When he finished, he washed the plate in the little sink at the back. He dried it. He put it away in the wrong place.

At the door, he stopped.

“Tomorrow,” he said. “Same time.”

It wasn’t a question.

“The contract—” Elowen started.

“Says you work your own hours,” said Zhao. “I know. I’m not working. I’m driving.”

He left. Through the window she watched him get into the car and sit there for a moment without starting it, his forehead almost touching the steering wheel, like a man who had run a very long way.

The next day, when she came down at three-thirty, he was in the kitchen with two cups of coffee.

The day after that, there were two new stools at the kitchen counter in the house on the hill. Tall ones, wooden, with backs. Nobody mentioned them.

But that night, when she came in from the shop, he was sitting on one of them, eating leftover soup from the second day.

Sitting down.

chapters.title: Aurelia Song Hears the News
chapters.desc: Her oldest rival arrives to gloat and finds out the worst part: their husbands are brothers.
chapters.content:
Aurelia Song arrived at the shop at twelve minutes past noon on a Thursday, which Elowen would later realise was the exact moment the lunch rush ended. Aurelia had always known how to time an entrance.

The bell over the door rang. A wave of perfume came in, something expensive with fig in it. Then Aurelia herself, in a cream coat and enormous sunglasses, her dark hair in a perfect low knot, heels that had never touched a wet market floor in their life.

She stopped just inside the door and took off the sunglasses, slowly.

“Lin Elowen,” she said. “Or should I say Mrs. Zhao.”

Elowen was wiring a corsage. She didn’t put it down.

“Aurelia,” she said. “Or should I say Mrs. Chen.”

They looked at each other across the shop the way they had looked at each other across a school corridor seven years ago, when the exam rankings went up on the noticeboard and one of them was first and the other one was second.

Then Aurelia smiled, a dazzling, dangerous smile, and walked to the counter, and put her handbag down on Elowen’s order book.

“Darling,” she said. “I had to see it for myself. You married the muscle.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In their final year of school, there had been two girls everybody talked about.

One was Aurelia Song, who had come from Milan at fifteen with a perfect accent and a mother who had expected her to be first at everything and told her so every night. Aurelia was loud and brilliant and beautiful and could not stand to lose. She was first in the rankings for two years straight. The teachers called her the Firebrand.

The other was Lin Elowen, who was quiet, who never put her hand up, who went home every day at four to look after a younger brother and three younger sisters, and who in their final year, without seeming to try at all, took first place.

The students called her the Ice Queen.

Aurelia had never forgiven her. Not for the ranking. For the not trying.

And then there had been Miles Wei, two years above them: the boy at the back of the advanced physics class who solved problems the teachers couldn’t, and didn’t care about rankings, and didn’t care about either of them. They had both wanted him, for different reasons, and fought over him with a viciousness that had made the whole school take sides. In the end, Miles had looked at them both, gone pale, and chosen physics.

Seven years later, Elowen still sometimes thought about that library, the quiet, the smell of old books, a boy who talked about light. It was the most peaceful thing she had ever wanted.

She did not plan to tell Aurelia that.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I didn’t marry the muscle,” Elowen said. She finished the corsage, tied it off, and put it in the box. “I married a businessman.”

“Oh, please.” Aurelia leaned on the counter and looked around the shop with bright, curious eyes. “I know exactly what Zhao Zhendong is. I’ve had him to dinner. He ate a whole fish with his hands and didn’t say one word for two hours and then he fixed our dishwasher.” She picked up a rose from the bucket beside the till and smelled it. “My husband is the brain. Yours is the fist. That’s what everyone says.”

“Does everyone also say your husband launders money through your shop?”

Aurelia’s smile didn’t move. Her eyes did.

“Our boutique,” she said sweetly, “is a very successful jewellery brand with stores in three cities. If some of our customers are generous, that’s their business.”

“And if some of my customers are frightening, that’s mine.”

They looked at each other.

And then, unexpectedly, Aurelia laughed. Not her dazzling laugh. A real one, short and surprised.

“God,” she said. “I missed this. Do you know nobody argues with me anymore? I married a Don. People bring me flowers and agree with everything I say. It’s killing me.”

“I can argue with you,” said Elowen. “It costs extra.”

Aurelia put the rose back in the bucket and pulled up the stool from behind the counter, the one Zhao had sat on with his plate of eggs. She sat down on it without asking, crossed her legs, and looked at Elowen with an expression of enormous, delighted malice.

“Do you understand,” she said, “what you’ve done?”

“I married a man.”

“You married Zhao Zhendong. My husband’s brother.”

“I know. Chen Si was at the registry.”

“Yes, but do you understand?” Aurelia spread her hands. “They’re not friends, Elowen. They’re not business partners. They’re brothers. The kind that cut their palms and shake hands. The kind that don’t need to talk. Zhendong comes to our house every New Year. Every birthday. Every time someone shoots at one of them, the other one is there in an hour.” She leaned forward. “Which means for the rest of your life, every family dinner, every holiday, every christening, every funeral, you and I will be at the same table.”

Elowen had a pair of florist’s scissors in her hand. She put them down.

She had not thought about it like that.

“Every New Year,” she said.

“Every single one.” Aurelia smiled. “Until we die. Probably at the same table as well.”

The shop was very quiet.

“You came here,” Elowen said slowly, “to tell me I’m going to spend the rest of my life having dinner with you.”

“I came here to watch your face while I told you.” Aurelia picked up her sunglasses and tapped them against her chin. “It was worth the drive.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed for two hours.

At first, it was war. Aurelia criticised the shop window. Elowen criticised the jewellery Aurelia was wearing, which was heavy and gold and very much like the ring on Elowen’s own finger, a fact both of them noticed and neither of them mentioned. Aurelia asked about the wedding and laughed until she had to wipe her eyes when Elowen said registry office, Tuesday. Elowen asked about Aurelia’s wedding and learned that it had been in Milan, with three hundred guests, and that Aurelia’s parents had found out about it from a magazine.

“A magazine,” Elowen repeated.

“They didn’t approve of Chen Si.” Aurelia shrugged. Something in her face went flat for just a second. “They don’t approve of anything I didn’t win first.”

Elowen thought of a school noticeboard. Of the look on Aurelia’s face, at seventeen, when she saw the number two beside her name. She had thought, back then, that it was jealousy. She thought now it might have been fear.

She didn’t say anything about it. She made two cups of jasmine tea instead, in the chipped mugs she kept behind the counter, and put one in front of Aurelia.

Aurelia looked at the mug. She looked at Elowen.

“This is a truce,” she said.

“It’s tea.”

“From you, it’s a truce.” But she drank it.

At half past two, she finally stood and picked up her handbag. Then she paused, opened it, and took out a folded sheet of paper.

“I’m launching a new collection next month,” she said. “At the gallery on Harbour Road. Two hundred guests. I need flowers. White, gold, nothing that smells too strong because it fights with the perfume. I’ve had three florists and they were all terrible.”

Elowen took the paper. It was a detailed brief, with sketches.

“You came to gloat,” she said, “and you brought a commission.”

“I came to gloat and I need flowers. I can do two things at once.” Aurelia put her sunglasses back on. “And you’re the only florist in this city I can’t bully.”

Elowen read the brief. She did the sum in her head.

She named a price. It was three times what she would have charged anyone else.

Aurelia didn’t even blink.

“Done,” she said. She walked to the door, and then turned back with her hand on the frame, and for a moment, behind the sunglasses and the perfect knot of hair, Elowen saw a seventeen-year-old in a school uniform.

“Elowen,” Aurelia said. “A serious thing. Just once.”

Elowen waited.

“They’re not like other men,” said Aurelia. “Not just dangerous. Other men are dangerous. These two—” She searched for the words. “When one of them bleeds, the other one does something terrible. And when we bleed, darling, they both do.” She paused. “Make sure you’re ready for that. I wasn’t.”

The bell rang as she went out. The fig perfume stayed in the shop for an hour.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night at dinner, at the clean table in the house on the hill, Elowen said, “You might have told me about Aurelia.”

Zhao looked up from his rice.

“I didn’t know you knew her,” he said. “I don’t know anything about your school.”

That was true. She realised with a strange jolt that he didn’t. He didn’t know where she had gone to school, or what she had studied, or who her friends had been. He knew the dates in her father’s files, and how she cut stems, and that she liked fish belly. He knew almost nothing else.

“She was first in our year,” Elowen said. “Then I was.”

He waited.

“And there was a boy,” she went on, before she had decided to. “Two years above us. Miles Wei. He did physics. We both wanted him. He didn’t want either of us. He chose physics.” She picked at her green beans. “It was very stupid. We were seventeen.”

Zhao put down his chopsticks.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t ask anything. His face did not change in any way she could point to. But something in the room changed, the way the air changes before a storm, and she looked up and found him watching her with an expression she couldn’t read at all.

“What was he like?” Zhao asked. His voice was very even.

She thought about the library.

“Quiet,” she said. “He talked about light. How it bends.” She smiled a little, without meaning to. “He was the only person at that school who didn’t care whose daughter I was.”

Zhao picked his chopsticks back up. He ate the rest of his dinner. He said the fish was good. He washed his own bowl.

At the top of the stairs, outside the little room, he said goodnight.

She went to bed. She didn’t think about it again.

He did.

At two in the morning, in the basement, under the hanging lamp, Zhao Zhendong took apart a rifle he had cleaned the night before, and cleaned it again, piece by piece, and thought about a boy who talked about light. A boy who hadn’t cared whose daughter she was. A boy she smiled about, seven years later, without meaning to.

Quiet. Physics. Libraries.

A different life. A clean one.

He put the rifle back together. It took fifty seconds. It worked perfectly, the way it always did.

Upstairs, in the big room at the end of the corridor, his wife was asleep under the window over the sea, with the heavy ring he’d bought her on the wrong finger.

chapters.title: The First Dinner as Mrs. Zhao
chapters.desc: A broker insults his wife at the table. Elowen sees what her husband does with his hands.
chapters.content:
The contract said she didn’t have to go to his dinners unless she chose to.

For the first month, she didn’t choose to. He went out two or three nights a week in a dark suit and came home after midnight, and she heard him on the stairs, and in the morning there were two cups of coffee in the kitchen as if nothing had happened.

She didn’t ask where he went. She didn’t ask who he saw. The contract didn’t say she couldn’t, but some part of her didn’t want to know, the same part that had learned at eight years old not to open the long boxes in the garage.

Then, at the end of the month, she found herself standing in front of her wardrobe holding a dark green dress, and she realised she had chosen.

“I’m coming tonight,” she said at breakfast.

Zhao stopped with his coffee halfway to his mouth.

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

He put the coffee down. He looked at her the way he had looked at her at the registry office, when the clerk asked the only question that mattered.

“It’s a man called Maartens,” he said finally. “He’s a broker. Dutch. He buys for a general in the south whose country can’t buy from anyone legally, so he buys from me.” He paused. “He’s not a good man, Elowen. None of them are. Neither am I.”

“I know what you are,” she said. “I want to see it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant was on the top floor of a hotel by the harbour, the kind of place with no prices on the menu and a private room behind a sliding door made of carved wood. The room had a round table, a window over the black water, and a lazy Susan in the middle already covered in cold dishes: jellyfish, sliced beef shank, cucumbers in garlic.

Maartens was already there. He was in his fifties, red-faced, with thinning sandy hair and a loud, pleasant laugh. He stood up when they came in and shook Zhao’s hand with both of his, and then turned to Elowen and looked at her the way men at the market looked at fish.

“So this is the wife,” he said, in English. “Zhao, you never told me she was so pretty.”

“Mr. Maartens,” said Elowen, also in English, and sat down.

There were two other men in the room. One stood behind Maartens’ chair with his hands folded in front of him: a big man with a shaved head and a jacket that didn’t close over what he was wearing under it. The other was Bao, standing by the door, looking at nothing.

The dinner went on for two hours.

Elowen said almost nothing. She ate small amounts of everything and listened, and slowly, from the edges of what the men said, she began to understand what her husband did.

It was not like a film. Nobody said guns. They said units and lots and the agricultural order. They talked about a cargo flight that would leave from one country and land in another, and about the papers, the end-user certificate, which had to say that the units were going to the army of a third country that was allowed to buy them. Elowen gathered, from a joke Maartens made, that the official in that third country who stamped the certificate had been paid more than the units were worth.

“And after?” said Zhao, turning his glass slowly on the tablecloth. “When they land?”

“After is my problem,” said Maartens cheerfully. “You’ll never see them again.”

But they will be used, Elowen thought. Somewhere. By someone. On someone.

She looked at her husband’s hands on the white tablecloth. Scarred knuckles. A thin white line across the back of one thumb. She thought about those hands carrying her mother’s lemon tree up the steps, both arms underneath, like something precious.

She didn’t know how both things could be true.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened at the end, over the fruit.

Maartens had drunk most of a bottle of baijiu by then, and he had stopped being careful. He leaned back in his chair, his face shining, and looked at Elowen across the table.

“A florist,” he said. “Zhao, you surprise me. All this time I thought you didn’t care about anything but money, and you go and buy yourself a florist.” He laughed. “Does she come with the shop? Or does the shop come with her?”

Elowen kept peeling her lychee.

Zhao didn’t move.

“Really, I’m jealous.” Maartens poured himself more. “My wife can’t even keep a cactus alive. Tell you what, Zhao. If you ever get bored, I’ll rent her for an evening. Name your price. You’ve always been reasonable about prices.”

He laughed again. The big man behind him smiled.

And under the table, Elowen felt a hand land on her knee.

It was hot and damp and heavy. It squeezed.

She went completely still.

It was a strange feeling. Not fear, exactly. It was as if her body had gone very far away and left her sitting at the table with a half-peeled lychee in her fingers and a man’s hand on her leg, and she couldn’t make any part of herself move. She had been in a lot of rooms with dangerous men in her life. Her father’s visitors. The man at the market with the short bunches. None of them had ever touched her.

She didn’t make a sound. She didn’t change her face. She had been keeping her face still for twenty years.

But Zhao was looking at her face. He had been looking at it all night.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood up.

He didn’t hurry. He walked around the table, past the lazy Susan, past the window, and stopped behind Maartens’ chair. The big man with the shaved head stepped forward and reached inside his jacket, and from the door Bao said, very calmly, in English, “I wouldn’t,” and there was a small sound of something metal clicking, and the big man stopped.

Maartens looked up over his shoulder, still smiling.

“Zhao? What—”

Zhao reached under the table, took hold of Maartens’ wrist, and pulled his hand off Elowen’s knee and up onto the tablecloth, flat, in one smooth movement, like a man laying down a card.

Then he picked up the fruit knife from beside Maartens’ plate and drove it straight down through the back of his hand and into the table.

The sound Maartens made was not a scream. Not at first. It was a sort of high, breathless huh, as if all the air had been knocked out of him. Then he looked down at his hand, at the knife standing up out of it, at the blood spreading in a slow dark circle on the white cloth, and then he screamed.

Zhao kept one hand on the handle of the knife. He leaned down, close to Maartens’ ear.

“Apologise to my wife,” he said.

Maartens was sobbing. “Jesus—Jesus Christ, Zhao—”

“Not to him. To her.”

“I’m sorry, I’m sorry, Mrs. Zhao, I’m sorry—”

Zhao turned the knife a quarter turn in the wood.

Maartens screamed again, and Elowen heard herself say, quite clearly, in a voice she didn’t recognise:

“Zhendong.”

He looked at her.

“Take it out,” she said. “He needs that hand to sign.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, she couldn’t remember deciding to say it.

She remembered that the room was very quiet except for Maartens crying. She remembered the blood on the white cloth. She remembered the lychee, still half-peeled, in her fingers, and that she put it down on her plate very carefully, the way she would put down a flower.

She remembered Zhao pulling the knife out, and Maartens folding over his hand, and the big man with the shaved head staring at her as if she were the frightening one.

And she remembered picking up the contract from beside Zhao’s empty plate, the one they had been talking about for two hours, and reading the last page, and saying in English, in her wedding-card voice:

“The price is twenty per cent higher. For the inconvenience.”

Maartens looked up at her through his tears. His face was grey.

“And you’ll pay for the tablecloth,” Elowen said.

He signed with his left hand. It was barely a signature. It didn’t matter.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car, she started to shake.

It started in her hands and went up her arms and into her shoulders, and she couldn’t stop it. She sat in the back seat beside her husband with her hands pressed together between her knees and shook so hard her teeth knocked together.

Zhao didn’t touch her. He sat at the other end of the seat with his hands on his own knees, looking straight ahead. There was blood on his right cuff. Bao drove very smoothly and didn’t look in the mirror once.

“You did that in front of me,” Elowen said, when she could speak.

“Yes.”

“You put a knife through a man’s hand at a dinner table.”

“He put his hand on you.”

“I would have handled it.”

He turned his head and looked at her.

“How?” he asked. Not unkindly. As if he really wanted to know.

She opened her mouth. She closed it. She thought about her body going far away, about her hands that wouldn’t move, about sitting there with a lychee in her fingers while a stranger squeezed her knee.

“I don’t know,” she whispered.

He looked away again.

“I know,” he said. “That’s why I did it.”

They didn’t say anything else all the way home.

✦ ✦ ✦

She couldn’t sleep.

She lay in the big bed at the end of the corridor and stared at the ceiling. Every time she closed her eyes she saw the knife going down. She heard the sound it made going into the wood: not loud, a dull, wet thock, like a spade going into soil.

And she saw his face. That was the worst part. Not the knife. His face while he did it, which had been completely calm, almost gentle, the face he wore when he carried buckets at the market.

I know what you are, she had said at breakfast. I want to see it.

She had seen it.

At two in the morning, she got up to get water, and opened her door, and nearly stepped on him.

He was sitting on the floor of the corridor with his back against the wall beside her door. He was still in his shirt from the dinner. He had changed the cuff, or rolled it; she couldn’t see the blood anymore. His knees were drawn up and his arms were resting on them, and he looked up at her in the dark without any surprise at all, as if he had been waiting for her to open the door.

“What are you doing out here?” she said.

“Sitting.”

“Why?”

He looked down at his hands.

“Because you were afraid,” he said. “And I didn’t know if you were afraid of him or of me. So I thought I’d sit here. If it was him, then I’m between you and the stairs. If it was me—” He stopped. “If it was me, then you know where I am. You don’t have to wonder.”

She stood in the doorway in her pyjamas and looked down at him.

“Did you do it because I’m yours?” she asked. “Like a car? Like the house? Because he touched something that belongs to you?”

He was quiet for so long she thought he wasn’t going to answer.

“I did it,” Zhao said slowly, “because he made you go still. You went completely still, like a rabbit. I’ve seen people do that. I’ve made people do that.” He lifted his head and looked at her. “I didn’t ever want to see you do it.”

Something in her chest turned over.

She didn’t say anything. She didn’t know what to say. She went past him to the bathroom and drank a glass of water, and came back, and he was still sitting there, exactly as she had left him.

She went into her room.

She didn’t close the door all the way.

She left it open a crack, a hand’s width, the way Evangeline had always left her door open at home when she couldn’t sleep, so she could hear the stairs.

On the other side of it, in the dark, she heard him let out a long breath. And she heard him stay.

chapters.title: The Night the Delivery Van Burned
chapters.desc: A message for Zhao, written in petrol on her shop’s van.
chapters.content:
Xiao Pan was nineteen and had worked for Elowen for two years. He delivered flowers on an electric scooter in the daytime and drove the van on weekends, and he was saving for a motorbike, and he talked about the motorbike so much that Elowen had once, as a joke, made him a bouquet shaped like one.

On Friday night, there was a big wedding in the morning: two hundred guests, thirty table arrangements, an arch of white roses for the hotel garden. Elowen and Xiao Pan worked until eleven. At half past, he went out to load the first boxes into the van so they could leave at six.

She was sweeping stems off the floor when she heard the sound.

It wasn’t loud. A soft whump, like a big rug being shaken out of a window. Then light, orange, flooding through the shop window and throwing the shadows of every flower across the far wall.

Then Xiao Pan screaming.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember running.

She was inside the shop, and then she was in the street, and the van was on fire. Not a small fire. The whole back of it was a roaring yellow column, the roof already black, the windows popping one after another. The heat hit her like a wall. Through the smoke she could see someone running away down the street, two figures, already turning the corner.

Xiao Pan was on his knees on the pavement beside the van. He was holding his hands out in front of him, away from his body, like something he didn’t want to touch.

“The roses,” he was saying. “I tried to get the roses out, Miss Lin, I opened the door and it just—it just—”

His hands were red. The skin on his palms was shiny and wrong and already starting to bubble.

Elowen dragged him back from the van by the collar of his jacket. She got him to the shop doorway. She got him to the little sink at the back and turned on the cold tap and held his hands under it while he shook and sobbed, and she kept them there, and kept them there, because her mother had taught her when she was small and had burned herself on the kettle: cold running water, twenty minutes, no ice, no butter, nothing else.

“Twenty minutes,” she told him. Her voice sounded very far away. “Count with me. Don’t take them out.”

Outside, the van’s fuel tank went with a bang that shook the windows.

She held his hands under the water and counted out loud, and called an ambulance with her other hand, and then, because her fingers were already moving, she called the only other number she could think of.

He answered on the first ring.

“Elowen.”

“The van,” she said. “They burned the van. Xiao Pan—his hands—”

“Are you hurt?”

“No. No, I’m—”

“Stay inside,” said Zhao. “Lock the door. I’m coming.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The burn unit at the City Hospital was on the sixth floor, and it smelled of antiseptic and something sweet and terrible underneath that Elowen didn’t want to think about.

Second-degree burns, the doctor said. Both palms and the inside of the fingers. Partial thickness. The cold water had helped; she had probably saved him a lot of damage. They would dress the burns, and watch for infection, and in a week or two they would know whether he needed skin grafts on the right hand. He would keep the use of his hands. He would have scars.

“He was trying to save the roses,” Elowen said.

The doctor looked at her with tired kindness. “They usually are,” she said. “People always try to save something.”

Xiao Pan was asleep now, full of painkillers, his hands wrapped in thick white dressings like boxing gloves. His mother was on a night bus from the countryside. Elowen sat beside the bed in her work apron, with soot on her face and her hair smelling of smoke, and didn’t move.

She heard him before she saw him: the change in the corridor, the way the nurses’ voices dropped.

Zhao stopped in the doorway of the ward. He looked at Xiao Pan. At the white dressings. At her.

He came and crouched beside her chair and looked at her face. He didn’t touch her. Then he took a clean handkerchief out of his pocket and held it out.

She didn’t understand. Then she realised she had soot all over her cheek.

She took the handkerchief and didn’t use it.

“The Qiu brothers,” she said.

“Yes.” He stood. “The younger one. Qiu Lei. He has a camera on his own warehouse door; he’s very stupid.” His voice was perfectly even. “They want me to know they can reach you. That’s what this is. A message.”

“Where are you going?”

He didn’t answer.

She stood up too.

“Don’t,” Elowen said. “Zhendong. Don’t.”

“It isn’t for you.” He was already turning toward the door. “It’s business. They burned a vehicle registered to my wife’s company. If I let that go, every man at the Docks will know they can burn anything of mine. This is about the business.”

She looked at him.

It was the voice he used with Maartens, with the men at the market. Flat and reasonable. And it was a lie, and they both knew it, because she had seen his face in the doorway when he looked at Xiao Pan’s hands.

“You promised,” she said quietly. “In the contract. You said you would tell me when you couldn’t tell me something. You said you would never make something up.”

He stopped.

The ward was very quiet. Somewhere a machine beeped steadily.

He stood with his back to her. Then he turned his head, just enough that she could see the side of his face.

“Then I can’t tell you,” he said.

And he went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Qiu brothers’ warehouse was on the old road to the market, a long, dark building with a rusted roof and a yard full of stolen scooters. Zhao had driven past it every morning for a month with his wife asleep against the window, and every morning he had looked at it, and every morning he had kept driving.

At two in the morning, he didn’t keep driving.

He took six men. He didn’t need six. He took them so that there would be witnesses, so that by morning everyone at the Docks would know exactly what had happened and exactly why.

Qiu Lei was in the office at the back with three friends and a bottle, still laughing about it. There was a phone on the table playing a video someone had taken of the van burning. They were watching it again.

They stopped laughing when the door came in.

It didn’t take long. Two of the friends ran. The third tried to pull something out of his belt and Bao put him on the floor and kept him there. Qiu Lei backed into the corner with his hands up and started talking very fast about his brother, about how it was his brother’s idea, about how nobody was supposed to get hurt, it was only a van, only a van, only flowers—

“A boy was standing next to it,” said Zhao.

“I didn’t know—I swear, I didn’t see him, I—”

“You didn’t look.”

There was a steel oil drum in the yard behind the office, the kind they burned rubbish in to keep warm at night. It was still smouldering. Zhao’s men dragged Qiu Lei out to it. Zhao picked up a can of petrol from beside the door, Qiu Lei’s own can, and poured a little into the drum, and the flames came up with a soft roar, yellow and hungry, exactly the colour of the van.

Then he took Qiu Lei by both wrists.

He held them over the drum.

Not in it. Over it. Close enough. He held them there, with Qiu Lei’s whole weight pulling against him, and Qiu Lei screamed and kicked and begged, and Zhao held his hands steady over the fire and counted, out loud, very quietly, the way his wife had counted for Xiao Pan under the cold tap.

He counted to twenty.

Then he let go, and Qiu Lei fell onto the concrete with his hands curled against his chest, sobbing, his palms red and blistered and shining.

“Cold running water,” Zhao told him. “Twenty minutes. No ice. Nothing else.” He turned away. “That’s more than you gave him.”

They burned the warehouse afterward. All of it: the stolen scooters, the stock, the office, the phone with the video still playing on the table. They stood in the road and watched it go up. The fire brigade came forty minutes later, which was about how long it took for the fire brigade to come to the old road, as everyone at the Docks knew.

Qiu Wen, the older brother, arrived in a car with no lights at three-fifteen. He got out and stood at the edge of the road and looked at the fire, and then at his brother on the ground, and then at Zhao.

Zhao walked over to him.

“Your brother will be fine,” he said. “He’ll have scars. The boy will have scars too.”

Qiu Wen was shaking with rage. “You’re a dead man, Zhao. You think you—”

“Next time,” said Zhao, “it won’t be your stock. It won’t be your brother. It’ll be you.” He looked at the fire for a moment, at the roof starting to sag. “And my wife isn’t business. Tell everyone. That’s the message.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home at half past five, as the sky was turning grey over the sea.

She was in the kitchen.

She had come home from the hospital at four, when Xiao Pan’s mother arrived, and she had not gone to bed. She had sat on one of the tall wooden stools at the counter, with her hands around a cup of tea that had gone cold, and waited.

He stopped in the kitchen doorway. He smelled of smoke. Not the smell of the van, sharp with rubber and plastic, but older and heavier, wood and petrol and something else.

They looked at each other.

“Is anyone dead?” Elowen asked.

“No.”

“Is that true?”

“Yes.” He didn’t move from the doorway. “Qiu Lei has burns on his hands. Their warehouse is gone. Nobody is dead.”

She looked at him. Then she looked down at his left arm, where his sleeve was pushed up, and saw the angry red patch on the inside of his forearm, the skin shiny and raised.

“You’re burned,” she said.

He glanced down at it as if it belonged to someone else. “It’s nothing.”

She got up. She took him by the wrist, the way she had taken Xiao Pan, and pulled him to the kitchen sink, and turned on the cold tap, and pushed his arm under it.

He went completely still.

It was the stillness she had felt at the registry office, in the photographer’s booth, when she leaned her head on his shoulder. As if nobody had ever done this. As if he didn’t know whether it would hurt.

“Twenty minutes,” Elowen said.

“It’s nothing—”

“Twenty minutes.” She held his wrist under the water. “Don’t take it out.”

So he didn’t.

They stood at the sink together in the grey morning light, her hand around his wrist, the water running over the burn, and neither of them said anything. Outside, the dogs had come to the kitchen door and were sitting with their noses against the glass. The lemon tree at the end of the hall was beginning to catch the light.

“I told you not to,” she said at last.

“You told me not to kill anyone.” He was watching the water. “I didn’t.”

“That isn’t what I said.”

“It’s what you meant.”

She looked down at his arm under the tap. At the scars on his knuckles, old and white. At the thin line across his thumb. At this new burn, which he had got holding a man’s hands over a fire, and which she was now, at five in the morning, nursing at her kitchen sink as if it were Xiao Pan’s.

She thought about the boy in the hospital bed with his hands wrapped in white. About the roses he had tried to save. About the two figures she had seen running down the street, laughing.

And somewhere very deep inside her, where she didn’t want to look, she was glad.

She was glad they were burned. She was glad the warehouse was gone. She was glad that somewhere in the city tonight, Qiu Lei was holding his hands under a cold tap and crying, and that he would be afraid for the rest of his life to come near her shop again.

She hated it. She hated the gladness more than she had ever hated anything.

“Thank you,” she whispered.

He turned his head and looked at her.

She didn’t look back. She kept her eyes on the water, and her hand on his wrist, and her face very still, because if she looked at him she didn’t know what would happen.

At twenty minutes, she turned off the tap. She dried his arm with a clean towel, very gently, without rubbing. She found cling film in a drawer, still in its box, and wrapped it loosely around the burn, the way the nurses had wrapped Xiao Pan’s hands before the proper dressings went on.

“Keep it clean,” she said. “Don’t pop the blisters. If it gets hot or starts to smell, you go to a doctor. A real one.”

“Yes.”

She put the cling film away. She rinsed her teacup. She walked past him to the stairs.

“Elowen,” he said.

She stopped with her hand on the banister.

“The hospital,” Zhao said. “The boy’s bills. The grafts, if he needs them. Rehabilitation. And a new van. I’ve already—”

“I know,” she said. “The nurse told me. At four. She said a man called Bao had come to the desk and paid for everything for a year, in cash, and asked them not to tell anyone.”

He didn’t say anything.

“She told me anyway,” said Elowen. “I think she was frightened of him.”

She went up the stairs. Behind her, she heard him stay at the kitchen sink, without moving, as if he were still under the cold water.

She didn’t sleep. But she lay in the big bed with the door open a hand’s width, and listened to him come up the stairs at last, and stop outside her room, and slide down the wall to sit on the floor.

And for the first time, it made her feel safe.

chapters.title: Zhendong, Stay
chapters.desc: A fever, a typhoon, and the first time she asks him for anything.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t touch me unless I ask.” — the contract, page two, line six
chapters.content:
The typhoon warning went up on Wednesday afternoon. By evening the sky over the Iron Docks had turned the colour of a bruise, and the cranes had stopped, and the sea below the house on the hill was white all the way to the horizon.

Elowen didn’t notice most of it, because by evening she had a fever of thirty-nine point four.

It had been coming for days. She had been at the hospital every afternoon with Xiao Pan, and at the market every morning at four, and at the shop in between, trying to fill the wedding orders without a van and without a delivery boy. She had stood in the rain at a bus stop with a box of peonies on Monday. She had not slept properly since the night of the fire. On Wednesday morning her throat hurt. By noon her whole body hurt. At three, standing at the workbench, she put down her knife because she couldn’t feel her fingers properly, and the next thing she knew, Bao was in the shop, and she was in the back of the car, and the city was sliding past the window in streaks of grey rain.

“He told me to bring you home,” Bao said, when she asked. “He saw your face this morning.”

“I was fine this morning.”

Bao looked at her in the mirror. He didn’t say anything. He didn’t have to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao met the car at the door. He took one look at her and picked her up.

She meant to protest. The contract. But the world tilted when she stood up and her legs didn’t work, and then she was off the ground with one arm under her knees and one behind her back, held against his chest as easily as he had carried the lemon tree. His shirt smelled of rain and soap.

“I can walk,” she said into his collar.

“I know.”

He didn’t put her down. He carried her up the stairs, past the little room by the stairs, down the corridor to the big room at the end, and laid her on the bed, and then stood back, very quickly, as if he had touched something hot.

“I’ll get Bao’s wife,” he said. “She can—”

“No.” Elowen closed her eyes. The room was spinning gently. “I don’t want anyone.”

There was a pause.

“Medicine,” he said. “What do you take?”

“Paracetamol. In my bag. And water. Lots of water.”

He went away. He came back. He held out two white tablets on his palm and a glass of water, and she took them, and some of the water went down her chin, and she was too tired to care. He took the glass from her hand before she dropped it. He pulled the duvet up to her shoulders, carefully, without touching her.

Then he went to the door.

“I’ll be outside,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The power went at nine.

She was half asleep when it happened, drifting in and out of strange hot dreams about the van, about Xiao Pan’s hands, about the knife going down into the table with that wet thock. The wind had been getting louder for hours, a long rising howl around the corners of the house. Then there was a crack, somewhere far down the hill, and every light went out at once.

The dark was total. No streetlights, no light from the Docks. Only the wind, and the rain hitting the bulletproof glass in hard, flat sheets, like handfuls of gravel.

Elowen lay where she was.

She was not afraid of the dark. She had never been afraid of the dark. But she was twenty-four and burning hot and very tired, and the house was enormous and strange around her, and for a moment, lying there, she felt about eight years old.

“Elowen.”

His voice came from the doorway. Low. Close.

“The generator will come on in a minute,” he said. “Bao’s gone down to it. Don’t be frightened.”

“I’m not frightened.”

“All right.”

She heard him move. Not toward her. She heard him sit down, just inside the door, on the floor, the way he sat outside her room every night.

The wind screamed. Something banged against the side of the house, a loose shutter, again and again.

The generator didn’t come on.

“Zhendong,” Elowen said into the dark.

“I’m here.”

She didn’t know she was going to say it. Afterwards she would wonder if it was the fever. Maybe it was. Maybe the fever only took away the part of her that would have stopped it.

“Stay,” she said.

The dark was very quiet. Even the wind seemed to pause.

“I am staying,” he said. “I’m right here.”

“No.” She turned her head on the pillow toward his voice. “Here. Not by the door.”

There was a long silence.

Then she heard him get up. She heard him cross the room, slowly, his feet finding their way in the dark. She felt the mattress dip slightly beside her as he put one hand on the edge of the bed to steady himself. He didn’t sit on it. He sat down on the floor beside it, with his back against the frame, so that his shoulder was level with her hand.

“Here,” he said.

She moved her hand across the sheet until her fingers found his shoulder. Then his arm. Then his hand, resting on his knee.

She held it.

He didn’t move. She felt him not move, felt his whole body go still the way it always did. His hand was big and rough and much cooler than hers. After a long moment, very slowly, as if he thought she might take it back, his fingers closed around hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

The generator never came on. Later, she found out a tree had come down across the line to the guardhouse, and Bao had spent half the night in the rain with a chainsaw and a torch.

She didn’t care. In the dark, with the storm going on outside like the end of the world, she lay with her hot hand in his cool one and listened to him breathe.

“Tell me something,” she said, after a while.

“What?”

“Anything. Something true.”

He was quiet for so long that she thought he had fallen asleep sitting up. Then he spoke, low and even, as if reading from something written down.

“When I was fifteen,” he said, “I was in a detention centre in the north. For young offenders. I’d stolen a truck. It was full of copper wire. I didn’t know how to drive it very well. I hit a wall.”

She waited.

“Chen Si was there too. He was sixteen. His family had been important, and then somebody made them disappear, and he had nowhere to go, and he did something clever and illegal to get money, and they caught him.” A pause. “He was very small then. Thin. The other boys didn’t like him because he talked like a rich boy. They used to wait for him in the showers.”

The wind howled. Her hand tightened around his.

“There was a riot in Block C,” Zhao said. “In the winter. Somebody set fire to the mattresses and the guards locked the doors and left us inside. Some of the older boys decided it was a good time to settle things. Three of them went for Chen Si. One of them had a piece of metal from a bed frame, sharpened.”

“What happened?”

“I was there.” He said it simply. “I got in the way.”

Elowen lay in the dark and thought about his body. The way he moved. The way he held himself, always slightly turned, always between her and the door.

Very slowly, she let go of his hand. She reached out in the dark and found his shirt, the side of his ribs, and laid her palm flat against it.

Under the cotton, under her fingers, she felt it: a long ridge of raised scar, running down from under his arm almost to his waist.

He had stopped breathing.

“Here?” she whispered.

“Yes.”

She left her hand there. She could feel his heart under her palm, beating hard and fast. Much too fast for a man who was sitting still.

“Chen Si got us out,” he said, after a long time. His voice was not quite even anymore. “Through the drains. He’d studied the plans of the building for months. He knew where every pipe went. He carried me half the way. I don’t remember most of it. When we came out, it was snowing, and he was covered in blood, and it was all mine.” He breathed out. “He’s my brother. That’s all. That’s the true thing.”

She moved her hand back down and found his again.

“Thank you,” she said.

“You can ask me something too,” she added, a moment later. “If you want. Anything. That’s fair.”

She felt him tense.

The storm roared against the glass. She waited. She could feel the question in him, could almost hear it, something big and heavy that had been sitting in him for a long time, the way the burn had sat under his skin. She didn’t know what it was. She only knew that he was holding it the way he held everything, very carefully, so it wouldn’t break.

“What was your mother like?” he asked instead.

She smiled in the dark.

So she told him. About her mother, who had been a florist too, before she married, and had kept a lemon tree on the balcony of the house in the Walled City for twenty years. Who had sung while she cooked, badly. Who had given her father the fish belly every night, and got it back every night. Who had taken Elowen to the flower market at four in the morning, wrapped in a coat, and bought her a hot soy milk from the man at the door. Who had gone into hospital to have Eliana and not come home.

She told him until her voice gave out, and then she lay there with her eyes closed, holding his hand, while the fever burned through her and the typhoon tore across the hill.

She didn’t remember falling asleep. She only remembered that the last thing she felt was his thumb moving, once, very lightly, across the back of her fingers.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she woke, the storm was over.

The light coming through the window was clear and clean and very bright, the kind of light that only comes after a typhoon, when the wind has scrubbed the whole sky. The fever had broken in the night. Her pyjamas were damp with sweat. Her head felt light and empty and her body felt as though it had been beaten all over, gently, by someone who loved her.

Her hand was still in his.

He was asleep.

He was sitting exactly where he had sat down in the dark, on the floor against the side of the bed, but at some point in the night his head had tipped sideways and come to rest on the edge of the mattress, next to their joined hands. His face was turned toward her. His mouth was slightly open. There was a crease in his cheek from the sheet.

Elowen didn’t move. She lay there and looked at him.

She had never seen him asleep. She had never seen his face without that stillness, that waiting. Asleep, he looked younger than twenty-five. He looked tired in a way that went all the way down. There was a small scar under his jaw she had never noticed. His eyelashes were longer than she had thought.

She lifted her other hand, slowly, and touched his hair.

It was soft. Softer than she expected. She moved a piece of it off his forehead. At the back, the piece that had stuck up at the registry office was sticking up again.

His eyes opened.

He didn’t move. He didn’t lift his head. He lay there with his cheek on the edge of the mattress and looked at her, and in the bright clean light she watched him wake up, watched him understand where he was, watched him realise that her fingers were still in his hair.

Neither of them looked away.

“Your fever broke,” he said. His voice was rough with sleep.

“Yes.”

“How do you feel?”

She thought about it.

“The contract,” she said. “Page two. Line six.”

Something moved in his face. He knew it by heart. She had known he would.

“You don’t touch me unless I ask,” he said quietly.

“I’m asking.”

He went still.

“Asking what?” he said.

She didn’t answer with words. She slid her fingers from his hair down to his jaw, and held it, very lightly, and leaned down toward him.

He didn’t move to meet her.

She understood. He wouldn’t. Not unless she was sure. Not unless she came all the way.

So she came all the way.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t like kisses in films.

Her lips were dry and cracked from the fever and his were warm and still. For a second he didn’t respond at all; he just stayed there, with her mouth on his, as if he couldn’t believe it was happening and was afraid that if he moved, it would stop. She could feel his breath catch. She could feel the rough edge of his jaw under her fingers where he hadn’t shaved.

Then, very slowly, he kissed her back.

He kissed her the way he had held her hand in the dark: slowly, as if asking a question with every second of it. His hand came up off the mattress and found her face, and it was shaking, she realised, this man who had held another man’s hands over a fire without blinking, his big scarred hand was trembling against her cheek. He touched her as if she were the most fragile thing he had ever held. His thumb moved along her cheekbone. His mouth softened against hers, opened a little, and she tasted salt, and coffee from yesterday, and something that was only him.

She heard herself make a small sound, low in her throat, that she had never made before.

He stopped.

He didn’t pull away. He just stopped, and rested his forehead against hers, and stayed like that, breathing hard. His hand was still on her face. His eyes were closed.

“You have a fever,” he said.

“It broke.”

“Last night you had a fever.” His voice was very low. “You might not—you might not mean it.”

She opened her eyes and looked at him from two centimetres away, at the closed lids, the long lashes, the crease in his cheek from the sheet. At a man who would rather stop kissing her than risk taking something she didn’t mean to give.

“Then I’ll ask again,” Elowen said. “When I don’t have a fever.”

He opened his eyes.

“And you’ll mean it?” he asked.

There it was. Just for a second, in his voice, she heard the edge of it: the big heavy question he had been holding in the dark and had not asked. It was there, under the words, under will you mean it, something much older and much more frightened.

She didn’t know what it was yet.

She would.

“Yes,” she said.

He looked at her. Then he closed his eyes again, and turned his face, and pressed his mouth to the inside of her wrist, to the place where her pulse was beating, very gently, the way you would kiss something you were afraid to wake.

“Okay,” he whispered against her skin.

Outside, the storm had left the whole hill wet and shining. Down in the garden, Dumpling and Noodle were barking at a fallen branch. Somewhere below, Bao’s chainsaw started up again.

And in the big bed at the end of the corridor, Elowen lay with her hand against her husband’s face and her wrist against his mouth, and thought, very clearly, for the first time:

Oh.

Oh, no.

chapters.title: Page Two, Line Six
chapters.desc: She asks again, a week later, with no fever and a thermometer to prove it.
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll ask again. When I don’t have a fever.”
chapters.content:
For a week, neither of them mentioned it.

He drove her to the market at four. He carried the buckets. He sat on the stool behind the counter and ate fried eggs on rice. In the evenings they ate dinner at the clean table, and she told him about Xiao Pan, who had been sent home with his hands in soft white gloves and a list of exercises, and who had texted her a photo of himself trying to hold a spoon, captioned MOTORBIKE IN 6 MONTHS.

At night, Zhao said goodnight at the top of the stairs and she went down the corridor to the big room, and she left the door open a hand’s width, and she lay awake listening to him sit down outside it.

He didn’t touch her. Not once. Not her hand when he passed her a cup, not her shoulder when she fell asleep in the car. If anything, he was more careful than before. He stood a little further away. He looked at her a little less. Once, at the market, a trolley swung round the corner too fast and he reached out to pull her back, and his hand stopped in the air a centimetre from her arm and hung there, and he said, “Watch out,” instead.

She understood. He had kissed a woman with a fever of thirty-nine point four, and he had decided it didn’t count. He was waiting. He would wait forever, if she let him. He would sit outside her door until they were both old, and never once ask, because the contract said unless I ask, and Zhao Zhendong had never broken a promise to her.

On the eighth day, she stopped letting him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home late. A meeting in the north of the city that had gone on too long, a broker who wanted to talk about prices until midnight. She heard the car on the gravel at twelve-twenty, and the dogs, and Bao’s voice, and the front door.

She was sitting at the kitchen counter, on one of the tall wooden stools he had bought without saying anything. She had heated the soup from the day before. There was a bowl of it waiting at his place, and a pair of chopsticks, and a spoon.

And beside the spoon, a thermometer.

He stopped in the kitchen doorway. He was in his dark suit, his tie pulled loose, and he looked tired the way he always looked after those dinners, as if he had spent the evening holding up something heavy and had only just put it down.

He looked at the soup. Then at the thermometer.

“Are you sick?” he said, and the tiredness went out of his face all at once, and he took a step toward her.

“No.” She picked up the thermometer and held it out so he could read it. “Thirty-six point six. I took it twenty minutes ago. And again ten minutes ago, to be sure. And again just now, when I heard the car.”

He stood there and looked at the little digital screen. Thirty-six point six. She watched him read it, and then read it again, and then she watched him understand.

His face didn’t change. But his hand, the one hanging at his side, closed slowly into a fist, and then opened again.

“Elowen,” he said.

“You said I might not mean it.” Her voice was steadier than she was. She had been rehearsing this since eight o’clock. She had rehearsed it in the shower and in the garden with the dogs and sitting at this counter for an hour, watching the soup, and none of the rehearsals had included the part where her heart would be going this hard. “Because of the fever. So I waited until I didn’t have one.”

She put the thermometer down on the counter.

“Page two,” she said. “Line six.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move for so long that she began to be afraid.

Not of him. Of the other thing. That she had misunderstood. That the man who sat outside her door every night did it for some reason she didn’t know, some reason that had nothing to do with wanting her, and that she was sitting in his kitchen at midnight with a thermometer making a fool of herself.

Then he crossed the kitchen.

He didn’t hurry. He came and stood in front of her stool, close, closer than he had stood in a week, and because she was sitting on the high stool and he was standing, their eyes were almost level. She could smell the restaurant on him, smoke and baijiu, and under it soap and him.

He lifted one hand and stopped it a centimetre from her face, the way he had stopped it at the market.

“Say it,” he said. His voice had gone very low. “Not the contract. You. Say what you’re asking.”

She looked at his hand, hanging in the air beside her cheek. At the scarred knuckles, the white line across the thumb. A hand that had put a knife through another man’s hand. That had carried her mother’s lemon tree like a sleeping child.

“I’m asking you to touch me,” Elowen said.

His hand came the last centimetre.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kissed her at the kitchen counter, and it was nothing like the first time.

The first time had been a question. This was an answer. He took her face in both hands and kissed her like a man who had been holding his breath for a week and had finally been told he could stop: deep and slow and certain, his mouth opening hers, unhurried, as if he had decided exactly how this would go a long time ago and was not going to let even himself rush it.

She made a sound against his mouth that she had never made in her life.

He heard it. She felt him hear it. His whole body went still for one second, and then his hands tightened on her face and he kissed her harder, and she grabbed the front of his shirt with both fists and pulled him in, and the stool rocked under her, and he caught her before it tipped and lifted her off it entirely, one arm round her waist, as easily as if she were a bucket of roses.

She found herself sitting on the edge of the counter, her knees on either side of his hips, the soup forgotten behind her. He stood between her knees and didn’t stop. He kissed her jaw. The corner of her mouth. The soft place under her ear that she didn’t know, until that moment, could make her shiver from her scalp to her heels. He found it, and felt her shiver, and stayed there, his mouth open against her skin, his breath hot, until she was gripping his shoulders and her head had gone back against the cupboard.

“Zhendong.”

“Mm.”

“That’s—you’re—”

“I know,” he said, against her throat. His voice was low and rough and not entirely steady. “I’ve been thinking about that spot for a week.”

“You’ve been—what?”

“Every night.” He kissed it again, slower. “Outside your door. On the floor. A week. I know exactly where it is. I could find it in the dark.”

Her stomach turned over like a coin spun on a table.

His hands were on her waist, over her jumper, and they hadn’t moved. They were very large and they were shaking slightly and they hadn’t moved one centimetre, as if he didn’t trust them, as if he had made them a promise.

She put her own hands over his.

“You can,” she whispered.

He lifted his head and looked at her. His eyes were black and his breathing was rough and he looked, for the first time since she had known him, completely undone.

She moved his hands. Herself. Up, under the hem of the jumper, until his palms were flat against the bare skin of her waist.

He shut his eyes.

His thumbs moved once, slowly, along the lowest edge of her ribs, and she gasped, and he opened his eyes and looked at her with an expression that made her forget her own name.

“Not here,” he said. His voice had gone to gravel. “Not on a kitchen counter. Not the first time.”

“What’s wrong with the counter?”

“Nothing.” He leaned in until his forehead was against hers. “That’s the problem.”

She laughed, shaky and astonished, against his mouth.

He answered by sliding one arm under her knees and the other behind her back and lifting her off the counter the way he had lifted her out of the car on the night of the typhoon. But this time she wasn’t burning with fever, and this time she put her arms around his neck and her mouth against his throat, where she could feel his pulse jumping wildly under her lips, and she kissed it, and then, because she didn’t know what had got into her, bit it, very lightly.

He stopped dead on the stairs.

“Elowen,” he said, in a voice she had never heard.

“Keep walking,” she said into his neck.

He kept walking. Faster. And this time, when he carried her up the stairs past the little room by the stairs, he didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

The big room at the end of the corridor was dark except for the lights of the Docks coming through the long window, orange and white, moving faintly on the ceiling as the cranes turned.

He set her down on her feet beside the bed. Then he stood in front of her and didn’t do anything.

She understood that too. He would not take a single step she hadn’t given him.

So she reached up and pulled his tie the rest of the way loose and dropped it on the floor. Then she started on the buttons of his shirt.

Her fingers were clumsy. Florist’s fingers, good with wire and ribbon and stems, and suddenly useless with ordinary buttons. He stood absolutely still and let her fumble, his hands at his sides, his chest rising and falling under her knuckles. When she got the last one undone and pushed the shirt off his shoulders, she heard him let out a breath he had been holding.

In the orange light from the window, she could see his scars.

She had felt one of them in the dark, the long ridge down his ribs. She hadn’t known there were others. A round, puckered mark on his left shoulder. A thin white line across his collarbone. Three short parallel scars on his forearm, neat as stitches. A rough, shiny patch low on his side, older than the rest, the skin pulled tight.

She put her fingertip on the round one, on his shoulder.

“This?” she asked.

“A bullet. In the south. Four years ago.” His voice was rough. “It went straight through.”

She bent her head and kissed it.

He made a sound she had never heard from him, low and broken, as if something had been pulled out of his chest.

She touched the line across his collarbone.

“A broken bottle,” he said. “I was nineteen.”

She kissed that one too. Then the three short lines on his forearm, one at a time.

“The yard,” he said. “Where I carried steel. A sheet slipped.” He swallowed. “I was eleven.”

She kissed them, and felt his hand come up, finally, and slide into her hair, not pulling, only holding, shaking very slightly against her scalp.

When she reached the long ridge down his ribs, the one from Block C, the one she had touched in the dark, she didn’t ask. She knew. She knelt on the edge of the bed so she could reach it properly and pressed her mouth to the top of it, under his arm, and then lower, and lower, all the way down to where it ended above his hip, the way you would follow a river on a map.

When she looked up, his eyes were wet.

“Nobody,” he said, and stopped, and tried again. “Nobody has ever done that.”

“Done what?”

“Asked.” He touched her face. “People see them and look away. Or they want to know if I killed the man who did it.” A breath. “Nobody asks where it hurt.”

She sat back on her heels on the bed and looked up at him: this big, scarred, dangerous man standing in the orange light with his shirt on the floor and his heart on his face. And she realised that she was not doing this for her father. She was not doing it for the contract, or for protection, or because she owed him for Xiao Pan’s hands. She was doing it because she wanted to. Because she wanted him, specifically, this man and no other, and had for longer than she had let herself know.

It frightened her so badly that she reached for the hem of her own jumper so she wouldn’t have to think about it.

He caught her wrists.

“Let me,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He undressed her the way he did everything that mattered: slowly, with total attention, and with a question in every movement.

He lifted the jumper over her head and folded it, actually folded it, and put it on the chair, which made her laugh out loud, and he looked at her laughing in the half-dark with an expression she would remember for the rest of her life. He found the heavy gold ring on her middle finger and took it off and put it in the empty vase on the bedside table, where it rang against the glass like a small bell.

Then he stood in front of her in the orange light from the cranes and just looked.

He looked for so long that she put her arms up to cover herself, and he caught her wrists, gently, and moved them back down to her sides.

“Don’t,” he said. “Please. I’ve waited a month to see you.” He swallowed. “Let me look.”

She let him look.

It was the most frightening thing she had ever done. Standing still in the half-dark while the most dangerous man in the city looked at her as if she were the only thing in it. Her skin went hot everywhere his eyes went. Her breath went shallow. And she understood, slowly, from the way his hands had closed into fists at his sides and the way his jaw had gone tight, that he was the one who was afraid.

“Zhendong,” she said. “Touch me.”

He went down on his knees in front of her.

He kissed her stomach first. Just above the waist of her trousers, very softly, his breath hot on her skin, and she felt it all the way through her, down into her knees, which nearly went. He kissed her hip. The inside of her wrist, where her pulse was, the way he had the morning after the storm. Her ribs, one by one, working upwards, slowly, as if he were climbing something. And every time, before he went further, he stopped, and looked up at her, and waited, until she said yes, or nodded, or put her hands in his hair and pulled him closer, which after a while she did without waiting to be asked.

His hands were rough. Calluses from rope and steel and the grip of a gun, scraping lightly over her ribs, her waist, the small of her back, the curve of her hip. They should have felt frightening. They didn’t. They felt like being held by someone who knew exactly how much force it took to break something, and was using none of it.

When he stood up again and kissed her mouth, it was different. Deeper. Hungrier. His hand at the back of her head, his other arm round her waist, pulling her in until there was nothing between them at all, his bare chest against hers, his heart going so hard she could feel it, and she made the sound again, and this time he made one too, low in his chest, almost a growl.

“Do you know,” he said against her mouth, “what I thought, the first night? In the rain. When you threw the towel at me.”

“What?”

“That I would kill any man who ever touched you.”

Heat went through her from her throat to her stomach. Some old, sensible part of her, the part that kept accounts and wrote three-page contracts, tried to be offended.

“That’s possessive.”

“Yes.”

“That’s—you can’t say things like that.”

“I know.” He bent and put his mouth on the curve of her shoulder, and bit, gently, and she gasped. “Tell me to stop.”

“Don’t you dare,” said Elowen, and heard herself, and nearly died.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he finally laid her back on the white sheets, he braced himself above her on his forearms and stopped, one last time, and looked down at her in the moving light from the cranes.

“Tell me to stop,” he said again, “and I’ll stop. Any time. Even now. Even—”

She put her hand over his mouth.

“Zhendong,” she said. “I am a very organised person. I wrote you three pages of terms. If I wanted you to stop, I would have written it down.”

He laughed against her palm, a real laugh, surprised out of him, and she felt it all the way through her. Then he took her hand away from his mouth and laced his fingers through hers and pressed it down into the pillow beside her head, gently, and lowered his face to hers.

He was slow. Agonisingly slow. He kissed her as if he had all night and intended to use every minute of it, and he touched her the way he had learned to strip a rose, finding every place that made her breath catch and going back to it, again and again, watching her face the whole time, until she was arching up off the sheets and gripping his shoulders and saying his name in a voice she didn’t recognise. Zhendong. Zhendong. Please.

He stopped and looked at her.

“Say it again,” he said hoarsely.

“Please.”

“No.” His forehead came down against hers. “My name. Say my name again.”

“Zhendong.”

He closed his eyes as if she had struck him.

And then there was no more asking, and no more waiting.

She would remember, afterwards, that it was not like anything she had imagined. That he was so careful at first that she had to pull him to her, and that when she did, something in him broke open, and he held her as if the world were ending and she was the only thing he was allowed to save. That he said her name into her throat, over and over, Elowen, Elowen, like a man praying in a language he had only just learned. That the lights of the cranes moved across the ceiling and across his back and she held on to his shoulders, to the scars she had kissed one by one, and that at the end, when everything in her went bright and blind and far away, his arms locked round her so tightly she couldn’t breathe and she didn’t want to, and he made a sound against her neck that she would hear in her sleep for weeks.

And then the quiet. The ship’s horn, out on the water. His weight, and his heart, and his breath, ragged, against her skin.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, she lay with her head on his chest and listened to his heart slow down.

The light from the Docks moved across the ceiling. Somewhere out on the water a ship sounded its horn, long and low. His arm was around her, his hand spread flat on her bare back, his thumb moving slowly up and down her spine as if he were counting the bones, one at a time, to make sure they were all there.

She traced the scar on his ribs with one finger. She had already learned it by heart.

“Is this all right?” he asked into the dark. His voice sounded strange, careful, as if he were afraid of the answer. “Are you—did I—”

She lifted her head and looked at him.

He was staring at the ceiling. His jaw was tight. This man, who had walked into the Qiu brothers’ warehouse at two in the morning without a second thought, was lying in her bed rigid with terror that he might have done something wrong.

She put her chin on his chest so he had to look at her.

“You folded my jumper,” she said.

He blinked.

“In the middle of everything,” Elowen said, “you stopped and folded my jumper and put it on the chair. And then you took off my ring like it was going to break. And you asked me four times if I was sure.” She felt her eyes sting and didn’t care. “Five. You asked me five times.”

“Six,” said Zhao quietly. “I counted.”

She laughed and hid her face in his chest, and felt his arm tighten around her, and felt him finally, finally let out a long breath and go soft underneath her, all the stiffness running out of him at once like water out of a bucket.

They lay like that until the ship’s horn sounded again, further out.

Then, very quietly, into her hair, he said, “Stay?”

She lifted her head again.

“This is my room,” she said. “You stay.”

So he did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her alarm went off at three-thirty.

She woke with her face against his shoulder and his arm heavy across her waist and the whole long warm length of him curled around her back. The room was cold. The bed was not. Outside, the Docks were dark, and the cranes had stopped, and the sea was a black, quiet line under the sky.

She reached out and turned off the alarm before it could ring twice.

Behind her, he didn’t wake. His breathing stayed slow and deep against the back of her neck. In the years that followed, she would learn—and laugh about it—that Zhao Zhendong slept like a guard dog, waking at the smallest sound, every night of his life. Except this one. This one night, he slept like a stone.

She lay in the dark and thought about the market. Granny Su. The ranunculus. The soy milk man.

She picked up her phone and typed, very slowly, one-handed so she wouldn’t move the arm across her waist:

Granny Su, I’m not coming today. Please keep the ranunculus for tomorrow.

She had not missed the market on a working day in five years. Not when she had flu. Not on the morning of her wedding.

She put the phone face down on the bedside table, next to the vase with her ring in it, and closed her eyes, and slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao woke at seven to full daylight and a feeling of total, physical panic.

Light. There should not be light. He had never once in a month woken up after her. He sat up so fast the duvet slid off, reaching for his watch, already planning: the car, the road past the Qiu warehouse, Granny Su would be closing up, the ranunculus—

A hand caught his wrist.

“I didn’t go,” Elowen said.

She was lying on her side, looking up at him. Her hair was everywhere. There was a crease on her cheek from his shoulder. She was wearing his shirt from last night, the one she had taken off him, which she must have picked up off the floor at some point in the night, and it was far too big for her, and he could not look at anything else.

“You didn’t go,” he repeated.

“I texted Granny Su.” She pulled gently on his wrist until he lay back down. “She replied at four-fifteen. She said, ‘About time.’”

He lay on his back and looked at the ceiling and tried to understand it.

She had not gone to the market. She had gone to the market on the morning of her wedding. She had gone to the market on the morning of the typhoon with her throat already burning; he had watched her from the car with his hands clenched on the wheel. She had not missed it once.

She had missed it today. For him.

She curled against his side, her head on his shoulder, his own shirt soft against his ribs, and he put his arm around her and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, he would remember that this was the happiest he had ever been.

He would also remember that even then, lying in the morning light with his wife asleep again on his chest, the old voice in the back of his head did not go quiet. It only got softer. It said:

She wanted you. Last night, she wanted you. That’s true.

It isn’t the same thing.

Wanting you isn’t the same as choosing you. And she didn’t choose you, did she? She chose a contract. She chose her father. You were just the price.

He looked down at her. At the crease on her cheek. At her hand, lying open on his chest, over his heart, with the pale mark around her middle finger where the heavy ring had been.

He could ask her. Right now. He could wake her and ask.

Did you marry me for love? Or to keep your father safe from me?

He opened his mouth.

Elowen sighed in her sleep and pressed her face harder into his shoulder, and her hand closed, very slightly, on his chest, as if holding on to something.

He closed his mouth.

Not today, he thought. Not this morning. He would not risk this morning for anything in the world.

He would ask her another day.

He didn’t know yet that it would take him almost three years, a bullet, and a long crawl home in the dark to do it.

chapters.title: The Florist’s Husband Is Not Allowed Behind the Counter
chapters.desc: House rules, broken daily. Also: what you can do in a walk-in cooler at one degree.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule one: no frightening the customers. Rule two: see rule one.” — handwritten sign, back wall of Elowen’s
chapters.content:
The trouble with sleeping with your husband, Elowen discovered, was that he started turning up at work.

Not every day. He had his own work, the kind that happened in the north of the city at midnight and came home smelling of cigarettes that weren’t his. But on the days when his meetings were late, or there were no meetings, or he simply decided there were none, he drove her to the market at four, carried the buckets in at six, ate his fried eggs on the stool, and then didn’t leave.

He stood in the corner. He read the newspaper. He watched the door.

By the end of the first week, her takings were down by a third.

“You’re frightening people,” she told him.

“I’m reading.”

“You’ve been on the same page for an hour.”

He looked down at the newspaper. It was the property section. He lowered it slowly.

“The man who came in at ten,” he said. “Grey jacket. He looked at the till twice before he looked at the flowers.”

“He was choosing between carnations and roses for his mother and checking whether he could afford the roses.” She snipped the end off a stem. “He bought carnations. Because you stared at him.”

Zhao considered this.

“He could have afforded the roses,” he said. “His shoes were new.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning she wrote a sign and stuck it to the back wall with tape, where he would see it every time he looked up from his newspaper.

HOUSE RULES

1. No frightening the customers.

2. The husband is not allowed behind the counter.

3. The husband does not count other people’s change.

4. The husband does not ask delivery drivers where they parked.

5. If the husband needs something to do, he can sweep.

He read it in silence. Then he took the broom from the corner and swept the shop floor so thoroughly that Xiao Pan, back at work with his hands in soft white compression gloves and strict orders not to lift anything heavier than a vase, came in from the back and stopped dead.

“Miss Lin,” he whispered. “Is the floor supposed to shine like that?”

“No,” said Elowen.

“He’s doing the corners. With his fingers.”

“I know.”

Xiao Pan watched Zhao Zhendong crouch beside the cooler and pick a single rose petal out of the gap under the door with the very tips of two fingers, as if defusing something.

“I think,” Xiao Pan said slowly, “he might be in love with you.”

Elowen dropped her scissors.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rules lasted four days.

On Wednesday, a woman came in to order flowers for her own funeral. She was eighty-one, tiny, sharp as a needle, and had very clear ideas. White lilies, but not the kind that smelled. Chrysanthemums, but yellow, because white was boring. And something blue, because her husband had always said blue suited her, and he would be waiting.

Elowen wrote it all down. She was good with people who were planning to die; she had been doing it for five years. She was halfway through the order when the old woman stopped talking and looked past her, at the corner of the shop.

“Who’s that?”

Elowen didn’t turn round. “My husband.”

The old woman peered at Zhao over her spectacles. Zhao lowered his newspaper. They looked at each other across the shop for a long, assessing moment, two people who had both seen a great deal of the world and didn’t think much of most of it.

“Young man,” the old woman said. “Come here.”

He came. Elowen watched him cross the shop floor and stand in front of an eighty-one-year-old woman with his hands at his sides like a soldier.

“You look like you’ve been to a lot of funerals,” the old woman said.

“Yes, Grandmother.”

“What flowers did they have?”

He was quiet for a moment.

“Mostly none,” he said.

The old woman looked at him. Then she nodded, as if he had passed some kind of test, and said, “Delphiniums. For the blue. My husband grew them.”

Zhao glanced at Elowen. Something passed across his face that she couldn’t name.

“They don’t like draughts,” he said. “Tell your family not to put them near the door.”

The old woman laughed, a dry, cracked, delighted laugh, and patted his arm, and paid in cash. When she had gone, Elowen stood at the counter holding the order form and looked at her husband.

“You were behind the counter,” she said.

He looked down. He was. He had walked round it without noticing.

“Rule two,” Elowen said.

“She called me over.”

“Rule two doesn’t have exceptions.”

He looked at the sign on the wall. He looked at her. And then, very slowly, the corner of his mouth went up, and stayed up, and became something she had never quite seen on him before: a real smile, crooked, a little rusty, like a door that hadn’t been opened in years.

“Then punish me,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

The walk-in cooler was at the back of the shop, behind a heavy insulated door with a rubber seal. Inside it was one degree, and dim, and smelled of wet leaves and roses and the faint chemical sweetness of flower food. Buckets stood in rows on metal shelves, packed with stems. Her breath came out in a small white cloud.

She had gone in to get the lilies for the funeral order.

He had followed her.

The door swung shut behind him with a soft thud and a click as the seal caught, and suddenly the noise of the street was gone, and it was only the hum of the cooling fan and the two of them standing very close in a space built for buckets.

“You can’t be in here,” she said. “You’re letting the cold out.”

“The door’s closed.”

“You’re—” She turned round with the bucket of lilies in her arms, and he was right there, and she had nowhere to go but backwards into the shelf of white roses. “You’re breathing on the stock.”

He took the bucket of lilies out of her arms and put it on the floor.

“Zhendong,” she said. “It’s one degree.”

“I know.” He put his hands on the shelf on either side of her, not touching her, his arms caging her in among the roses. “You’re shivering.”

She was. Her bare arms had gone to gooseflesh. Her breath was clouding between them, mixing with his.

“Then let me out.”

“In a minute.”

He bent his head and kissed her.

His mouth was the only warm thing in the room. She made a small sound and grabbed the front of his shirt, and he pressed closer, and the shelf rattled behind her, and a dozen white roses shivered on their stems and dropped cold water down the back of her neck. She gasped.
