He laughed against her mouth, low, and caught the drop with his thumb at the nape of her neck, and then his whole warm hand was there, under her hair, holding her head, and his other arm was around her waist, pulling her off the cold shelf and against him.

It was the strangest kiss of her life. Freezing air on her arms and his heat against her front. The smell of roses so thick she could taste it. The fan humming. His heart going hard under her palm. The danger, faint and thrilling, that Xiao Pan might open the door at any moment, and the knowledge, deeper and better, that he wouldn’t, because the boy had taken one look at Zhao following her into the cooler and fled to the front of the shop with a look of deep, personal embarrassment.

When they finally broke apart, her lips were tingling and her nose was cold and she had forgotten what she came in for.

“That,” she said, a little breathless, “was not a punishment.”

“No,” Zhao agreed. He bent and picked up the bucket of lilies and handed it to her. “But now you’re warm.”

She was. All the way through.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they came out, Xiao Pan was standing at the counter wrapping a bouquet with enormous concentration and the tips of his ears bright red.

Elowen put the lilies down and went back to the funeral order as if nothing had happened.

Zhao went back to his corner, picked up the newspaper, and opened it at the property section.

After a while, Xiao Pan cleared his throat.

“Mr. Zhao,” he said, without looking up from the bouquet. “I wanted to say thank you. For the hospital. Miss Lin told me.”

Zhao didn’t lower the paper.

“How are your hands?”

“Better. The doctor says no grafts. I have to squeeze a ball a hundred times a day.” A pause. “I can’t ride a scooter yet. Or a motorbike. Not for six months.”

“I know,” said Zhao. “I asked.”

Xiao Pan looked up.

Behind the newspaper, very casually, Zhao said, “There’s a garage near the Docks. A woman called Jinx builds bikes. She owes me a favour. In six months, when your doctor says yes, you go and see her, and you tell her my name.”

Xiao Pan stared at the newspaper. His mouth opened. Nothing came out.

“It’ll be a small one,” Zhao added. “And you’ll wear a helmet. And if I ever see you without the helmet, I’ll take it back.”

The boy made a sound that was not quite a word, put down the bouquet, and fled into the back of the shop.

Elowen looked at her husband over the top of the funeral order.

“Rule one,” she said quietly. “No frightening the customers.”

“He’s not a customer.”

“You made him cry.”

Zhao turned a page of the property section.

“He was going to cry anyway,” he said. “I just gave him a reason.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, she took the sign down from the back wall and put it in the drawer under the till.

She didn’t throw it away. She kept it, and years later, when people asked how long the arms dealer had been helping out in the flower shop, she took it out and showed them.

By then, rule two had a line through it in her handwriting, and next to it, in his, square and blunt: Except when she says so.

And underneath, added a long time afterward, in hers again:

She always says so.

chapters.title: Thorns at Six in the Morning
chapters.desc: He learns to strip roses. He bleeds a lot. Chen Si comes to buy flowers and stays to watch.
chapters.content:
“Give me the knife,” said Zhao.

It was six-fifteen on a Monday, and the market haul was spread across the workbench: four hundred roses from the south, still wrapped in their cardboard sleeves, heads packed tight as fists. Every one of them had to be unwrapped, stripped of its lower leaves and the worst of its thorns, cut at an angle with the knife, and dropped into a bucket before the shop opened at nine. On a normal Monday it took Elowen and Xiao Pan two hours. With Xiao Pan’s hands still healing, it would take her three.

“You don’t know how,” she said.

“Show me.”

She looked at him. He had taken off his jacket and rolled up his sleeves. The burn on his forearm had healed into a shiny pink patch. He was looking at the roses the way he looked at the pieces of a gun laid out on a cloth.

She handed him a stem and a rose stripper: a small metal tool, like a pair of tongs with a hole in the end, that you closed around the stem and pulled down to tear off the leaves.

“Hold it here,” she said. “Squeeze. Pull down, toward you. Not too hard or you’ll strip the bark and the stem will rot. Leave the top two sets of leaves. They help it drink.”

He squeezed and pulled.

The stripper went down the stem in one clean movement and took every leaf and every thorn with it, and also, somehow, a strip of skin off the side of his thumb.

He looked at his thumb. A bead of blood came up, bright red.

“The thorns go in the tool,” Elowen said. “Not in you.”

“I see that now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By seven o’clock, he had stripped sixty roses and bled on about twenty of them.

He was slow. He was very, very careful, which made him slower. He held each stem as though it might go off. He checked every one after he stripped it, turning it in the light, running his finger down the bark to find the thorns he’d missed, and finding them, and saying nothing, and bleeding again.

He did not complain once.

She had worked with a lot of people over five years: part-timers, students, a cousin of Xiao Pan’s for one disastrous Valentine’s Day. All of them complained about the roses. Roses were the worst job in the shop. They tore your hands to pieces and there were always more of them.

Zhao stripped his sixty-first rose, found a thorn, pulled it out of the pad of his finger with his teeth, and reached for the sixty-second.

“Stop,” Elowen said.

He stopped.

She took his hand and turned it over.

It was a mess. Little cuts all over the fingers and the side of the palm. A thorn still lodged in the web of skin between his thumb and first finger, black and tiny. Old calluses and old scars and fresh red scratches, all on top of each other.

“You’re holding it like it’s going to bite you,” she said.

“It does bite me.”

“Because you’re holding it like that.” She stood behind him at the workbench and reached round him, her chest against his back, and put her hands over his. “Loose. Like this. Let it move in your hand. You’re not fighting it.”

She guided his hands. The stripper closed around the stem. She pulled down with him, smooth, not too hard.

The leaves came away. The thorns came away. His skin stayed where it was.

“Oh,” he said.

She didn’t let go.

They stood like that for a moment at the workbench, in the grey early light, her arms around him from behind and her hands over his hands and her cheek resting against his shoulder blade. She could feel him breathing. She could feel how still he had gone, the way he always went still when she touched him without warning, waiting to find out whether he was allowed to have it.

“Again,” she said into his back.

They stripped the next one together. And the next.

“Where did you learn to be so careful?” she asked, after the tenth.

His hands paused under hers.

“The yard,” he said.

“Where you carried steel.”

“Old Zhao used to say that if you dropped something, it cost him money. And if it cost him money, it cost you.” He reached for another stem. His voice was perfectly level. “So I learned not to drop things.”

Elowen kept her hands on his.

“What did it cost you?” she asked. “When you did?”

He was quiet. A delivery van went past outside. The cooler fan hummed.

“There’s a scar on my side,” he said finally. “Low. Older than the others. You found it.”

She remembered. A rough, shiny patch, the skin pulled tight. She had kissed it without asking where it came from, because by then he had told her about the bullet and the bottle and the steel sheet, and she had thought there was no more to tell.

“He kept a stove in the office,” Zhao said. “For winter. I dropped a box of bolts when I was nine.”

He stripped the rose. Leaves, thorns. Smooth. Perfect.

Elowen took her hands away from his. She put her arms around his waist instead, from behind, and held on, her face pressed between his shoulder blades, and didn’t say anything at all.

After a moment, he put down the stripper. He put his hand over both of hers, where they were locked together over his stomach. His thumb was bleeding a little. She didn’t care.

“It was a long time ago,” he said.

“I know.”

“He’s dead.”

“I know.”

“I don’t think about it.”

“You think about it every time you pick up something that might break,” Elowen said into his shirt. “You carried my mother’s lemon tree like a baby. You carry the buckets like they’re made of glass.” She tightened her arms. “You hold me like that.”

He didn’t answer.

“Is that bad?” he asked at last, very low.

She thought about the knife going into the table at the dinner. The oil drum. All the things those hands could do.

“No,” she said. “It’s the opposite.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight-fifteen, the bell over the door rang and Chen Si walked in.

He was wearing a camel coat and carrying a takeaway coffee, and he stopped just inside the door with the expression of a man who has walked into a room and found his brother in an apron.

Because Zhao was in an apron. Elowen had put it on him at seven-thirty, after the third time he bled on his own shirt. It was green and said ELOWEN’S across the chest in white letters, and it was too short for him by a head.

“Good morning,” said Chen Si.

“Si,” said Zhao, without looking up from his rose.

Chen Si walked slowly to the workbench. He looked at the buckets of stripped roses, two hundred of them now, standing in neat rows. He looked at the floor, which was covered in leaves and thorns. He looked at his brother’s hands.

“You’re bleeding,” he said.

“Roses.”

“I can see that.” Chen Si set his coffee down on the counter, very precisely. “I’ve watched you take a bullet in the shoulder and finish your noodles before you let anyone look at it. I’ve never seen you bleed for a flower.”

“There are four hundred of them.”

“That explains everything.” Chen Si turned to Elowen with a small, courteous bow. “Mrs. Zhao. I’m here to buy flowers for my wife. It’s our anniversary on Thursday and I would like to be the first to order.”

“What does she like?”

“Everything expensive.” He considered. “And whatever you would never put in an arrangement for her. She’ll want to know why.”

Elowen almost smiled. “Peonies, out of season. Gold ribbon. And one stem of something cheap in the middle. Carnation.”

“Why the carnation?”

“So she has something to complain about. She’ll enjoy it more.”

Chen Si looked at her for a moment with genuine interest, the way you look at a chess player who has just made an unexpected move.

“Yes,” he said slowly. “She will.” He turned to Zhao. “Your wife understands my wife better than I do.”

“They went to school together,” said Zhao.

“So I’ve heard. Endlessly.” Chen Si picked up his coffee again. Then he paused, and looked at Zhao’s hands, and his face changed slightly. “Zhendong. A word.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went outside. Elowen watched them through the window while she wrote up Chen Si’s order: two men standing on the pavement in front of her shop, one in a camel coat and one in a too-small green apron, talking in low voices.

She couldn’t hear what they said. She saw Chen Si say something short and Zhao shake his head. She saw Chen Si say something longer, and Zhao look away down the street. She saw Chen Si put a hand on his brother’s shoulder, briefly, and then take it away.

Then Chen Si said something else, and Zhao laughed.

Not the rusty smile from the funeral order. A full laugh, out loud in the street, his head going back. She had never heard him laugh like that in daylight. Two women walking past with shopping bags stopped and stared.

When he came back in, he was still half smiling.

“What did he say?” Elowen asked.

Zhao picked up his stripper and a rose.

“He asked if I was all right,” he said.

“And?”

“I said yes.” He stripped the rose. “He said, ‘You’re in an apron, Zhendong, and you’ve bled on two hundred roses, and you look happier than I have ever seen you in ten years. I’ve known you since you were a feral fifteen-year-old with no front tooth. I would like to know who this woman is and how she did it.’” He dropped the rose in the bucket. “And I said, ‘She showed me how to hold them.’”

Elowen put down her pen.

“That’s why you laughed?”

“No.” Zhao reached for another rose. “I laughed because he said, ‘Teach me. Aurelia keeps giving me back the roses I buy her and saying they’re not good enough.’”

Elowen laughed so hard she had to sit down on the stool.

✦ ✦ ✦

They finished the four hundred at nine minutes to nine.

Afterward, she sat him down on the stool and took his hands, one at a time, and went over them with tweezers and antiseptic and a little torch, the way her mother had gone over hers when she was small and had played in the rose buckets. She found six more thorns. She pulled them out one by one. He watched her do it without moving.

When she had finished, she put a plaster on the worst cut, on his thumb, and then, because the shop was empty and the sign said CLOSED for nine more minutes, she lifted his hand and kissed the plaster.

He looked at her.

“Tomorrow,” he said, “I’ll be faster.”

“Tomorrow you’re wearing gloves.”

“Real florists don’t wear gloves.”

“Real florists didn’t learn to hold things from Old Zhao,” said Elowen.

He was quiet for a moment, his hand still in hers.

“No,” he said. “I’m learning from you now.”

She turned the sign on the door to OPEN, and the first customer of the day walked in, and found a woman behind the counter with pink cheeks, and a large man in a too-short green apron sweeping thorns into a dustpan with enormous care.

chapters.title: The Rare Flower He Should Not Have Bought
chapters.desc: She mentions one camellia. He buys the mountain it grows on.
chapters.epigraph: “There are two in the world. One in London. One in New Zealand. Everyone says there might be a third.”
chapters.content:
It started with a magazine.

Elowen subscribed to three: a trade magazine for florists, full of wholesale prices and new varieties of chrysanthemum; a Japanese one about ikebana that she couldn’t read but liked to look at; and a British gardening quarterly that cost a fortune to import and that she read in the bath, slowly, one article a night, like a novel.

On a Sunday evening at the end of summer, she was reading it at the dinner table, which she did not normally allow, because Zhao was eating soup and reading a shipping report, which she also did not normally allow, and they had silently agreed that tonight the rule was off.

“Listen to this,” she said.

He looked up.

“There’s a camellia called Middlemist’s Red.” She turned the magazine so he could see the photograph: a flower so full and so deep a pink that it looked almost like a rose, every petal laid over the last in perfect overlapping circles. “A man called John Middlemist brought it to England from China in 1804. Then it disappeared from China completely. Nobody knows how. Now there are only two known plants in the whole world. One in a glasshouse in London. One in a garden in New Zealand.”

Zhao looked at the picture.

“Two,” he said.

“Two.” She turned the magazine back and read. “But there’s always been a rumour that it survived in China somewhere. In an old private garden, or a temple, or on a tea estate in the south. The article says a botanist went looking for it in the nineties and found a plant on an estate in the Cangshan hills that might be one. Might. The owner wouldn’t let anyone take a cutting to test it. He said the plant was older than his family and it wasn’t for sale.”

She put the magazine down.

“I’ve wanted to see one since I was a girl,” she said. “My mother had a picture of it on the kitchen wall. She cut it out of a calendar. She said it was the rarest flower in the world, and that rare things should be left where they are, because the minute someone tries to own them, they die.”

She smiled a little and went back to her soup.

Zhao didn’t say anything. He finished his own soup, and his shipping report, and washed his bowl.

She forgot about it.

He didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

The envelope came to the shop three weeks later, by courier, at eleven in the morning on a Wednesday.

It was thick and cream-coloured and had a law firm’s name embossed on the corner, the same firm Chen Si used for everything. Inside were forty pages, stapled, in small dense type. She read the first page standing at the counter, holding a bunch of eucalyptus in her other hand.

Then she put the eucalyptus down.

Then she read it again.

It was a deed. A transfer of land use rights. Three hundred and twenty mu of terraced hillside in the Cangshan hills, a hundred and sixty years of continuous cultivation, a main house, two drying sheds, a walled garden. The Wen Family Tea Estate. Previous owner: Wen Guoliang, aged eighty-four. New owner—

Lin Elowen.

Not Zhao. Her. Her name, alone, on the deed, the way her name was alone on the sign above the shop.

At the back, in an envelope inside the envelope, there was a single photograph. A garden wall covered in moss. A dark, glossy shrub against it, taller than a man. And on the shrub, half-hidden in the leaves, three flowers, each one so full and so deep a pink that it looked almost like a rose.

Xiao Pan, who had been wrapping a bouquet, looked up at the sound she made.

“Miss Lin?” he said. “Are you all right?”

Elowen was already reaching for her phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the Docks. She went there.

She didn’t take the bus. She took a taxi, which she never did, and she walked past Bao at the door without a word, and up the stairs, and into the long bare office, where Zhao was standing at the whiteboard with three men she didn’t know and a map of somewhere with a great many arrows on it.

All four of them turned round.

She held up the envelope.

“Out,” said Zhao to the three men, without taking his eyes off her.

They went. Quickly. One of them forgot his coffee.

When the door had shut, Elowen walked to the desk and put the envelope down on it, very precisely, the way she had once put down three pages of terms.

“You bought a mountain,” she said.

“A hill.”

“Three hundred and twenty mu.”

“The house needs a new roof,” said Zhao. “The tea is good. Mr. Wen says the oolong from the upper terraces won a prize in 1987.”

“Zhendong.”

He stopped talking.

She found that her hands were shaking, and she didn’t know if it was anger or something else. She pressed them flat on the desk.

“You can’t,” she said. “You cannot buy me things like this. I told you about a flower. A flower, in a magazine. And three weeks later, there’s a deed on my counter with my name on it and a photograph and eighty-four-year-old Mr. Wen has sold his family’s land for—how much? How much did you pay him?”

He told her.

She sat down in the chair in front of the desk because her legs stopped working.

“That’s more than my father’s whole business,” she said.

“It’s less than two containers.”

“That isn’t the point.”

“Then what is the point?” He came round the desk. He didn’t touch her. He crouched down beside the chair, the way he had crouched beside the car door on the day of Kang, so their eyes were level. “Tell me what I did wrong. I want to understand.”

She looked at him.

He meant it. He wasn’t defending himself. He was looking at her the way he had looked at the roses on the first morning: a man who had picked something up the wrong way and wanted to be shown how to hold it.

“My mother said,” Elowen said slowly, “that rare things should be left where they are. That the minute someone tries to own them, they die.” Her voice wobbled. “And you went and bought it. Like a car. Like the house. Like—”

“Like you?” said Zhao quietly.

She stopped.

The office was very quiet. Down in the warehouse, a forklift beeped.

“I didn’t buy it to own it,” he said. “I read the rest of the article. After you went to bed.” He reached past her to the desk and picked up the magazine she hadn’t known he had. It was her magazine. He had taken it from the bathroom. There was a coffee ring on the cover. “Page forty. The last paragraph. You didn’t read that part out.”

He opened it and handed it to her.

She read it.

Mr. Wen, now in his eighties and in poor health, has said that his children intend to sell the estate after his death. Two developers have already made offers for the land. It is not known what would become of the plant.

She looked up.

“Developers,” Zhao said. “A golf course, Mr. Wen thinks. Or holiday villas. They’d have bulldozed the walled garden in a week. Or someone would have dug the plant up and sold it to a collector in Japan.” He took the magazine back, gently. “The two in London and New Zealand have guards. Did you know that? People have tried to steal cuttings. Someone tried to dig the London one up.”

“I didn’t know.”

“So I bought the hill.” He put the magazine on the desk. “Not the flower. The hill around it. So nobody else could. Mr. Wen stays in the house as long as he lives. His grandson keeps running the tea. The garden doesn’t change. Nobody touches the plant without your permission. That’s in the contract. Page twelve.” He paused. “I put your name on it because I don’t know anything about flowers. You do.”

Elowen sat in the chair and looked at him.

At this big, dangerous man crouching beside her in his office, who had read her magazine at midnight after she went to bed, who had found a paragraph she hadn’t bothered to finish, and who had then spent more than her father’s entire business so that one old flower on a hill a thousand kilometres away could stay exactly where it was.

“You could have asked me,” she said. Her voice was very small.

“You would have said no.”

“Yes.”

“That’s why I didn’t ask.” He almost smiled. “It’s the only time. I promise. Next time I want to buy you a mountain, I’ll ask first.”

She laughed. It came out wet. She put her hand over her mouth.

“You’re impossible,” she said through her fingers.

“Chen Si says that.”

“Chen Si is right.”

He reached up and took her hand away from her mouth. He held it. His thumb moved over the place where the heavy ring sat on her middle finger.

“Is it a real one?” she asked. “The plant. Is it really Middlemist’s Red?”

“I don’t know,” said Zhao. “Mr. Wen won’t let anyone test it. He says it’s his grandfather’s grandfather’s, and it came from a nursery in Guangzhou in 1850, and that’s good enough.” He looked at her. “He says if the new owner wants to test it, that’s her business. But he wants to meet her first.”

“Meet me?”

“He says,” Zhao said, very seriously, “that he wants to see the face of a woman a man would buy a mountain for.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, she couldn’t sleep.

She lay in the big bed at the end of the corridor with the photograph of the camellia on the pillow beside her, and looked at it in the light from the Docks, and thought about her mother’s calendar picture taped to the kitchen wall in the Walled City, gone yellow and curling at the corners. She had looked at that picture every morning of her childhood while she ate her breakfast.

Beside her, Zhao was asleep. He slept in her bed now. Not every night. Some nights he still came in late, smelling of other people’s cigarettes, and sat down outside her door out of habit, and she had to go out and get him. But most nights.

She turned on her side and looked at him.

He slept on his back, one arm flung up over his head, the other on his chest. In the dark, without the stillness, without the waiting, he looked like a boy. She could see the edge of the scar on his ribs where the sheet had slipped.

I didn’t buy it to own it.

Like you?

She put her hand on his chest, over his heart.

He didn’t wake. But his hand came up in his sleep and covered hers, and held it there, and stayed.

“I’ll go,” she whispered into the dark. “To the hill. I want to see it.”

She didn’t expect him to answer. He was asleep.

“I booked the tickets,” Zhao said, without opening his eyes. “Friday. Two seats. The hills are very wet in September. Bring boots.”

She hit him in the chest with the photograph.

He laughed, low and sleepy, and pulled her down against him, and she lay with her face in his neck and the photograph crushed between them and laughed into his neck until her eyes were wet.

chapters.title: The Estate in the Rain
chapters.desc: An old tea estate, an older gardener, a shooting lesson, and a night with nothing in the way.
chapters.epigraph: “Rare things should be left where they are.”
chapters.content:
The Cangshan hills were green in a way the city never was.

They flew south for three hours and drove for four more, up a road that got narrower and steeper and wetter with every kilometre, until the car was crawling along a ledge cut into the side of a mountain with tea bushes falling away below them in neat dark terraces, like the steps of a giant staircase. Mist sat in the valleys. It had been raining since the airport. The windscreen wipers went back and forth, back and forth, and Elowen sat with her face almost against the glass and didn’t say a word for the last hour.

Zhao drove. He had sent Bao and two other men ahead the day before. He didn’t say so, but she saw them at the bottom of the estate road, standing beside a car under a tree, and Bao lifted one hand as they passed.

“You brought guards,” she said.

“I brought Bao.”

“Bao is a guard.”

“Bao is a man who likes tea,” said Zhao. “He asked to come.”

She looked at him sideways. He kept his eyes on the road. She decided not to argue. There was mist on the terraces and the air coming through the vents smelled of wet leaves and woodsmoke, and she was too happy to argue about anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house at the top of the estate was old and low and grey, built around a courtyard, with a curved tiled roof that sagged in the middle like a tired horse. Part of it was clearly falling down. Part of it had smoke coming from the chimney.

Mr. Wen was waiting under the eaves.

He was tiny and bent and very old, with a face like a walnut and a long white wisp of beard, and he was leaning on a stick made from a twisted tea branch. Beside him stood a young man of about twenty in a waterproof jacket who looked mortified, the way grandsons look when their grandfathers are about to do something.

Elowen got out of the car into the rain.

Mr. Wen looked at her. He didn’t say anything. He looked at her face, her hair coming loose in the wet, her muddy boots, the heavy gold ring on her middle finger. Then he looked past her at Zhao, getting out of the driver’s side, and his eyebrows went up into his hat.

“Hm,” said Mr. Wen.

His grandson closed his eyes.

“So,” said Mr. Wen to Elowen, in a thick southern accent she had to concentrate to follow. “You’re the one.”

“I’m sorry?”

“The one he bought the mountain for.” The old man pointed his stick at Zhao, who had come round the car and was standing behind her shoulder with rain running off his hair. “A man like that. When his lawyer called, I said no. I said it three times. Then he called.” The stick waggled. “He said, ‘My wife looks at a picture of your flower the way I look at her. I don’t want anyone to dig it up.’ That was all. I said yes.”

Elowen turned slowly and looked at her husband.

Zhao was looking at the roof. Very hard. As if it were extremely interesting.

“Grandpa,” said the grandson faintly.

“What? It’s true.” Mr. Wen turned and started shuffling toward the courtyard. “Come. Come and see it before the light goes. Then we eat. Then you can tell me if you want to test it with your machines, and I can tell you no.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The walled garden was at the back of the house, up a flight of mossy stone steps. The wall was taller than Zhao and green with moss and fern, and the gate in it was so old the wood had gone silver.

Mr. Wen pushed it open with his stick.

Inside, it was very quiet. The rain was softer here, broken up by the trees. There were beds of herbs gone wild, and an old stone basin full of water with leaves floating in it, and a pomelo tree, and a bench.

And against the far wall, taller than a man, dark and glossy and dripping with rain, the camellia.

It was in flower, which should have been impossible. Camellias bloomed in late winter; she had sold them every February for five years. Behind her, Mr. Wen said only, “It does that sometimes. When it likes someone.”

Not many. Five, maybe six, half-hidden in the leaves. But each one was exactly like the photograph in the magazine, exactly like the faded calendar picture on her mother’s kitchen wall: so full, so many petals laid over each other in perfect overlapping circles, so deep a pink that in the grey wet light it almost glowed. A rose that wasn’t a rose. A flower that had disappeared from a whole country and survived, maybe, here, on one hill, behind one wall, because one family had refused to sell it for a hundred and seventy years.

Elowen walked across the wet grass and stopped in front of it.

She didn’t touch it. She stood very close and looked, with the rain running down her face, for so long that Mr. Wen sat down on the bench and his grandson went to fetch him an umbrella.

Zhao didn’t come closer. He stood by the gate.

When she finally turned round, her face was wet, and not only with rain.

“My mother,” she said. And couldn’t finish.

Zhao crossed the garden. He stood beside her in front of the camellia and didn’t say anything, and after a moment she leaned against his arm, and he put it around her, and they stood there in the rain together looking at a flower.

On the bench, Mr. Wen watched them from under his grandson’s umbrella.

“Hm,” he said again, quite softly, and this time it sounded different.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t test it.

Over dinner—soup with bamboo shoots, cured pork, greens from the garden, and a pot of the oolong from the upper terraces that had won a prize in 1987 and that Bao drank with his eyes closed like a man in church—Mr. Wen asked her, and she said no.

“Why not?” said the old man, narrowing his eyes. “Don’t you want to know?”

Elowen thought about it.

“If it is,” she said, “then it’s the rarest flower in the world, and everyone will want it, and someone will try to steal it, and we’ll need walls and cameras and guards. And if it isn’t, then it’s a beautiful old camellia your grandfather’s grandfather planted, and everyone will lose interest and leave it alone.” She turned her teacup in her hands. “Either way it stays in the garden. Either way it’s the same flower. I don’t think the test changes anything that matters.”

Mr. Wen looked at her.

Then he turned to Zhao and said, “You chose well.”

Zhao, who had been eating his soup in silence, put down his spoon.

“She chose,” he said.

Something in the way he said it made Elowen look up. But he had gone back to his soup, and his face didn’t tell her anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning the rain stopped for two hours, and he taught her to shoot.

She hadn’t asked. But after breakfast he took a canvas bag out of the car and walked her down to the bottom terrace, where an old drying shed stood against the hillside with nothing behind it but rock, and set six empty tin cans along a fence rail.

“No,” said Elowen.

“Yes.”

“I’m a florist.”

“You live in a house with fourteen locks and a steel room in the basement.” He opened the bag. Inside was a small black pistol and two boxes of ammunition. “The code gets you into the room. This is for if you can’t get to the room.”

She looked at the gun. She thought about Maartens’ hand on her knee, and how her body had gone far away and left her sitting there.

She held out her hand.

He was a good teacher. She would think that later, and be surprised by it. He was patient. He didn’t raise his voice. He showed her how to check it was empty, how to stand, how to hold it with both hands, the right hand high on the grip and the left wrapped around it. How to breathe out before she squeezed. How not to flinch.

The first shot went into the hillside a metre to the left of the cans. The noise was enormous. She dropped the gun on the grass.

He picked it up. He checked it. He put it back in her hands.

“Again,” he said.

By the twentieth shot she had hit two cans. By the fortieth, five. Her arms ached and her ears rang through the ear defenders he had made her wear and her hands smelled of metal and smoke.

On the forty-first, she hit the last can dead centre, and it spun off the rail and bounced down the terrace into the tea bushes, and she let out a whoop she didn’t know she had in her.

Behind her, he laughed.

She turned round, the gun pointing safely at the ground the way he had taught her, and found him standing a little way back with his hands in his pockets, looking at her with an expression she had never seen before. Pride, she thought. And something else. Something hungry.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing.” He came and took the gun from her and checked it and put it away. His fingers brushed hers. “You’re good at that.”

“I hit six cans.”

“You hit six cans and didn’t close your eyes once.” He zipped up the bag. Then he straightened and looked at her, standing on the wet terrace with her hair coming down and her cheeks red and her hands still shaking a little from the noise. “You have no idea,” he said quietly, “what you look like right now.”

The rain started again before she could answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

It didn’t stop for two days.

The road down the mountain washed out at the second bend. Mr. Wen’s grandson came back from looking at it soaked to the waist and said nobody was going anywhere until the county sent a digger, which would be Tuesday, if they were lucky.

They were given the room at the end of the east wing. It was the only one with a roof that didn’t leak. It had whitewashed walls and a wooden floor, a wide old bed with a carved frame and a quilt that smelled of camphor, a charcoal brazier in the corner, and a window that looked out over the terraces, which today were nothing but grey cloud and the sound of water running everywhere, down the gutters, down the steps, down the hill.

There was no electricity in the east wing. Mr. Wen’s grandson brought them candles.

Elowen sat on the edge of the bed in her socks and watched Zhao light the brazier.

He did it the way he did everything with his hands: carefully, competently, without wasted movement. The charcoal caught. Red light came up over his face from below, and the candles flickered on the white walls, and outside the rain went on and on.

She realised that she had never been anywhere with him where nobody could reach them.

No phone signal; she had checked. No road. No Docks, no Chen Si, no brokers at midnight, no Qiu brothers, no father. No market at four in the morning. No reason to get up. No fever. No contract. Nothing either of them had to ask or prove or wait for.

Just a room, and a fire, and rain.

“Zhendong,” she said.

He looked up from the brazier.

She didn’t say anything else. She didn’t have to. He got up from his crouch and crossed the room and stood in front of her where she sat on the edge of the bed, and she reached up and took his hand and pulled him down.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was different from the first time.

The first time had been a question, asked over and over, six times; he had counted. This time there was no question. This time it was slow because they had nowhere to be. It was slow because the rain was slow, because the candlelight was slow, because for the first time in either of their lives there was nothing at all waiting on the other side of the door.

She undressed him by the brazier, with the red light on his skin, and this time she didn’t ask about the scars. She knew them. She kissed them in order, like a path she had walked before. He let her. He stood with his head bowed and his eyes closed and his hands in her hair and let her, and when she reached the long one on his ribs he said her name in a voice that wasn’t steady at all.

Then he turned her round.

He did it gently, his hands on her shoulders, until her back was to him and she was facing the fire. He undid her hair first. Every pin, one at a time, dropping them into his palm, and when it fell down her back he gathered it up in one hand and moved it over her shoulder and put his mouth on the back of her neck.

She gasped. She had not known about the back of her neck.

He found out about it for her. Slowly. Every centimetre of it, his mouth warm and open, his stubble rough, until she had reached back blindly and grabbed his thigh to stay upright. Then his hands came round her from behind, and undid her shirt, button by button, with his chin on her shoulder, watching his own hands do it in the red light, and when the shirt was open he spread his palms flat against her stomach and held her back against him and just breathed, his face in her hair.

“I can feel your heart,” he said. “From here.”

“It’s going very fast.”

“I know.” His hands moved, very slowly, upwards. “I’m going to make it go faster.”

She laughed. It turned into something else halfway through, because his hands had reached where they were going.

✦ ✦ ✦

He laid her down on the camphor-scented quilt and took his time. More time than she knew a person could take.

There was nowhere to be. He seemed to have decided to prove it. He learned her the way he had learned to strip a rose, slowly, completely, paying attention to everything. The inside of her elbow. The back of her knee. The soft skin just inside her hip, where his breath made her whole body tighten. He found every place that made her breath catch and went back to it, again, and again, and when she reached for him he caught her wrists and held them, gently, in one hand above her head, and said, Not yet, against her stomach, and she could have killed him.

“Zhendong.”

“Not yet.”

“I’m asking.”

He lifted his head. In the candlelight his eyes were black and his mouth was soft and he was smiling, slightly, the smile almost nobody ever saw.

“I know,” he said. “Page two, line six. I want to hear you ask properly.”

So she asked properly. She told him exactly what she wanted, in a voice that shook, in words she had never in her life said out loud to anyone, and watched them land on him one by one. Watched his breathing change. Watched his hand tighten on her wrists and then let go.

“Again,” he said hoarsely.

She said it again.

And he stopped making her wait.

At some point she opened her eyes and found him watching her face in the candlelight with an expression so naked that it frightened her more than anything she had ever seen him do with a knife.

“What?” she whispered.

He shook his head. He didn’t answer. He bent and put his mouth against her throat, where her pulse was, and stayed there, and she felt him tremble, all through him, and she wrapped her arms and legs round him and held on while the rain came down and the charcoal burned and the whole slow world went bright and narrow and then broke, for both of them, one after the other, his name in her mouth and hers in his.

Outside, the rain ran down the hill in a thousand little streams. Inside, the charcoal burned down to red. Neither of them noticed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, much later, she lay on her stomach across his chest with the quilt pulled up over them both and her chin on her folded hands, and looked at him.

He was lying on his back, one arm behind his head, the other moving slowly up and down her bare back under the quilt. His eyes were half closed. His face in the last of the candlelight was soft in a way she had never seen it.

“You said something,” she said, “at dinner. Yesterday.”

His hand paused on her back.

“Mr. Wen said, ‘You chose well.’” She watched his face. “And you said, ‘She chose.’”

He didn’t say anything.

“What did you mean?”

For a long time he was quiet. The rain filled the silence. She could feel his heart under her chin, slow and heavy.

“I meant,” he said finally, “that it was you who walked into my office. Not me who walked into yours.”

It was true. It was exactly true. But she lay there on his chest and listened to the way he said it and felt, very faintly, something underneath the words: the shape of something larger, something he wasn’t saying, the way you can feel the shape of a stone under a quilt.

She almost asked.

But his hand had started moving on her back again, slow, warm, and the rain was loud, and she was so tired and so happy, happier than she could remember being since she was a girl eating breakfast under a yellowing calendar picture, and she didn’t want anything at all to come into this room.

So instead she said, “I’m happy.”

His hand stopped.

“Here,” she said. “Right now. I don’t think I’ve been happy since my mother died. Not like this. I didn’t know I wasn’t, until now.”

He looked at her in the dark. She couldn’t read his face. Then he pulled her up the length of his body until her face was beside his on the pillow, and wrapped both arms around her, and held her so tightly she could barely breathe.

She fell asleep like that, held, in a room with no phone and no road and no door anyone could knock on, with the rain coming down on a hill she owned and a flower in a walled garden that would never be sold.

He stayed awake until the candles went out.

I’m happy, she had said. Here. With you.

She had said happy.

She had not said the other word. And he lay in the dark and held her, and told himself it didn’t matter, and listened to the rain, and almost believed it.

chapters.title: Lin Jian Comes to Dinner
chapters.desc: Her father, her husband, one table, a lemon tree, and the sentence Lin Jian should never have said.
chapters.content:
Her father had not set foot in the house on the hill.

Seven months of marriage. Seven months of Elowen going home to the Walled City every Sunday for lunch, alone, and her father asking how the shop was, and never once asking how her husband was. Seven months of Lin Jian working for Zhao Zhendong the way he always had—moving containers, paying officers, sending reports—and somehow never being in the same room with him for longer than it took to hand over a folder.

“He’s coming on Saturday,” Elowen announced at breakfast.

Zhao put down his coffee very slowly.

“Who?”

“My father. For dinner. I asked him and he said no, and I asked him again and he said no, and then I told him I’d stop coming to Sunday lunch, and he said yes.”

“You blackmailed your father.”

“I negotiated with my father.” She buttered her toast. “It’s a family skill.”

Zhao looked at her for a moment. Then he looked down at his coffee.

“He hates me,” he said.

“He’s frightened of you. It looks the same in my family.” She put the toast on his plate. “Seven o’clock. Wear the blue shirt. Don’t bring a gun to the table.”

“I never bring a gun to the table.”

“You brought one to our wedding.”

“That was a registry office,” said Zhao, “and Chen Si was there. Somebody had to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday, Lin Jian arrived at six fifty-eight, in a car he drove himself, wearing the suit he wore to funerals.

He stopped at the bottom of the front steps and looked up at the house. At the concrete. The long windows. The cameras. The two dogs, who came running down the drive and then stopped exactly three metres from his feet and sat, tails sweeping the gravel, because Elowen had spent four months teaching them that people who came to the front door were usually carrying something to eat.

“They have names now,” Elowen said from the top step. “Dumpling and Noodle.”

Her father looked at the dogs. Then at her.

“Your mother named our first dog Mantou,” he said. “Steamed bun.” And he came up the steps.

She took his coat. She led him down the hall. And halfway down the hall, he stopped.

The lemon tree stood at the end of the corridor in front of the long window, where Zhao had put it on the first day. It had grown. It had put out new shoots in the summer and there were five lemons on it now, small and green, and its leaves shone in the light from the Docks.

Lin Jian stood in the hallway of the arms dealer’s house and looked at his dead wife’s lemon tree.

He didn’t say anything.

Then he walked to it and touched one leaf, very lightly, with the tip of one finger.

“She kept it twenty years,” he said, without turning round. “On the balcony. It never had more than three lemons. Never.”

“It likes the window,” said Zhao.

Lin Jian turned.

Zhao was standing in the kitchen doorway in the blue shirt, his hands at his sides, the way he had stood in front of the eighty-one-year-old woman in the shop. He looked at his father-in-law. His father-in-law looked at him.

“He waters it,” Elowen said. “On Thursdays. I forgot one week and it nearly died. Now he has an alarm on his phone.”

Lin Jian looked at the man who had made his hands shake for six years.

“An alarm,” he repeated.

“Once a week,” said Zhao. “And it doesn’t like the cold.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was bad.

Not a disaster. Nobody shouted. Nobody threw anything. It was bad the way a long drive in silence is bad: every minute felt like ten.

Elowen had cooked all day. Her mother’s fish with ginger. Red-braised pork, her father’s favourite. Green beans. Lotus root soup from the day before. She talked the whole time, about the shop, about Xiao Pan’s hands getting stronger, about Raiden’s new job drawing buildings for a firm in the south. Her father answered in single words. Zhao didn’t answer at all.

She gave her father the fish belly. He gave it back to her.

She gave it to Zhao. He looked at it for a moment and gave it to her father.

Her father looked at the piece of fish in his bowl, back again for the second time, and something in his face moved.

“Her mother did that,” he said to Zhao, abruptly. The first full sentence he had said at the table. “Every night. Gave me the belly. Twenty years.”

“She told me,” said Zhao.

“Did she tell you I gave it back? Every night?”

“Yes.”

Lin Jian picked up the fish belly with his chopsticks. He held it for a moment. Then he put it in his daughter’s bowl.

“Eat,” he said to her, roughly. “You’re too thin. He doesn’t feed you.”

“He feeds me,” said Elowen. “He makes breakfast at four in the morning.”

Her father looked at Zhao again. For a long time.

“Four in the morning,” he said.

“The market,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, she went to make tea and left them alone.

She did it on purpose. She knew it was a risk. But she also knew her father, and she knew that he would never say what he needed to say with her in the room, and she knew that whatever it was, it had been sitting in him for seven months like a stone.

She made the tea slowly. She stood in the kitchen with the kettle and listened.

At first there was nothing. Then her father’s voice, low.

“She did it for me.”

The kettle began to murmur. Elowen stood very still.

“You know that,” Lin Jian went on. His voice was quiet and very hard, the voice he used with officers who had changed the price. “Whatever she tells you. Whatever this is—the dogs, the tree, the four in the morning. She married you because she was afraid of what you would do to me. She put herself between us. That’s all. That’s my daughter. She’s been doing it since she was seven.”

Silence from the dining room.

“So I want you to remember it,” said her father. “Every day. When you look at her. Remember that she didn’t choose you. She chose me. You were only the price she paid.”

The kettle boiled. It screamed. Elowen didn’t move to take it off.

In the dining room, there was a long, terrible silence.

Then Zhao said, very evenly, “I know.”

That was all. I know. No anger. No argument. Two words, flat and quiet, the way he said yes when the clerk at the registry office asked if he married of his own free will.

Elowen took the kettle off the heat with a hand that didn’t feel like hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

She carried the tea in. Neither of them looked at her. She poured three cups and sat down and talked about the weather, and her father drank his tea in four swallows and said he had to go, and she walked him to the door.

On the front steps, in the dark, with the dogs sniffing hopefully at his shoes, he turned and looked at her.

“Elowen,” he said. “Are you all right? Truly?”

She looked at her father. At his funeral suit, and his grey hair, and his hands, which were not shaking tonight, for the first time in years.

“You shouldn’t have said that to him,” she said.

He went very still.

“I heard you,” said Elowen. “In the kitchen. Every word.”

“It’s the truth.”

“It was the truth.” Her voice was shaking. She made it stop. “Seven months ago, it was the truth. You don’t know what it is now. You haven’t asked. You come to my house for the first time, and you look at my mother’s lemon tree, and you see that he set an alarm on his phone to water it, and you still walk into that room and tell him—”

She stopped, because she was going to cry, and she would not cry on the front steps in front of her father.

Lin Jian looked at her in the light from the door.

“And what is it now?” he asked quietly.

She opened her mouth.

And found that she couldn’t say it. Not here, on the steps, to her father. Not before she had said it to the man inside.

Her father saw her face. Something changed in his. He looked, suddenly, very old and very sorry.

“Ah,” said Lin Jian softly. “Ah, Elowen.”

He touched her cheek, the way he had when she was small. Then he went down the steps to his car, and the dogs followed him to the gate, and he drove away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao was in the basement.

She found him at the workbench under the hanging lamp, with a rifle in pieces on the cloth in front of him. He wasn’t cleaning it. His hands were resting on either side of the pieces, flat on the bench, and he was looking at them.

She came down the stairs. He didn’t turn round.

“He was wrong,” Elowen said.

“He was right.” Zhao didn’t look up. “You did choose him. You told me so. In my office. I don’t run. I cut things cleanly. You were very clear.”

“That was seven months ago.”

“Yes.”

“Things change.”

He picked up one piece of the rifle. Put it down again.

“I know,” he said.

It was the same voice. The same I know he had said to her father. Flat. Final. As if he were agreeing to a price he had already decided to pay.

She came and stood beside him at the bench. She wanted to say it. She could feel it in her throat, the word she hadn’t been able to say on the front steps, enormous and frightening. It’s not true anymore. I didn’t choose you then. I choose you now. I—

He looked up at her.

And she saw his face in the light of the hanging lamp, and it was not angry. It was not even hurt, exactly. It was the face of a man who had heard something he had always known, said out loud for the first time by someone else, and was now carefully putting it away somewhere safe, the way he put away guns, so it would never go off by accident.

If she said it now, he wouldn’t believe her. She could see that. He would think she was saying it because of her father. Because she felt sorry for him. Because she was a woman who put herself between people and the things that would hurt them, and had been since she was seven.

He would think it was another contract.

So she didn’t say it.

She put her arms round him from behind, the way she had at the workbench in the shop on the morning of the roses, and pressed her face between his shoulder blades.

“Come to bed,” she said.

After a moment, his hand came up and covered both of hers.

He came to bed. He held her all night. He didn’t sleep; she could tell from his breathing. Neither did she.

And neither of them said anything about the sentence her father had left in the dining room, sitting on the table between the empty teacups like a loaded gun.

chapters.title: The Shop Gets a New Floor
chapters.desc: Raiden “renovates.” The panic room is under the tulips. And Zhao says it out loud, to the wrong Lin.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve always wanted to put a bunker under a bucket of tulips. Is that strange? Don’t answer that.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
Raiden arrived at the shop on a Monday in October with three builders, a van full of tools, a roll of drawings under his arm, and an expression of sunny, total innocence that Elowen had learned to fear when he was nine.

“Jie!” he said, and kissed her on the cheek. “You look wonderful. Have you lost weight? Don’t answer that, it’s rude. I’m here to fix your floor.”

“There’s nothing wrong with my floor.”

“There is everything wrong with your floor.” He unrolled a drawing across her workbench, on top of a half-finished wedding bouquet. “It’s concrete laid directly on fill from 1964. No damp-proofing. It’s cold, it’s cracked, and it’s going to give you arthritis by forty.” He tapped the drawing. “Also, it doesn’t have a reinforced steel chamber underneath it with its own air supply and a hatch hidden under the second row of buckets.”

Elowen looked at the drawing. Then at her brother.

“Who asked you to do this?”

Raiden widened his eyes. “Nobody! It was my idea. Entirely. A gift. From a loving brother to his beloved sister.” He paused. “Who is married to a man who gets shot at.”

“Raiden.”

“And who called me last Thursday at two in the morning and said, and I’m quoting, ‘How long would it take you to build a room nobody can get into under a flower shop,’ and when I said ‘Who is this,’ said, ‘Your brother-in-law,’ and when I said ‘It’s two in the morning,’ said, ‘Yes,’ and hung up.”

Elowen closed her eyes.

“He didn’t tell me.”

“Of course he didn’t tell you. You’d have said no.” Raiden rolled up the drawing again. “He’s paying triple. I’ve already spent it. Move your roses.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop was closed for six days.

Elowen ran her orders out of the back of Bao’s car and a borrowed cooler in the guardhouse at the house on the hill. She went past the shop twice a day anyway, because she couldn’t help it, and stood on the pavement watching her brother in a hard hat and a paint-spattered hoodie directing three builders with the cheerful, slightly vague air of a rich young man who had no idea what he was doing.

He knew exactly what he was doing. She had known that since he was fourteen and turned up at the gate of the house in the Walled City, alone, filthy, eight hundred kilometres from the safe house their father had hidden him in, and said, I followed the railway lines. They all go somewhere.

But the builders didn’t know that. To them, he was the boss’s silly brother-in-law who sang along to the radio and forgot their names. They didn’t notice that he checked every weld himself after they went home. They didn’t notice him standing in the empty shop at midnight with a torch and a tape measure and a face like stone, walking the floor, counting steps from the door to the hatch, from the hatch to the cooler, from the cooler to the back exit, again and again, until he could have done it blind.

Zhao noticed.

On the fourth night, she came down to the shop at eleven with a flask of soup for her brother and found both of them there. Raiden was sitting on an upturned bucket with a drawing on his knees. Zhao was standing over the open hatch in the floor, looking down into the dark.

Neither of them heard her at the door. She stopped.

“Two metres by three,” Raiden was saying, without his silly voice. His real voice was lower, flatter, a lot like their father’s. “Steel plate under the concrete. The hatch looks like a drain cover. It’ll be under the second row of buckets: tulips, she always keeps tulips there, I checked her order books going back three years. Air comes in through a pipe that runs up inside the wall and out above the cooler’s vent, where nobody looks. Water for three days. A phone line that goes through the building next door, not this one.” He glanced up. “Eliana is doing the alarm. She says she can make it so the shop calls you before anyone outside knows something’s wrong.”

Zhao nodded slowly, still looking into the hole.

“You’ve built these before,” he said.

“Four for Baba. One for Chen Si.” Raiden shrugged. “And one when I was nine. At the safe house. Out of a chest freezer and a lot of earth.” He looked back down at his drawing. “There were men on the road one night. I didn’t want to be in the house when they came.”

Zhao turned and looked at him.

Raiden didn’t look up. He drew a careful line on the paper.

“Did they come?” Zhao asked.

“No.” Raiden smiled, very faintly, at the drawing. “But I was in the freezer for eleven hours anyway. Just in case.” The pencil moved. “I was very small. It was very dark. I counted. I counted to forty thousand and something. I lost track.”

Zhao didn’t say anything.

Then he crouched down on the other side of the hatch, so that he and Raiden were level, the open hole in the floor between them.

“Make it bigger,” he said. “Not two by three. Make it so she can lie down. Make it so there’s a light. A good one. Not a torch. A light that stays on.”

Raiden looked up.

“That’ll cost more,” he said.

“I know.”

For a long moment, the two men looked at each other across the hole in the floor of Elowen’s shop. Her brother, who had counted to forty thousand in a chest freezer when he was nine. Her husband, who had held a man’s hands over a fire.

“Okay,” said Raiden softly. “A light that stays on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen should have gone in then. She knew she should. She stood in the doorway with the flask of soup going cold in her hands and didn’t move, because her brother had just said a thing she had never heard him say in eight years, not to her, not to anyone, and she didn’t want to make him stop.

Raiden put down his pencil.

“Can I ask you something?” he said.

Zhao waited.

“Do you love her?”

It was said very simply. No silly voice. No widened eyes. Just a brother, sitting on a bucket in the middle of the night, asking.

Elowen stopped breathing.

Zhao looked down into the hole for a moment. Then back at Raiden.

“Yes,” he said.

She had to put her hand flat on the doorframe.

“Have you told her?” asked Raiden.

“No.”

“Why not?”

Zhao stood up. He walked to the counter, where she had left a bucket of eucalyptus that hadn’t gone to the guardhouse, and stood looking at it with his back to the room.

“Because she married me to protect your father,” he said. “And if I say it, she’ll say it back. Because she’s kind. Because that’s what she does. She puts herself between people and the thing that will hurt them.” He touched one eucalyptus leaf with a fingertip. “I don’t want her to say it because she’s kind. I don’t want her to say it because she thinks she owes me.”

Raiden was quiet.

“So you’re just going to never tell her,” he said. “Ever. For the rest of your life.”

“I’m going to wait,” said Zhao, “until I know she would say it even if I didn’t.”

“And how will you know that?”

Zhao didn’t answer.

Raiden looked at his brother-in-law’s back for a long time. Then he picked up his pencil again, and his voice, when he spoke, was back to its normal cheerful brightness, as if nothing had happened.

“You know,” he said, drawing a line, “for a very frightening man, you’re extremely stupid.”

Zhao turned round.

“My sister,” Raiden went on serenely, “has looked after five people since she was seven years old. She has never, once, done a single thing in her whole life just for herself. Not the shop—the shop was so she could pay for Elara’s school fees. Not her friends—she didn’t have time for friends. Not the boy at school with the physics—she wanted him because he was quiet and she was tired.” He shaded something. “And seven months ago she walked into your office and married you, and I thought, okay, that’s the same. That’s another thing she’s doing for someone else.”

“It is,” said Zhao.

“It was.” Raiden looked up. “Then I came to Sunday lunch last month, and she was late, because she’d been on a mountain looking at a flower. Her own flower. On her own mountain. And she sat at Baba’s table and told us about it for an hour, and she was happy, Zhendong. Not looking-after-us happy. Happy for herself. I haven’t seen that since our mother died.” He went back to his drawing. “I don’t know what that means. I’m only a draftsman. But if I were a frightening, extremely stupid arms dealer, I might think about it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen backed out of the doorway as quietly as she had ever done anything in her life.

She walked to the end of the street and stood under the streetlight with the flask of soup and her heart going so hard she could feel it in her teeth.

Yes.

He had said yes. To her brother. In the middle of the night, over a hole in her floor. Not to her.

I’m going to wait until I know she would say it even if I didn’t.

She stood there. Then she walked back to the shop, loudly this time, scuffing her shoes on the pavement, and pushed open the door with her shoulder and said, “I brought soup. It’s cold now. That’s your fault, Raiden, you should have finished by ten.”

Her brother looked up from his bucket with wide, innocent eyes, and she knew, from the way he didn’t look at the doorway, that he had seen her there the whole time.

Zhao took the flask from her hands.

“You walked here,” he said. “Alone. At eleven at night.”

“Bao was across the road.”

He looked at her. She looked back. She thought: I heard you. I heard every word. She thought: If I say it now, you’ll think it’s because I heard.

She took the flask back and poured him a cup of cold soup and put it in his hands.

“Drink it,” she said.

He drank it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop opened again on Sunday.

The new floor was warm under her feet, pale grey, smooth as a pebble. The cooler had a new seal. There was a new drain cover in the floor under the second row of buckets, where the tulips always were, and you would never, ever have known it was anything else.

On Monday morning, before anyone else arrived, she lifted the tulips aside and opened it.

Underneath, a ladder went down into a room big enough to lie down in. There were blankets, and water, and a phone on the wall. And when she reached the bottom rung, a light came on by itself: warm and steady and bright, the colour of late afternoon, like a lamp in a window.

She stood in the room under her shop for a long time, in that light.

On the wall beside the phone, someone had taped a small piece of paper. On it, in square, blunt handwriting she would have known anywhere, were two lines.

This light stays on.

I’ll come.

chapters.title: A Reunion Invitation With One Name on It
chapters.desc: The school turns sixty and every year is invited. Miles Wei is giving a speech. Zhao reads three of his papers and understands none of them.
chapters.content:
The invitation came on thick white card with the school crest in gold.

Sixty Years On. Former students of every year, most especially Lin Elowen and Aurelia Song, would be delighted by your company. That wasn’t what it actually said, but that was how Aurelia read it out over the phone, at nine in the morning, while Elowen was trying to wire a funeral wreath.

“The fourteenth of December,” Aurelia said. “The Harbour Hotel. Black tie. And darling, read the second page.”

“I haven’t opened it.”

“Open it.”

Elowen put down the wire. The envelope was on the counter where Xiao Pan had left it with the rest of the post. She slit it with her florist’s knife and pulled out the card and the folded sheet tucked behind it.

Programme for the evening.

7:00 — Reception.

8:00 — Dinner.

9:30 — Address by a distinguished former student: Dr. Miles Wei, Lecturer in Physics, City University. “Light, and Other Things That Bend.”

She stood at the counter and read it twice.

On the other end of the phone, Aurelia was laughing so hard she had to stop and breathe.

“He’s going to bend light at us,” she said. “For half an hour. Seven years later. In a hotel ballroom. Elowen, I’ve already bought the dress. It’s red. I’m going to sit in the front row and not blink.”

“I’m not going.”

“Of course you’re going.”

“I have a wedding on the fifteenth. Two hundred arrangements.”

“You’ve had a wedding every weekend for five years and you went to my launch on a Saturday.” Aurelia’s voice changed, went lower and sharper. “Are you afraid?”

“Of Miles?”

“Of your husband.” A pause. “Seeing Miles.”

Elowen looked down at the card in her hand. Dr. Miles Wei.

She thought about her father’s voice in the dining room. She didn’t choose you. You were only the price she paid. She thought about Zhao in the basement, saying I know in that flat, finished voice.

“I’ll call you back,” she said, and hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t mention it at dinner. She meant to. She opened her mouth three times and closed it again, and talked about the wedding on the fifteenth instead.

She left the invitation on the kitchen counter, under the bowl of mandarins, the next morning, without saying anything, because she was a coward, and because she thought that if he saw it there by himself, he could decide what to feel about it without her watching.

When she came home that evening, it had moved.

It was sitting on the counter beside the mandarins, squared exactly to the edge. The second page was on top.

Zhao was at the stove. He was making noodles. He had learned how in the last month: badly at first, then less badly, and now he made them most nights she worked late, very slowly and seriously, with the recipe she had written out for him propped against the salt.

“You saw it,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I was going to tell you.”

“I know.” He stirred the noodles. “You put it under the mandarins.”

She sat down on the stool at the counter.

“I don’t have to go,” she said.

He stirred the noodles for a long moment. Then he turned off the heat and divided them between two bowls and put one in front of her, and sat down on the other stool, and looked at her.

“Do you want to?” he asked.

She thought about it honestly. He deserved that.

“I want to see Aurelia lose her mind in a red dress,” she said. “I want to see the teachers. Some of them were kind to me when my mother died. And—” She stopped. “I want to see if he’s still the same. Miles. I don’t know why. Not because of anything. Just because he was the only person at that school who didn’t look at me and see my father.”

Zhao looked at his noodles.

“Then go,” he said.

“Will you come?”

His chopsticks stopped.

“To your school reunion,” he said.

“Partners are invited. It says so.” She turned the card over and pointed. Plus one. “Aurelia’s bringing Chen Si. I don’t want to walk in on my own. Please.”

He looked at the card. At plus one, in gold.

“I don’t dance,” he said.

“Neither does anyone from my year. We were very serious students.”

“I don’t know how to talk to teachers.”

“You talked to an eighty-one-year-old woman about delphiniums.”

He looked at her. And she saw it again, briefly, that thing in his face she couldn’t name, the shape of a stone under a quilt.

“All right,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, she woke at two and the bed beside her was empty.

She didn’t hear the basement door. She lay listening, waiting for the metal sound of the lock, and it didn’t come. Instead there was a faint glow under the door from the corridor.

She got up.

He was in the small room at the top of the stairs, the one he had slept in for the first month of their marriage. He was sitting on the narrow bed with his laptop on his knees, and the screen was full of mathematics.

Not numbers. Mathematics. Symbols she half-remembered from school, integrals and Greek letters and long equations that ran across the whole width of the page.

He hadn’t heard her. He was frowning at the screen with the expression he wore when he took apart a gun he’d never seen before.

She looked at the title at the top of the page.

Gravitational lensing of light by low-mass compact objects: a perturbative approach. M. Wei, City University.

She stood in the doorway and felt something happen in her chest that was halfway between laughing and crying.

“Zhendong,” she said.

He shut the laptop so fast it made a noise like a gunshot.

They looked at each other.

“I couldn’t sleep,” he said.

“You’re reading Miles Wei’s research papers.”

“One.”

She looked at the stack of printouts on the bed beside him. There were three. One of them had notes in the margin in his square, blunt handwriting. She could read one of the notes upside down. It said: ?

“Three,” she said.

He looked at the stack. He didn’t deny it.

She came in and sat down on the narrow bed beside him. It creaked. She picked up the top paper and looked at his note in the margin. Next to an equation that went on for six lines, he had written: What is this. And under it, a few lines down: Light bends because of mass. Heavy things pull it. And under that, in smaller letters, as if written later: She said he talked about how light bends.

Elowen put the paper down.

“Did you understand any of it?” she asked quietly.

“No.” He looked at the closed laptop. “The first paragraph. Something very heavy, like a star, can make light from behind it go around it, instead of straight. So you see it in the wrong place. That’s all I understood.” He paused. “I read it eleven times.”

“Why?”

He didn’t answer.

“I wanted to know what you liked,” he said finally. “About him. What it was. You said he was quiet. You said he talked about light. I thought—if I knew what he knew, I’d understand what you—” He stopped. “I don’t know. It was stupid.”

“It was,” said Elowen.

He looked at her.

“It was very stupid,” she said again, and she was smiling now, and her eyes were wet. “You sat up at two in the morning reading eleven times about light going round a star, because you thought that’s what I wanted.”

“Isn’t it?”

She took the laptop off his knees and put it on the floor. She took the papers and put them on top of it. Then she took his face in both hands.

“I liked Miles because he was quiet,” she said. “Because I was seventeen and I had a brother and three sisters and a father who was frightened all the time and a house full of people who wanted things from me. And he was the only person who didn’t want anything. He wanted physics. He didn’t even want me.” She held his face. “That was what I liked. That he didn’t want anything. It was restful.”

Zhao looked at her.

“I want everything,” he said, very low.

“I know.”

“I’m not restful.”

“No,” said Elowen. “You’re not.” She leaned in until her forehead touched his. “You sit outside my door. You buy mountains. You learned to strip roses and bled on two hundred of them. You read physics papers in the middle of the night because you’re jealous of a man I haven’t spoken to in seven years.” Her voice cracked. “Nobody has ever wanted me that much. Nobody has ever wanted anything that much. It’s not restful at all. It’s terrifying.”

“Then why are you smiling?”

She didn’t answer. She kissed him instead.

He made a low sound against her mouth and pulled her into his lap, and the narrow bed groaned, and the printouts slid off the laptop and scattered across the floor. Gravitational lensing. Perturbative approach. Neither of them looked at them.

She pushed him down onto the narrow bed in the smallest room in the house, the room where he had slept for a month to be between her and the stairs, and kissed him until he stopped thinking about light.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, when he had gone down to make coffee, she picked up the printouts from the floor and put them in order.

She read his notes in the margins. All of them. What is this. Mass bends light. She said he talked about light. And on the last page, at the very bottom, under a final equation he had clearly not understood either, a line that he must have written at the end, just before she came in:

He made her feel calm. I make her feel afraid. I should let her go to the reunion alone.

Elowen sat on the narrow bed and looked at that line for a long time.

Then she took a pen from the bedside table and wrote underneath it, in her small, neat, wedding-card handwriting:

No. You come with me. Plus one.

And for the record, I said terrifying. That isn’t the same as afraid.

She left it on his pillow in their room.

He didn’t mention it. But that night the page was gone from his pillow, and the next morning, when he leaned over the bed to kiss her goodbye before a meeting, she saw the corner of it, folded very small, in the inside pocket of his jacket, where he thought she wouldn’t see.

chapters.title: Zhao Zhendong Is Absolutely Fine About the Physics Lecturer
chapters.desc: He is not fine. He goes to a public lecture in disguise. Chen Si finds him there.
chapters.epigraph: “I am completely fine.” — Zhao Zhendong, to nobody, eleven times
chapters.content:
Two weeks before the reunion, the City University held a public lecture.

It was advertised on a poster on the noticeboard outside the old library, and on the university website, and in the culture section of the evening newspaper, which Zhao did not read, except that one Tuesday he did.

FREE PUBLIC LECTURE. “Why the Universe Lies to Us About Where Things Are.” Dr. Miles Wei. Thursday, 7 p.m., Lecture Theatre B. All welcome.

He read it three times. Then he folded the newspaper very small and put it in the bin in the garage, under an empty oil can, where his wife would never find it.

On Thursday, he told her he had a meeting in the north of the city.

It wasn’t a lie. He had made sure of that. He had called a broker in the north of the city that afternoon and arranged to meet him at ten for fifteen minutes about nothing. That way, when he told her I have a meeting, it was true.

He told himself that this was keeping the contract.

He knew perfectly well it wasn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lecture Theatre B was enormous and full.

He hadn’t expected that. He had expected a small room with twenty students. Instead there were three hundred seats rising in steep rows, almost every one taken: students with laptops, old men with notebooks, a group of schoolgirls in uniform, a woman with a baby asleep on her chest. He came in late, at five past seven, in a grey hoodie and a baseball cap pulled low, and stood at the very back, against the wall, beside the door.

He had chosen the hoodie carefully. He did not own a hoodie. He had borrowed it from Xiao Pan, who had handed it over without a word and then, as Zhao was leaving the shop, said very quietly, Mr. Zhao, it says ‘FLOWER POWER’ on the back, and Zhao had said I know, and the boy had nodded and gone back to his bouquet with the face of someone who had decided not to ask any more questions for the rest of his life.

On the stage, a man stood behind a lectern in front of a huge screen showing a picture of stars.

He was thin. Thinner than Zhao had imagined. He wore glasses with dark frames and a grey jumper with a hole in one elbow, and his hair stood up at the back as if he had been running his hands through it. He was holding a clicker for the slides and seemed to have forgotten what it was for.

“So,” said Miles Wei, into the microphone. “I want to start with a question. Can you trust your own eyes?”

Three hundred people waited.

“The answer,” said Miles, “is no. Not if you’re looking at the sky.”

He clicked the clicker. The picture changed to a bright yellow blob in the middle of the screen, with four smaller blobs around it in a cross.

“This,” he said, “is one quasar. One. Ten billion light-years away. You can see four of it. Why?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao had expected to hate him.

He had come prepared. He had read the three papers eleven times each and understood one paragraph. He had stood in the shower that morning and thought about what kind of man would make his wife smile like that, seven years later, without meaning to, and he had decided it must be the kind of man who made you feel small. Clever, and cold, and careless with people. A man who had looked at two seventeen-year-old girls fighting over him and chosen physics, because physics didn’t need anything from him.

He stood at the back of Lecture Theatre B and listened, and slowly, against his will, understood.

Miles Wei did not make you feel small. That was the worst part. He made you feel like the universe was a secret he was telling you personally. He spoke quickly and then stopped and apologised and went back and said it again more slowly. He drew on the screen with his finger and went pink in the face about a picture of a galaxy bent into a ring of light. When a schoolgirl in the third row put her hand up and asked a question, a good question, he stopped the whole lecture for five minutes and answered her as if she were the most important person in the room, and when she understood, he looked so delighted that the whole theatre laughed.

“Something very heavy,” Miles said, drawing a circle, “bends the space around it. And light has no choice. It has to follow the shape of the space. So light from something far behind comes round it, instead of straight to you. And you see the thing in the wrong place. Or you see it four times. Or you see it as a ring.” He stepped back from the screen. “The heavy thing in the middle is invisible. You can’t see it at all. You only know it’s there because of how everything around it bends.”

Zhao stood very still against the back wall.

He thought about a dining room, and a fish belly passed back and forth three times between three people.

He thought about a lemon tree with five lemons on it, where there had only ever been three.

He thought about a woman on a mountain in the rain, saying I’m happy, I didn’t know I wasn’t, until now.

You only know it’s there because of how everything around it bends.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re wearing a hoodie that says FLOWER POWER,” said a quiet voice at his shoulder.

Zhao didn’t turn round.

“How long have you been there,” he said.

“Since the quasar.” Chen Si leaned against the wall beside him, in a camel coat, with his hands in his pockets, looking at the stage with polite interest. “Bao called me. He was worried. He said you’d borrowed a teenager’s clothes and told your wife you had a meeting and driven yourself to a university. He thought you might be having some kind of breakdown.”

“I’m fine.”

“Of course you are.”

On the stage, Miles had dropped his clicker. He crawled under the lectern to find it, still talking into the microphone, and the theatre laughed again.

“He’s not what I expected,” Zhao said, after a while.

“No,” Chen Si agreed. “He’s nice. That’s very annoying, isn’t it.”

Zhao didn’t answer.

“Aurelia told me about him,” Chen Si said. “When we were first married. She said he was the only thing she ever wanted and didn’t get. She said it like she was talking about a necklace. She said she didn’t love him. She said she loved that she couldn’t have him.” He glanced sideways. “Is that what you’re afraid of? That Elowen feels the same?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

Zhao watched the man on the stage climb out from under the lectern with the clicker in his hand and his glasses crooked, beaming.

“That she’d have been happy,” he said. “With someone like that. Quiet. Kind. A library. Physics. Nobody shooting at her. A man she didn’t have to make a contract with.” He stopped. “That I took that from her.”

Chen Si was quiet.

“Zhendong,” he said at last. “I have known you for ten years. In ten years, I have seen you afraid twice. Once in Block C, when you thought I was dead. Once now.” He took his hands out of his pockets. “And both times, you were wrong.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I know that a woman who wanted a quiet life with a physics lecturer would not have walked into the Iron Docks with three pages of terms.” Chen Si straightened his coat. “Come on. I’ll buy you dinner. You can’t meet your broker in that hoodie, you look like a delinquent.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home at midnight.
