She was waiting in the kitchen. On one of the tall stools, with a cup of tea, and on the counter in front of her, laid out flat, was a baseball cap and a grey hoodie with FLOWER POWER across the back in yellow letters.

He stopped in the doorway.

“Xiao Pan,” Elowen said, “cannot lie. It’s his worst quality. I asked him where his hoodie was and he went red and said a man had borrowed it for an important mission, and then he said, and I quote, ‘Please don’t make me say more, Miss Lin, I have to live.’” She turned her teacup. “And then Aurelia called. Because Chen Si told her. Because Chen Si tells her everything. She laughed for ten minutes. She said you stood at the back of Miles Wei’s lecture for an hour and a half looking like someone had shot your dog.”

He didn’t say anything.

“So,” said Elowen. “How was your meeting in the north of the city?”

“Fifteen minutes,” said Zhao. “About nothing.”

“You made a meeting so you wouldn’t be lying.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him. He braced himself. For anger. For the cold, quiet voice she used on the man at the market who had short-counted her roses. For you promised.

Instead, she put her face in her hands and started to laugh.

It wasn’t a small laugh. It came up from somewhere very deep and shook her whole body, and she put her head down on the counter next to the FLOWER POWER hoodie and laughed until she was gasping, until there were tears running down her face, and he stood in the doorway of his own kitchen and had absolutely no idea what to do.

“You—” she managed. “You borrowed a hoodie—”

“It was a disguise.”

“It says FLOWER POWER.”

“I didn’t know until I was wearing it.”

She laughed harder.

He came across the kitchen slowly and stood beside her stool. After a while, carefully, he put his hand on her back. She was still shaking with laughter under his palm.

“Was he good?” she asked into the counter, when she could speak. “The lecture?”

He thought about lying. He didn’t.

“Yes,” he said. “He was very good. He made a schoolgirl understand quasars. He dropped the clicker twice.” He paused. “He’s kind. He’s the kind of man who stops everything to answer a question. You were right about him.”

She lifted her head and looked at him. Her face was wet and pink from laughing.

“And?”

“And he said that sometimes you can’t see the heaviest thing in the middle,” Zhao said slowly. “You only know it’s there because of how everything around it bends.”

She went very quiet.

He didn’t know why he’d said it. He hadn’t planned to. He stood there with his hand on her back and wished he could take it back, because he didn’t know what it meant, not really, only that he had stood at the back of that lecture theatre and thought about a lemon tree with five lemons on it and had not been able to breathe properly for the rest of the hour.

Elowen reached up and took his hand off her back and held it.

“Zhendong,” she said. “Come to the reunion. Stand next to me. Meet him. I want you to meet him.”

“Why?”

She looked at him with an expression he couldn’t read.

“Because I want to see,” she said, “how everything around you bends.”

He didn’t understand. Not then. But she pulled him down by his hand and kissed him, slowly, in the kitchen at midnight, with a teenager’s hoodie on the counter between them, and he decided that understanding could wait.

chapters.title: The Reunion, Table Nine
chapters.desc: Miles, Aurelia, Elowen, a red dress, a balcony, and a husband standing by the wall like a loaded gun.
chapters.content:
The ballroom at the Harbour Hotel had been decorated by someone who thought sixty years meant as much gold as possible.

Gold chairs. Gold tablecloths. A gold balloon arch over the door with the school crest on it, slightly deflated on one side. Two hundred former students in evening dress stood under the chandeliers holding glasses of champagne and pretending not to check who had got fat.

Elowen stopped in the doorway with her hand on her husband’s arm.

She felt it go through the room. Not all at once. In a ripple, out from the door, like a stone dropped in water. Heads turning. Conversations pausing. People who had not thought about Lin Elowen in seven years looking at her, in her dark green dress with her hair up and her mother’s pearl earrings, and then looking at the man beside her.

She had expected whispers. The Ice Queen. Didn’t she marry—? Isn’t that—?

She had not expected them to step back.

But they did. A little. Without knowing they were doing it. The crowd near the door eased away from Zhao the way the couples on the registry office steps had curved around him, the way the market went quiet when he walked in. He wasn’t doing anything. He was standing in a black suit with his tie very slightly crooked and his hands at his sides, looking at the gold balloon arch with an expression of mild, polite confusion.

“Why is everything gold?” he asked her quietly.

“Aurelia was on the committee.”

“Ah,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia arrived at seven fifteen in a red dress the head teacher pretended not to see.

She came down the three steps into the ballroom on Chen Si’s arm as if they were the steps of a palace, and the whole room turned to look, and she let them, and then she saw Elowen across the room and her face lit up with pure, wicked joy.

She crossed the ballroom in a straight line. People got out of her way too, but differently.

“Darling,” she said, and kissed the air beside Elowen’s cheek. “You came. And you brought him.” She turned to Zhao and looked him up and down. “Your tie is crooked.”

“I know,” said Zhao.

Aurelia reached up and fixed it in three sharp movements, the way she might have adjusted a necklace on a mannequin, and stepped back to look.

“Better,” she said. “Now you look like you could have murdered someone in a nicer suit.” She turned back to Elowen. “Table nine. I arranged the seating. You’re next to me.”

“Of course I am.”

“And opposite him.” Aurelia’s eyes sparkled. “He said yes to dinner. I asked him personally. He sounded terrified.”

“Aurelia.”

“What? I’m a good committee member. I put old friends together.” She hooked her arm through Elowen’s and turned her toward the tables. “Chen Si, look after your brother. He looks like he wants to check the exits.”

“He’s already checked the exits,” said Chen Si mildly. “Twice. There are four, and one of them is a kitchen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles Wei arrived late, in a suit that didn’t fit him, holding a folder of notes against his chest like a shield.

He came in through the side door, the kitchen one, as if he had got lost on the way, and stood blinking at the gold balloons. He was exactly as she remembered and completely different. Taller. Thinner. Glasses with dark frames instead of wire ones. The same way of standing, slightly hunched, as if apologising to the ceiling for being so tall.

Then he saw her.

She watched him recognise her. She watched it go across his face: surprise, and then something warmer, and then, as his eyes moved to Aurelia beside her, a look of such pure, schoolboy alarm that Elowen laughed out loud before she could stop herself.

“Oh no,” said Miles Wei, from across the ballroom. She saw his mouth make the words. “Both of them.”

He came over anyway. He was brave like that. He always had been.

“Elowen,” he said. “Aurelia.” He looked from one to the other. “You’re—you’re standing next to each other. Voluntarily. Without any—”

“Bloodshed?” said Aurelia sweetly.

“I was going to say ‘shouting.’”

“We’re grown women now, Miles. We save the shouting for galas.” Aurelia tilted her head. “You look exactly the same. It’s very upsetting.”

“You look—” Miles hesitated. “Very red.”

Aurelia laughed, delighted.

And then Miles looked past them both, at the man standing a little way back, by the pillar, with his hands at his sides and his tie freshly fixed.

He looked. Elowen watched his face change. Miles Wei had always been oblivious to most things. He didn’t notice when girls liked him, or when teachers were angry, or when he had chalk on his face. But he noticed patterns. He noticed when the numbers didn’t add up.

And he looked at Zhao, standing very still by the pillar, watching Elowen; and at the way the other guests had left an empty circle around him without knowing they’d done it; and something in his expression went careful.

“Hello,” Miles said to Zhao. “I’m Miles.”

“I know,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was strange.

Aurelia talked. Chen Si listened to Aurelia. Miles answered questions about his work with the slightly desperate enthusiasm of a man who would much rather be talking about galaxies than people. Elowen ate very little.

And Zhao said nothing at all.

He sat beside her and ate his food and didn’t speak. When Miles asked him, politely, what he did, he said, “Import and export,” and Chen Si coughed into his napkin. When Aurelia told the story of the time Elowen had corrected the head teacher’s maths in front of the whole school, he looked at Elowen with an expression so unguarded that Miles, across the table, put down his fork.

At nine-thirty, Miles stood up, picked up his folder, and went to give his speech.

He was good. He was nervous for the first minute and then he forgot to be, and talked about light and how it bends, and the whole ballroom of former students who had once slept through physics went quiet and listened. Elowen watched him. She thought about a library. Quiet. The smell of old books. A boy explaining why the sky was blue.

She felt nothing.

Not nothing. She felt a kind of soft fondness, the way you feel about a house you lived in as a child: grateful, a little sad, and very glad you didn’t live there anymore.

She turned her head.

Zhao was not watching Miles. He was watching her. He had been, she realised, the whole time.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, she went out on the balcony for air.

The ballroom was too hot and too gold and too full of people asking her what her husband did. The balcony was cold, and dark, and looked out over the harbour, where the lights of the ships moved slowly on the black water.

She heard the door open behind her.

“Hello again,” said Miles.

He came and stood beside her at the rail. He had taken off his tie. He was holding two glasses of water and gave her one.

“You were good,” she said. “The speech.”

“I dropped my notes.”

“Nobody noticed.”

“Aurelia noticed. She gave me a thumbs-up.” He drank his water. “I think she was being sarcastic.”

“She was being Aurelia. It’s the same thing.”

They stood in silence for a while. It was a comfortable silence. It had always been comfortable, with Miles. That had been the whole point.

“Can I ask you something?” he said.

“Yes.”

He looked at the water.

“At school,” he said, “you used to talk about running away. Do you remember? In the library. You said one day you would take a train to the end of the line and get off and nobody would know who your father was.” He turned the glass in his hands. “You said it every week. I used to think about it.”

She had forgotten. She remembered now. Sitting at the long table in the library with her chemistry homework, seventeen, so tired she could barely see, saying one day like a prayer.

“Are you happy?” Miles asked. Quietly. Without looking at her. The way he asked about galaxies: because he wanted to know the answer, not because he had already decided what it should be.

She opened her mouth to say what she always said. Yes, of course, the shop is doing well.

And then she thought about it. Properly. The way Zhao had taught her to think about things, by refusing to let her answer too fast.

The market at four in the morning with two cups of coffee waiting. A man in a too-short green apron, bleeding on roses. A lemon tree with five lemons. A note taped to a wall underground: This light stays on. A mountain in the rain. A hoodie that said FLOWER POWER.

“Yes,” said Elowen. And then, hearing it, surprised by it: “Yes. I am.”

Miles looked at her then. For a long moment. Then he smiled, his old crooked smile, the one he used to give her across the library table when she finally solved a problem.

“Good,” he said. “You don’t look like someone who wants to get on a train anymore.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the other side of the glass, in the gold ballroom, Zhao stood by the pillar and watched them.

He couldn’t hear what they said. He saw his wife at the rail in her green dress. He saw the thin man in the badly fitting suit beside her, close, closer than anyone but Aurelia had stood to her all night. He saw Miles say something quiet. He saw Elowen turn her head and look at him, and think about it, and then say something, and smile.

He saw Miles smile back.

Something cold went through him and settled.

“Zhendong.” Chen Si’s voice, at his elbow. Quiet. Careful. “Whatever you’re thinking—”

“I’m not thinking anything.”

The balcony door opened. Miles came back in alone, holding an empty glass. He looked around the ballroom, and saw Zhao by the pillar, and stopped.

Then, to Chen Si’s visible surprise, he walked straight over.

“Mr. Zhao,” said Miles. He was a little out of breath. He looked as if he had decided something on the way across the room and was doing it before he could change his mind. “Can I say one thing? Then I’ll go away. I’m not very good at—” He gestured vaguely at the ballroom, the balloons, the people. “This.”

Zhao looked at him.

Miles pushed his glasses up his nose. “I just asked her if she was happy. She thought about it. She actually thought about it, for about ten seconds, which she never used to do, she always just said yes. And then she said yes anyway.”

Zhao didn’t move.

“She doesn’t look like she wants to run,” said Miles. “That’s all. I thought you should know. I don’t know what you did. But she never looked like that at school. Not once.”

He nodded awkwardly, as if ending a lecture, and turned, and walked straight into a waiter carrying a tray of champagne.

In the noise that followed, Chen Si turned to his brother.

Zhao was standing by the pillar, very still, looking at the balcony door.

“Well,” said Chen Si softly. “That was unexpected.”

Zhao didn’t answer.

When Elowen came back in from the cold a minute later, her cheeks pink, her eyes bright, he crossed the ballroom before she had taken three steps, and took her hand, and held it so tightly that she looked up at him in surprise.

“What?” she said.

He didn’t answer. He just held on.

They didn’t dance. He didn’t know how. But for the rest of the evening, he didn’t let go of her hand once, and two hundred former students watched the most frightening man any of them had ever seen stand beside the Ice Queen all night like a man holding onto the side of a boat; and not one of them could have said, afterwards, which of the two of them looked happier.

chapters.title: Two Women, One Gala, Zero Ceasefire
chapters.desc: Elowen and Aurelia trade daggers. A ghost from the old road walks in. And Zhao learns to dance, badly, on purpose.
chapters.epigraph: “Floral is a tablecloth. Jewellery is a crown.” “Jewellery is a rock someone dug out of a hole.” — overheard, Chen Foundation Spring Gala
chapters.content:
The Chen Foundation Spring Gala was the most expensive night of the year, and every single person in the city who mattered was there, and some of them were there because they were afraid not to be.

Officially, it raised money for a children’s hospital. Unofficially, it was where the people who ran the city came to look at each other: property developers and port officials, two judges, a deputy mayor, and, at a table near the stage, a man from the provincial security bureau who was very carefully not looking at the table where Chen Si sat.

Aurelia had organised everything. The flowers, she had insisted, would be done by the best florist in the city.

“You can’t mean that,” Elowen had said on the phone, two months earlier.

“I mean exactly that,” Aurelia had said. “And then I am going to stand next to every single arrangement all night and tell people how much I would have done it differently.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“The peonies are leaning,” said Aurelia.

“They’re not leaning. They’re reaching.”

“Toward what?”

“The light. It’s what flowers do.” Elowen adjusted a stem by a millimetre. “Not that you’d know. You only work with things that are already dead.”

Aurelia touched the diamond collar at her throat. “Diamonds aren’t dead, darling. They’re eternal.”

“They’re rocks. Someone dug them out of a hole.”

“And someone dug your peonies out of a field.”

“Peonies grow back.”

They were standing in the middle of the ballroom in front of the largest arrangement Elowen had ever made: a column of white peonies and gold-leafed branches and trailing jasmine, two metres high, in the very centre of the room. Around them, the gala swirled in black and silver. People stopped to look at the arrangement, and then at the two women standing beside it, one in deep blue silk, one in gold, both smiling with all their teeth.

“They do this every time,” said Chen Si, by the bar, to the deputy mayor, who had asked. “It’s how they say hello.”

At the end of the bar, Zhao drank water and watched the room.

He did that at these things. Chen Si worked the room; Zhao watched it. Who came in with whom. Who looked at the exits. Who had something under their jacket that wasn’t a wallet. The deputy mayor, who was nervous, had a bodyguard who wasn’t very good. The man from the security bureau had two, who were. A property developer by the window was drunk already and would need to be taken home before the speeches.

And by the side door, the one the waiters used, a man in a grey suit had just come in with a woman on his arm whom Zhao had never seen before.

The man had a scar on the back of his left hand. Old, white, shaped roughly like a coin.

Zhao put down his water.

✦ ✦ ✦

Qiu Wen had changed.

A year ago, he had stood at the edge of the old road with his warehouse burning behind him and his brother crying on the ground with blistered hands, and said, You’re a dead man, Zhao. He had been fat then, and loud, a man who wore gold chains and drove a car with no lights.

Now he was thinner. His suit was good. His hair was cut by someone expensive. The woman on his arm was a minor actress whose face Zhao had seen on a billboard by the Docks. He walked into the Chen Foundation Spring Gala as if he had every right to be there, and looked around the room, slowly, and when he found Zhao at the end of the bar, he smiled.

It was not a friendly smile.

Then he looked past Zhao. At the centre of the room. At the column of white peonies. At the woman in deep blue silk standing beside it, laughing at something Aurelia had said.

Zhao was moving before he had decided to.

He didn’t hurry. Hurrying would have made people look. He walked along the edge of the room, past the bar, past the deputy mayor’s bad bodyguard, past the drunk developer, the way water moves along the edge of a basin; and he arrived beside his wife at the exact moment Qiu Wen did.

“Mrs. Zhao,” said Qiu Wen pleasantly. “What beautiful flowers.”

Elowen turned.

She had never seen Qiu Wen. She had seen his brother, running, two black shapes in the firelight at the end of her street. But she saw her husband’s face, and Aurelia’s, and she understood.

“Thank you,” she said, in her wedding-card voice.

“I’ve always loved peonies.” Qiu Wen reached out and touched one of the white flowers, lightly, with the hand that had the scar on it. “They’re so delicate. So easy to bruise.” He turned the flower toward him. “You have to be very careful where you keep them, don’t you? I hear even a little heat can ruin them.”

The air around the arrangement went very cold.

Aurelia’s smile didn’t move. But her hand, which had been holding a glass of champagne, set it down on a passing waiter’s tray without looking, and Elowen saw her fingers close around the small gold clutch she was carrying in a way that suggested it held more than lipstick.

Zhao didn’t say anything. He didn’t move toward Qiu Wen. He only looked at him.

It was Elowen who spoke.

“You’re right,” she said. She reached out and took Qiu Wen’s hand off the peony, firmly, the way she would have taken a child’s hand off a cake, and let it go. “They bruise easily. Which is why I never let anyone touch them who doesn’t know what they’re doing.” She smiled. “I’m sure your brother told you about heat, Mr. Qiu. He must know all about it. How are his hands?”

There was a silence.

Qiu Wen’s smile stayed exactly where it was. But his eyes changed. He looked at her, really looked, the way men in her father’s house had sometimes looked at her when they realised she had been listening to every word.

“Healing,” he said softly. “Slowly.”

“Cold water,” said Elowen. “Twenty minutes. I’m told it helps.”

Behind her, very quietly, Aurelia made a sound that might have been a laugh.

Qiu Wen inclined his head. He looked at Zhao one last time—a long, flat look that said this isn’t over—and then he took the actress’s arm and walked away into the crowd.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao let out a breath.

“You shouldn’t have done that,” he said, very low.

“He touched my flowers.”

“He was threatening you.”

“I know.” Her hands were shaking. She hid them in the folds of her dress. “That’s why I did it.”

Aurelia looked at her. Then she picked up a new glass of champagne from a passing tray and handed it to Elowen.

“Darling,” she said, “I take back everything I said about the peonies.” She clinked her glass against Elowen’s. “And I’m telling Chen Si to find out exactly who brought that man into my gala, and then I’m going to ruin their entire life.”

“You can’t do that.”

“I absolutely can. I organised the seating. I have a list.” Aurelia drank. “And next time someone threatens you in front of me, tell me first. I want to say something too. That was my line. The cold water. I’d been saving it for months.”

Elowen laughed. It came out unsteady. Zhao put his hand on the small of her back and kept it there.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven, the band started playing something slow.

Couples drifted onto the floor under the chandeliers. Chen Si took Aurelia’s hand without asking, and she rolled her eyes and let him, and they moved across the floor together with the ease of two people who had been doing this for years and had never once agreed on who was leading.

Elowen watched them from the edge of the floor.

“I don’t dance,” said Zhao, beside her.

“I know.”

He looked at the dance floor. At Chen Si, turning Aurelia under his arm. At the deputy mayor, stepping on his wife’s feet. At all the people who had stepped back from him in doorways for as long as he could remember.

Then he held out his hand.

She looked at it.

“You’ll have to lead,” he said. “I’ll follow. I’m good at following instructions.”

She took his hand.

He was terrible. He had no idea what to do with his feet, and he held her like the first box of eucalyptus at the market, at arm’s length, very carefully, as if she might break, and every time she tried to move him he went the wrong way. Twice he stepped on her hem. Once, turning, they bumped into Chen Si and Aurelia, and Aurelia said “Oh, for heaven’s sake,” and Chen Si said “Leave them, my queen,” and steered her away.

Elowen started to laugh.

“Closer,” she said. “You’re not carrying me. You’re dancing with me.”

He came closer. Her cheek ended up against his shoulder. His hand on her back spread wide, warm through the silk. They stopped trying to move their feet properly and simply swayed, slowly, in a small circle, while the band played and the chandeliers turned and the most dangerous people in the city watched the arms dealer and the florist rock back and forth in the middle of the floor like two teenagers at a school dance.

“Everyone’s looking,” she whispered.

“Let them.”

“You said you don’t dance.”

“I’m not dancing,” said Zhao, into her hair. “I’m holding you in public. It’s different.”

She closed her eyes and leaned into him.

Across the room, by the side door, Qiu Wen stood in the shadows with an untouched drink and watched them.

Zhao saw him. He didn’t stop swaying. He didn’t let go of his wife. He looked at Qiu Wen over her head, steadily, for a long moment, until the other man looked away first.

Then he bent his head and kissed his wife’s hair, and kept dancing.

chapters.title: The Question He Almost Asks
chapters.desc: In the car home, he gets as far as her name. A year to the day, a fourteenth key. Then the phone rings at three.
chapters.content:
In the car home from the gala, she fell asleep against his shoulder.

Bao drove. The city slid past the windows: the harbour, the bridges, the long dark road out toward the Docks. Zhao sat very straight so as not to wake her. Her head was heavy and warm against his arm. Her hair smelled of jasmine from the arrangement and one of the gold leaves had got caught in it, above her ear. He didn’t take it out.

He thought about Qiu Wen’s hand on the white peony.

He thought about the way she had taken that hand off the flower, firmly, the way you take a child’s hand off a cake.

How are his hands?

He thought about Miles Wei standing in front of him with an empty glass, out of breath. She doesn’t look like she wants to run.

And under all of it, as always, quieter than everything else and heavier: her father in the dining room. She didn’t choose you. She chose me. You were only the price.

“Elowen,” he said.

He didn’t mean to say it out loud. It came out of him very quietly, into the dark of the car.

She stirred against his shoulder.

“Mm?”

He looked down at her. Her eyes were still closed. The gold leaf trembled above her ear.

“When you married me,” he said.

And stopped.

She didn’t open her eyes. She was mostly asleep. He could see it in her face, soft and slack, her mouth slightly open. In the front seat, Bao’s hands had gone very still on the wheel.

When you married me, did you ever think you might—

When you married me, was it only for him?

When you married me, would you have married me at all, if your father hadn’t lost three containers?

“What about it?” Elowen murmured, against his arm.

The car went over a bump. She sighed and pressed her face harder into his shoulder, and her hand came up in her sleep and curled into the front of his shirt, and held on.

He looked at her hand.

“Nothing,” he said. “Go back to sleep.”

She did.

Bao drove the rest of the way home without once looking in the mirror. When they pulled up at the house on the hill, Zhao lifted her out of the car without waking her and carried her up the steps, past the lemon tree, up the stairs. He laid her on the bed in her blue silk dress and took off her shoes and pulled the duvet over her. He took the gold leaf out of her hair, finally, and put it on the bedside table, in the glass vase, beside the heavy ring she had taken off in the car.

Then he went down to the basement and didn’t come up until four, when it was time to drive her to the market.

✦ ✦ ✦

The anniversary was on a Wednesday.

She thought he’d forgotten. He gave no sign. He drove her to the market at four, as always. He carried the buckets. He ate his fried eggs on the stool behind the counter. Granny Su looked at both of them, said “One year, hm,” and slipped an extra bunch of lily of the valley into Elowen’s order without being asked, the same as she had a year ago, on the morning of the registry office.

Elowen had remembered. Of course she had. She had been planning for a month.

She had gone back to the Cangshan hills in February, on her own, for two days, to see the camellia flower again and to talk to Mr. Wen’s grandson about the tea. And when she left, Mr. Wen had pressed something into her hands, wrapped in rice paper: a single camellia flower from the walled garden, pressed flat between the pages of a book, deep pink, every petal laid perfectly over the last.

For the husband, the old man had said. Tell him I said he’s an idiot. A good one.

She had taken it to a framer in the old town. It was in a narrow glass frame now, the flower floating between two panes, with a thin black border. It was wrapped in brown paper on the shelf in the back of the shop, behind the ribbon.

She gave it to him that evening, at dinner, at the clean table, after the fish.

He unwrapped it slowly. He took off the brown paper and folded it, the way he folded everything of hers, and then he held the frame in both hands and looked at the flower.

“Mr. Wen says you’re an idiot,” she said. “A good one.”

He didn’t smile. He was looking at the camellia.

“You went back,” he said.

“In February. When you were in the south.”

“By yourself.”

“Bao came.” She paused. “Bao always comes. I don’t know how you do it, he’s always just there.”

He didn’t answer. He put the frame down on the table very carefully, face up, beside his bowl. Then he reached into his jacket pocket.

He took out a key.

It was small and plain and steel. It had a little red tag on it. He put it on the table in front of her, next to her chopsticks.

She looked at it.

“The fourteenth key,” said Zhao.

The basement. The steel door. The one key he had kept back on the first day, when he gave her the ring of thirteen with their little coloured tags, and said you don’t need that one.

“You gave me the code,” she said. “On the first night. I don’t need the key.”

“I know.” He didn’t take his eyes off her. “The code is for if something happens. For if you need to hide.” He pushed the key a centimetre closer. “The key is for if you just want to come in.”

She picked it up. It was warm from his pocket.

“There’s nothing in this house you can’t open,” he said. “Not anymore. I wanted you to have all of them.”

She sat at the table holding a small steel key and could not say anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him upstairs.

She didn’t say anything. She stood up from the table and held out her hand, and he took it, and she led him up the stairs, past the little room at the top, down the corridor. She was still holding the key in her other hand. She put it in the vase on the bedside table with the heavy ring and the gold leaf from the gala, and it rang against the glass like a bell.

He reached for her. She stopped his hands.

“Let me,” she said. The way he had said it, a year ago, in the dark.

He let her.

She undressed him slowly in the light from the Docks, the way he had once undressed her: one button at a time, folding each thing, putting it on the chair. He stood and watched her do it with his hands at his sides and his breathing getting rougher, and when she folded his shirt and laid it on the chair, very neatly, on top of his trousers, he made a sound that was almost a laugh and almost something else.

She pushed him back onto the bed.

He went down easily, on his back, and lay there looking up at her in the light from the Docks, and she climbed up and knelt over him with her knees on either side of his hips, and took his wrists, and put them up above his head, on the pillow.

“Don’t move,” she said.

His eyes went very dark.

“Elowen.”

“Page two, line six,” she said. “You don’t touch me unless I ask.” She bent down until her mouth was an inch from his. “I’m not asking. Not yet. Don’t move.”

He didn’t move.

It nearly killed him. She could see it nearly killed him. She kissed him the way he usually kissed her: slowly, deliberately, as if she had all night. His mouth. His jaw. The pulse in his throat, which was going so fast she could feel it against her lips. The scar on his collarbone, the bullet scar on his shoulder, the long ridge down his ribs, all the way down, the way you would follow a river on a map. His hands, above his head, had closed into fists in the pillow. His breathing had gone rough and loud in the quiet room. When she reached the end of the long scar, above his hip, and put her mouth there and stayed, he said her name through his teeth like a man being burned.

“Elowen. Please.”

She lifted her head and looked at him.

The most frightening man in the city, lying in her bed with his hands in fists above his head because she had told him not to move, saying please.

She had never felt so powerful in her life. She had never been so in love.

“Say it again,” she said.

“Please.”

“What do you want?”

He told her. In that low, rough voice, staring up at her in the orange light, he told her exactly what he wanted, and her whole body went hot, and she sat back on her heels and looked at him, and then, very slowly, smiled.

“You can move now,” she said.

He moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was not like the first time, or the mountain. It was not careful. A year of marriage was in it, a year of knowing exactly what made him lose his breath and exactly how long to make him wait. He rolled her under him in one movement and kissed her so hard her head pressed back into the pillow, and she laughed into his mouth and then didn’t laugh, because his hands were everywhere at once, greedy and sure, and he was saying things against her skin, low and rough, half in words and half not, mine, you’re mine, say it, and she said it, yours, and meant it more than she had ever meant anything.

She took her time and then she didn’t. He said her name into her shoulder in a voice she had only ever heard from him in this bed, low and broken, Elowen, Elowen, and she wrapped herself round him and held on, and at the end she held his face in both hands and watched it come apart, and thought, this. This is what I chose.

She almost said it. Afterwards, lying on his chest in the dark with his heart thudding under her ear and his hand spread on her back.

It isn’t a contract anymore. It hasn’t been for a long time. I love you.

It was right there. In her mouth. She could taste it.

And she thought about her father on the front steps, and Zhao in the basement saying I know in that flat, finished voice, and she thought: not like this. Not in bed, after. He’ll think it’s the moment talking. He’ll think it’s because of the key.

I want to say it when he can’t mistake it for anything else.

So she said instead, into his chest, “Happy anniversary.”

His hand stopped moving on her back.

“You remembered,” he said.

“You remembered,” she said.

“I remember everything.” His voice was very quiet. “The fourteenth of March. Nine forty-one in the morning. The clerk stamped the book at nine forty-one. You had soil under your nails. You smelled of eucalyptus.” A pause. “I remember every date. I’m very bad at forgetting things.”

She lifted her head and looked at him in the dark.

“Nine forty-one,” she said.

“I looked at the clock on the wall.”

“Why?”

He didn’t answer.

“In case it was the only one,” he said finally. “In case you changed your mind. I wanted to know exactly when it started.”

She put her head back down on his chest so he wouldn’t see her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

The phone rang at three.

Not hers. His. The one he kept on the bedside table that only four people had the number for. It buzzed against the wood, loud in the dark, and he was awake and sitting up with it at his ear before the second buzz.

“Si,” he said.

She sat up too, the sheet around her shoulders. In the light from the screen she could see his face. She watched it change.

He listened. Once he said, “When?” And once, “Which ones?” And once, very quietly, “Does she know?”

Then he said, “No. I’ll tell her.” And hung up.

He sat on the edge of the bed in the dark with the phone in his hand and his back to her.

“Zhendong?”

“Turn on the news,” he said.

She found the remote. The television on the wall flickered on, too bright. A news channel, the international one, a woman at a desk with a graphic behind her. INTERPOL NOTICE. And underneath it, a photograph.

It was a bad photograph. Taken from a distance, a long lens, years ago. A younger man in a cheap suit, standing beside a car at a port somewhere, half turned away.

It was her husband.

…issued a Red Notice tonight for a man described as one of the most significant illegal arms brokers in the region, following the publication of a United Nations panel report linking a network of shell companies to weapons shipments in at least four conflict zones under embargo…

Elowen stared at the screen.

…Zhao Zhendong, twenty-six, believed to be based in the Iron Docks district…

The newsreader moved on to the weather.

Neither of them did.

Zhao put the phone down on the bedside table. Beside the glass vase, with the heavy ring in it, and the gold leaf, and the fourteenth key.

“It’s a request,” he said, without turning round. His voice was perfectly even. “Not a warrant. It asks police in other countries to find me and hold me. Here, it doesn’t mean much. Not yet. Chen Si has people in the right offices.” A pause. “But I can’t leave the country now. And everyone I do business with saw that. And everyone who wants me gone saw it too.”

She looked at his back. At the long scar down his ribs, pale in the light of the television.

“How many people want you gone?” she asked.

He was quiet for a long time.

“After tonight,” he said, “more.”

She moved across the bed. She put her arms around him from behind and pressed her cheek against his back, between his shoulder blades, where she had pressed it on the morning of the roses.

He didn’t move. But after a moment his hand came up and covered both of hers, where they were locked over his heart, and held on, very tightly, the way he had held her hand all night at the reunion.

Like a man holding on to the side of a boat.

chapters.title: A Red Notice With His Face on It
chapters.desc: A detective from her childhood walks into the shop. A UN report with a familiar name buried on page sixty.
chapters.epigraph: “Someone wants him gone, Elowen. People like that don’t check who’s standing next to him.” — Detective Song Wei Long
chapters.content:
For a week after the news, the phone on the bedside table never stopped.

Zhao answered it at three in the morning and at four and at six. He stood at the kitchen window with it pressed to his ear, saying very little: yes, no, when, how many. He went to the Docks before the market and came back after midnight. He stopped eating at the table. She found him in the basement at two, every night, not cleaning anything, just sitting at the workbench under the lamp with his hands flat on the wood.

Buyers cancelled. She could tell, without him saying, from the way his jaw set after certain calls. Two brokers he had worked with for years stopped answering. A shipment that should have gone out of the Docks on Thursday didn’t, because the captain of the ship had seen the news too, and suddenly remembered that his engine needed repairs.

And at the shop, people began to stare.

Not everyone. Most of her customers didn’t watch the international news, and the ones who did didn’t connect a bad photograph of a man in a cheap suit with the large, quiet husband who sometimes swept the floor. But some did. A woman she had sold wedding flowers to two years before came in, saw who was standing in the corner with the newspaper, went white, and walked out without a word. A regular, an old man who bought chrysanthemums for his wife’s grave every Sunday, didn’t come on Sunday.

“It’ll pass,” Zhao said. He didn’t look at her when he said it. “People forget.”

“Do they?”

He didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday, a man came into the shop and didn’t buy anything.

He was about her age, tall, in a plain dark coat, with a face so still and expressionless it looked carved. He stood just inside the door and looked around: at the buckets, at the cooler, at the second row of tulips over the drain cover in the floor. He looked at everything for exactly as long as it took to remember it.

Then he looked at her, and something in that carved face moved, just slightly.

“Lin Elowen,” he said.

She knew him. It took her a second. Then it came back all at once: a skinny boy with a buzz cut, sitting on the wall between her family’s house in the Walled City and the policeman’s house next door, eating an ice lolly and refusing to come down even when his father shouted.

“Song Wei Long,” she said.

“Detective Song now.” He took a small leather wallet out of his coat and showed her the badge inside without any ceremony, the way you might show someone a bus ticket. “I’m not here officially.”

“You showed me your badge.”

“So you’d know I was telling the truth about the not-officially part.” He put it away. “Can we talk?”

Xiao Pan, at the counter, had gone the colour of paper.

“It’s all right,” Elowen told him. “He grew up next door. He used to steal our persimmons.”

“Your sister Eliana used to throw them at me,” said Song Wei Long. “From the upstairs window. She had very good aim for a four-year-old.” He glanced at Xiao Pan. “Your boy can stay. I won’t say anything he can’t hear.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t sit down. He stood by the counter with his hands in his coat pockets, looking at the roses, and told her things in a flat, quiet voice, the way he must have given evidence in court, facts first, no adjectives.

“The Red Notice isn’t the problem,” he said. “Not here. Your husband has friends in the right offices. Chen Si made sure of that years ago. Nobody in this city is going to arrest him because Lyon asked politely.” He touched a rose petal. “The problem is the report.”

“The UN panel.”

“You read it?”

“All two hundred pages.” She had. Every night that week, in the big bed, while he was on the phone. “It names eleven companies. Seven of them are his. It describes four shipments. It has photographs of crates in places I’ve never heard of.” She paused. “It’s very detailed.”

“Too detailed.” Song Wei Long finally looked at her. “Panels like that work from seizures and flight records and paperwork. They don’t usually get the names of shell companies registered in back offices in this city. They don’t usually get the right dates.”

“Someone told them.”

“Someone told them a great deal.” He let that sit for a moment. “And now every man your husband ever cheated, or embarrassed, or put out of business knows two things. That he can’t leave the country. And that his buyers are nervous. A wolf with a wounded leg.” His voice didn’t change. “Somebody wants him gone, Elowen. And the kind of people who want that don’t check who’s standing next to him when they try.”

The shop was very quiet. Outside, a bus went past.

“Why are you telling me this?” she asked.

Song Wei Long was silent.

“When I was eleven,” he said, “my father arrested a man who owed your father money. The next morning, someone left a dead cat on our doorstep. My mother cried for a day. And that afternoon, you came over the wall with a shoebox and a trowel, and you buried it in our garden, under the persimmon tree, and you made a little cross out of lolly sticks. You were ten. You didn’t say anything. You just did it, and went home.”

She had forgotten that. She remembered it now: the weight of the shoebox, the smell of the earth.

“I owe you a cat,” said Song Wei Long. “This is the cat.”

He turned to go. At the door, he stopped.

“One more thing. Page sixty-one of the report. Footnote nine.” He didn’t turn round. “Look at who registered the third company. Then tell your husband.”

The bell rang as he went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the footnote that night, in the big bed, with the report on her knees and Zhao downstairs on the phone.

Page sixty-one. Footnote nine. Small print.

Northgate Agricultural Holdings Ltd. was incorporated in this city in 2015. The original registering agent, a Mr. Kang Ji, is understood by the Panel to have provided substantial documentary assistance to its inquiries.

Kang.

She sat in the bed and looked at the name.

He won’t hold a pen again, her husband had said, standing beside the car at the Docks, with water drying on his wrists.

Kang couldn’t hold a pen. So he had found someone to hold it for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took it down to the basement.

He was at the workbench, as usual, under the hanging lamp. He had his phone on the bench in front of him, face down. He looked up when she came down the stairs, and she saw how tired he was, the shadows under his eyes like bruises, the way they had been on the day she first walked into his office.

She put the report on the bench in front of him, open at page sixty-one, and put her finger on the footnote.

He read it.

He read it twice. His face didn’t change. But she watched his hand, lying on the bench beside the report, close very slowly into a fist, and then open again, and then lie flat.

“Song Wei Long,” he said. “The detective.”

“He came to the shop. Not officially.”

“I know. Bao told me.” He didn’t look up from the footnote. “What did he want?”

“To give me back a cat.”

He did look up then.

“It’s a long story,” said Elowen. “He’s a friend. He was warning me. He said someone wants you gone, and they won’t care who’s standing next to you.”

Zhao looked at her for a long moment in the lamplight.

“He’s right,” he said.

“I know he’s right.”

“Then you should—”

“Don’t.” She said it before he could finish. “Don’t tell me to close the shop. Don’t tell me to go to my father’s house. Don’t tell me to go and stay on the mountain until it’s over.”

He was quiet.

“I was going to say,” he said slowly, “that you should take the gun. The small one. From the drawer. Keep it at the shop.”

She stopped.

“Oh,” she said.

“I know you won’t close the shop.” The corner of his mouth moved, too tired to be a smile. “You went to the market the morning of our wedding. You’re not going to hide because of a footnote.”

She looked at him. At this exhausted, hunted man sitting under a lamp in a room full of guns, who knew her well enough not to ask her to run.

She came round the bench and stood beside him, and put her hand on the back of his neck, and he leaned his head against her ribs and closed his eyes and stayed there, very still, breathing.

“Kang,” she said quietly. “What will you do?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

“He’s in a hospital in Singapore with a new name and a lawyer somebody else is paying for.” His voice was muffled against her. “I can’t reach him. Not now. Not with the world watching.” A pause. “And I should have killed him a year ago, at the Docks. I didn’t. Because you were on the stairs.”

She went very still.

“I’m not blaming you,” he said. “I’m telling you so you know. That was the choice. I made it. I’d make it again.” He breathed out against her ribs. “But somebody is going to pay for it. And I don’t know yet who.”

She stood in the basement with her hand on the back of her husband’s neck, and the UN report open on the bench, and thought about the sound she had heard on the stairs at the Docks: a branch snapping, a man screaming.

She had been glad, that day, that it was only his hands.

She wasn’t sure, anymore, what she was glad of.

chapters.title: The Order She Wouldn’t Fill
chapters.desc: A client wants funeral wreaths for a man who isn’t dead yet. Their worst fight. Their best apology.
chapters.content:
The man came in on a Wednesday at eleven, which was the quiet hour between the office workers and lunch.

He was ordinary. That was the first thing she noticed later, when Song Wei Long asked her to describe him. Middle-aged, medium height, a grey jacket, a face you would forget the moment it left the room. He smelled faintly of cigarettes. He paid in cash.

“Two funeral wreaths,” he said. “The large ones. White chrysanthemums. White lilies.”

Elowen took out her order book.

“The name for the ribbon?” she asked.

He told her.

She wrote the first character before her hand understood what her ears had heard, and stopped.

She looked up. He was smiling, pleasantly, the way men smile at waitresses.

“And the dedication,” he said. “In deepest sympathy. Taken too soon. Deliver them to Northgate Industrial Pumps, the Iron Docks. On the ninth.”

The ninth. Two weeks away.

“The ninth,” Elowen repeated.

“That’s right.” He put a stack of notes on the counter. Far too much. “Keep the change. You’re the best florist in the city. Everyone says so. It should be done properly.” He paused, as if remembering something. “Oh. And a small one. A bunch of white peonies. For the widow.”

He turned and walked out. The bell rang behind him.

Xiao Pan, who had been sweeping at the back, put down his broom very slowly.

“Miss Lin,” he said. “Was that—”

Elowen was looking at the first character she had written on the order form. Zhao.

She tore the page out of the book. Her hands were steady. She folded it in half, and then in half again, and then she picked up the stack of notes he had left on the counter, walked to the door, opened it, and stood on the pavement looking up and down the street.

He was gone.

She went back inside and called Song Wei Long, not her husband.

She would think about that later, a great deal.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao found out anyway. Bao had been across the street. Bao was always across the street.

He came into the shop at noon, and she knew from his face, and from the way he shut the door behind him and turned the sign to CLOSED without looking at it, that he knew everything.

“You called the detective,” he said.

“He’s the police.”

“You called the police,” said Zhao, “before you called me.”

There was something in his voice she had never heard before. Not anger. Something rawer.

“Because if I called you,” said Elowen, “you would have gone after that man. And then you would have done something to him. And he was a messenger, Zhendong. Someone paid him to walk in here and smile at me. That’s all.”

“That isn’t all.” He stood in the middle of the shop with his hands at his sides. “He came into your shop. He stood at your counter. He looked at you. He ordered flowers for my funeral from my wife and asked for peonies for the widow.” His voice dropped. “Do you understand what that means?”

“It means someone wants to frighten you.”

“It means someone wants me to know they can reach you whenever they like.” He took a step toward her. “The van was a message. This is a message. The next one won’t be.”

“Then what do you want me to do?”

He was silent.

“Say it,” said Elowen. “Say what you want.”

“I want you to close the shop.”

The words fell into the room like a dropped bucket.

“For a month,” he said. “Two. Until this is finished. You can work from the house. Bao’s cousin can run deliveries. I’ll pay the rent, the staff, the—”

“No.”

“Elowen—”

“No.” She heard her own voice go cold and flat and very quiet, the way it had gone with the man at the market who short-counted her roses. “You said you wouldn’t ask me that. In the basement. You said, ‘I know you won’t close the shop.’ You said it a week ago.”

“A week ago nobody had ordered my funeral wreath from you.”

“And next week it’ll be something else. And the week after that, something else. There will always be something else, Zhendong, as long as you’re you.” She came round the counter. “I knew what you were when I married you. I knew it when I walked into your office. You told me yourself, at the dinner with Maartens—he’s not a good man, none of them are, neither am I. I said I wanted to see it. I saw it. I stayed.”

He didn’t argue.

“Then don’t ask me to hide from it.” Her voice cracked and she made it stop. “I won’t live in your house with fourteen locks and wait for you to come home. I won’t. I’ve spent my whole life being careful so other people could be safe. My father. My brother and sisters. You. This shop is the only thing in my whole life I ever made just for me, and I am not closing it because a man in a grey jacket smiled at me.”

The shop was very quiet. In the cooler, the fan hummed.

He looked at her.

“It’s not the only thing,” he said finally, very low.

“What?”

“You said it’s the only thing you ever made just for you.” He didn’t look away. “There’s a mountain with your name on it. There’s a dog called Dumpling. There’s a man who sweeps your floor.” His jaw was tight. “I thought maybe some of those were yours too.”

She opened her mouth. Nothing came out.

He turned round and went out of the shop, and the bell rang behind him, and she stood in the middle of her new warm floor with a folded order form in one hand and a stack of a stranger’s money in the other, and for the first time since she had known him, he had walked away from her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t come home for dinner.

She ate alone at the clean table. Then she didn’t eat; she sat there in front of the cold fish and looked at his empty chair.

At ten, she went down to the basement with the fourteenth key and let herself in. The lamp over the workbench was off. The room was dark and cold and smelled of oil, and he wasn’t there, and she stood at the bottom of the stairs feeling as though she had walked into a church after the funeral.

At eleven she sat on the stairs in the hall, by the lemon tree, and waited.

At one, she heard the car.

He came in quietly, the way he always did. He saw her sitting on the bottom stair in her pyjamas with her arms around her knees, and stopped in the doorway, and they looked at each other across the hall.

He had been drinking. Not much. She could tell from the careful way he shut the door.

“Where were you?” she asked.

“Chen Si’s.”

“Did you talk?”

“He talked.” Zhao took off his coat and hung it up. He didn’t come any closer. “Aurelia talked more. She called me a coward and an idiot and a Neanderthal. In Italian. Then in English, so I’d understand.”

“What did Chen Si say?”

Zhao looked at the lemon tree for a long moment.

“He said that the day he married Aurelia, she told him that if he ever tried to keep her somewhere safe, she would leave him and take half of Chen Si’s people with her.” He paused. “He said she meant it. He said that was why he married her.”

Elowen didn’t say anything.

“He said,” Zhao went on slowly, “that I didn’t marry a woman who would let me lock her in the basement. I married the woman who walked into the Iron Docks with three pages of terms and read my shipping routes better than my own men.” He finally looked at her. “He said if I wanted someone to keep safe in a room, I should have bought a bird.”

She laughed. It came out wet. She put her face against her knees.

He crossed the hall and sat down on the stair beside her. Not touching her. Their shoulders an inch apart.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

She lifted her head.

She had never heard him apologise for anything he had done. Not once in a year. Not to her, not to anyone. I won’t make something up, he had said, I’ll tell you when I can’t tell you something. He had never said he was sorry.

“I was afraid,” he said, to the floor. “When Bao called. When he told me what the man ordered. I was in a meeting and I stood up in the middle of it and walked out, and I drove to the shop, and the whole way I was thinking: she’s alone at the counter. She’s alone at the counter and he’s standing in front of her.” His hands were clasped between his knees. They were not quite steady. “I’ve never been afraid of anything that much. Not in Block C. Not when I got shot. I didn’t know what to do with it. So I tried to put you somewhere it couldn’t reach.”

“I know,” said Elowen.

“It was wrong.”

“It was.” She leaned her shoulder against his, closing the inch. “And I should have called you. Not Wei Long. You. First.”

“You were right. I would have gone after him.”

“I know. I should have called you anyway. I should have trusted you to hear me say don’t.” She took his hand, unclasped it from the other one, held it. “At the Docks, a year ago, Kang lived because I was on the stairs. At the Qiu warehouse, nobody died because I asked you not to. You listen to me. I should have let you.”

He looked down at their hands.

“And you were right,” she added, more quietly. “About the other thing. The mountain. Dumpling. You.” She swallowed. “It isn’t the only thing I made for myself. Not anymore. I don’t know when that happened.”

He didn’t say anything. But his hand turned over in hers and held on.

“The shop stays open,” she said.

“The shop stays open.”

“Bao comes inside. Not across the street. Inside, in the corner, with your newspaper.”

“Yes.”

“And I keep the gun in the drawer under the till.”

“Yes.”

“And if anyone comes in and orders anything with your name on it again, I call you first.” She squeezed his hand. “And you don’t kill them.”

He was quiet for a moment.

“I don’t kill them,” he said, “first.”

She laughed, despite everything, and put her head on his shoulder.

They sat on the stairs in the hall at one in the morning, by the lemon tree, with their hands together. After a while he put his arm around her and she curled into his side, and neither of them moved to go up.

Outside, in the dark, on the far side of the city, someone had paid a man in a grey jacket to smile at a florist and order two wreaths for the ninth.

Neither of them knew yet that it was not the wreaths that mattered.

It was the peonies. For the widow.

chapters.title: Glass
chapters.desc: The shop window comes in at 4:12 in the afternoon. The light under the tulips stays on.
chapters.epigraph: “This light stays on. I’ll come.” — note taped to a wall, under the second row of buckets
chapters.content:
At 4:11 on the ninth, Elowen was wrapping a bouquet of sunflowers for a little girl’s mother.

The little girl was six. Her name was Mimi. She had chosen the sunflowers herself, for her grandmother, who was in hospital, and she was standing on tiptoe at the counter watching Elowen tie the ribbon with the total concentration of a child who has been allowed to choose the colour. Yellow. Obviously.

Bao was in the corner with the newspaper. He had been there every day for two weeks. He read the sports section very slowly and looked at the door every time it opened and the customers had stopped noticing him, mostly, the way you stop noticing a large piece of furniture.

Xiao Pan was at the back, by the cooler, squeezing his rubber ball. Ninety-one. Ninety-two.

It was a grey afternoon. Not raining. The street outside was quiet. Elowen had been thinking all day about the date: the ninth, the day on the funeral order. She had thought about it at the market before dawn, with Zhao beside her carrying the buckets, both of them pretending not to think about it. She had thought about it at lunch. And then a woman had come in at four with a little girl who wanted sunflowers for her grandmother, and for ten minutes she had stopped thinking about it at all.

“Is it pretty?” Mimi asked.

“It’s very pretty,” said Elowen. “Your grandmother will—”

At 4:12, a car came down the street too slowly.

Bao’s newspaper came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

She would remember it in pieces, afterwards. Never all at once.

Bao moving. Not standing up: moving, already across the shop before the newspaper hit the floor, shouting a word she didn’t hear.

A dark car outside the window. A back window rolling down.

The sound.

It wasn’t like films. It wasn’t a bang. It was a flat, hard, enormous cracking, over and over, so loud it seemed to come from inside her own head, and the big front window of the shop went white all at once, the whole pane, and then it came in.

Glass everywhere. A wave of it. Glittering, flying, falling over the buckets and the counter and the floor like hard rain. The sunflowers exploded off the counter in a burst of yellow. The bucket of white peonies by the window jumped and fell over. Something hit the wall behind her head with a sound like a hammer and the shelf of ribbons came down.

She was on the floor. She didn’t remember getting there. Bao had come over the counter—actually over it, the way you’d jump a fence—and knocked her down and was on top of her, and the little girl was screaming, somewhere, and the cracking went on and on and on—

Then it stopped.

A car engine, roaring, going away.

Silence. A ringing silence, high and thin, in both her ears.

“Miss Lin.” Bao’s voice, close, very far away. “Miss Lin. Are you hit? Talk to me.”

“The girl,” she said. Her mouth didn’t feel like hers. “The girl. Mimi—”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mimi’s mother was on the floor by the door with her daughter underneath her, both arms wrapped round her. Xiao Pan was lying across both of them. He had thrown himself from the back of the shop the moment the window went white, and he was lying across a stranger and her child with his hands in their compression gloves over his own head, and his back was covered in glass.

“Is anyone hurt?” Elowen heard herself say. Her voice was steady. She didn’t know how. “Xiao Pan. Are you hurt?”

“I don’t—I don’t know—”

“Bao.”

Bao was already up, already at the empty window frame with a gun in his hand that she hadn’t known he had, looking up and down the street, his whole body like a drawn bow. “They’ve gone,” he said. “For now. They might come back. We have to get you out of—”

“The floor,” said Elowen.

He turned.

“Raiden’s floor,” she said. “Under the tulips.”

She was crawling before she had finished saying it. Across her own shop floor, through broken glass, on her hands and knees, to the second row of buckets. The tulips were still standing. Somehow. Pink and white, in their bucket, untouched, while everything else around them lay in pieces.

She pushed the bucket aside. Water slopped over her hands. She found the drain cover with her fingers, the edge Raiden had shown her, and pulled.

It came up.

Underneath, a ladder going down into the dark. And then, as the light from the shop fell across the first rung, another light came on below, warm and steady and gold, the colour of late afternoon.

“In,” said Elowen. “All of you. Now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mimi went first. Her mother passed her down to Elowen, who had gone two rungs down the ladder, and Elowen held her tight and carried her the rest of the way down and set her on the blankets at the bottom. The little girl had stopped screaming. She was staring at the light on the ceiling with enormous eyes.

Then the mother. Then Xiao Pan, shaking, glass falling off his back in little tinkling showers onto the floor of the room.

“Bao,” Elowen called up.

Bao’s face appeared in the square of the hatch, dark against the grey light of the ruined shop.

“I stay up here,” he said. “Close it from inside. There’s a bolt. Don’t open it for anyone who isn’t me or him.”

“Bao—”

“Miss Lin.” He looked down at her. His face was very calm. “That’s my job. Close it.”

The hatch came down. The light stayed on.

She found the bolt, where Raiden had told her it would be, and slid it home with a heavy, final sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room under the shop was three metres by four, and warm, and smelled of new concrete and clean blankets.

The light stayed on. Mimi sat on the blankets with her mother’s arms around her, staring at it. Xiao Pan sat with his back against the wall, breathing in short, fast gulps, looking at his hands.

Elowen picked up the phone on the wall.

She didn’t dial. There was nothing to dial. It was a line that went through the building next door, Raiden had said, and it only rang one number, and Eliana had made it so that the moment the receiver came off the hook, that number would already be ringing.

It rang once.

“Elowen.”

His voice. Very calm. Much too calm.

“They shot the window,” she said. “At four twelve. A car. Bao’s up top. We’re under the tulips. Me, Xiao Pan, a mother, a little girl. Nobody’s—” She stopped. She looked at Xiao Pan’s back, glittering with glass. “I don’t think anyone’s badly hurt.”

“Are you hurt?”

“No,” she said. “I don’t think so. I don’t—”

She put her free hand up to her neck, because something there felt warm and wet.

Her fingers came away red.

She looked at them for a moment in the gold light. Red. Bright, real red, running down between her fingers and into her palm.

“Elowen,” said the voice on the phone. “Elowen. Talk to me.”

She found it with her fingertips. Low on the side of her neck, just above her collarbone. A cut. Not deep, she thought; she could feel the edges of it. A sliver of glass had come through the air when the window went white, and opened her skin like a knife opens a stem.

A clean cut.

“A little,” she said. Her voice had started to shake now, finally. “A piece of glass. On my neck. It’s—I think it’s small. It’s bleeding.”

There was a sound on the other end of the line.

She had never heard him make a sound like that. It was not a word. It was the sound of something very big breaking very quietly, a long way down.

“Press on it,” said Zhao. His voice had gone strange. Too careful, every word laid down like a foot on ice. “Something clean. The blankets. Press hard. Don’t look at it. Keep pressing.” A breath. “I’m in the car. I’m eight minutes away. Keep the hatch shut. Stay on the phone. Don’t hang up. Talk to me.”

“I’m talking.”

“Keep talking.”

She pressed a corner of the blanket hard against her neck. Mimi was watching her with huge eyes. Elowen smiled at her, and the little girl, unbelievably, smiled back.

“The sunflowers,” Elowen said into the phone. “I’d just finished the ribbon. Yellow. She chose it herself. They went everywhere.”

“I’ll buy her more.”

“And the window. Raiden will be furious. He only did the floor.”

“I’ll buy a new window.”

“And Bao jumped over the counter. Did you know Bao could jump over a counter?”

“Yes.”

“And Xiao Pan.” She looked at the boy against the wall, glass in his hair. “Xiao Pan threw himself on top of a stranger and her little girl. With his hands still healing. He didn’t think. He just did it.”

On the other end of the phone there was a long silence. Only the sound of an engine, going too fast.

“Tell him,” said Zhao finally, “that his motorbike is going to be a very good one.”

She laughed. It came out as a sob. She pressed the blanket harder against her neck and closed her eyes, and on the ceiling above her, Raiden’s light stayed on, warm and gold and steady, exactly as promised.

This light stays on.

I’ll come.

At 4:23, there was a knock on the hatch above her head. Three knocks, then two.

“It’s me,” said her husband’s voice, through the steel.

She slid back the bolt.

chapters.title: Nobody Else Touches Her
chapters.desc: He sends the doctor out of the room and closes a three-centimetre cut with hands that will not stop shaking.
chapters.content:
He came down the ladder so fast he missed the last three rungs.

She saw his face in the gold light and wished she hadn’t. It was white. Completely white, the colour of the plaster on the walls, and his eyes went straight to her neck, to the blanket she was pressing there, to the red soaking through it, and his face changed.

He didn’t say anything. He crossed the little room in two steps and went down on his knees in front of her on the blankets, and put his hand over hers where it was pressing the cloth to her neck.

His hand was shaking so badly she could feel it through hers.

“Let me see,” he said.

“It’s small.”

“Let me see.”

She took her hand away. He lifted the corner of the blanket. She watched his eyes while he looked at it. They didn’t blink.

“Three centimetres,” he said, after a moment. His voice was very low and very steady and completely wrong. “Clean. It missed everything. It’s not deep. It’s not—” He stopped. His jaw moved. “It missed everything.”

“I told you,” she whispered. “Small.”

He pressed the blanket back against her neck. He didn’t take his hand away. With his other hand, very slowly, he touched her face, her hair, her shoulder, her arm, down to her hand, as if counting, the way he had counted the bones of her spine on the first night. Checking that all of her was there.

Behind him, Mimi’s mother was staring at him with open terror. Xiao Pan had pressed himself against the wall.

“Bao,” Zhao said, without turning round. “Get them out. Take them to the hospital. The boy has glass in his back. The child goes to the children’s ward and someone stays with her. Pay for everything.” A pause. “And get the girl some sunflowers.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara came at five.

She was twenty-one, the fourth of the five Lin children, in her fourth year at medical school. She arrived at the house on the hill in a taxi with her hair half falling out of its clip and a bag over her shoulder that clinked when she put it down. Their father had called her. Somebody had called their father. Everyone in the family knew within an hour; it was that kind of family.

Elowen was sitting on the edge of the bath in the big bathroom upstairs, holding a towel to her neck. Zhao was standing in front of her. He hadn’t let go of her since the shop. He had carried her up the ladder, through the wreck of the glass and the sunflowers and the overturned buckets, and out to the car, and up the stairs here, and he had not once put her down long enough to let her walk.

Elara came into the bathroom, took one look at the towel, and became someone Elowen had never seen before.

“Okay,” she said briskly, setting her bag on the counter and unzipping it. “Let me see it. Jie, tilt your head. Brother-in-law, move, please. Thank you. Lights. More light. There we go.” She bent close and looked. “Oh, that’s nothing. That’s barely anything. That’s a paper cut with ambitions. Two, maybe three centimetres, clean edges, superficial, not near anything important. Steri-strips. Maybe one stitch at the deepest bit if you want it neater. I can do that here.” She pulled on gloves with two sharp snaps. “Brother-in-law, you can wait outside.”

Zhao didn’t move.

Elara looked up at him.

“It’s fine,” she said, more gently. “I’m good at this. I’m the best in my year at suturing. I practise on bananas. I’ll be very careful with her.”

“No,” said Zhao.

Elara blinked.

“I’ll do it,” he said.

The bathroom went quiet.

“With respect,” Elara said carefully, “you’re not a doctor.”

“No.” He didn’t look at her. He was looking at Elowen’s neck. “Tell me what to do. I’ll do it.”

“You’re shaking.”

“I know.”

Elara looked at him, the way she would look at a patient who was saying something more important than the words. Then she looked at her sister.

Elowen was looking at her husband.

At his white face. At his hands, hanging at his sides, trembling so hard he had clenched them into fists to stop it. At the blood on his shirt. Hers. All down the front, where he had carried her.

She understood.

“Elara,” she said quietly. “Show him. Then wait outside.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara showed him. She laid everything out on a clean towel on the counter: the saline, the gauze, the tiny strips of white tape, the scissors, a little tube of glue. She explained it twice, slowly, in plain words. Clean it. Dry it. Pull the edges together. Strips across, close together, not too tight. Leave it alone.

“If it bleeds through,” she said, “you call me. If it gets hot or red or starts to smell, you call me. I’m downstairs.” She stripped off her gloves. At the door, she stopped and looked back at Zhao. “You’ve done this before,” she said. It wasn’t a question.

“On myself,” said Zhao.

Elara looked at the scars on his forearms. At the shiny patch from the burn.

“Yes,” she said quietly. “I suppose you have.”

She went out and closed the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He washed his hands for a full two minutes. She watched him do it at the basin, scrubbing between his fingers, under his nails, the way she had once watched him clean a gun piece by piece under a lamp. When he turned round, his hands were red from the hot water. They were still shaking.

He knelt down on the bathroom floor in front of her where she sat on the edge of the bath, so that her neck was level with his face.

“Tilt your head,” he said.

She tilted it.

He took the towel away. She felt the air touch the cut. She felt him look at it.

He didn’t move for a long moment.

Then he soaked a square of gauze in saline and began to clean it.

It stung. She hissed. His hand stopped instantly.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“It’s all right.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Zhendong. It’s all right.” She put her hand over his wrist, the one holding the gauze. “Keep going.”

He kept going. Very slowly. So gently she could barely feel it. Little dabs, one after another, cleaning the dried blood from around the edges of the cut, from her collarbone, from the hollow of her throat where it had run down. His face was so close to hers she could feel his breath. Every time she flinched, he stopped. Every time he stopped, she said keep going, and he did.

His hands didn’t stop shaking. Not once. But they didn’t slip, either. Not once.

She watched his face while he worked. She had seen this man put a knife through a man’s hand at a dinner table without blinking. She had seen him come home smelling of smoke from a burned warehouse. She had seen him in the basement at two in the morning with a rifle in pieces on the bench, calm as stone.

She had never seen him afraid.

She was seeing it now. All of it. It was in his white face and his shaking hands and the way he was breathing, short and careful, as if every breath had to be checked before he took it. It was in his eyes, which hadn’t left the cut since he knelt down. It was the face of a man who had lived his whole life in a world full of knives and bullets and broken glass, and had never once been frightened of any of it, because nothing in that world had ever been his to lose.

Until now.

✦ ✦ ✦

He dried the cut with clean gauze, a little at a time. He opened the packet of strips with his teeth because his fingers couldn’t manage it.

He laid the first one across the cut, pulling the edges together, so carefully that she felt nothing at all.

Then the second. The third. Close together, the way Elara had said. Not too tight.

When he laid the fifth one, his hand finally slipped, just slightly, and his knuckle brushed the side of her throat, and she heard him make a sound like a man who has been hit.

“Zhendong.”

He didn’t answer. He laid the sixth strip. The last one. He smoothed the ends down with the tip of one finger. Then he sat back on his heels on the bathroom floor and looked at it: six white strips across a small cut on his wife’s neck, the edges pulled neatly together.

And then he put his face in his hands.

He didn’t make a sound. His shoulders shook. That was all. He knelt on the bathroom floor with his face in his hands and his shoulders shaking, silently, and she understood that he was crying, and that he had possibly not done it since he was a child, and that he did not know how to do it with any sound.

She slid off the edge of the bath onto the floor in front of him. She took his wrists and pulled his hands gently away from his face.

His eyes were red. His face was wet. He looked at her the way he had looked at the camellia on the mountain: as if she were the last one of something, the only one left in the world.

“I should have been there,” he said. His voice was barely there. “I was at the Docks. I knew it was the ninth. I knew. I should have closed the shop. I should have made you—”

“You couldn’t have made me.”

“I should have tried.”

“You did try. I said no.” She held his wrists. “And I’d say no again. Zhendong, listen to me. Bao was there. Raiden’s floor was there. The light stayed on. You put all of it there. Every single thing that saved us today, you put there. You thought of it before I did. You called Raiden at two in the morning. You wrote that note on the wall.” Her voice broke. “I’ll come. You came. In eleven minutes. I counted.”

He looked at her.

“Eight,” he said. “I said eight. It was eleven. There was a bus.”

She laughed, and cried, and pulled him in, and he came: he fell forward onto her on the bathroom floor and put his arms round her and held on, his face in the side of her neck that wasn’t cut, his whole big body shaking, and she held him back and stroked his hair and said nothing at all, for a very long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, he lay beside her in the big bed and didn’t sleep.

She knew because she didn’t sleep either. She lay on her side with her back to him and his arm around her waist and his face against her hair, and she could feel him awake. Every so often his hand moved, up to her neck, to the edge of the white strips, and stopped there, just touching, as if checking they were still in place.

Just before six, he got up.

She heard him dress in the dark. She heard him open the drawer of the bedside table, the one where he kept things she didn’t ask about.

She didn’t turn over.

“How long?” she said into the dark.

He stopped.

He came round to her side of the bed and crouched down beside it, the way he had crouched beside the car at the Docks a year ago, so their faces were level. In the light from the window she could see his face. It wasn’t white anymore. It wasn’t frightened anymore. It was something else, something flat and cold and very far away, like a lake frozen all the way down.

“Forty-eight hours,” he said.

She looked at him.

She thought about Mimi’s yellow ribbon. About Xiao Pan lying across a stranger with glass in his back. About the man in the grey jacket, smiling, saying a bunch of white peonies, for the widow.

She thought about I don’t kill them first.

She should say don’t. She knew she should. She had said it before, at the hospital, and he had listened. He would listen now. If she said it, he would take off his coat and get back into bed and hold her until morning.

She put her hand on his face.

“Come back,” was all she said.

He turned his head and kissed her palm. Then he stood up and went out, and she heard him on the stairs, and the front door, and the car on the gravel.

And then the house was very quiet, and the light from the Docks moved slowly on the ceiling, and Elowen lay alone in the big bed with six white strips on her neck and her hand still warm from his mouth, and did not sleep, and did not cry, and did not once let herself wonder what it meant that she hadn’t said the word.

chapters.title: Forty-Eight Hours
chapters.desc: He finds the cell. This chapter does not look away.
chapters.epigraph: “When one of them bleeds, the other does something terrible. And when we bleed, darling, they both do.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
The clock started just before six in the morning, when he walked out of the front door and down the steps to the car.

Hour 1.

The car was waiting at the bottom of the drive with the engine running. Bao was at the wheel. His left arm was bandaged where a piece of the shop window had opened it from wrist to elbow. He had not mentioned it. He would not mention it for the next forty-eight hours.

“Where?” Bao said.

“The Docks,” said Zhao. “Then wherever it goes.”

Hour 2.

The office above Northgate Industrial Pumps had every light on.

Eliana was on a video call on the laptop on his desk. She was eighteen and had been told by her father not to get involved and had ignored him. Her face on the screen was small and pale and absolutely steady, and behind her three monitors glowed with grey traffic-camera footage.

“Black saloon,” she said. “Stolen plates. Stolen from a car park by the airport two nights ago. It went west after the shop, then north on the ring road. Camera seventy-four lost it at 4:31. Camera seventy-nine picked up a fire in an empty lot behind the cement works at 4:58.” She clicked. A grainy image: a shape in flames. “They burned it.”

“Faces?”

“No. Masks.” She hesitated. “But whoever stole the car didn’t wear one at the airport. He’s a kid. Sixteen, maybe. He steals for whoever pays. I already have his name and the address of his grandmother’s flat.” She looked at him through the screen. “Brother-in-law. Is my sister really all right?”

“Six strips,” said Zhao. “Elara did the instructions. I did the strips.”

Eliana looked at him. Then she nodded once and sent him the address.

Hour 3.

Raiden called. Then Chen Si.

“Who do you need?” said Chen Si.

“Nobody.”

“Zhendong.”

“Keep the police off the roads I’m on. Keep Song Wei Long busy. That’s all.” A pause. “Look after Aurelia. She’ll want to go to the house. Let her. Elowen shouldn’t be alone.”

A long silence on the line.

“Come back,” said Chen Si quietly. It was what Elowen had said.
