Hour 9.

The car thief was sixteen and lived with his grandmother on the eleventh floor of a block by the railway. He opened the door in a vest and saw who was standing there and wet himself.

Zhao didn’t touch him. He sat on the grandmother’s sofa, under a calendar picture of a mountain, and waited while the boy shook and cried and told him everything he knew, which wasn’t much. A man had paid him two thousand to steal a car. The man was called Little Fu. Little Fu drove for anyone. Little Fu played mahjong every night above a pharmacy in the old town.

When he had finished, Zhao stood up.

“If anyone pays you to steal a car again,” he said, “you think about the little girl who was buying sunflowers.”

The boy didn’t understand. Zhao didn’t explain. He left two thousand on the grandmother’s table, under the teapot, so the boy would have to explain it to her.

Hour 17.

Little Fu was harder.

Little Fu was thirty and thin and fast and had been driving for bad men since he was twelve, and when he saw Zhao in the doorway of the mahjong room above the pharmacy, he went out of the back window without stopping to think. He made it across two roofs. On the third, Bao was waiting.

They took him to the harbour.

The old fishing pier at the north end, where nobody went at night. Black water slapping against the pilings. A smell of diesel and rot. Bao held him. Zhao asked him once who had held the gun, and Little Fu laughed and spat and said he didn’t know what Zhao was talking about.

So Zhao put him in the water.

Not all of him. Bao held his ankles. Zhao held him by the collar and pushed his head and shoulders under the black surface and held them there, and counted, out loud, quietly. The way his wife had counted for Xiao Pan under the cold tap. The way he had counted over the oil drum.

At twenty, he pulled him out.

Little Fu came up choking and retching. Zhao asked him again. Little Fu said something about his mother.

Zhao put him back.

At thirty, he pulled him out. Little Fu was crying now, coughing up harbour water, his whole body jerking. Zhao asked him again, in exactly the same voice.

“Tian,” Little Fu gasped. “Tian Haoyu. He did the shooting. I only drove, I only drove, I swear, I didn’t know there was a kid—”

“Who paid Tian?”

“A man. Grey jacket. Lu. He works for—” Little Fu choked. “He works for Qiu Wen. Everyone knows. Qiu Wen’s new partner sent the money. A foreigner. The Dutchman. The one with the hand.”

Zhao went very still on the pier.

The one with the hand.

He had pinned that hand to a restaurant table with a steak knife, a year ago, for touching his wife’s knee. He had let the man live, and sign, and go home to the south with a hole through his palm.

Kang, whose fingers he had broken and left alive, had given the UN his companies.

Maartens, whose hand he had pinned and left alive, had paid for the bullets.

He stood on the black pier in the cold and understood, finally, what Chen Si had told him years ago, the night after Block C, in the back room of a clinic, when Zhao woke up and asked what had happened to Gao. You don’t leave them behind you, Zhendong. Not ever. Everything you leave behind you comes back.

They left Little Fu on the pier, alive, shaking, coughing, with a broken arm and a phone number for Song Wei Long in his pocket and instructions to call it and confess to stealing cars. He would. Zhao had looked into his eyes and seen it. He would do anything, for the rest of his life, rather than see that pier again.

Hour 30.

Tian Haoyu had a rented room above a karaoke bar in the east of the city, and a rifle case under the bed, and a bag packed by the door for a bus to the south in the morning.

He was a professional. He heard them on the stairs.

He came out of the door with a pistol in his hand and Zhao shot him twice in the chest before he could lift it.

It was very fast. It was very loud, in the narrow stairwell, louder than the cracking at the shop window, and then very quiet. Below them, through the floor, someone in the karaoke bar was singing an old love song badly, and didn’t stop.

Tian lay on his back on the landing. He was looking up at the ceiling. He was younger than Zhao had expected. Twenty-five, maybe. His eyes were open. He had a tattoo of a fish on his wrist.

Zhao stood over him for a moment.

He felt nothing. That was what he would remember afterward. He had expected to feel something—satisfaction, or anger, or the old cold quiet that came over him in Block C—and there was nothing at all. Only a man on a landing who had fired a rifle through a shop window at a woman wrapping sunflowers for a six-year-old girl, and was now dead, and would never do it again.

He went into the room and found the rifle case and the bag and, in the bag, an envelope of cash and a photograph. The photograph was of Elowen, taken through the shop window, a week ago. She was laughing at something Xiao Pan had said. Someone had drawn a circle around her face in red pen.

He put the photograph in his pocket.

Hour 38.

Lu, the man in the grey jacket, was found at his sister’s house in the suburbs, under a bed.

He told them everything before anyone asked him anything. He talked so fast that Bao had to tell him to slow down. Qiu Wen had planned it. Maartens had paid. The wreaths were Qiu Wen’s idea—he’d thought it was funny. The peonies for the widow were Maartens’. Tell him, Maartens had said, on the phone from Rotterdam, it’s for the hand.

“Where is Qiu Wen?”

Lu told them.

Zhao looked at him. Lu began to cry.

“You smiled at her,” Zhao said. “At the counter. You put money on her counter and smiled at her and ordered flowers for my funeral and peonies for my widow.” His voice didn’t change. “You looked her in the face.”

“I’m sorry, I’m sorry, I’m so sorry, I didn’t—they paid me—please—”

Zhao reached down and took Lu’s face in one hand, his thumb under one cheekbone and his fingers under the other, and held it, not hard, the way you would hold a child’s face to make it look at you.

“Every time you see a flower shop,” he said, “for the rest of your life, you cross the street.”

He let go.

Lu was still crying on the floor of his sister’s spare room when they left. He was alive. He had not been touched except for that one hand on his face. He would cross the street, Zhao knew. Every time. For the rest of his life. He would never be able to look at a florist again without feeling that thumb under his cheekbone.

Some people you left behind you because they would come back.

Some people you left behind you because they never, ever would.

Hour 46.

Qiu Wen had bought a villa on the coast with the money from his new partner. White walls. A gate. A garden with a koi pond lit from underneath, so the fish glowed orange and gold in the dark like coins.

He had four guards. Two of them took one look at who was coming through the gate at four in the morning and laid their guns down on the gravel and walked away. The third tried, and Bao put him on the ground. The fourth was Qiu Lei, the younger brother, with the scarred palms, who had been holding a cigarette in his ruined hand and dropped it when he saw Zhao and ran.

Zhao let him run.

He found Qiu Wen in the garden in a silk dressing gown, standing by the koi pond with a phone at his ear, shouting at someone. He turned. He saw Zhao.

He did not run. Zhao would give him that, afterward. He stood his ground by the glowing pond and lifted his chin.

“I can pay,” said Qiu Wen. “Whatever the Dutchman gave me. Double. Triple. I can give you his accounts. His routes. I can give you the man who gave Kang to the UN. I can—”

“You ordered flowers,” said Zhao, “for my widow.”

Qiu Wen’s face changed.

“That was a joke,” he said. “A message. Business. You burned my warehouse. You burned my brother’s hands. You know how this works, Zhao, this is how it works, we send each other messages—”

“You put a red circle,” said Zhao, “around her face.”

He took the photograph out of his pocket and held it up in the orange light of the pond.

Qiu Wen looked at it. Something in him understood, then. Zhao saw it go across his face. The understanding that there was no price. That there was nothing on the table at all.

He opened his mouth to shout for his guards.

Zhao hit him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He broke Qiu Wen’s jaw first, so there would be no more offers. Then he took him by the collar of the silk dressing gown and put him into the pond, the way he had put Little Fu into the harbour, and held him under among the glowing fish, and counted. At twenty he brought him up. Qiu Wen tried to speak through the broken jaw and couldn’t. Zhao put him back. He didn’t ask him anything. There was nothing left that he wanted to know. At forty, Qiu Wen stopped fighting. Zhao kept counting anyway, out loud, quietly, in the same voice he had used on the pier, all the way to a hundred.

It took longer than the stairwell. It was quieter. When it was finished, Qiu Wen was in the water, face down, among the glowing orange fish, and the fish had scattered to the edges of the pond, and the water was very still.

Zhao stood at the edge of it with his sleeves wet to the elbow and looked down.

He took a single white peony out of his coat. He had taken it from the floor of the ruined shop at four-thirty in the afternoon, two days ago, from the bucket that had fallen over by the window, and carried it in his pocket ever since. It was crushed and brown at the edges.

He dropped it in the pond. It floated beside Qiu Wen’s head.

He took a photograph with his phone. The pond, the man, the flower.

He sent it to a number in Rotterdam.

He typed one word underneath it.

Next.

Hour 48.

He washed at the Docks.

There was a shower in the back of the warehouse, behind the office, that the forklift drivers used. He stood under it for forty minutes. The water was as hot as it would go. He scrubbed his hands and his arms and his face and his hair, over and over, until his skin was red and raw, until the water running off him into the drain had been clear for a long time.

He put on clean clothes from the cupboard in the office. He threw the old ones in the furnace in the yard and stood and watched them burn.

Then Bao drove him home, and neither of them spoke, and the sun came up grey over the sea as they turned onto the hill, exactly forty-eight hours after he had left.

chapters.title: He Came Home Washed
chapters.desc: He showered before he came to her. She asks one question. He doesn’t lie. Then she asks a second.
chapters.content:
She was in the kitchen when he came in.

Not on the stairs this time. Not in bed. She was standing at the stove in her dressing gown making congee, because it was what her mother had made when someone came home from a hospital, and it was what she had made for her father the night the containers were seized, and it was the only thing she could think of to do with her hands.

Aurelia had stayed with her for two days. She had arrived an hour after he left, in a tracksuit with no makeup on, which Elowen had never in her life seen, and had sat on the end of the bed and talked about nothing for six hours straight, and slept in the guest room with the door open, and made terrible coffee. She had left at five this morning, when Chen Si called her. She hadn’t said why. She had kissed Elowen on the forehead at the front door, very hard, and said, “He’s coming home now. Make him eat something.” And gone.

So Elowen was making congee.

She heard the car. The dogs. Bao’s door, and then his. She heard the front door open and close.

She didn’t turn round from the stove.

He stopped in the kitchen doorway. She could feel him there behind her, the way you feel a change in the weather.

She stirred the congee.

“You showered,” she said.

He didn’t answer.

“Your hair’s wet. I can smell the soap from here. The cheap kind. From the Docks.” She stirred. “You stood in that shower for a long time.”

“Yes.”

She turned off the heat. She put the spoon down on the counter, very carefully, the way he put things down. Then she turned round.

He was standing in the doorway in clean clothes that didn’t fit quite right, a grey sweatshirt and old trousers from the cupboard at the office. His hair was wet. His face was scrubbed raw and red, especially his hands; she could see them from across the kitchen, the skin on his knuckles pink and shining as if he had tried to take it off. His eyes were very tired and very far away.

Under the soap, faintly, so faintly she could have imagined it, he smelled of something else. Harbour water. Smoke. And something metal and sweet that she didn’t have a name for and didn’t want one.

They looked at each other across the kitchen.

“Is anyone dead?” Elowen asked.

He had promised her, at the very beginning, on a third page in square blunt handwriting, that he would never make something up.

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t move. She didn’t look away.

“Who?”

“The man who held the rifle. Tian. He was twenty-five. He had a tattoo of a fish.” His voice was flat and level, like the weather report. “Qiu Wen. In his garden. And one of Qiu Wen’s guards, who drew on Bao.” A pause. “Three.”

Three.

She stood at the stove and let the number go through her.

“The driver,” said Zhao. “Little Fu. Alive. He’ll go to Song Wei Long and confess to stealing cars. The boy who stole the car. Alive. He’s sixteen. The man in the grey jacket. Alive.” He paused again. “I left him alive because he will never come near a flower shop again as long as he lives. I made sure of that.”

“And the money? Who paid?”

He looked at her.

“Maartens,” he said.

She went cold.

“The dinner,” said Elowen. “The hand.”

“He said the peonies were for the hand.” Zhao’s voice didn’t change. “He’s in Rotterdam. I can’t reach him. Not with the notice. Not yet.” A pause. “I sent him a photograph.”

She didn’t ask what was in it. She didn’t need to.

“Kang,” she said slowly. “And Maartens. Both of them.”

“Both of them.”

“Because you left them alive.” She said it very quietly. “Because I was on the stairs. Because I was at the table and said take it out.”

“No,” said Zhao. “Because I left them alive. Me. I made the choice.” He finally moved, one step into the kitchen. “I won’t make it again. I need you to know that. Not with men like that. Not anymore. I need you to know what I am, Elowen, all of it, because I won’t lie to you about it, and I won’t ever—”

His voice stopped.

She saw it happen. She saw it reach his face. He was standing in the middle of her kitchen with his scrubbed red hands at his sides, and his jaw was moving, and his eyes had gone suddenly very bright, and his hands—

His hands had started to shake.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started in his fingers, like hers had in the car after the dinner with Maartens. Then it went up his arms. Then his whole body. He stood in her kitchen in borrowed clothes and shook, hard, from head to foot, like a man who has been out in the snow too long, and he didn’t seem to know it was happening. He looked down at his own hands as if they belonged to somebody else.

“I’m sorry,” he said. His teeth were chattering. “I don’t—this doesn’t happen. I don’t know why it’s—”

She crossed the kitchen.

She didn’t say anything. She took him by both wrists, the way she had at the sink after the warehouse, and pulled him down, and he came, folding up onto the kitchen floor like something with its strings cut, and she went down with him and wrapped her arms around him and held on.

He shook. He shook so hard she could feel it in her own teeth. His face was against her shoulder, the one without the cut, and his breath was coming in short, hard gasps that weren’t quite sobs, and his hands, his scrubbed raw hands, were fisted in the back of her dressing gown, holding on as if she were the only fixed thing in a moving world.

She held him on the kitchen floor beside the stove, with the congee going cold in the pot above them, and stroked his wet hair, and didn’t say anything at all.

It took a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

When it was over, he lay with his head in her lap on the kitchen floor, with his eyes closed, and she sat with her back against the cupboard and her hand on his hair.

The shaking had stopped. He was breathing slowly. The kitchen was full of grey morning light. Outside, the dogs had come to the glass door and were sitting with their noses pressed against it, very quietly, watching.

“The photograph,” he said, without opening his eyes. “In the shooter’s bag. There was a photograph of you.”

Her hand paused in his hair.

“Through the shop window. Last week. You were laughing at something.” He swallowed. “Someone had drawn a red circle around your face.”

She didn’t say anything.

“When I saw that,” Zhao said, “I stopped being afraid. I’ve been afraid since the phone call. Since I saw the blood on the blanket. I was afraid all the way through the first day. Then I opened the bag and saw the photograph, and it stopped.” He opened his eyes and looked up at her. “And after that I didn’t feel anything. For a whole day. At the karaoke bar. At the pond. Nothing. That’s what frightens me now. Not what I did. That I didn’t feel it.”

She looked down at him.

At the scarred, dangerous, broken man with his head in her lap, who had just killed three people, and was telling her so, and was more frightened of the fact that he hadn’t been frightened than of anything he had done with his hands.

And somewhere very deep inside her, where she had felt it before, at the kitchen sink after the warehouse, she felt it again. The terrible thing. The gladness.

She was glad the man with the fish tattoo was dead. She was glad Qiu Wen was in his koi pond. She had lain awake in the big bed for two nights with six strips of tape on her neck and Aurelia talking in the dark, and she had thought about Mimi’s yellow ribbon and Xiao Pan’s glittering back, and she had wanted them dead. She had wanted it the way she had once wanted the Iron Docks to be a place she never had to go.

It was not the gladness that frightened her this time. She had known it was in her since the warehouse.

It was that she wasn’t ashamed of it.

“You felt it,” she said quietly.

He looked up at her.

“Just now. On this floor. You shook for twenty minutes.” She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart. “That was you feeling it. It just took a day to catch up.”

He looked at her.

Then he turned his face into her stomach and put his arms round her waist and held on, and she sat on the kitchen floor and held his head and looked out at the grey sea.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when he had eaten two bowls of congee at the counter on one of the tall stools, sitting down, without being asked, she sat across from him and said the thing she had been thinking for two days.

“They knew the schedule.”

He looked up from his bowl.

“The shooter. The photograph.” She turned her teacup. “He took a picture through the window a week ago. He knew what time I’d be at the counter. He knew Bao reads the paper in the corner and only looks up when the door opens. He knew the ninth was a Wednesday and Wednesdays are slow at four.” She looked at him. “Somebody told them.”

“Yes,” said Zhao.

“Did Lu say who?”

He was quiet for a moment.

“He said the schedule came from the fixer’s people,” Zhao said. “That was all he knew. ‘The fixer’s people.’ Qiu Wen had someone inside.”

The fixer.

Her father.

She sat very still.

“I was going to go myself,” he said. “Tonight. After I slept. To the Walled City. To find out who.”

“No.”

He looked at her.

“No,” Elowen said again, and her voice was steady, and very clear. “My family. Page three. Paragraph two. In everything that concerns my family, you answer to me.” She held his eyes. “You don’t go to my father’s house. I go.”

“Elowen—”

“You’ve done your forty-eight hours,” she said. “This one’s mine.”

He looked at her across the kitchen counter for a long time. At the white strips on her neck. At her hands around the teacup, perfectly steady.

Then he nodded.

“Take Bao,” he said.

“Bao has a bandaged arm and hasn’t slept in two days.”

“Take Bao anyway.”

She almost smiled.

“I’ll take Bao,” she said.

chapters.title: Elowen Goes to Her Father’s House
chapters.desc: Not to leave him. To find out who sold her schedule. The youngest Lin has already started looking.
chapters.content:
The house in the Walled City looked exactly the same.

That was the strangest part. Elowen stood at the gate with Bao behind her, his left arm in a fresh white bandage, and looked up at the tall old house with its narrow windows and its balcony where her mother’s lemon tree had stood for twenty years, and it was exactly the same. The same crack in the third step. The same red paper charm on the door from last New Year, faded pink. The same smell of the neighbour’s birds.

As if nothing had happened. As if nobody in this house had sold her.

Raiden opened the door before she could knock.

He had been watching from the window. Of course he had. He looked at her neck, at the six white strips, and his face did something she had only seen once before, when he was fourteen and had walked eight hundred kilometres to stand at this same gate.

He didn’t say anything. He put his arms round her on the doorstep and held on.

“Jie,” he said into her hair. “Jie, I’m sorry. The floor—I should have made the window stronger, I should have—”

“The floor saved four people,” said Elowen. “And a little girl’s sunflowers. Mostly.”

He laughed, a cracked sound, and let her go.

“Baba’s out,” he said. “He went to the office at six. He’s been going at six every day since it happened. He doesn’t come back until midnight.” Raiden looked at her carefully. “He sent flowers to your shop, did you know? Yesterday. Your boy Xiao Pan told me. White lilies. Baba hasn’t bought flowers since Ma died.”

“I didn’t know.”

“He didn’t put a card in.” Raiden stepped back to let her in. “Eliana’s upstairs. She hasn’t slept since Wednesday. She wants to see you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana’s room at the top of the house had always been dark, even in daytime. Blackout curtains. Three monitors on the desk and two on the wall. Cables everywhere, taped neatly along the skirting boards in colour-coded bundles. A camp bed in the corner that she apparently slept on instead of her real bed, which was covered in hard drives.

She was eighteen now. She sat in her chair in a hoodie three sizes too big, with her knees up to her chin, and when Elowen came in she didn’t get up. She looked at the white strips on her sister’s neck for a long moment, and her face went very still.

Then she said, in a small flat voice, “I found him.”

Elowen sat down on the camp bed.

“I started on Wednesday night,” Eliana said. “After I sent your husband the camera footage. I thought, they had to know when you’d be at the counter. They had to know about Bao. So I made a list. Everyone who knows your schedule. The shop staff. The family. Zhao’s people.” She turned to her keyboard. “And Baba’s people. Because Baba always knows where we are. He has his drivers report it. He’s done it since Ma died.”

“I know,” said Elowen quietly. She had always known. Every night at eight, the phone call. Have you eaten? He had always known where she was. She had thought it was love. It was. It was also a list.

“I went through all of it,” said Eliana. “Phones. Bank accounts. Messages. I’m not supposed to be able to see Baba’s staff accounts. I can.” She clicked. A spreadsheet came up on the main screen, columns of dates and numbers. “Somebody who works for Baba got paid. Four times. Cash deposits, all under the reporting limit, all into an account in his mother’s name. The first one was six weeks ago. The last one was the day before the shooting.”

She clicked again. A face came up on the screen. A photograph from a driving licence.

Elowen knew the face.

A man in his forties, square-jawed, with a gun under his jacket. She had first seen him getting out of her father’s car at two in the morning, a year ago, the week Old Tan was found in the alley with both legs broken.

Protection, her father had said, not meeting her eyes. I hired him.

“Feng,” said Elowen.

“Feng Jun,” said Eliana. “Baba’s bodyguard. He drives Baba everywhere. He was with Baba on Sundays when you came for lunch. He sat in the kitchen. He heard everything.” Her voice wobbled, just slightly, and she made it stop. “He heard you tell Baba that Wednesdays are slow. He heard you say Bao reads the paper in the corner. He heard you, Jie. At Sunday lunch. And then he sold it.”

Elowen sat on the camp bed and looked at the face on the screen.

Every Sunday for a year, she had walked into this house and talked about her week over lunch, and that man had been sitting in the kitchen eating rice, listening.

“There’s something else,” said Eliana.

She didn’t turn round from the screen. Her knees were pulled up very tight.

“I wasn’t going to show you. I thought about deleting it. But you’d find out. You always find out.” She clicked. A message thread appeared. Two phones. Short messages, dated. “Baba knew.”

The room went very quiet.

“Not about the shooting,” Eliana said quickly. “I don’t think he knew that. I don’t. But he knew Feng was selling something. He found out eight days before. He found the account. Look.” She pointed. “Baba sent this. To Feng. On the first.”

Elowen read it.

I know about your mother’s account. Come to the office tonight. We need to talk.

And underneath it, from Feng, an hour later:

Talk all you like, old man. But if I go, the story about the paper twins goes with me. To people who pay a lot more than Qiu Wen.

And then nothing.

No reply from her father. No more messages. Eight days of nothing. And then a black car coming down her street at 4:12 on a Wednesday afternoon.

“What story about the paper twins?” Eliana whispered. “Jie. What does that mean? Raiden and Evangeline? What story?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen didn’t answer.

She sat on the camp bed in her sister’s dark room and looked at the message on the screen and felt something enormous move in her chest, the way she imagined the earth moved before it opened.

She knew what it meant.

She had known for as long as she could remember, and had been told never to know it. A night when her father came home with a baby wrapped in a foreign silk blanket and her mother cried in the kitchen. Two days later, her mother came home from hospital with Raiden. And then Raiden was gone—sent away, somewhere, she was told he was sick—and there was only the foreign baby, who was now called Evangeline, and who everyone said was Raiden’s twin. And when Raiden came back at fourteen, walking up to the gate filthy and alone, the whole family had simply gone on saying it. Twins. As if saying it enough times made it true.

She didn’t know where the baby had come from. Not exactly. Only that her father had once said, very drunk, at New Year, that Evangeline was worth more than this house, and her mother had told him to be quiet, and he had been.

Eight days. Her father had known for eight days that the man sitting in his kitchen every Sunday was selling things. And Feng had said: if I go, the paper twins go with me. And her father had chosen.

He had chosen Evangeline’s secret over Elowen’s Wednesdays.

Or he hadn’t known it was her Wednesdays. He had thought it was routes, money, the usual. He hadn’t asked. He hadn’t wanted to know.

Either way, he had been silent for eight days.

Either way, a black car had come down her street.

“Jie?” Eliana said. Very small. “Are you all right?”

Elowen stood up.

“Print it,” she said. “All of it. The deposits, the messages, his photograph. Two copies.”

“Where are you going?”

Elowen looked at her little sister, curled in her enormous hoodie in the glow of the monitors, eighteen years old and so tired her eyes were red, who had stayed awake for three days to find the man who had sold her big sister to a shooter.

She bent down and kissed the top of Eliana’s head.

“To Baba’s office,” she said. “He’s been there since six every morning. I think he’s waiting for me.”

chapters.title: The Man in Her Father’s Office
chapters.desc: Feng is sitting in the outer room, eating sunflower seeds. Her father has known for eight days.
chapters.content:
Her father’s office was on the second floor of an old building near the river, above a shop that sold fishing nets.

She had been there a hundred times as a child. She knew the smell of the stairwell: damp concrete and tobacco and the faint fishy tang from the shop below. She knew the outer room where the secretary used to sit, with its plastic chairs and its calendar of beautiful women holding bottles of beer. She knew the inner door with her father’s name on a brass plate.

She did not expect Feng to be sitting in the outer room.

But he was. In the secretary’s chair, with his feet up on her empty desk, eating sunflower seeds out of a paper twist and dropping the shells on the floor. He looked up when Elowen came through the door, with Bao behind her.

For a moment, his face didn’t change at all.

Then he saw Bao. He saw Bao’s bandaged arm. And he saw the folder in Elowen’s hand, and something in his square face went very still, the way an animal goes still when it hears something in the grass.

“Miss Lin,” he said. He took his feet off the desk. “Your father’s busy.”

“I know,” said Elowen. “He’s been busy for eight days.”

Feng’s hand went inside his jacket.

Bao said, very quietly, “Don’t.”

Feng’s hand stopped.

They looked at each other across the outer office: Feng in the secretary’s chair, his hand halfway inside his jacket, and Bao in the doorway with his arm in a sling and his other hand in his own coat pocket, holding something that made a shape against the fabric.

“He’s been up for three days,” said Elowen pleasantly, to Feng. “He has forty stitches in his arm. He’s very tired and very angry, and he’s very fond of me. I wouldn’t.”

Feng took his hand out of his jacket. Slowly. Empty.

“Good,” said Elowen. “Stay there.”

She walked past him to her father’s door and opened it without knocking.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian was sitting at his desk.

He wasn’t working. The desk was covered in papers, but he wasn’t looking at them. He was sitting with his hands folded on the blotter in front of him, very still, looking at the door, as though he had been sitting exactly like that for a long time.

When he saw her, he closed his eyes.

“Elowen,” he said.

She shut the door behind her. She walked to his desk. She put the folder down on it, on top of his papers, and opened it, and laid out the pages one by one, the way she laid out stems on the workbench. The bank deposits. The dates. Feng’s driving licence photograph. And on top of everything, the two messages.

I know about your mother’s account. Come to the office tonight.

If I go, the story about the paper twins goes with me.

Her father looked down at the messages.

He didn’t ask how she had got them. He didn’t say Eliana. He didn’t pretend. He just looked at the printouts on his desk, and his face slowly crumpled, the way paper crumples in a fire.

“I didn’t know it was you,” he said. His voice was barely there. “Elowen. I swear on your mother. I didn’t know he was selling your—your days. Your hours. I thought it was routes. Money. The usual. Men like Feng always sell something. I thought it was the business.”

“You didn’t ask.”

“No.”

“You found out he was selling information to Qiu Wen. Qiu Wen, Baba, the man whose warehouse my husband burned. The man whose brother burned my van. And you didn’t ask what.”

“No.”

“Why?”

He didn’t answer.

“Because of this,” said Elowen, and put her finger on the second message. The paper twins. “Because he said he’d sell that.”

Her father looked up at her. His eyes were red and wet and very old.

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat down.

She hadn’t meant to. Her legs gave way and there was a chair behind her, the visitor’s chair, the one she used to sit in when she was eight and came here after school to do her homework while he made phone calls. She sat in it and looked at her father across his desk.

“Tell me,” she said.

He was quiet.

“You know some of it,” he said at last.

“I know that a baby came home in a silk blanket when I was two. I know Ma cried. I know Raiden went away and Evangeline stayed, and we were all told to call them twins.” Her voice was steady. “I know you once said she was worth more than our house. I don’t know anything else. Nobody ever told me anything else.”

Her father unfolded his hands. He laid them flat on the desk. They were shaking.

“I was hired,” he said slowly, “to make a baby disappear.”

Elowen didn’t move.

“A woman came to me. From a foreign court. A country you would know the name of, if I said it. I won’t say it. The king had a child with someone who wasn’t the queen. The child was a problem. The family wanted the problem moved. Somewhere far away. Permanently.” He swallowed. “They didn’t say kill. They never say kill. They said moved permanently, and paid me more money than I had ever seen.”

“And you didn’t.”

“I looked at her,” said her father, “in the back of the car. In her silk blanket. She was three days old and she didn’t cry. She just looked at me. And I thought about you, at home, two years old, and your mother pregnant with Raiden.” His voice cracked. “And I thought—I thought, a royal child. A king’s daughter. If I kept her, hid her, one day she might be worth something. As a secret. As leverage. Against a throne.”

He looked at Elowen with an expression of such naked shame that she almost looked away.

“That’s the truth,” he said. “I want you to have the truth, for once in your life. I didn’t save her because I was kind. I saved her because I thought she was valuable. And then your mother held her, and cried, and named her Evangeline, which means bringer of good news, and I couldn’t do anything with her after that. She was ours. But the secret was still worth more than this house. It still is. If the wrong people knew she was alive, and where—”

“Traffickers,” said Elowen. “Ransom. Her father’s enemies.”

“Yes.”

“And so you hid Raiden. Your real son. You sent him away to a safe house in the borderland so nobody would ever count the babies and notice there were two.” She heard her voice rising and couldn’t stop it. “He was in a freezer, Baba. When he was nine. For eleven hours. Did you know that? Did he ever tell you? He counted to forty thousand in the dark because he thought men were coming for him.”

Her father’s face went grey.

“I didn’t know,” he whispered.

“You didn’t ask.” She was on her feet now. She didn’t remember standing. “You never ask. You didn’t ask Raiden what it was like. You didn’t ask Evangeline what it was like being worth more than a house. You didn’t ask Feng what he was selling. You didn’t ask me if I was happy when I married Zhendong. You came to dinner and told him I didn’t choose him and you never once asked me—”

She stopped.

Her father was crying.

He was sitting at his desk with his face in his hands and his shoulders shaking, silently, the way Zhao had cried on the bathroom floor, and she stood over him with the printouts spread between them and found she couldn’t finish the sentence.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a long time before either of them spoke.

When her father finally lifted his face, he looked like a man who had been beaten.

“Eight days,” he said hoarsely. “I sat in this chair for eight days and told myself it was routes. Money. I told myself Feng was bluffing. I told myself I would deal with him after the holiday, quietly, when it was safe. I told myself everything except the truth, which was that I was afraid. I was afraid for Evangeline, and I was afraid of Zhao Zhendong finding out that one of my men had been talking to Qiu Wen, and I was afraid of losing everything I have ever built.” He looked at her. “And then on Wednesday, Raiden called me from the hospital. And said your name. And said glass.”

Elowen didn’t say anything.

“I’ve been sitting here every day since,” said Lin Jian. “Waiting. I knew Zhao would come. I thought he would come and kill me, and I would let him. I thought that was fair.” He wiped his face with the back of his hand. “I didn’t think he would send you.”

“He didn’t send me.” She picked up the printouts and squared their edges. “He wanted to come. I told him no. I told him this was mine.”

Her father stared at her.

“He listened to you,” he said slowly.

“He always listens to me.”

“The arms dealer,” said Lin Jian, “who made my hands shake for six years, who put a knife through a man’s hand at dinner, who I hear”—his voice dropped—“put Qiu Wen in his own fish pond last night. He wanted to come here. And you said no. And he stayed home.”

“Yes.”

Her father looked at her for a very long time.

“I was wrong,” he said. “At your dinner table. What I said to him.” He swallowed. “Wasn’t I?”

She thought about her husband on the kitchen floor that morning, shaking, holding on to the back of her dressing gown as if she were the only fixed thing in the world. About a man saying I’m sorry, for the first time in a year, on the bottom stair. About a note taped to a wall underground. I’ll come.

“Yes,” said Elowen. “You were.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Through the door, she could hear the scrape of a chair. Feng. Moving.

She turned to the door.

“What will you do?” her father asked. “About Feng?”

She stood with her hand on the door handle.

She could open it now and tell Bao to call her husband. One phone call. Feng would be gone by tonight. Nobody would ever find him. The paper twins would stay a secret, because dead men don’t sell anything, and Evangeline would be safe, and she would never have to think about Feng again.

She thought about the koi pond. About Tian with his fish tattoo. About Zhao shaking on the kitchen floor, saying I didn’t feel anything, more frightened of that than of anything he had done.

She thought about I don’t kill them first.

“Not that,” she said.

“Then what?”

Elowen took out her phone. She scrolled. She found a name she had never called before, a number Aurelia had put into her phone on the night of the gala, saying for emergencies, darling, the real kind.

“I’m going to call the only person in this city,” she said, “who can make a man disappear without anyone dying.”

She pressed the name.

It rang once.

“Mrs. Zhao,” said Chen Si.

chapters.title: What a Daughter Owes
chapters.desc: The truth about the paper twins comes out at the kitchen table in the Walled City. Evangeline already knew.
chapters.content:
Chen Si came to the fishing-net building in a quarter of an hour, in a camel coat, with two men who stayed in the stairwell and a lawyer who stayed in the car.

He looked at Feng in the secretary’s chair. He looked at Bao in the doorway with his bandaged arm. He looked at the printouts in Elowen’s hand and read them standing up, all of them, in silence, while Feng watched him and slowly understood who he was.

Then Chen Si turned to Elowen and said, “Go home to the Walled City and have dinner with your family. I’ll take it from here.”

“I want to know what you’re going to do.”

“I’m going to have a conversation with Mr. Feng about his mother’s bank account,” said Chen Si mildly, “and about where he was on the night a warehouse manager called Old Tan had both his legs broken behind the fish market, a year ago. I think he’ll find it a very interesting conversation.” He glanced at Feng, whose face had gone the colour of old rice. “And then I’m going to call your friend Detective Song. Nobody will die, Mrs. Zhao. I promise. I keep promises. Your husband can tell you that.”

She looked at him.

“He told me,” she said, “that you carried him through the sewers when he was fifteen.”

Something moved in Chen Si’s calm face.

“He was very heavy,” he said. “Go home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went home. Not the house on the hill. The house in the Walled City.

Her father came with her, in the back of Bao’s car, with his hands folded in his lap. Neither of them spoke.

Raiden was in the kitchen. Evangeline was in the kitchen. Eliana came down from her dark room at the top of the house with her laptop clutched against her chest like a shield, and stood in the doorway, and looked at her father’s face, and at Elowen’s, and sat down very quietly on the bottom stair.

Elara was on the phone, on speaker, propped against the teapot. She had a shift at the hospital and couldn’t come. “I’m listening,” she said. “Go on. I’m listening.”

Elowen looked at her father.

“You tell them,” she said. “I’m not doing it for you this time.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told them.

He sat at the head of the kitchen table, in his funeral suit, and told them everything he had told her in his office. The woman from the foreign court. The baby in the silk blanket. Moved permanently. The money. The decision to keep her, not because he was kind, but because she was valuable. The other baby, his real son, born two days later and sent away to a borderland safe house so nobody would ever count. The lie the whole family had told for twenty-three years.

He didn’t look away from any of them while he said it. Elowen would give him that, later. He looked at each of them in turn, and when he reached the part about valuable, he looked straight at Evangeline, and his voice broke, and he kept going.

Nobody said anything when he finished.

Raiden was staring at the table. His hands were flat on the wood, very still. He looked, suddenly, much younger than twenty-three. He looked nine. He looked like a boy sitting in the dark in a chest freezer, counting.

Eliana was crying silently on the stairs, her face pressed against the lid of her laptop.

On the phone, Elara said, very quietly, “Oh, Baba.”

And Evangeline—

Evangeline sat at the far end of the table where she always sat, with her hands folded around a cup of tea, and looked at her father with a calm, clear, quiet face.

“I know,” she said.

Everyone turned.

“I’ve known since I was fifteen,” said Evangeline. Her voice was soft. She almost never spoke at the table. They all leaned in to hear her, the way they always had. “I found the blanket. In the cedar chest in the attic. Silk. With a crest on it in gold thread. I looked the crest up in the library.” She turned her teacup. “I didn’t say anything. I thought—if I said it, it would become real. And then I would have to be it. A princess. A problem. A thing worth more than a house.” She looked at her father. “I didn’t want to be worth anything. I just wanted to be your daughter.”

Lin Jian made a sound that Elowen had never heard a human being make. He put his face down on the kitchen table, on his folded arms, and his shoulders shook.

Evangeline got up.

She walked down the length of the table, past Raiden, past Elowen, and stopped beside her father’s chair. She stood there for a moment. Then she put her hand on his back, between his shoulder blades, very lightly, and left it there.

She didn’t say anything else. Evangeline almost never did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden stood up so suddenly his chair fell over.

Everyone jumped. He didn’t pick it up. He stood in the middle of the kitchen with his fists clenched and his face white, looking at his father’s bowed head.

“Eleven hours,” he said.

His father lifted his head.

“When I was nine,” said Raiden. His voice was shaking. His silly, cheerful, empty-headed voice was gone; this was his real one, low and flat, like their father’s. “There were men on the road. I thought they were coming for me. I hid in a chest freezer in the yard for eleven hours. I counted to forty thousand. I lost track. I wet myself. I didn’t come out until the sun came up.” He swallowed. “And I thought, all those years, that it was because I was in danger. That you sent me there because someone wanted to hurt me. That I was important. That I was being protected.”

He laughed. It was a terrible sound.

“I wasn’t being protected,” he said. “I was being hidden. So nobody would count. I was the spare. I was the one you could lose.”

“Raiden—”

“Don’t.” Raiden held up his hand. “Don’t. Not yet. I can’t—” He stopped. He looked at Evangeline, standing beside their father with her hand on his back. His twin. His not-twin. The girl he had argued with about who was older their whole lives.

Then he crossed the kitchen and put his arms around her.

Evangeline went still for a second, the way she always did when anyone touched her. Then she put her arms around him too, and held on, and the two of them stood beside their father’s chair, holding each other, the real son and the stolen princess, and neither of them said anything.

Elowen sat at the table and watched them and could not see properly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when the others had gone up to bed and the kitchen was dark except for the lamp over the stove, she sat with her father at the table.

He looked smaller than he had that morning. He looked like a man who had put down something very heavy and didn’t know how to stand up straight without it.

“What happens now?” he asked.

“Chen Si called. Feng confessed. About Old Tan. He was working for the Qiu brothers the whole time, Baba. They put him with you. He was the one who broke Old Tan’s legs, a year ago, and then he came to you the next week and said he could protect you.” She watched her father’s face. “You hired the man who did it.”

Lin Jian closed his eyes.

“Wei Long arrested him an hour ago,” said Elowen. “For Old Tan, for the money, for helping plan a shooting. Chen Si’s lawyer will make sure he never gets bail. And Chen Si told him that if he ever says one word to anyone about twins, his mother’s bank account will be the least of his problems.” She paused. “I believe Chen Si. Feng believed him too. Wei Long said he was shaking.”

“And Zhao?”

“I’ll tell Zhendong everything. Tonight. Tomorrow.” She turned her teacup. “I don’t lie to him. That was the deal.”

“Even about Evangeline?”

“He’ll keep it,” said Elowen. “He keeps everything I give him. He’s very good at keeping things.”

Her father was quiet.

“What do I owe you?” he said finally. “Tell me. Whatever it is. I owe you. I’ve owed you since you were seven and your mother died and you put on her apron and made dinner for five children and never once asked me for anything.” His voice cracked. “You married a man you were afraid of, for me. And then I sold your Wednesdays to keep a secret. What do I owe you, Elowen? Tell me.”

She looked at her father across the kitchen table where she had grown up.

She thought about all the things a daughter owes. And all the things a father does.

“Ask,” she said.

He looked at her.

“That’s all,” said Elowen. “Ask Raiden what it was like. Ask Evangeline what she wants to be. Ask Eliana why she never sleeps. Ask Elara if she’s happy at the hospital.” She stood up. “And next time you see my husband, ask him something. Anything. Ask him how the lemon tree is. Don’t tell him who I chose. Ask him.”

Her father sat very still.

“And me?” he said quietly.

She stopped at the door.

“I won’t come to Sunday lunch for a while,” she said. “I need some time. I’ll come back. But not for a while.”

He nodded slowly. He didn’t argue. He didn’t tell her she was being dramatic, or ungrateful, or a hundred other things he would once have said.

“All right,” said Lin Jian. And then, after a moment, so quietly she almost didn’t hear: “Elowen. Are you happy? With him?”

She stood in the doorway with her hand on the frame and looked back at him.

He had asked.

“Yes, Baba,” she said. “I am.”

chapters.title: Chen Si Makes a Phone Call
chapters.desc: The software fixes what the hardware can’t. Then Aurelia, in a bathtub full of champagne, tells Elowen the thing she’s never told anyone.
chapters.epigraph: “Zhendong is the hammer. I am the hand that decides where it falls. Your wife, it turns out, is the hand that decides when it doesn’t.” — Chen Si
chapters.content:
She didn’t go home that night.

She meant to. She stood at the gate of the house in the Walled City at eleven, with Bao holding the car door, and her phone in her hand, and her husband’s name on the screen, and found that she couldn’t make herself press it.

Not because she was angry. Because she was empty. Because she had spent twelve hours pulling the truth out of her family one thread at a time, and she had nothing left, and she knew that the moment she saw his face, she would fall apart, and she didn’t want to fall apart on him. Not yet. Not when he had only just stopped shaking on the kitchen floor.

So she texted him instead.

Feng. Baba’s bodyguard. Arrested. Chen Si helped. Nobody dead. I’m safe. I need one night. I’ll tell you everything. I promise. Don’t come.

The reply came in less than ten seconds.

Ok.

And then, a minute later:

Where will you sleep?

She looked at the screen.

Then a black car pulled up behind Bao’s, very quietly, and the back window rolled down, and Aurelia Chen leaned out in a cashmere coat with her hair in a messy knot and no makeup and said, “Get in, darling. You’re sleeping at ours. Chen Si already told your husband. He said ‘ok’ to him too. They’re both very articulate tonight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Chen penthouse was on the forty-fourth floor of a tower in the Coastal High-Rise, and it was everything the house on the hill was not. Glass on every side. White marble floors. Art on the walls that Elowen suspected was real. A view over the entire city, every light of it, all the way to the dark line of the sea and the cranes of the Iron Docks, small and far away.

Aurelia walked straight through it all, kicked off her shoes, and ran a bath.

“I don’t want a bath,” said Elowen.

“It’s not for you,” said Aurelia. “It’s for me. You can sit on the edge. I’m not drinking alone.”

The bathtub was the size of a small swimming pool, black stone, sunk into the floor in front of a window that looked straight down forty-four floors. Aurelia filled it with bubbles that smelled of fig, got in wearing nothing at all, and opened a bottle of champagne with a loud pop and poured two glasses and held one out to Elowen.

Elowen sat on the edge of the bath in her clothes, with six white strips on her neck, and took it.

“To Feng,” said Aurelia, “who is going to spend a very long time in a very small room, thinking about his choices.”

They drank.

“What did Chen Si do?” Elowen asked.

“The usual.” Aurelia leaned her head back against the stone. “He made three phone calls. One to Detective Song, to say where to find Feng and what to find with him. One to a judge who owes him a great deal, to say that Feng is a danger to society and must not be granted bail under any circumstances. And one to Feng’s lawyer, who works for us, to say that if Feng ever says the word ‘twins’ in any language, the lawyer should make sure Feng understands exactly what happens next.” She sipped her champagne. “Nobody shouted. Nobody bled. My husband is very good at making problems quiet.”

“That’s why I called him.”

“I know.” Aurelia turned her head and looked at her. “Do you know what he said when he hung up the phone with you? He was standing in the kitchen. He put the phone down and he looked at me, and he said, ‘Zhendong’s wife just stopped him killing a man by calling me instead.’ And then he said, ‘That has never happened before. Not once since Block C.’” Aurelia smiled faintly. “He sounded impressed. He doesn’t sound impressed very often. It was quite attractive.”

Elowen looked down into her glass.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You stayed with me,” she said, after a while. “For two days. When he was gone. You slept in the guest room with the door open.”

“Somebody had to.”

“You didn’t have to.” Elowen looked at her. “We’ve hated each other since we were fifteen.”

“We have never hated each other,” said Aurelia. “We’ve competed. It’s different. You hate people you don’t respect.” She set her glass on the edge of the bath. “And I came because I know what it’s like. The waiting. The phone that doesn’t ring. The man walking out of the door at two in the morning and you not knowing what will come back.”

Elowen waited.

Aurelia looked out of the window, at the city spread below like spilled jewels.

“The spring after we married,” she said, “Chen Si was poisoned.”

Elowen went still.

“At a dinner. Someone inside the Syndicate. A glass of wine. He drank it, and he finished his sentence, and then his hand started shaking and he put the glass down and said, very calmly, ‘Aurelia, I think you should call a doctor,’ and then he fell off his chair.” Her voice was perfectly steady. “He was in a bed for eleven days. He couldn’t move. He couldn’t speak for four of them. And the man who did it was still in the Syndicate, sitting at the table, waiting to see if he would die.”

“What did you do?”

Aurelia turned her head and smiled. It was not a nice smile. It was a beautiful one.

“I ran everything,” she said. “For eleven days. In his name. I signed his signature on forty documents. I sat in his chair at his meetings and told his men he was in Zurich on business and if anyone questioned me I would remember their name. I found the man who poisoned him by the sixth day.” She picked up her glass again. “I won’t tell you what I did to him. You’d think less of me.”

“I wouldn’t.”

Aurelia looked at her.

“No,” she said slowly. “You wouldn’t. Not anymore. Would you?”

Elowen thought about a koi pond. About Tian with his fish tattoo. About the gladness, and how she was not ashamed of it.

“No,” she said.

Aurelia nodded, as if something had been confirmed.

“When he woke up,” she said, “on the eleventh day, he looked at me. I was sitting beside the bed with a laptop on my knees and a gun in my lap. I hadn’t slept properly in a week. I looked terrible. And he looked at me for a very long time, and he said, ‘Ah. I didn’t marry a wife. I married a co-ruler.’” She laughed softly. “A month later he asked me to sign a new marriage contract. Seventy pages. Co-ruler, in writing. I made him rewrite clause forty.”

Elowen laughed despite herself.

“That’s why I came,” said Aurelia. “Not because I like you. I do, God help me. But because the night I sat by that bed with a gun, I was more alone than I have ever been in my life. Nobody sat with me. Nobody slept in my guest room with the door open. My own mother didn’t call.” She turned her head. “I wasn’t going to let that happen to you. Not while I’m alive. That’s all.”

They looked at each other across the black stone bath.

Then Elowen put down her glass, stood up, took off her shoes, and got into the bath with all her clothes on.

Aurelia stared at her.

“You’re wearing jeans,” she said.

“I know.”

“Those are wet jeans. In my bath. With my fig bubbles.”

“I know,” said Elowen, and sat down in the warm water up to her chest, fully dressed, with six white strips on her neck, and leaned her head back against the stone beside Aurelia’s, and started, finally, after three days, to cry.

Aurelia didn’t say anything. She put her arm around Elowen’s wet shoulders and pulled her in, and let her cry into her neck, and poured more champagne with her other hand, and looked out over the whole lit city.

“There,” she said softly, after a long time. “There. It’s all right. Your husband’s waiting for you. He’s sitting on your stairs. Chen Si checked. He’s been sitting there since you texted him.”

Elowen lifted her head.

“He’s on the stairs?”

“Since eleven,” said Aurelia. “With the dogs. Bao says he hasn’t moved.” She smiled. “Tomorrow, darling. Go home tomorrow. Tonight you’re in my bath, getting my champagne in your wet jeans, and we’re going to talk about how terrible Miles Wei’s suit was at the reunion. And then you’re going to sleep. And in the morning, you’ll go home to the man on the stairs and tell him everything, and he’ll look at you the way he always looks at you, and you’ll finally, finally say it.”

“Say what?”

Aurelia gave her a long, pitying look.

“Elowen,” she said. “I’ve known you for ten years. I know when you’re holding something in your mouth. You’ve been holding it for months. Everyone can see it but him.”

Elowen didn’t answer.

Far below, at the edge of the city, the cranes of the Iron Docks stood dark against the sea. And somewhere beyond them, on a hill, in a concrete house with fourteen locks and a lemon tree in the hall, a man was sitting on the bottom stair with two dogs at his feet, waiting, the way he had waited outside her door every night of the first month of their marriage.

So she would know where he was.

So she wouldn’t have to wonder.

chapters.title: She Comes Back Through the Front Door
chapters.desc: He has been sitting on the stairs all night. She tells him everything. Then she tries to tell him one more thing, and he stops her.
chapters.content:
She came home at seven in the morning, in a pair of Aurelia’s trousers that were too long for her and a cashmere jumper that probably cost more than her van.

Bao drove. He had slept, finally, in the Chens’ guest room, and he looked almost human. When they turned onto the hill and the house came into view, grey and square against a pale sky, he said, without looking in the mirror:

“He hasn’t moved. The guardhouse says. Since eleven last night.”

Elowen looked out of the window at the house.

“Has he eaten?”

“No.”

“Slept?”

Bao was quiet for a moment.

“Miss Lin,” he said. “When you had the fever, in the typhoon—no. Before that. The first month. When you slept with your door open, and he sat outside it.” He turned onto the gravel drive. “He did that every night. I used to check on him at three, on my rounds. Every night, he was awake. Sitting there. Every single night for a month.”

She hadn’t known that. She had thought he slept, sitting up. She had thought he dozed.

“He doesn’t sleep when he doesn’t know where you are,” said Bao. “He never has.” He stopped the car at the foot of the steps. “I thought you should know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The dogs met her at the door. They didn’t bark. They pressed themselves against her legs, one on each side, whining very softly, the way dogs do when someone in the house has been sad for a long time.

She opened the front door.

He was sitting on the bottom stair.

He was in the same grey sweatshirt from the Docks, the one that didn’t fit. He was sitting with his elbows on his knees and his hands hanging loose between them, looking at the front door, as if he had been looking at it all night and had forgotten how to look at anything else. The lemon tree stood at the end of the hall behind him in the grey light.

When she came in, he didn’t move. He just looked at her.

Then he stood up, slowly, like an old man. One hand on the banister.

“You came back,” he said.

His voice was rough, as if he hadn’t used it in a long time.

She stood in the doorway in Aurelia’s clothes and looked at him.

“You thought I wouldn’t?”

He didn’t answer. He didn’t have to. She could see it in his face: a whole night on the bottom stair, with the dogs and the lemon tree, waiting to find out if the woman who had married him to protect her father would come back, now that she knew her father had been the one to sell her.

Now that she didn’t need protecting from Zhao Zhendong anymore.

Now that there was no reason left.

“Oh, Zhendong,” she said.

She crossed the hall. She walked right into him. She put her arms around his waist and her face against his chest and held on, and for a second he didn’t move at all, he stood there with his hands hanging at his sides like a man who has been told good news and doesn’t believe it.

Then his arms came round her so hard it hurt.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him everything. Sitting on the bottom stair beside him, with his hand in hers and the dogs at their feet.

Feng. The bank deposits. Sunday lunches, and Feng in the kitchen eating rice, listening. Her father and the eight days. The messages. The paper twins.

She told him about Evangeline. All of it. The foreign court, the silk blanket, moved permanently, the crest in gold thread in the cedar chest. Raiden in the freezer. Her father at the head of the kitchen table, telling them with his face open, not looking away.

She had promised him, at the very beginning, that she wouldn’t lie. So she didn’t. Not about any of it.

He listened without interrupting. He didn’t say anything when she told him about Evangeline. He only went very still beside her, and when she had finished, he said one thing.

“She’s safe. Evangeline. Nobody will hear it from me.”

“I know.”

“Not Chen Si. Not anyone.”

“I know, Zhendong. That’s why I told you.”

He nodded slowly. He looked at their joined hands.

“And Feng,” he said.

“Arrested. Wei Long took him. Chen Si made the calls. The judge, the lawyer.” She watched his face. “Nobody died. I chose that.”

He was quiet.

She waited for it. For you should have called me. For the flat, cold look, the lake frozen all the way down. For him to say that Feng had sat in her father’s kitchen and listened to her talk about her Wednesdays and sold them to a man who put a red circle round her face, and that men like that should not be left behind you, ever, because everything you leave behind comes back.

He looked at her.

“You chose that,” he repeated.

“Yes.”

“Not me. You.”

“Yes.”

He looked at her for a long, long moment in the grey morning light.

“Okay,” said Zhao.

That was all. Okay. He turned her hand over in his and held it.

She stared at him.

“You’re not angry?”

“I’m angry at Feng. I’m angry at your father.” He looked down at the floor. “I’m not angry at you. You had a choice. You made it your way. It worked. Nobody is dead and he can never hurt you again.” His jaw moved. “Yesterday I put a man in his own fish pond. I don’t get to tell you your way is wrong.”

She put her head on his shoulder.

“Chen Si said,” she told him quietly, “that I’m the hand that decides when the hammer doesn’t fall.”

Zhao breathed out, something that was almost a laugh.

“Chen Si says a lot of things,” he said. “He’s usually right. It’s very annoying.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him upstairs.

Not because she meant to. Because he was swaying where he sat, grey with exhaustion, and because she was too, and because she wanted, more than she had ever wanted anything, to lie down next to him somewhere soft and stop.

But when she pulled him into the big room at the end of the corridor and turned to him in the grey light, he put his hands on either side of her face, very gently, the way he had in the dark the first time, and looked at her, and she forgot about sleeping.

It was not slow. It was not careful. It was two people who had each spent two days believing they might have lost the other, finding out they hadn’t. He kissed her hard and badly, as if he’d forgotten how and didn’t care. She pulled his ugly grey sweatshirt over his head and threw it across the room, and he laughed into her mouth, ragged and disbelieving, and tugged at Aurelia’s expensive jumper until she had to stop him because she was laughing too hard to help.

“It’s cashmere,” she gasped. “It’s Aurelia’s. She’ll kill me—”

“Let her,” said Zhao, and pulled it off her anyway, and dropped it on the floor without folding it.

She stared at him.

He looked down at the jumper on the floor. Then at her.

“I didn’t fold it,” he said, as if he had only just noticed.

“No.”

“I always fold it.”

“I know you do.”

He looked at her for a second, with his chest heaving and his hair wild and an expression on his face she had never seen there before, something raw and astonished, as if he had finally let go of something he had been holding very carefully for a very long time and had just discovered that it didn’t break.

Then he picked her up and put her on the bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, in the full grey light of a morning that had become day, she lay on her side facing him with their legs tangled together and the sheet half off, and looked at his face on the pillow.

He was nearly asleep. His eyes were half closed. He looked younger than he had on the stairs. His hand was on her hip, his thumb moving slowly back and forth.

She thought about Aurelia in the black stone bath. You’ve been holding it for months. Everyone can see it but him.

She opened her mouth.

“Zhendong,” she said. “I—”

His eyes opened.

He looked at her. And she saw him see it, in her face: the word that was coming. She watched him understand what she was about to say.

He put two fingers against her lips. Very lightly.

“Don’t,” he said.

She stopped.

“Not today.” His voice was very low and very rough. “Not after this. Not after your father, and Feng, and the stairs. Not lying here like this.” His fingers stayed on her lips. “If you say it today, I’ll never know if it was true or if it was—” He swallowed. “If it was because you came home. Because you were sorry I sat on the stairs all night. Because you’re kind, and I looked tired, and you put yourself between people and the thing that hurts them. You’ve done it since you were seven.”

She looked at him over his fingers.

“I want to believe it,” said Zhao. “When you say it. I want to believe it so much it frightens me. So don’t say it on a day like this. Please.” His thumb moved, once, along her lower lip. “Say it on a day when nothing has happened.”

She was quiet.

Then she took his hand away from her mouth, and held it, and pressed a kiss to his scarred knuckles, one at a time.

“All right,” she said. “A day when nothing has happened.”

“A boring day.”

“The most boring day there has ever been,” said Elowen. “No glass. No fathers. No men in grey jackets. I’ll go to the market at four, and you’ll carry the buckets, and nobody will order anything with your name on it, and at the end of the day I’ll make fish, and you’ll sit down at the table, and then I’ll tell you.”

He looked at her.

“And you’ll mean it,” he said.

It wasn’t a question. It was the same thing he had said the morning after the typhoon, two centimetres from her face. And you’ll mean it?

“I already mean it,” said Elowen. “I’ve meant it for a long time. You just have to wait for a boring day to hear it.”

Something happened in his face. She couldn’t name it. It was like watching ice crack on a lake in spring: not breaking, not yet, but the first long line running across it, deep and quiet.

He pulled her in against his chest and held on.

“Okay,” he whispered into her hair. “A boring day.”

They fell asleep like that, at nine in the morning, with the curtains open and Aurelia’s cashmere jumper lying unfolded on the floor.

Neither of them knew that it would be two years before a boring day came.

Or that before it did, he would crawl home in the dark with a bullet in his side, and lie on the floor of the armory, and ask her first.

chapters.title: A Shipment With Children’s Names on It
chapters.desc: The biggest deal of his life. She reads the buyer’s file the way she reads everything. Then she says one word.
chapters.epigraph: “They’re all bad people, Elowen. Every buyer I have ever had.” “I know. But I can’t see the others’ names.”
chapters.content:
Two springs after the glass, the business had come back.

Not all of it. The Red Notice was still there, and the UN report, and he still couldn’t leave the country. Two of his oldest buyers had gone to other brokers and wouldn’t return his calls. But Qiu Wen was gone, and the Qiu brothers’ network had scattered like birds after a gunshot, and the men who had been watching to see if the wolf would fall had watched him walk into a koi pond garden at four in the morning and walk out again forty minutes later, and had quietly decided to keep doing business with him after all.

Elowen read his files now.

Not all of them. She had told him at the very beginning that she would read his routes and find his leaks, and for a long time she had only done that: shipping schedules, warehouse ledgers, the dull paper bones of the thing. She found two more small leaks the first year. She found a warehouse manager in the south who was skimming. She found an accountant who had been rounding numbers in his own favour for six years. She did it at the kitchen counter in the evenings with a pencil and a cup of tea, and he watched her do it with an expression she had once seen on Granny Su’s face when a new apprentice cut a stem correctly the first time.

She didn’t read the buyer files. He didn’t offer them. It was the one door in the house, now, that neither of them opened.

Until the night he brought one home and put it on the counter in front of her and said, “I want you to read this.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was thick. A grey cardboard folder, the kind her father used, held together with an elastic band.

“What is it?” she asked.

“The biggest deal I’ve ever been offered.” He sat down on the stool beside her. “A militia in the Velde highlands. They’re fighting a government that is also very bad. They want enough to arm four thousand men for two years. Rifles. Ammunition. Some heavier things.” He said it the way he said everything about the business: flat, factual, no colour in it. “If I take it, I’m back. Completely. The Red Notice won’t matter. Nobody will remember the UN report. Three hundred million.”

She looked at the folder.

“Why do you want me to read it?”

He didn’t answer for a moment.

“Because the broker is Maartens,” he said.

She went cold.

“He’s alive?”

“He’s alive. He’s in Rotterdam. He hasn’t replied to the photograph.” Zhao’s jaw tightened. “He’s been very quiet for two years. Then last week, his office sent this. Very polite. Very professional. As if the pond never happened. As if the peonies never happened.” He looked at the folder. “Either he’s desperate, or it’s a trap. I can’t tell which. I’ve been looking at it for a week. I can’t tell.” He turned his head and looked at her. “You see things in paper I don’t. You always have.”

She took the elastic band off the folder.

✦ ✦ ✦

She read it the way she read everything. Every page. Slowly. With a pencil.

The militia was called the Highland Liberation Front. There were maps. Lists of what they wanted, in the dry language she had learned at the dinner with Maartens: units, lots, the agricultural order. There was a proposed end-user certificate from a government in a third country, a small one, whose name she had to look up. There were flight routes. There was a payment schedule, in three parts, through banks in four countries.

It all looked very professional. It all looked like every other file her father had ever kept in the bottom drawer.

Then, near the back, between the payment schedule and a list of delivery coordinates, there was a section she almost turned past. It was not from Maartens. It looked as if someone had attached it by accident: a few pages photocopied from a longer document, slightly crooked, the stamp of an aid agency in the corner.

She stopped.

It was a report about the Highland Liberation Front. From a children’s charity. About how the militia found its soldiers.

They took them from schools. From villages. From refugee camps. Twelve years old. Thirteen. Fourteen. They gave them rifles that were too big for them and pills to make them brave, and they put them in the front lines, because children didn’t run, and didn’t ask questions, and were cheaper than men.

There was a photograph.

Five boys standing in a line in front of a mud wall. The tallest one might have been fourteen. The smallest couldn’t have been more than eleven. They were all holding rifles. The rifles were almost as tall as the smallest boy. They were all looking at the camera with the same flat, empty eyes.

And underneath the photograph, on the next page, there was a list.

Names. Ages. Villages. Children the charity had managed to identify, who had been taken. Some of them had a small cross beside them.

The list went on for four pages.

Elowen sat at her kitchen counter and read every single name.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she looked up, he was watching her.

He hadn’t moved. He had been sitting beside her for an hour and twenty minutes, not speaking, while she read. He looked at her face.

“What is it,” he said quietly.

She turned the folder round and pushed it toward him, open at the photograph.

He looked at the five boys in front of the mud wall. He didn’t say anything. He looked at the list on the next page. He turned the pages, one by one. Four pages. She watched his eyes move down the names.

When he reached the end, he closed the folder.

“I didn’t see that,” he said.

“I know. It was at the back. It looks like somebody put it there by mistake.”

“Maybe somebody did.”

“Or maybe someone in Maartens’ office wanted you to see it.” She folded her hands on the counter to keep them still. “Someone who doesn’t want this deal to happen either.”

He didn’t answer.

“Zhendong,” she said. “No.”

The kitchen was very quiet.

He looked at her. She could see him thinking. She could see the whole weight of it behind his eyes: three hundred million, and the Red Notice, and the brokers who had stopped returning his calls, and the men at the Docks who depended on him for their wages, and the long years of building something out of nothing in a world where nobody ever gave you anything.

“They’re all bad,” he said finally. Not arguing. Just telling her, the way he would tell her the truth about anything. “Every buyer I have ever had, Elowen. Every single one. The general Maartens bought for, at that dinner—he burned villages. The men in the south. The ones in the north. I don’t sell to good people. Good people don’t need what I sell.” He touched the folder with one finger. “If I don’t do this, someone else will. They’ll get the rifles anyway. From the Russians, or the Serbs, or a man in Dubai. Those boys will still be standing in front of that wall.”

“I know,” said Elowen.

“Then why this one?”

She looked at the closed folder. At the edge of the photograph, sticking out where he hadn’t pushed it back in properly. Five pairs of feet in the dust. The smallest pair barefoot.

“Because I can see their names,” she said.

He went very still.

“All the others,” she said, “I never saw. The villages the general burned. The people in the south. I knew. I knew what you did. I married you knowing it. I said at that dinner that I wanted to see it, and I saw it, and I stayed.” Her voice was shaking now, and she let it. “But I never saw a name. I never saw a face. And now I have, and I can’t not have seen them. There are four pages, Zhendong. I read every one. There’s a boy called Samuel who was eleven. There’s a cross next to his name.”

He didn’t say anything.

“I can’t live in this house,” said Elowen, “and sleep in that bed, and go to the market at four in the morning, and know that the rifles in that file went to the people who took Samuel. I can’t. I’ve tried to think of a way. I can’t find one.” She looked at him. “So I’m saying no. Not for the business. Not because it’s a trap, although it might be. Because of the names. That’s all. That’s the only reason I have.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was quiet for so long that she began to be afraid.

Not of him. Of the other thing. That this was the place where it ended. That she had walked up to the edge of what he was, and pointed over it, and he would look at her and say, very gently, Elowen, this is who I am. You knew.

He picked up the folder.

He opened it again, at the photograph. He looked at it. Then he turned to the list and ran his finger down the first page, slowly, until it stopped.

Samuel Okonjo. 11. Marisi village. ✝

He looked at the name.

“When I was eleven,” he said, very quietly, “I was carrying steel at Old Zhao’s yard. Twelve hours a day. He didn’t pay me. He fed me, if the work was good. When I dropped something, he burned me.” He didn’t look up from the page. “Nobody ever came to the yard to see what was happening to me. Nobody wrote my name on a list.”

She put her hand over his, on the page.

“I’m not a good man,” he said. “I’ll never be a good man. I don’t think I know how.” He closed the folder slowly, under her hand. “But I know what it’s like to be eleven and holding something too heavy for you because a man with a stove told you to.”

He stood up.

He walked to the kitchen bin. He opened it. He dropped the grey folder inside, on top of the onion skins and the fish bones from dinner, and closed the lid.

Then he came back and sat down on the stool beside her and put his face in his hands.

She didn’t say anything. She put her arm around his back and leaned against him and held on.

“Three hundred million,” he said, through his fingers, after a long time.

“I know.”

“Chen Si is going to be very angry.”

“I’ll talk to Chen Si.”

“Maartens is going to be angrier.”

“I know that too.”

He lifted his head and looked at her. His eyes were red. He looked, suddenly, very tired and very young, like a boy at a steel yard who has put something down for the first time in his life and doesn’t know what to do with his empty hands.

“You understand what this means,” he said. “If I say no to this. In front of everyone. To Maartens. After the pond.”

“Yes.”

“It means something is going to happen.”

“Yes,” said Elowen.

He looked at her for a long moment. Then he took her hand off his back and held it, and pressed his mouth to her palm, the way he had on the night he left for forty-eight hours.

“Okay,” he said against her skin. “Then something is going to happen.”

chapters.title: He Cancels the Deal
chapters.desc: Three hundred million, gone, because his wife said one word. Chen Si is furious. One of his men is worse.
chapters.content:
“No,” said Chen Si.

He said it calmly. He said everything calmly. But he had put down his coffee cup on the edge of Zhao’s desk with a small, precise click that Elowen had learned meant the same thing as another man throwing a chair.

“It’s done,” said Zhao.

“It is not done. Nothing is done until Maartens’ office gets the message, and his office hasn’t got it, because I told them you were ill.” Chen Si stood in the middle of the long bare office at the Docks with his hands in the pockets of his camel coat. “Zhendong. Three hundred million. It would put you back where you were before the notice. It would make every broker who stopped calling you crawl back. It would—”

“There are children in it, Si.”

“There are children in all of it.” Chen Si didn’t raise his voice. “There have always been children in all of it. You know that. I know that. Every rifle you have ever sold has ended up, at some point, in the hands of someone too young to hold it. That’s the business.” He turned to Elowen, who was sitting on the metal chair by the shelves where she had sat on the first day, the day of Kang. “Mrs. Zhao. With the greatest respect. You married an arms dealer.”

“I know what I married,” said Elowen.

“Then you know this is what he does.”

“It was what he did,” said Elowen. “He’s allowed to stop.”

Chen Si looked at her. Then he looked at his brother.

“Is that true?” he said. “Are you stopping?”

Zhao was standing at the whiteboard. It was covered in the routes for the Velde deal: flights, ports, arrows. He had been looking at it when Chen Si came in. He hadn’t wiped it.

“I don’t know,” he said. “I’m stopping this one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si was angry for exactly one day.

Elowen knew because Aurelia told her. Aurelia called at nine that night and said, “He came home and sat in the dark in his study for three hours and didn’t speak to me, and then he came out and said, ‘Your friend has ruined my brother,’ and I said, ‘Good,’ and he looked at me like I’d shot him, and then he laughed.” A pause. “He doesn’t laugh. He laughed. Then he went back into the study and made phone calls until two in the morning. I think he’s working out how to do it without anyone getting killed. He likes a puzzle.”

“Is he still angry?”
