“Oh, furious,” said Aurelia cheerfully. “But not at you. He said you were right. He said it in the voice he uses when he hates that someone else was right.” She paused again. “He said, ‘She read every name on the list. Zhendong never reads every name on anything. He reads the numbers.’”

The next morning, Chen Si sent his lawyer to the Docks with a letter for Maartens’ office in Rotterdam, very polite, very professional, regretting that due to unforeseen circumstances Northgate Agricultural Holdings was unable to proceed.

He sent a second letter, privately, to the children’s charity whose report had been in the back of the folder. Elowen didn’t know what was in that one. She only knew that a month later, the charity received an anonymous donation large enough to build a school.

✦ ✦ ✦

The men at the Docks were angrier than Chen Si.

Not all of them. Bao didn’t say anything. He never did. But on the morning the letter went to Rotterdam, he came into the shop at six, with the buckets, and put down the eucalyptus very carefully, and then stood in the middle of the floor for a moment looking at Elowen with an expression she couldn’t read.

“Miss Lin,” he said.

She looked up.

“My younger brother,” said Bao. “When I was twelve. A man came to our village. He offered money for boys. My father said no. The man came back with a truck.” He looked at the eucalyptus. “I was at the market in town. My brother was not.”

Elowen put down her knife.

“I never saw him again,” said Bao. “He was nine.” He picked up the empty boxes. “I wanted to say. I’ve worked for Mr. Zhao for eight years. I have never been proud of it until yesterday.”

He went out to the van before she could say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

But Wu was a different matter.

Wu was one of Zhao’s oldest lieutenants: a broad, heavy man in his fifties who managed the warehouses in the north and had known Zhao since he was twenty and carrying boxes for Kang. He had a wife and three children and a mortgage on a big house and a gambling habit he thought nobody knew about. A third of what he earned came from the big deals. The Velde deal would have paid off his house.

He came into the office on the third day without knocking.

Elowen was there. She was at the desk, going through the warehouse ledgers with a pencil, the way she did on Thursdays now. Zhao was at the whiteboard, finally wiping off the Velde routes.

Wu looked at her. Then at Zhao.

“So it’s true,” he said. “You turned down the Velde. Because of her.”

Zhao kept wiping the whiteboard.

“I turned it down,” he said.

“Because your wife read a charity pamphlet.” Wu’s face was dark red. “Three hundred million. My share was six. Six, Zhendong. I’ve given you eight years. I carried boxes beside you. And you throw it in the bin because a florist cried over some photographs.”

Elowen didn’t move. She kept her pencil on the ledger.

Zhao put down the eraser.

He turned round. He didn’t come closer. He stood by the clean whiteboard with his hands at his sides and looked at Wu, and the office went very quiet, the way the market went quiet, the way the gold ballroom had gone quiet.

“She didn’t cry,” he said.

Wu laughed, short and ugly. “Oh, I’m sorry. She didn’t cry. She just told you what to do, and you did it. Like a dog.” He took a step forward. “Everyone’s saying it, Zhendong. All down the Docks. The wolf’s been muzzled. He sits in a flower shop in an apron. He lets his wife read the books. He lets his wife pick the buyers.” Another step. “And now he’s scared of a little blood. The great Zhao Zhendong, who put Qiu Wen in his fishpond—”

“Wu,” said Elowen.

Both men turned.

She hadn’t looked up from the ledger. She turned a page. She ran her pencil down a column of figures.

“Warehouse seven,” she said. “In the north. Your warehouse. Last March, you reported a shipment of eight hundred cases arriving. The port records say six hundred. The difference was sold to a buyer in the south for cash. It happened again in June. And September.” She turned another page. “I found it the first time it happened. I wrote it down.” She looked up at him, finally. “I didn’t tell my husband. I thought you had three children and a gambling problem and you’d stop on your own. You didn’t.”

Wu’s face had gone from red to grey.

“Eight years,” said Elowen. “You’ve been stealing for one of them.” She closed the ledger. “I think if anyone in this room should be worried about a little blood, Mr. Wu, it isn’t my husband.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Wu didn’t look at her. He looked at Zhao.

Zhao was looking at his wife.

For a long moment, he didn’t say anything. Something moved in his face, slowly, the way it had moved the night she asked for terms in this same office: a surprise that went all the way down, followed by something warmer and much more dangerous.

“Is that true?” he said to Wu. Not looking away from Elowen.

Wu didn’t answer.

Zhao finally turned his head.

“Get out,” he said, very quietly.

Wu opened his mouth.

“You have three children,” said Zhao. “That is the only reason you are walking out of this room. Take your family and leave the city tonight. Don’t come back. If I see you again, at the Docks or anywhere, I won’t remember your children.”

Wu stood there for a second longer, breathing hard.

Then he turned and went out, and his footsteps went down the stairs very fast, and the door at the bottom banged, and the office was quiet.

Zhao looked at his wife.

She looked back at him over the closed ledger.

“You knew for a year,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You didn’t tell me.”

“I told you I’d find your leaks,” said Elowen. “I didn’t say I’d hand them all to you. Some of them I was saving.” She stood up and put the ledger back on the shelf. “For a day when someone called you a dog in front of me.”

He stared at her.

Then he laughed. Out loud, his head going back, the way he had laughed on the pavement outside the shop with Chen Si on the morning of the roses. It filled the bare office. Down in the warehouse, two men on the forklift looked up.

He crossed the room in three steps and took her face in both hands and kissed her, hard, in the middle of the office, with the door open and the forklift men watching, and she laughed into his mouth and held onto his shirt.

“You’re terrifying,” he said, against her lips.

“Terrifying isn’t the same as afraid. I wrote it in your margin.”

She pulled back and looked at him. “Zhendong. Wu’s going to talk. Everywhere. About the muzzle. About the apron.”

“Let him.”

“It’ll make people think you’re weak.”

He looked at her.

“Weak men,” he said, “don’t throw three hundred million in the bin.” He touched her cheek. “And the ones who think I’m weak will find out. One way or another.”

She heard it then, under the words. The thing she had felt in the kitchen, when the grey folder went into the bin on top of the fish bones.

Something is going to happen.

She didn’t say anything. She put her arms round his neck and held on, in the middle of the long bare office, and he held her back, and down in the warehouse the forklift started up again, beeping as it reversed.

chapters.title: The Buyer Does Not Take No Well
chapters.desc: A warehouse burns at three in the morning. Maartens comes to the city in person. Zhao goes to meet him. He doesn’t come back.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll be home for dinner. Make fish.”
chapters.content:
Warehouse four went up at three in the morning, nine days after the letter went to Rotterdam.

Elowen heard it from the house on the hill. Not the explosion itself; a low thud, far away, like a door slammed in another building. Then the dogs, both of them, howling. Then his phone, on the bedside table, buzzing against the wood.

By the time she sat up, he was already dressed.

From the bedroom window, she could see it. Down at the Docks, beyond the dark cranes, a column of orange fire going straight up into the black sky, and the flashing blue lights of fire engines crawling toward it along the harbour road like beetles.

“Two men,” Zhao said. He was standing at the door with the phone still in his hand. His face was very still. “The night guards. Old Ming and his nephew. Ming’s dead. The boy’s on his way to the burns unit.”

“Will the boy—”

“They don’t know.”

She closed her eyes.

Old Ming had been sixty-three. He had brought her a bag of lychees from his garden in the summer, shyly, holding them out at arm’s length, and said for the lady of the house. His nephew was twenty and wanted to be a chef.

When she opened her eyes, Zhao was looking at her.

“It’s Maartens,” he said. “He left a card. On the gate. A florist’s card.” His voice didn’t change. “It said For the widow.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Maartens came to the city a week later.

He came openly, on a commercial flight, with a Dutch passport and two lawyers and six men who did not look like lawyers. He checked into the best hotel on the harbour, the one with the restaurant on the top floor where he had once had his hand pinned to a table. He booked the same private room. And he sent a message, through Chen Si, very polite, very professional.

Mr. Maartens believes there has been a misunderstanding. He would like to meet Mr. Zhao in person to settle the matter, in a neutral location, so that both parties can move on. He suggests the old Hengli shipyard, Thursday, midnight. Mr. Zhao may bring two men. Mr. Maartens will bring two men.

“It’s a trap,” said Chen Si.

“Of course it’s a trap,” said Zhao.

They were in the kitchen of the house on the hill. Chen Si had come at eleven at night, which he never did, and stood by the counter in his camel coat, not taking it off. Aurelia had come with him. She was sitting on one of the tall stools beside Elowen, not saying anything, which was more frightening than anything she could have said.

“Then don’t go,” said Chen Si.

“If I don’t go, he burns another warehouse. Then another. Then the shop.” Zhao was leaning against the sink with his arms folded. “He came here. He came to my city, on a plane, with his own face. He knows about the notice. He knows I can’t go to him. So he came to me.” A pause. “He wants it finished. So do I.”

“He wants you finished,” said Chen Si. “Zhendong, he has six men and two lawyers and the protection of a country that wants to extradite you. If something happens to him in this city, the whole world will be watching. Song Wei Long won’t be able to look away even if he wants to.”

“I know.”

“Then let me handle it. Let me make the calls. I can have his visa revoked. I can have the hotel—”

“And then he goes home,” said Zhao, “and he waits. A year. Two. And one day a car comes down Elowen’s street at four twelve in the afternoon again.” He shook his head. “No. I left him behind me once. At that table. With his hand. I told myself I wouldn’t do it again.”

Chen Si looked at him.

Then he looked at Elowen.

She was sitting very still on her stool, with her hands around a cup of tea she hadn’t drunk. She had been listening to every word. She had not said anything.

“Mrs. Zhao,” said Chen Si quietly. “Tell him not to go.”

Everyone looked at her.

She looked at her husband, leaning against the sink with his arms folded. At his face, which had gone flat and cold and very far away. She had seen that face once before, before dawn, crouched beside the bed, saying forty-eight hours.

She thought about Old Ming and his lychees. His nephew who wanted to be a chef.

She thought about for the widow.

She thought about a boring day, and a word she had been holding in her mouth for two years.

“Will you come back?” she asked him.

He looked at her.

“Yes,” he said.

“You promised you’d never make something up.”

His jaw moved.

“I’ll come back,” said Zhao. “I promise.”

She held his eyes for a long moment. Then she turned to Chen Si.

“I can’t,” she said. “I can’t tell him not to. He’s right. Maartens will never stop. Not after the pond. Not after the Velde.” Her voice held. “I said no to the deal. This is what happens when you say no. I knew that. I said it to him in this kitchen.”

Chen Si closed his eyes.

Aurelia reached over without a word and took Elowen’s hand, and held it so tightly her rings dug in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He left at eleven on Thursday night.

She walked him to the door. He was in black: a black coat, black gloves. Bao was waiting in the car, his arm healed now into a long pink scar. Another man she didn’t know well, Deng, was in the passenger seat.

At the door, by the lemon tree, he stopped.

“I’ll be home for dinner,” he said. “Tomorrow. Make fish.”

“You said you’d come back last time. Before the forty-eight hours.”

“And I came home.”

“You came home washed.”

He looked at her.

“I’ll come home,” he said again.

She reached up and straightened the collar of his coat, which didn’t need straightening, the way her mother had once straightened her father’s every morning. She smoothed it flat with both hands. She left her hands there, on his chest.

She opened her mouth.

He saw it. He saw the word coming. He put his gloved fingers against her lips, very gently, the way he had in the big bed on the morning she came home from Aurelia’s.

“Not today,” he said. “Today isn’t boring.”

“Zhendong—”

“Tell me tomorrow. At dinner. Over the fish.” He took his fingers away and bent and kissed her, softly, once. “Then I’ll know it’s true. Because I’ll be home, and nothing will be happening, and you’ll still say it.”

He went out. The dogs followed him down the steps to the car and then stood on the gravel, both of them, very still, watching it go down the drive, out of the gate, down the hill toward the Docks.

She stood in the doorway until the tail lights were gone.

Then she went to the kitchen and took the fish out of the fridge and put it on the counter, ready for tomorrow.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 12:40, her phone rang.

Not his number. Chen Si’s.

She was sitting on the bottom stair in the hall, by the lemon tree, in her coat, because she hadn’t been able to make herself take it off. She answered before the first ring finished.

“Elowen.” Chen Si’s voice. Not calm. For the first time since she had known him, not calm at all. “Listen to me. Something happened at the shipyard. There was shooting. A lot of it. My people are there now. Maartens is dead. Two of his men are dead.”

“Zhendong.”

“Bao is alive. He’s hurt. He’s in the car with my people, they’re taking him to Elara. Deng is—Deng is dead.”

“Zhendong.”

A silence on the line. Short. Terrible.

“We can’t find him,” said Chen Si.

She didn’t say anything. She sat on the bottom stair and held the phone.

“Bao says he was hit,” Chen Si said. His voice was very careful now. “In the side. Bao saw him go down by the water. And then Maartens’ other men came round the cranes, and Bao was hit too, and when he looked again, Zhendong was gone. Just gone. There’s blood on the edge of the dock. A lot of it.” A breath. “And then nothing.”

“The water,” said Elowen.

“We’re searching the water. And the shipyard. And every boat in the harbour. I have forty men out. Song Wei Long has the police out, unofficially. Eliana is in the traffic cameras.” He stopped. “Elowen. I need you to go to the basement. I need you to put in the code and lock the door and stay there until I call you. Maartens had more than six men. We don’t know where the others are. We don’t know if they’ll come to the house.”

She looked down the hall, at the lemon tree, at the dark window behind it.

At the kitchen, where the fish was sitting on the counter, ready for tomorrow.

“Elowen?”

“I heard you,” she said.

She stood up. She walked down the hall, past the lemon tree, through the kitchen. She opened the door to the basement stairs. At the bottom, the steel door was waiting, the one that took six numbers or one small steel key with a red tag on it.

She went back up the stairs first.

She went to the hall and took his coat off the hook, the old one, the black wool one he had worn the night it rained in her shop, three years ago, and had kept wearing until the elbows went thin. She held it against her chest.

Then she went down and put in the code and locked the door from the inside, and turned on the lamp over the workbench, and sat down on the floor of the armory with her back against the wall and his coat in her arms.

On the bench, in the drawer, was the small black pistol he had taught her to shoot on a wet terrace on a mountain.

She took it out. She checked it, the way he had shown her. She put it on the floor beside her.

Then she waited.

For him.

The way he had told her to, on the very first night.

For how long?

For me.

chapters.title: Three Days
chapters.desc: She waits in the armory with his coat and a gun she knows how to use. Everyone who loves her comes to the steel door. She doesn’t open it.
chapters.content:
The first night, she didn’t sleep.

She sat on the floor of the armory with her back against the cold concrete wall, under the hanging lamp, with his coat in her arms and the small black pistol on the floor beside her knee, and listened.

The basement was very quiet. The walls were thick. She could hear the faint hiss of the air coming in through the vent he had built, from outside, from somewhere up the hill. She could hear her own heart. Nothing else.

She knew every object in the room now. She had come down here with the fourteenth key many times in the last year: sometimes to sit with him while he cleaned something, sometimes just to sit, because it was the one room in the house where the phone didn’t ring. She knew the racks of rifles along both walls, each one in its place. She knew the drawers of the workbench, the oiled cloths, the small brushes. The water in the cupboard. The phone on the wall that didn’t go through the house.

It rang at three. She picked it up before the first ring finished.

“Nothing yet,” said Chen Si. “The divers are in the water. The coastguard. Eliana has every camera within five kilometres of the shipyard. Nothing.” A pause. “Are you safe?”

“Yes.”

“Stay where you are.”

She put the phone back on the wall.

She looked at his coat in her arms. The black wool, thin at the elbows. It smelled of him: soap and gun oil and the cold air off the sea. In the inside pocket, she could feel something stiff and flat. She took it out.

It was a page. Folded very small, many times, worn soft at the creases.

She unfolded it under the lamp.

Gravitational lensing of light by low-mass compact objects: a perturbative approach. M. Wei.

The last page of Miles’s paper. With his handwriting in the margin. He made her feel calm. I make her feel afraid. I should let her go to the reunion alone.

And underneath, in hers: No. You come with me. Plus one. And for the record, I said terrifying. That isn’t the same as afraid.

He had kept it. For more than two years. In the inside pocket of his oldest coat, against his heart.

She held it in her lap and looked at it for the rest of the night.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first day, people came to the door.

She heard them on the stairs. Footsteps, then a knock on the steel, then a voice.

Aurelia came first, at nine. “Darling. It’s me. Open the door.”

“No.”

“I brought coffee. Terrible coffee. Mine. You know how terrible.”

“Chen Si said to stay in here.”

“Chen Si says a lot of things.” A pause. Then, quieter, through the steel: “Elowen. Please. Let me sit with you. I sat with you last time. You let me then.”

Elowen pressed her forehead against her knees.

“Last time I knew he was coming back,” she said. “He told me. Forty-eight hours. This time I don’t know anything.” Her voice broke. “If I open the door, I have to come out. And if I come out, I have to be in a house he isn’t in. I can’t. Not yet. In here, it’s still his. In here, I’m still waiting.”

There was a long silence on the other side of the door.

Then the sound of someone sitting down on the concrete steps. The rustle of a coat.

“All right,” said Aurelia, through the steel. “Then I’ll wait out here.”

She did. For six hours. Elowen could hear her: talking on the phone in Italian, sharp and low; the click of her lighter, once, and then nothing, because she had remembered where she was and put it away. At three in the afternoon, she knocked once, and said, “I’m leaving a sandwich on the step. Eat it or I’ll tell everyone you cried in my bath in wet jeans,” and went away.

Elowen didn’t eat the sandwich.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came at five.

She knew it was him from the footsteps, slow and heavy on the stairs. He didn’t knock. He stood on the other side of the door for a long time without saying anything.

“Baba,” she said.

“Elowen.” His voice was rough. “Chen Si told me. I came.” A pause. “I don’t know what to say.”

She didn’t say anything either.

“I was wrong,” said Lin Jian, through the steel. “At your table. I told him you didn’t choose him. I told him he was the price. I said it to his face, in his own house.” She heard him lean against the door; the steel creaked. “And then he put his hand up in that office, at the Docks, every time I came in with a file. Every time. Before I could speak. Mr. Lin, how is your back. Mr. Lin, did Eliana get her exam results. Mr. Lin, I heard Raiden won a prize.” A breath. “He asked. Every time. I didn’t understand why. I thought it was a trick.” Another pause. “Then you told me. In my kitchen. Ask. And I understood he’d been doing it for a year. Because you told him to. Because he does what you say.”

Elowen closed her eyes.

“The next week,” said her father, “I went to the Docks with a file. And before he could say anything, I said, ‘How is the lemon tree?’” His voice cracked. “He looked at me for a very long time. Then he said, ‘Seven lemons. The most it’s ever had.’ And then he smiled. At me. I didn’t know he could.”

She was crying now. Silently, into the wool of his coat.

“He’ll come back,” said Lin Jian. “Elowen. He’ll come back. He’s too stubborn to die in the harbour. He hasn’t had his dinner.”

She laughed, wetly, into the coat.

“Go home, Baba,” she said. “Ask Raiden how he is. He’ll be pretending to be fine.”

She heard him stand there for a moment longer. Then his footsteps, going slowly back up the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second night, she cleaned a gun.

She didn’t decide to. Her hands decided. Sometime after midnight she got up off the floor, stiff and cold, and went to the workbench and turned on the hanging lamp, and took a pistol from the drawer: not the small one, one of his, a heavier one he cleaned more often than the others. She laid out the cloth. She found the little brushes.

She had watched him do it a hundred times. She had never done it herself.

She took it apart slowly. She did it wrong twice and had to start again. She laid the pieces out on the cloth in a straight line, the way he did, and picked them up one at a time and cleaned them with the small brush and the rag. Slowly. Paying attention to each one.

When I was sixteen, the only thing in my life that did what it was supposed to do was a gun. You clean it, you put it back together, it works. Every time.

People don’t.

It took her an hour to put it back together. When she finished, she held it in her hands under the lamp and felt it click into place, solid and complete, and she understood, finally, why he came down here at two in the morning. It wasn’t the gun. It was that for an hour, you could hold something in your hands and know exactly what it was and that it wouldn’t break.

She put it back in the drawer.

The phone on the wall rang at four. Chen Si.

“They found his phone,” he said. “In the harbour. A diver. At the bottom, by the edge of the dock.” A pause. “Nothing else.”

She held the receiver against her ear and didn’t say anything.

“Elowen,” said Chen Si, very quietly. “I’m not stopping. Do you understand? I carried him through a sewer when he was fifteen. I am not stopping.”

“I know,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second day, Raiden came. He sat on the step outside the steel door and didn’t say anything for an hour. Then he slid a piece of paper under it.

It was a drawing. A floor plan of the house on the hill, every room, every door, every window. And in the corner, in his neat draftsman’s hand: Every way back in. He knows all of them. I built three of them.

Evangeline came, and said nothing, and sat on the step for three hours. When she left, there was a cup of tea outside the door, still warm, and one orchid in a glass.

Eliana didn’t come. Eliana sent messages every hour through Chen Si, and he read them out at the end of every call in his flat, careful voice, word for word, because she had made him promise to: Still looking. Still looking. Camera 112 has nothing. Still looking. Jie I’m not sleeping either.

Xiao Pan came at six, on his motorbike, the small red one Jinx had built him, and left a bunch of white tulips on the step, and a note in careful handwriting: Miss Lin, the shop is open. I did the market with Granny Su. She says to tell you she counted every bunch. She says, “Tell the girl her husband carries better than anyone I’ve ever had, so he has to come back.”

Elowen read the note through the gap under the door and laughed and cried at the same time.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third night, she stopped crying.

There was nothing left. She sat on the floor of the armory in the light of the lamp with his coat around her shoulders and Miles’s folded page in her lap and the gun beside her knee, and she was very calm and very empty, and she thought about all the things she had not said.

She had said happy. On the mountain, in the rain. She had said I’m happy.

She had not said the other word.

She had held it in her mouth for two years. She had almost said it on the anniversary, and stopped, because she wanted him to believe it. She had almost said it on the morning she came home from Aurelia’s, and he had stopped her. Say it on a day when nothing has happened. She had almost said it at the front door, by the lemon tree, with her hands on his chest, and he had put his gloved fingers on her lips.

Tell me tomorrow. At dinner. Over the fish.

The fish was still in the fridge upstairs. She had not been able to throw it out.

She thought: if he doesn’t come back, he will never know.

She thought: he will die thinking I married him for my father, and stayed because I’m kind.

She thought: he sat outside my door every night for a month and never slept, so that I would know where he was, so that I would never have to wonder.

And I let him wonder. For three years.

She put her face in his coat and stayed there.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 3:10 in the morning on the third night, the dogs started barking.

Not the way they barked at a fox, or a car. A high, wild, frantic sound she had never heard from them. Both of them. Far away, up through the concrete, through the thick walls of the basement. Barking and barking, and then a sound that was almost a scream.

She was on her feet with the pistol in her hand before she knew she had moved.

The phone on the wall rang.

She snatched it up.

“Miss Lin.” Not Chen Si. One of the guards from the gatehouse, a young man called Peng, his voice high and shaking. “Miss Lin. The gate. Someone’s at the gate. On the ground. We—the dogs got there first, they won’t let us near, they’re—” He was almost crying. “Miss Lin, it’s him. It’s Mr. Zhao. He’s—he crawled. From the sea road. There’s a trail all the way up the hill. He’s—”

She dropped the phone.

She didn’t remember putting in the code. She didn’t remember the stairs, or the kitchen, or the hall, or the lemon tree with its seven lemons glowing in the dark. She remembered the front door, and the cold, and running down the gravel drive in her bare feet with his coat still around her shoulders and the pistol still in her hand, toward the gate, where the floodlights were on and two dogs were standing over something dark on the ground, barking and barking and barking, and wouldn’t let anyone come near.

Until they saw her.

Then they stopped.

And stood aside.

chapters.title: He Crawled the Last Mile
chapters.desc: A bullet in his side, a fever, a kitchen table, and the fourth Lin child with a bag full of stolen hospital supplies.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m late. For dinner.”
chapters.content:
He was lying on his side at the foot of the gate, curled around himself, the way a dog curls around a wound.

He was soaked. Salt water and something darker. His black coat was gone. His shirt was gone, or most of it; what was left was wound round his middle in a thick, filthy knot, pressed against his left side, and the knot was black with blood. His face was grey. His lips were blue. His hands were raw, the palms shredded, as if he had pulled himself along by them over stone. Behind him, down the gravel and out through the open gate and away down the dark road toward the sea, there was a trail: a long, dark, broken line on the tarmac, glistening under the floodlights.

He had crawled. Up the whole hill. From the sea road.

Elowen went down on her knees beside him on the gravel.

“Zhendong.”

His eyes were half open. They didn’t move.

“Zhendong. Look at me.”

She put her hand on his face. His skin was cold and wet and burning at the same time, the terrible heat of fever under the cold of the sea. She felt for the pulse in his neck, the way Elara had once shown her, and found it: fast and thin and fluttering, like a bird against glass.

But there.

His eyes moved. Slowly. They found her face.

For a long moment, he just looked at her. As if he didn’t believe it. As if he had seen her face so many times in the last three days, in the dark, in the hold of a boat, on the long road up the hill, that he couldn’t be sure this one was real.

Then his cracked lips moved.

“Late,” he whispered. “For dinner.”

She made a sound she didn’t recognise. She put her forehead down on his cold wet shoulder and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Miss Lin.” Peng, the young guard from the gatehouse, crouching beside her. His hands were shaking. “Miss Lin, we have to move him, he’s—”

She lifted her head. Something in her went cold and clear and very calm, the way it had gone in the shop when the glass came in.

“Call Elara,” she said. “My sister. Her number’s on the wall in the guardhouse. Tell her: gunshot, left side, three days, fever, he’s lost a lot of blood, he’s been in the sea. Tell her to bring everything. Tell her to steal it if she has to.” She looked at Peng. “Then call Chen Si. Then call nobody else. No hospital. No police. Not even Wei Long. Do you understand?”

Peng stared at her.

“A hospital,” he said. “He needs a hospital, he—”

“He has a Red Notice and a dead Dutchman at the shipyard and a dead man of his own,” said Elowen. “If he goes to a hospital, he wakes up in handcuffs. If he wakes up.” She took off his coat, the old black one she had been wearing for three days, and laid it over him. “Elara. Now. Then help me carry him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They put him on the kitchen table.

It was the only surface in the house big enough, and the light was good, and it was close to the sink. Elowen pushed everything off it onto the floor: the fruit bowl, Bao’s mandarins, a stack of post. Peng and another guard carried him in between them, and he made a sound when they lifted him, low and awful, and then didn’t make any sound at all.

She cut the filthy knot of shirt away from his side with her florist’s knife.

Underneath was the wound.

She had expected a hole. It was not a hole. It was a mess: a torn, swollen, angry place low on his left side, just above his hip, below the long old scar from Block C. The skin all round it was red and hot and tight and shiny. There was a second wound on his back, a few inches round from the first, ragged at the edges, where the bullet had come out. Both of them were packed with something dark—cloth, she realised, torn strips of cloth, stuffed into the wounds and gone black and stiff. And the smell coming off it was sweet and wrong, like flowers left too long in old water.

Infection. She had read about it, once, in the burns unit, waiting for Xiao Pan.

She didn’t touch it. She put a clean towel over it and pressed, gently, and held his hand with her other hand, and talked to him.

“Elara’s coming,” she said. “She’s very good. She practises on bananas. She’s the best in her year.”

His eyes were closed. His hand in hers didn’t move.

“You crawled up the hill,” she said. “Peng says there’s a trail all the way from the sea road. That’s two kilometres. That’s further than the market. You’ve never once carried the buckets further than the van.”

Nothing.

“The fish is in the fridge,” said Elowen. Her voice was starting to go now. She made it stop. “I didn’t throw it out. It’s probably bad. I’ll make it anyway. You promised you’d eat it. You don’t make things up. You said so. On page three.”

His fingers moved in hers. Very slightly. Just once.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara came at 3:52, in a taxi that drove straight through the gate and up the gravel to the front steps.

She was twenty-three now, in her final year of medicine, and she came into the kitchen at a run with her hair in a mess and a huge bag over each shoulder, both of them clinking. She stopped in the doorway and looked at the man on the kitchen table, and Elowen watched her sister’s face go white and then go completely still and then become someone else entirely.

“Okay,” said Elara. “Okay. Okay.”

She dropped the bags on the counter and unzipped them. Bags of fluid. Tubing. Needles in sterile packets. Boxes of gloves. Bottles with hospital labels. A green surgical drape. Instruments in a metal case.

“I stole all of this,” she said, very fast, already pulling on gloves. “From the hospital. From the supply room. If anyone ever finds out, I will never be a doctor, and I’ll go to prison, and I don’t care, Jie, I don’t care, move his arm, I need a vein.”

She found one on the inside of his elbow, on the second try. She put a needle in it and taped it down and hung a bag of clear fluid from the cupboard door above the table with a coat hanger. Then another needle in the other arm. Then she held up a small bottle and a syringe.

“Antibiotics,” she said. “The strongest I could find. Into the drip. He needs fluids, he needs these, and he needs—” She stopped. She looked down at the towel over his side. “Show me.”

Elowen lifted the towel.

Elara looked at the wound for a long, silent moment.

“Okay,” she said again, more quietly. “Okay. It went through. In and out. It’s low and to the side. I don’t—I don’t think it went into his belly. I think it went through the muscle. If it had gone into his belly, he’d be dead by now. Three days. He’d be dead.” Her voice wobbled. She made it stop. “But it’s infected. Badly. He packed it himself, with his shirt. It kept him alive. Now it’s killing him. All of that has to come out. All the dead tissue. It has to be washed out. It has to be left open, to drain. Then we pump him full of antibiotics and we pray.” She looked up at her sister. “I can’t put him to sleep. I don’t have the drugs for that, I don’t know how. I have local anaesthetic. It won’t be enough. It’s going to hurt him. A lot. Even like this.”

“Do it,” said Elowen.

“Jie—”

“Elara. Do it.” Elowen took her husband’s hand in both of hers. “I’ll hold him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It took two hours.

Elara worked under the kitchen light with her stolen instruments, sweating, biting her lip, saying nothing except short words to herself, okay, okay, there, okay. She pulled out the black strips of shirt, slowly, one by one, and he arched off the table and made a sound that Elowen would hear in her sleep for a year. She washed the wounds out with bag after bag of saline, the water running pink and then red and then pink again off the edge of the table onto the kitchen floor, where the guards kept mopping it up with towels. She cut away the dead tissue, the grey and the black, with small, careful snips. She packed the wounds with clean white gauze. She did not close them.

Elowen held him.

She stood at the head of the table with his face between her hands, and talked to him the whole time. She talked about the market. About Granny Su, counting every bunch. About Xiao Pan’s red motorbike. About the seven lemons. About the reunion, and the FLOWER POWER hoodie, and the night he read Miles Wei’s paper eleven times. About the cooler at one degree, and the roses dropping cold water down the back of her neck. About the camellia on the mountain in the rain.

When he screamed, she put her forehead against his and kept talking.

When he stopped screaming and went limp, she kept talking.

At one point, his eyes opened and looked straight up at her, and he said, very clearly, through his teeth, “Elowen. Go upstairs. Don’t watch this.”

“No,” she said.

“You shouldn’t see—”

“I married you,” said Elowen. “I said I wanted to see it. All of it. I’m seeing it.” She held his face. “I’m staying. Look at me. Don’t look at anything else. Look at me.”

He looked at her. He didn’t look away again until he passed out.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six, the sky outside the kitchen window started going grey.

Elara stripped off her gloves. They were red to the wrist. She dropped them on the floor and stood with her hands braced on the edge of the counter, her head down, breathing.

“That’s all I can do,” she said. “It’s clean. It’s open. The antibiotics are going in. Now it’s his body. If the fever breaks in the next two days, he lives. If it doesn’t—” She stopped. “If it doesn’t, we take him to a hospital, Jie, Red Notice or no Red Notice. I won’t let him die on a kitchen table because of a piece of paper.”

“Neither will I,” said Elowen.

Elara lifted her head and looked at her sister. At the blood on Elowen’s hands, and her nightdress, and her bare feet, cut from the gravel. At her face, which was perfectly calm.

“You held him for two hours,” Elara said. “You didn’t look away once. You didn’t even cry.”

“I’ll cry later.”

“Jie—”

“Later,” said Elowen.

Chen Si was standing in the kitchen doorway.

She didn’t know how long he had been there. He had come in at some point during the two hours and stood against the wall without a word. His camel coat was soaked and filthy at the hem. His shoes were ruined. He had been on the harbour all night, all three nights; she could see it in his face.

He looked at his brother on the kitchen table: grey, still, a drip in each arm, white gauze packed into his side, breathing.

Then he turned and walked out into the hall, and Elowen heard him stop by the lemon tree, and heard a sound she had never expected to hear from Chen Si: a long, shaking breath that broke in the middle.

✦ ✦ ✦

They carried him upstairs at seven, on a door Raiden had taken off its hinges, to the big room at the end of the corridor. Elara hung the drips from the curtain rail.

Elowen sat down on the floor beside the bed, the way he had sat beside her on the night of the typhoon, with her back against the frame so that her shoulder was level with his hand.

She took his hand.

It was hot. Too hot. The palm was torn and scabbed from the hill. She held it very gently, between both of hers, the way you would hold something you were afraid to break.

“The light stays on,” she told him quietly. “I’ll come.”

She didn’t sleep. She didn’t move. She sat on the floor in her ruined nightdress with her husband’s burning hand in hers, and watched him breathe, and waited.

For him.

chapters.title: “I Stained Your Life”
chapters.desc: Two days of fever. He comes up out of it once, and thinks he’s apologising for the last time.
chapters.epigraph: “I married a man who keeps the world away.”
chapters.content:
The fever didn’t break the first day.

He burned. She had never touched anything that hot that was alive. His skin was dry and tight and his breath came short and fast, and he shook under the blankets in long, hard waves, his teeth chattering, though the room was warm. Elara came every four hours to change the drips, and morning and evening to change the packing in the wounds. Each time, Elowen held his hand while she did it, and each time he didn’t wake.

He talked, sometimes. Not to her. To people she couldn’t see. Once, in a boy’s voice, high and frightened: I didn’t drop it, I didn’t, it fell. Once, very low and fierce: Si. Si. Get down. Get behind me. Once, in the middle of the night, so quietly she had to bend close to hear: She’s at the counter. She’s alone at the counter. Bao. Bao, drive faster.

She sat on the floor beside the bed and held his hand and answered all of them.

“It fell,” she told the boy. “It’s all right. It’s not your fault.”

“Si’s safe,” she told the fierce voice. “He’s downstairs. He’s been here all night. He’s asleep on the sofa in his coat.”

“I’m not at the counter,” she told the last one. “I’m here. I’m right here. You came.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fever didn’t break the second day either.

Elara looked at the thermometer at noon and didn’t say anything, and then went out into the corridor, and Elowen heard her crying out there, very quietly, with her hand over her mouth so nobody would hear.

At two, Chen Si came up and stood at the foot of the bed.

He had shaved. He had changed his clothes. He looked almost like himself, except for his eyes.

“The search is over,” he said quietly. “Officially. The police found Maartens and his two men at the shipyard. And Deng. Song Wei Long is calling it a dispute between foreign criminals. He has written that the man known as Zhao Zhendong was not present and his whereabouts are unknown.” A pause. “He came to me at six this morning and gave me the report to read before he filed it. He said, ‘Tell her this is the cat.’ I don’t know what that means.”

“It means he owed me something,” said Elowen. “It means we’re even.”

Chen Si looked at his brother in the bed. Grey. Burning. Two drips hanging from the curtain rail.

“Elara says if it hasn’t broken by tonight,” he said, “we take him to a hospital. I’ve arranged one. Private. A surgeon who owes me. Nobody will know.” He paused. “He’d hate it.”

“I know.”

“He made me promise once,” said Chen Si. “In Block C. When he was fifteen and bleeding into the snow. He said, ‘Si, if I’m dying, don’t take me to a hospital. Hospitals have records. Take me somewhere quiet and let me go.’” He looked at Elowen. “I didn’t listen then. I carried him to a clinic in the next town and lied about his name. I won’t listen now.”

“Neither will I.”

“Good,” said Chen Si.

He went to the door. Then he stopped, with his hand on the frame, and turned round.

“Mrs. Zhao,” he said. “Elowen. I’ve never asked you this. I should have, three years ago, at the registry office. I didn’t, because I thought I knew the answer. I thought you were doing it for your father.” His face was very still. “Do you love him?”

She looked up at him from the floor beside the bed.

“I haven’t told him,” she said.

“That isn’t what I asked.”

She looked at her husband’s hand in hers. Torn and scabbed and burning.

“Yes,” said Elowen.

Chen Si closed his eyes. When he opened them again, something in his face had changed.

“Then tell him,” he said. “When he wakes up. Don’t wait for anything. Don’t wait for a good day. Zhendong has never in his life had a good day that he didn’t think someone would take away. He won’t believe it’s good until you say it.”

He went out and closed the door softly behind him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven that night, he woke up.

Not all the way. She saw his eyes open in the light from the Docks, glassy and too bright, and move around the room without seeing anything. Then they found her face, on the pillow beside his, where she had finally lain down on top of the covers, unable to sit on the floor any longer.

He looked at her.

“Elowen,” he said. His voice was a cracked thread.

“I’m here.”

“Are you real?”

“Yes.”

“I saw you. On the boat.” His eyes wandered, came back. “In the dark. In the hold. For two days. I saw you on the market road at four, with the van. I saw you in the cooler with the roses. I saw you on the mountain.” He swallowed. It looked like it hurt. “I thought if I stopped looking at you, I would die. So I didn’t stop.”

She took his hand.

“I came up the hill,” he said. “I don’t remember most of it. I remember the dogs. I remember thinking, I said I’d be home for dinner.” His mouth moved, almost a smile, and then it went away. “I didn’t keep my promise. I was three days late.”

“You kept it. You came home.”

He was quiet. His eyes closed. She thought he had gone under again.

Then he opened them, and looked at her, and his face was terrible: open and naked and full of something she had never seen in it before, not even on the bathroom floor, not even in the dark on the night of the typhoon.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“You don’t have to—”

“Let me.” His hand moved in hers, weakly. “Let me say it. I might not—” He stopped. Started again. “I’m sorry. For all of it. For your father, at the Docks, for six years. For the van. For the boy’s hands. For the glass. For the man in the grey jacket at your counter. For the circle round your face.” His voice was breaking now, a little more with every word. “For Old Ming. For his nephew, who wanted to be a chef. For the kitchen floor, and the blood on your nightdress, and making you hold me on a table while your sister cut me open.” He was crying. Silently, the way he had on the bathroom floor, the tears running sideways across his face into the pillow. “You were a florist. You had a shop with your name on it. You had a lemon tree. You were going to get on a train one day and go somewhere nobody knew your father. And then you walked into my office, and I said yes, and I—”

He stopped.

“I stained your life,” said Zhao Zhendong. “Everything I touched, I stained. I knew I would. I said yes anyway. Because I wanted you. Because I am a selfish, ugly, dangerous man, and I wanted the only clean thing I had ever seen, and I took it, and look—” His torn hand moved, weakly, toward the drips, the gauze, the bloodstained sheets on the floor where Elara had dropped them. “Look what I did to it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen didn’t say anything for a long time.

She lay on her side on the pillow and looked at her husband’s face, wet and grey and burning, two inches from hers.

Then she leaned in and kissed him.

Not carefully. Not the way he always kissed her, as if asking a question. She kissed him as if she were answering one, hard, her hand on his burning face, her mouth on his cracked lips, until he made a sound against her and his torn hand came up off the sheet and found her hair and held on.

When she pulled back, he was staring at her.

“Listen to me,” she said. “Zhendong. Are you listening?”

He nodded, very slightly.

“I didn’t marry a man who stained my life,” said Elowen. “I married a man who keeps the world away from it.”

He went still.

“The world was always there,” she said. “It was there when I was seven and my mother died and I put on her apron. It was there in my father’s garage when I was eight, in long boxes I wasn’t allowed to open. It was there in the Walled City every day of my life. Men like Feng, sitting in our kitchen. Men like Maartens. Men like Kang. They were always there. I just didn’t have anyone standing between me and them.” She held his face. “Then you sat outside my door. Every night. For a month. Bao told me. You never slept.”

His eyes were very wide.

“You put a room under my shop with a light that stays on,” she said. Her voice cracked. She let it. “You went to the shipyard so a car would never come down my street again. And when they shot you, you crawled two kilometres up a hill on your hands, with a hole in your side, because you said you’d be home for dinner.”

She put her forehead against his.

“You didn’t stain anything,” said Elowen. “You’re the wall. You’re the thing that keeps it out. You always were. From the first night, in the rain, when you made a woman with an umbrella walk away from my window and then gave her the tulips.”

He was crying again. So was she. Their faces were wet against each other on the pillow.

“I don’t believe you,” he whispered.

“I know.”

“I want to.”

“I know that too.”

His eyes were closing. The fever was pulling him back down; she could feel it, the heat coming off him in waves.

“Elowen,” he said. Barely a breath. “I need to ask you something.”

She went very still.

She knew what it was. She had known for three years. She had felt it in him in the dark on the night of the typhoon, the big heavy question, and on the mountain in the rain, the shape of a stone under a quilt, and in the car home from the gala, when you married me—

“Ask me,” she said.

But his eyes had closed. His breathing went long and slow and deep. His hand in her hair loosened and slid down to the pillow.

He was asleep.

She lay beside him in the dark and held his hand, and listened to him breathe.

At four in the morning—the hour she always got up for the market, the hour he always had two cups of coffee waiting—she felt it. Under her palm, on his forehead. Something changing.

The heat was going out of him.

Slowly. Like a tide. His skin, under her hand, had gone damp, and then wet, sweat breaking out all over him, soaking the pillow, soaking the sheets. His breathing slowed. His shaking stopped. His face, in the first grey light from the window, lost its terrible flush and went pale and ordinary and quiet.

She put her hand flat on his chest and felt his heart. Slow. Steady. Strong.

She didn’t call Elara. Not yet. She lay beside him in the soaked sheets with her hand on his heart, and at last, after three days in the armory and two on the floor beside the bed, she put her face in his shoulder and cried, silently, the way he did, until the sun came up.

chapters.title: The Question He Never Asked
chapters.desc: Two weeks later, on the most boring day there has ever been, he finally asks. She tells the truth.
chapters.epigraph: “Did you marry me to control your father’s boss?”
chapters.content:
It took him two weeks to walk to the bathroom on his own.

He hated every minute of it. He hated the drips, and then the tablets. He hated Elara changing the packing in his side every morning, very cheerfully, while he lay on his back with his jaw clenched and his eyes on the ceiling. He hated the walking stick Raiden brought, which had a silver dog’s head on the handle and which Raiden claimed, with total seriousness, had belonged to a general.

Most of all he hated not being able to drive her to the market.

“Bao can drive me,” Elowen said, on the first morning she went back, at three-thirty, in the dark.

“Bao drives badly.”

“Bao drives very well. He drove you for eight years.”

“He brakes too hard on the corner by the Qiu warehouse.” He was sitting up in bed against the pillows, grey and thin, watching her dress. “There’s a pothole. He always forgets.”

“There is no Qiu warehouse anymore. You burned it.”

He considered this.

“There’s still a pothole,” he said.

She came and sat on the edge of the bed and kissed his forehead. He closed his eyes.

“Go back to sleep,” she said.

“I don’t sleep when I don’t know where you are.”

“You know exactly where I am. The flower market. Stall forty-two. Granny Su. Ranunculus.” She stood up. “I’ll be back at seven with eggs.”

He didn’t sleep. She knew, because when she got home at seven, Bao told her the light in the big room had been on the whole time, and Zhao was sitting exactly where she had left him, looking at the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fifteenth day, nothing happened.

She noticed it at about noon, standing at the counter of the shop wrapping a birthday bouquet for a schoolteacher. Nothing had happened. Nobody had come in with a strange order. Nobody had smiled at her in a way she didn’t like. No phone had rung at three in the morning. No car had come down the street too slowly. The new window, which Raiden had installed himself and claimed would stop a small missile, let in ordinary grey spring light. Xiao Pan was singing along to the radio, badly. A woman bought tulips for her mother’s birthday. An old man bought chrysanthemums for his wife’s grave.

It was, she realised, the most boring day there had ever been.

She put down the scissors.

Then she picked up her phone and called a number in the Cangshan hills.

“Mrs. Zhao,” said Mr. Wen’s grandson, sounding surprised. “Is everything all right? Grandpa says he heard there was trouble.”

“Everything is fine,” said Elowen. “Everything is very, very boring. I need a favour. Is the camellia still flowering?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came home at six, with fresh fish from the market by the Docks, and cooked it the way her mother had: with ginger and spring onion and a little soy, steamed whole. She made rice. She made green beans with garlic. She did not make soup, because there wasn’t time, and because it was better on the second day, and she was planning on there being one.

She carried it upstairs on a tray, because he still couldn’t manage the stairs without Raiden’s ridiculous stick, and she put it on the bed between them, and sat down cross-legged on the other side.

He looked at the fish.

“You made fish,” he said.

“You said to make fish. At the door. I’ll be home for dinner, make fish.” She picked up her chopsticks. “You were seventeen days late. It’s a different fish. The first one went bad. I threw it out on Tuesday. I cried.”

He looked at her.

Then he picked up his chopsticks and took the belly, the best piece, and put it in her bowl.

She took it out and put it in his.

He took it out and put it in hers.

They looked at each other across the tray.

“My father,” said Elowen, “gave it back to my mother every night for twenty years. Neither of them ever ate it.”

“I know.”

“So one of us has to eat it, or we’ll be like them.”

He looked at the fish belly in her bowl. Then, slowly, he reached over with his chopsticks, took it, and ate it himself.

She laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate. It was a good dinner. The fish was perfect. He ate everything, slowly, sitting up against the pillows, and she watched him eat, and the light from the Docks came in through the long window the way it always did, orange and white, moving on the ceiling as the cranes turned.

When he had finished, he put his chopsticks down across his bowl, neatly, the way she had taught him.

He didn’t say anything.

She waited. She had been waiting for three years.

“Elowen,” he said.

He wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at the tray. At the fish bones, and the empty rice bowls, and the green beans.

“On the night with the fever,” he said. “After I came back. I said I needed to ask you something.”

“I remember.”

“I fell asleep.”

“I remember that too.”

He was quiet. She watched his hands, lying on the blanket on either side of the tray. Scarred. Still scabbed, on the palms, from the hill. They closed slowly into fists. Then opened.

“It’s a boring day,” he said.

“It’s the most boring day there has ever been.”

“Nothing happened.”

“Nothing at all.”

He nodded slowly, as if confirming something he had already checked.

Then he looked up at her.

And she saw it. All of it. Three years of it. The big heavy question he had carried in him since the night she walked into his office with three pages of terms. She saw it in the dark on the night of the typhoon. She saw it on the mountain, under the quilt, the shape of a stone. She saw it in the car home from the gala, when you married me—. She saw it in the basement after her father came to dinner, put carefully away where it would never go off by accident.

It was right there now. On his face. Out in the open, in the light from the Docks.

“Did you marry me,” said Zhao Zhendong, “to control your father’s boss?”

✦ ✦ ✦

The room was very quiet.

She thought about lying. She had promised him she never would, on page three, in his square blunt handwriting. Lie to everyone else. Not to me. Ever. She thought about it anyway, for one second, because she could see what the truth was going to do to his face.

Then she didn’t.

“Yes,” said Elowen.

He didn’t move. He didn’t look away. But she watched it go into him, the way the knife had gone into the table at the dinner with Maartens: straight down, all the way, without a sound.

“Yes,” she said again, steadily, because he deserved to hear all of it. “I married you for my father. Every word Baba said at our table was true. When I walked into your office, I wasn’t thinking about you at all. I was thinking about Old Tan in hospital with his legs in plaster. I was thinking about a hired gun in my father’s car who would run the first time someone shot at him. I was thinking about a brother and three sisters asleep upstairs.” She held his eyes. “You weren’t a man to me that night. You were a wall. I wanted to put you between my family and the world. That’s all. That’s the truth.”

He nodded, very slowly.

“Thank you,” he said.

His voice was quite steady. Quite calm. It was the voice he used for weather reports, for I know.

“Thank you for not lying,” he said. “I always knew. I just—” He stopped. He looked down at his hands. “I wanted to hear you say it. Once. So I could stop wondering.” He swallowed. “Now I can stop.”

“Zhendong.”

“It’s all right.” He wasn’t looking at her. “I said yes anyway. I knew. I signed it. It’s all right, Elowen. You don’t have to—”

“That was one question,” said Elowen.

He stopped.

“You asked me why I married you,” she said. “I told you. Now ask me the other one.”

He looked up.

“What other one?”

“Why I stayed.”

He stared at her.

She watched him not understand. She watched him look at her face, and look for something in it, and not find it, because he had spent three years teaching himself not to look for it. She watched his hands close on the blanket.

He didn’t ask.

He couldn’t, she understood. He opened his mouth, and nothing came out. He had carried one question for three years, and it had nearly killed him to ask it. He didn’t have another one left in him. Not tonight.

She reached across the tray and took his scabbed hand.

“It’s all right,” she said. “You don’t have to ask. I’m going to tell you anyway.”

“Elowen—”

“But not here.” She squeezed his hand. “Not in bed. Not with a tray. Not after you nearly died and I sat on the floor for two days.” She smiled, though her eyes were wet. “You said I had to say it on a day when it couldn’t be mistaken for anything else. On a boring day. With nothing in the way.”

He was looking at her as if she had stopped speaking his language.

“So tomorrow,” said Elowen, “you’re going to get up, and get dressed, in a real shirt, with buttons. And you’re going to use Raiden’s silly stick, and Bao is going to drive you, and you’re going to come to the shop at closing time.”

“The shop.”

“Where it started. At closing time. When it rains.” She glanced at the window. “The forecast says rain.”

He didn’t say anything for a long time.

“And then?” he asked finally. Very quietly. Like a boy at a steel yard, holding something too heavy, asking if he’s allowed to put it down.

She leaned across the tray, past the fish bones, and kissed his forehead.

“And then,” said Elowen, “you won’t have to wonder ever again.”

chapters.title: The Flower in His Lapel
chapters.desc: Closing time. Rain. One camellia, flown in from a mountain. Her answer.
chapters.epigraph: “You are the man who fought the world to give me one.”
chapters.content:
It rained at six, which meant nobody would come in after seven.

She had sent Xiao Pan home at five, and he had looked at her face and at the small white box on the workbench and gone without arguing, with the tips of his ears bright red. She had swept the floor. She had re-cut the roses. She had moved the delphiniums away from the door.

At six forty, a courier on a motorbike pulled up outside in the rain and handed her a small wooden box packed with damp moss, with a note on top in a shaky old hand.

For the wife. From the idiot’s mountain. Don’t let him touch it, he’ll crush it. — Wen.

Inside, on the moss, was a single camellia.

So full. So many petals, laid one over the other in perfect overlapping circles. So deep a pink that in the light of the shop it almost glowed. Picked that morning, from the dark glossy shrub against the mossy wall in the walled garden, and flown a thousand kilometres in a box on someone’s lap.

She held it in her palm and looked at it.

Then she cut the stem short, very carefully, with her knife, at an angle, the way you cut something so it will heal. And she waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven, the bell over the door rang.

She didn’t look up. She was standing behind the counter, wiring a single stem of eucalyptus that didn’t need wiring.

“We’re closed,” she said, though the sign still said OPEN.

Nobody answered.

She looked up.

He was standing in the doorway. Soaked to the skin, because he had refused the umbrella Bao held out for him, she found out later; he had said, Not tonight, and walked from the car in the rain. His black coat was dark with water. His hair was flattened against his forehead. He was leaning on Raiden’s ridiculous silver-headed stick, and he was thinner, and greyer, and he had dark shadows under his eyes. Water ran off him onto her clean floor.

Under the coat, he was wearing a white shirt. With buttons. He had done them up wrong, one button off, all the way down.

She almost laughed. She didn’t.

“You’re dripping on my floor,” she said.

He looked down at the puddle spreading round his shoes. Then he looked at her, and something moved in his face, too fast to read, and he took off the wet coat and folded it over his arm and stood on the doormat like a schoolboy who has been told off.

Exactly where he had stood, three years ago, on a night exactly like this one.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came round the counter.

She didn’t throw him a towel this time. She walked across the shop floor, past the buckets, past the cooler, past the second row of tulips over Raiden’s floor, and stopped in front of him on the doormat. Close. Close enough to smell the rain on him.

She reached up and undid the buttons of his shirt, one by one, all the way down, and did them up again properly. He stood very still and let her. His breathing changed.

When she had finished, she smoothed the front of the shirt flat with both hands, the way her mother had smoothed her father’s collar every morning.

Then she took the camellia out of her apron pocket.

He saw it. She watched him see it. His whole body went still.

She took the lapel of his jacket in her fingers—he had worn the black suit, the one from the reunion—and tucked the short stem of the camellia into the buttonhole. She settled it there, carefully, so the petals sat just right, deep pink against the black. Then she left her hand on it, flat, over his heart.

He looked down at the flower. Then at her.

“Zhendong,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I married you for my father,” said Elowen. “I told you that last night. It was true.”

He didn’t move.

“But I didn’t stay for him.”

The rain hammered on the new window. Inside the shop, under the lights, it was very quiet.

“I stayed,” she said, “because on the night of the rain, a man came into my shop and bought every flower in it so he could wait for my father without frightening my customers. And then he frightened a woman away from my window, and when I told him she wanted tulips for her mother, he walked out into the rain and gave them to her. And I stood here, behind that counter, and I thought: that’s not what a monster does.” Her voice wobbled. “I thought about it all night. I didn’t tell anyone. I didn’t tell myself.”

His eyes were very wide.

“I stayed,” she said, “because you sat outside my door every night for a month, and Bao says you never once slept. Because you carried my mother’s lemon tree up the steps like a baby, and set an alarm on your phone to water it. Because you read eleven times about light bending round a star, in the middle of the night, because you thought that was what I wanted. Because you bled on two hundred roses and didn’t complain once.” She was crying now. She let herself. “Because you put a light under my shop that stays on. Because you bought a mountain so nobody could dig up a flower. Because you threw three hundred million in a bin full of fish bones because I read four pages of names.”

She pressed her hand flat against the flower, against his heart.

“You are the man who fought the world to give me one,” said Elowen. “One flower. The rarest one. And I don’t want the world. I don’t want a train to the end of the line. I don’t want a quiet library and a man who talks about light. I want you. I want this. I chose you, Zhendong. Not that night in your office. Later. Every day after. Every morning at four, with two cups of coffee waiting. Every night you sat outside my door. I kept choosing you. I never stopped.”

She looked up at him through the tears.

“It’s a boring day,” she said. “Nothing happened. Nobody ordered anything. Nobody shot at anyone. I went to the market at four and Granny Su counted every bunch and Xiao Pan sang along to the radio and an old man bought chrysanthemums for his wife.” She took a breath. “And I love you. I’ve loved you for so long I can’t remember not loving you. I love you, and I mean it, and I would mean it if you were nobody and owned nothing and had never once carried a bucket in your life.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

He stood on the doormat of her shop with the camellia in his lapel and her hand over his heart, and looked down at her, and for a very long moment his face did nothing at all.

Then it broke.

She had seen him cry before. On the bathroom floor, silently, with his face in his hands. In the fever, the tears running sideways into the pillow. This was not that. This was like watching ice on a lake in spring, the long line she had seen run across it on the morning she came home from Aurelia’s, finally, finally giving way. All at once. All the way down.

He dropped Raiden’s stick. It clattered on the floor.

He took her face in both his hands, his scabbed, scarred, shaking hands, and he looked at her as if he still couldn’t believe he was allowed to.

“Say it again,” he said.

His voice was gone. It was barely there.

“I love you.”

“Again.”

“I love you, Zhendong.”

He made a sound she had never heard from him. Then he bent his head and kissed her, and his face was wet, and hers was wet, and the camellia was crushed between them, and neither of them cared.

✦ ✦ ✦

He reached into his back pocket, after.

She didn’t understand what he was doing. He took out his wallet. He opened it, with his hands still shaking, and slid his fingers behind his identity card, and drew something out, and held it out to her on his palm.

It was a flower. Very small. Pressed flat. Dried paper-thin and faded almost to grey, but still, if you looked closely, the faintest ghost of blue. A single delphinium floret, no bigger than a fingernail.

She stared at it.

“The night of the rain,” said Zhao. “It was stuck to my sleeve. When I got in the car. From the delphiniums by your door.” He swallowed. “I should have brushed it off. I didn’t. I put it in my wallet. It’s been there every day since.” He looked at her. “It was there at the registry office. It was there at the dinner with Maartens. It was there at the pond, and the shipyard, and the boat. It went into the sea with me. I had it laminated the week after the wedding, so it wouldn’t break.” His voice cracked. “It’s been there for three years. I never told you. I never told anyone.”

“Since the night of the rain,” she whispered.

“Since the night of the rain,” said Zhao. “Since you threw a towel at me and told me I was dripping on your floor. I went home and sat in my office all night and thought about your hands. How you cut the stems. Like a wound. I knew then. I didn’t know what it was called. I didn’t have the word. I’d never needed it.” He closed his hand around the delphinium and pressed it against her palm. “I love you. I’ve loved you since before you walked into my office. I married you knowing you didn’t love me, because I would rather have you without it than not have you at all.” He was crying again. “I love you. I love you. I didn’t think I would ever be allowed to say it.”

She closed her hand around his, around the tiny grey flower.

Then she reached past him and turned the sign on the door to CLOSED.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him into the back of the shop, behind the cooler, where the workbench was.

She cleared it with one sweep of her arm: the wire, the ribbon, the eucalyptus, a bucket of offcuts that tipped over and scattered stems and petals all across the new warm floor. She didn’t care. He was laughing, low and wet and astonished, and then he wasn’t laughing, because she had pulled him down by his crooked collar and kissed him again.

“Your side,” she said, against his mouth. “Elara said—”

“I don’t care what Elara said.”

“I care. You crawled up a hill with a hole in you.”

“Then be careful with me,” said Zhao. His voice was very low. “You always are.”

She was careful. He let her be. She undid the buttons she had done up properly, and pushed the shirt off his shoulders, and kissed the scars she knew by heart, in order, and then the new one: the dressing low on his left side, the edges of the healing wound under it. She kissed the skin all round it, very gently, the way you would kiss something you were afraid to wake, and he put his head back and closed his eyes and said her name, once, very low.

Then he opened his eyes, and looked at her, and she saw that careful was not going to last.

He took her face in both hands and kissed her as if he had been dead for a week and had only just come back to find her, which, she thought later, was more or less true. It wasn’t slow. It wasn’t gentle. It was desperate and wet with both their tears and tasted of salt and rain, and his hands went from her face into her hair and pulled the pins out, all of them, scattering them across the workbench among the petals, and she grabbed his shoulders and pulled him down and heard herself make a sound that should have embarrassed her and didn’t.

“Your side,” she gasped.

“I don’t care about my side.”

“I care about your side.”

“Then hold still,” said Zhao, against her throat, “and let me.”

He backed her up against the edge of the workbench. He kissed her neck, her collarbone, the hollow at the base of her throat, hard enough to leave a mark, and then another, and she let him, she wanted him to, she wanted to walk into the shop tomorrow with his mouth written all over her. He undid her blouse with shaking hands, and swore under his breath when the last button wouldn’t give, and she laughed and pulled it off over her head herself, and threw it somewhere behind the cooler, and he looked at her in the yellow light from the shop window with an expression that made her knees go.

“I thought about this,” he said. His voice was barely there. “In the water. When I was going down. I thought, I never told her. And I thought about your face.” He put his hand flat over her heart. “This. I thought about this.”

She put her hand over his.

“You’re here,” she said. “You’re here. Touch me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She had thought, three years ago, that it would always be him asking.

It wasn’t. Not tonight. Tonight, she was the one who laid him back on her coat on the workbench among the scattered petals and the crushed camellia and the smell of roses, carefully, mindful of his side, and climbed up over him, and took her time. She was the one who kissed him slowly, everywhere she could reach, until he was gripping the edge of the bench with both hands. She was the one who made him wait, and made him say it again, I love you, and again, and again, until he was saying it without being asked, over and over, into her hair, into her shoulder, into her mouth, his voice breaking on it every time, as if three years of not saying it were coming out of him all at once.

“Again,” she said.

“I love you.”

“Again.”

“I love you. Elowen. I love you. I love you—”

She kissed it out of his mouth.

And then neither of them could speak at all. She moved with him, slow and then not slow, his hands on her hips, holding her, the rain on the window and the fan humming in the cooler and the petals sticking to their skin, and she watched his face the whole time, the way he had watched hers in a candlelit room on a mountain, and saw everything in it. Every one of the three years. Every night outside her door. The delphinium in his wallet. The water. All of it, right there, open, for her.

When he finally pulled her down against him, careful of his side, and held her so tightly she could barely breathe, and said her name one last time like something breaking, she wasn’t afraid of anything at all.

Not the world. Not the glass. Not the men in grey jackets or the notice with his face on it or the long boxes in her father’s garage.

There was a wall between her and all of that now. A wall made of a man.

She had chosen it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, they lay on the floor of the shop under her coat, among the petals, because the workbench had turned out to be too narrow for two people to lie on together for more than about four minutes.

The rain had eased. The light from the window was soft and yellow. Somewhere in the cooler, the fan hummed.

He was holding the crushed camellia. He had found it on the floor and picked it up and was turning it in his fingers, very carefully, looking at it.

“Mr. Wen said not to let you touch it,” she said, against his chest. “He said you’d crush it.”

“I did crush it.”

“I know.”

He looked at the flower. Then he tucked it, crushed and perfect, behind her ear.

“I don’t have to wonder,” he said. Very quietly. As if trying the words out to see if they would hold. “Anymore.”

“No.”

“You chose me.”

“Every day.”

He was quiet for so long that she lifted her head to look at him.

He was looking at the ceiling of her shop, at the lights, at the rain on the window, at nothing, and on his face was an expression she had never seen there in three years. Not stillness. Not waiting. Not the look of a dog that hasn’t decided whether to bite.

Peace.

Just that. Plain and simple and complete.

She put her head back down on his chest and listened to his heart, slow and steady and strong, and closed her eyes.

Outside, the rain stopped. The street was empty. Nobody came in after seven.

And on the doormat by the door, where he had stood, there was a perfect wet outline of two shoes.

chapters.title: Closing Half an Empire
chapters.desc: He starts selling what he can stop selling. Chen Si helps him lie about it. Elowen keeps the books. Wei Long gets a list.
chapters.epigraph: “You can’t stop being what you are overnight, Zhendong.” “I know. I’m going to do it slowly.”
chapters.content:
He didn’t stop overnight.

He couldn’t. She understood that, and he explained it anyway, at the kitchen counter one night a month after the shop, with the ledgers spread between them and a cup of tea going cold at her elbow.

“There are a hundred and forty people,” he said, “who get paid because of what I do. Bao. The men at the Docks. The warehouse workers in the north. The drivers. Old Ming’s widow.” He turned a page. “If I close everything tomorrow, they don’t get paid. Some of them go to work for someone worse. Some of them get killed by people who think I’ve gone soft and want what’s left.” He looked at her. “And the rifles don’t stop. Someone else sells them.”

“I know.”

“So I can’t stop.” He put his finger on a column of numbers. “But I can stop some.”

She looked at the column.

It was a list of buyers. Not names; codes, the way he wrote everything. She had learned to read them. Beside each one, in his square blunt handwriting, he had written a single letter.

K. K. S. K. S. S. S.

“K is keep,” he said. “For now. Governments. Licensed buyers. Paperwork that’s real, or close enough. Private security companies. People who were going to buy anyway, from someone, and might as well buy from someone who checks.” He moved his finger. “S is stop. Militias. Anyone the UN has a report on. Anyone who uses children. Anyone Maartens sold to. Anyone I wouldn’t want you to read about.”

She counted.

There were more S’s than K’s.

“That’s more than half,” she said.

“Sixty per cent of the business.”

“Zhendong. That’s—”

“I know what it is.” He closed the ledger. “Chen Si says it’s insane. He says I’ll lose half my men and all my reputation and someone will put me in a koi pond.” He almost smiled. “He also says he’ll help.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si helped by lying.

That was what he was best at, he told Elowen, quite cheerfully, at dinner at the penthouse on the forty-fourth floor. Lying very well, in the right offices, to the right people.

“The world thinks Zhao Zhendong nearly died at the Hengli shipyard,” he said, cutting his steak into exact squares. “The world thinks he was shot by the Dutchman and hasn’t been the same since. The world thinks he’s scaling back because he’s frightened, and because his health is poor, and because the Red Notice makes travel impossible.” He ate a square. “All of which is true. None of which is the reason. I simply make sure everyone believes the true things, so that nobody looks for the real one.”

“And the men who think he’s gone soft?”

“Will be told, very quietly, by people they trust, that the last man who thought Zhao Zhendong had gone soft is in a fish pond on the coast.” Chen Si smiled faintly. “Fear is very useful. It lasts much longer than money.”

Aurelia, across the table, rolled her eyes.

“He’s enjoying this,” she said to Elowen. “Look at him. He hasn’t had a puzzle this good in years. He was up until four last night drawing diagrams.”

“It’s an interesting problem,” said Chen Si. “How to dismantle sixty per cent of an arms empire without anyone noticing, getting killed, or going to prison.” He looked at his brother, who was sitting at the end of the table eating his steak with his hands, the way he always did at Chen Si’s, because Chen Si had stopped trying to make him use cutlery a decade ago. “I find I quite like building something for once,” he said. “It’s more interesting than winning.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen kept the books.

Not all of them. The K side, the side that stayed. She sat at the kitchen counter in the evenings with his ledgers and her pencil and checked every number, every shipment, every end-user certificate, every buyer. When something was wrong, she wrote it in the margin in her small, neat, wedding-card handwriting, and he read it the next morning over coffee and fixed it.

His accountant, a nervous man called Mr. Yao who had worked for him for nine years, came to the house on the hill once to discuss it. He sat at the clean dining table with Elowen for three hours, going through the ledgers line by line, and came out looking like a man who had been through a very thorough interrogation.

“Mr. Zhao,” he said, in the hall, by the lemon tree. “Your wife found an error in the third quarter accounts from four years ago.”

“Yes,” said Zhao.

“I made that error.”

“Yes.”

“Nobody ever found it. I didn’t find it. I’ve been looking for four years.” Mr. Yao took off his glasses and wiped them. His hands were shaking. “She found it in twenty minutes. With a pencil.”

Zhao looked down the hall at his wife, who was still sitting at the dining table, frowning at a ledger, chewing the end of her pencil.

“Yes,” he said. “She does that.”

Mr. Yao put his glasses back on.

“I think,” he said carefully, “I might be afraid of her.”

“Good,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

And Song Wei Long got a list.

Elowen took it to him herself. She met him at a noodle shop in the old town, near the police station, on a Tuesday afternoon. He was sitting in the corner with a bowl of beef noodles, in his plain dark coat, with his carved, expressionless face, and he looked up when she sat down opposite him and didn’t say anything.

She put an envelope on the table.

“What is it?” he asked.
