“Names,” said Elowen. “People my husband used to do business with. People he’s stopped doing business with. Traffickers. Men who move people as well as guns. Men who buy children from refugee camps and sell them across the border.” She pushed it across. “Some of them are in this city. Some of them have offices you can walk into.”

Song Wei Long looked at the envelope. He didn’t touch it.

“Why?” he said.

“Because he can’t do anything about them without killing them,” said Elowen. “And I’ve asked him not to kill people first. So I thought, maybe you could do something about them without killing them instead.”

“And in return?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at her.

“Nothing,” she said again. “No deal. No favour. My husband isn’t asking you to look away from anything. He knows you won’t. He doesn’t want you to.” She stood up. “He said, ‘Tell the detective I owe him a cat.’ I told him that was my line. He didn’t care.”

Song Wei Long looked up at her. Something moved in the carved stone of his face. It might, on another man, have been a smile.

“I’ll read it,” he said.

He put the envelope inside his coat.

Six weeks later, the evening news showed a raid on a warehouse by the railway in the east of the city. Fourteen men arrested. Twenty-two people found in a shipping container, alive, among them nine children. A detective with a carved, expressionless face stood behind the reporter, not looking at the camera.

Elowen watched it at the kitchen counter, with her husband sitting beside her on one of the tall stools.

When it finished, he reached over without a word and took her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t become a good man.

She knew that. He knew it. He still sold weapons, to governments, to licensed buyers, to people who would buy them anyway. He still had a Red Notice. He still came home some nights smelling of other people’s cigarettes, and some nights he still went down to the basement at two in the morning and cleaned something that didn’t need cleaning. He still had a hundred and forty people on his payroll, and some of them had done terrible things, and some of them would again.

But the S column got longer every month. The K column got shorter. And in the spring, he sold the warehouse in the north where Wu used to steal from him, and gave the money, all of it, to Old Ming’s widow and the nephew who wanted to be a chef, who opened a small noodle restaurant near the Docks.

It was very good. They ate there every Friday.

“You know,” said Elowen, one Friday, watching the nephew through the kitchen hatch, chopping spring onions very fast with a cleaver and singing to himself, “you could keep going. One day. All the S’s. All of it.”

Zhao didn’t answer for a long time. He was eating his noodles, slowly, sitting down.

“One day,” he said finally. “Maybe.”

“Maybe?”

“I don’t know who I am if I’m not this.” He put down his chopsticks. “I’ve been this since I was nineteen. Since before that. Since the yard.” He looked at her. “I don’t know what else I’m for.”

She reached across the table and took his scarred hand.

“You carry buckets very well,” she said. “Granny Su says you’re the best she’s ever seen.”

He looked at her.

Then, slowly, the corner of his mouth went up, and stayed up, rusty and crooked and real.

“That’s not a job,” he said.

“It could be,” said Elowen. “I’m very short-staffed.”

chapters.title: The Wedding They Eloped From
chapters.desc: A real ceremony in the flower shop. Every Lin. Every friend. Two dogs. One father who finally asks the right question.
chapters.epigraph: “You never had a wedding.” “We had a registry office on a Tuesday.” “That isn’t a wedding, darling. That’s an appointment.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
It was Aurelia’s idea.

Of course it was. She announced it at the penthouse in June, over dessert, with the air of a general announcing an invasion.

“You’re having a wedding,” she said.

Elowen put down her spoon. “We’re married.”

“You had a registry office on a Tuesday. With soil under your nails. And a ring two sizes too big. And Chen Si as a witness nobody needed.” Aurelia pointed her fork across the table. “That isn’t a wedding, darling. That’s an appointment.”

“It was a very good appointment,” said Zhao.

Everyone turned to look at him.

He was eating his cake with his hands. He looked up, mildly, and met his wife’s eyes across the table.

“Nine forty-one,” he said. “I remember the time.”

Aurelia looked from one of them to the other. Then she put down her fork.

“Oh, for heaven’s sake,” she said. “You’re having a wedding. In September. I’m organising it. Nobody is allowed to argue. Chen Si, write it down.”

Chen Si took out a pen.

✦ ✦ ✦

They had it in the shop.

Aurelia wanted the Harbour Hotel. Elowen said no. Aurelia wanted the Chen penthouse. Elowen said no. Aurelia wanted a garden, a ballroom, a yacht, a temple, a castle somewhere in the hills that belonged to a man who owed Chen Si money. Elowen said no to all of them.

“The shop,” she said.

“It holds thirty people,” said Aurelia. “Standing.”

“Then thirty people,” said Elowen. “Standing.”

Aurelia looked at her. Then her face changed.

“Where it started,” she said quietly.

“Where it started.”

So they had it in the shop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden took the shelving off the back wall for the day and put it back the next morning. He built an arch over the doorway out of reclaimed timber from the old Hengli shipyard, which he said was poetic and Chen Si said was in very poor taste and Zhao said nothing about at all, but stood under it for a long time the evening it went up, with one hand on the wood.

Eliana rigged the lights. Thousands of them, tiny and warm, strung across the ceiling like stars. She programmed them to come on at exactly 9:41, and refused to tell anyone why, and was found the night before the wedding asleep on the floor of the shop under a ladder with her laptop on her chest.

Elara did the cake, because she had steady hands and was used to working at very small scales, and because she said it would be relaxing after surgery. It was four tiers. It had sugar camellias on it, deep pink, every petal laid perfectly over the last. She made each one with tweezers.

Evangeline did nothing, as far as anyone could tell, except stand at the back of the shop for three days with her arms folded, watching everyone else work. Then, on the morning of the wedding, she brought in a small potted orchid, white, and put it on the counter beside the till, and Elowen looked at it and burst into tears, because it was a cutting from the orchid Evangeline had given her the week she moved into the house on the hill, which she had thought had died.

“I kept a piece,” said Evangeline quietly. “Before you moved. In case.”

Elowen held her sister for a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

And Elowen did the flowers.

Of course she did. She would not let anyone else touch them. Aurelia tried to hire a florist from Milan and Elowen looked at her across the penthouse dining table with such an expression that Aurelia put her phone down mid-sentence and said, “Fine. Fine. But I’m choosing the ribbon.”

She went to the market at four in the morning on the day, as always. He drove her, as always. He carried the buckets.

Granny Su was waiting at stall forty-two with a cigarette and a box.

“For the bride,” she said, and pushed the box across the counter.

Inside, packed in damp moss, were five stems of lily of the valley. Out of season. Very expensive. The same as on the morning of the registry office, three and a half years ago.

“I don’t know how you get these,” said Elowen.

“Trade secret,” said Granny Su. She looked at Zhao, standing behind his wife with three boxes of eucalyptus in his arms, held correctly, like he was carrying them and not like they were a baby. “You. You carry well now.”

“Thank you, Grandmother.”

“The ring,” said Granny Su. “Still too big?”

Zhao looked at Elowen. Elowen held up her left hand.

The heavy gold ring with the square green stone was on her fourth finger. Where it belonged. It fitted perfectly.

Granny Su looked at it. Then she looked at Zhao.

“Hm,” she said, and lit another cigarette, and that was all; but when they had walked away down the aisle, Elowen looked back and saw the old woman wiping her eyes with the back of her hand, very quickly, and pretending it was the smoke.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine o’clock, thirty people stood in a flower shop.

Lin Jian, in his funeral suit, which was the only suit he owned, standing by the cooler with his hands clasped in front of him, trying not to cry and failing.

Raiden, in a silver waistcoat he had designed himself, beside a tall, quiet, broad-shouldered woman in a black leather jacket with grease under her nails whom he introduced to everyone as Jinx, my girlfriend, she built Xiao Pan’s bike, don’t touch her tools.

Evangeline, at the back, alone, in pale blue, watching the door.

Elara, flushed and proud beside her cake, with a tall, serious young doctor in glasses standing very close beside her whom nobody had been introduced to yet and everyone noticed.

Eliana, in a hoodie, with a laptop, because she had refused to wear anything else and nobody had the energy to argue; and beside her a lanky boy from next door with a medical textbook under his arm, who had apparently come because Eliana told him to.

Chen Si, in grey, by the counter, where he had stood at the registry office with an untouched coffee. Aurelia, in gold, in the front, in charge of everything.

Bao, in a new suit that didn’t fit across the shoulders, with the long pink scar on his arm, standing by the door the way he always stood by doors.

Xiao Pan, with his motorbike helmet under his arm, because he had ridden there and wouldn’t leave it outside.

Mr. Wen’s grandson, who had flown up from the Cangshan hills with a box of oolong from the upper terraces and a message from his grandfather, which he delivered loudly, to the room, before anything else: “Grandpa says: Tell the idiot I was right.”

Old Ming’s widow and her nephew. Mr. Yao the accountant, who sat as far from Elowen as the shop allowed. Detective Song Wei Long, in his plain dark coat, at the very back, who said he wasn’t there officially and then stood through the whole thing with his carved face perfectly still and his eyes suspiciously bright.

A card had come from Miles Wei, from a conference somewhere cold. It was on the counter. It said: Light bends around heavy things. I hope you’re very happy. I think you are. — M.

And two dogs, Dumpling and Noodle, with white ribbons tied round their necks, lying on the doormat in the exact place where a man had once stood dripping in the rain.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian walked her down the aisle.

The aisle was four metres long, between the buckets of white roses. It took them twenty seconds. Her father’s arm was shaking. Halfway down, past the second row of tulips over Raiden’s floor, he stopped.

Everyone waited.

He looked at Zhao, standing at the far end under the arch from the shipyard, in his black suit, with a camellia in his lapel: one of Elara’s sugar ones, because Mr. Wen said the shrub had given enough this year. Zhao looked back at him. Steady. Waiting. The way he had stood in the dining room on the night of the fish belly.

“Zhendong,” said Lin Jian.

The shop went very quiet.

“How is the lemon tree?” Lin Jian asked.

For a moment, Zhao didn’t say anything.

Then something happened in his face, slowly, like a door opening.

“Nine lemons,” he said. “The most it’s ever had.”

Lin Jian nodded. His eyes were wet. He walked the last two metres and put his daughter’s hand into the hand of the man who had made his own shake for six years, and held them both together for a moment between his.

“Look after her,” he said.

“She looks after me,” said Zhao.

Lin Jian looked at him for a long time. Then he smiled, his whole face crumpling, and stepped back to stand beside Raiden, who put an arm around him without looking.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t have a priest or an official. They were already married; the little red book was in the drawer under the till. Aurelia had asked Chen Si to say a few words, and he stood at the side of the arch and said exactly four sentences, which was how many he had prepared.

“Thirteen years ago, I carried this man through a sewer. He was very heavy. He has been carrying people ever since, and nobody has ever carried him. I am very glad to see that somebody finally does.”

Then he stepped back, and Aurelia, beside him, looked up at her husband with an expression that made Elowen look away to give them privacy.

They said their own vows. Nobody had written them down. Nobody needed to.

“I don’t run,” said Elowen, holding his hands. “I cut things cleanly. And then I keep them. I keep you. Every day. At four in the morning. I keep choosing you.”

He looked at her. His jaw was moving.

“I’ll sit outside your door,” said Zhao. “Every night. For as long as I live. So you’ll always know where I am.” He swallowed. “So you’ll never have to wonder.”

“You sleep in my bed now,” said Elowen. “You don’t have to sit outside the door.”

“I know,” he said. “I’ll still be there.”

At 9:41, Eliana pressed a key on her laptop, and every one of the thousands of tiny lights on the ceiling came on at once, warm and gold, like a sky full of stars.

He kissed her under them, in her shop, in front of everyone she loved; and for the first time in her life, Lin Elowen didn’t keep her face still at all.

chapters.title: Every Flower in the Shop
chapters.desc: Epilogue. Five years after the first rainy night. Closing time. He buys them all again.
chapters.epigraph: “How much, for everything?”
chapters.content:
The rain started at six, which meant nobody would come in after seven.

Lin Elowen knew the rhythm of the shop the way other people knew their own heartbeat. Morning was for brides and funerals. Lunch was for office workers who had forgotten a birthday. Late afternoon was for men who had done something wrong. And when it rained in the Walled City, the narrow streets filled with water and umbrellas and bad tempers, and the last hour before closing belonged to her.

She was twenty-nine. The shop was ten years old. The sign above the door still said Elowen’s in white paint, because she had repainted it twice and both times, standing on the ladder with the brush in her hand, had not been able to think of anything better.

She was stripping the lower leaves from a bucket of white stock when the bell over the door rang.

“We close in ten minutes,” she said, without looking up. “If it’s for an apology, I recommend the peonies. They look expensive.”

Nobody answered.

She looked up.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man in the doorway was soaked to the skin. His black coat was dark with rain, his hair flattened against his forehead, and water ran off him onto her clean floor in a steady, careless stream. He was tall and very still.

Behind him, through the glass, a man stood under the awning of the noodle shop across the street. He was eating noodles. Bao had started eating noodles there every evening about two years ago, and the noodle shop owner had started keeping a stool for him.

“You’re dripping on my floor,” said Elowen.

Zhao Zhendong looked down at the puddle spreading round his shoes. Then he took off his wet coat, folded it over his arm, and stood on the doormat like a schoolboy who had been told off.

It was the same coat. The old black wool, thin at the elbows, that he had worn the first night and kept wearing until the elbows went through, and then had taken to a tailor in the old town who had patched them with black leather and shaken his head the whole time.

“You don’t have an umbrella,” she said.

“Bao had one.”

“And?”

“It’s raining,” said Zhao, as if that explained everything. “It was raining the first time.”

She threw him a towel from the workbench.

He caught it without looking.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came round the counter. He wasn’t allowed behind the counter. He had not been allowed behind the counter for five years. The sign was still in the drawer under the till, with rule two crossed out in her handwriting and Except when she says so written beside it in his, and She always says so under that in hers.

He put his arms round her from behind and rested his chin on top of her head and looked at the stock she was stripping.

“You’re tired,” he said.

“I’m fine.”

“You were at the market at four.”

“I’m always at the market at four.”

“Elara said you should stop going at four.” His hands moved, very gently, down from her waist to rest on the curve of her stomach under her apron. Four months. Just beginning to show. “Elara said, ‘Tell her to let you go alone. Tell her Granny Su will count every bunch.’”

“Granny Su is eighty-three,” said Elowen. “She can barely see the bunches.”

“She can see them. She counts them by feel now. She told me.” His thumbs moved slowly on her stomach. “She said, ‘Tell the girl I’ve been counting since before she was born, and I’ll be counting after this one is.’”

Elowen laughed, and leaned back against him, and closed her eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven forty, a woman knocked on the glass with an umbrella and pointed at the tulips.

Elowen opened her eyes.

She was young, the woman. Twenty, perhaps. A student, with a backpack and a cheap umbrella that had blown inside out on one side. She was standing in the rain pointing at the bucket of red tulips by the window with an expression of hopeless, apologetic longing, the way people point at things they know they can’t afford.

Zhao looked at the woman through the glass.

Elowen felt him go still behind her. Not the old stillness. Something else.

“Wait,” he said.

He let go of her, stepped to the till, and opened his wallet, and took out a stack of notes, and put it down on the counter beside her scissors.

“How much,” he said, “for everything?”

She stared at him.

Five years ago, standing in this exact spot, with rain running off him onto her floor and a holster under his arm, he had said exactly that. She had done the sum without meaning to. Four thousand two hundred.

She looked at the buckets. At the roses and the stock and the lilies in the cooler and the delphiniums she had moved away from the door. At the tulips in the window, and the girl standing outside them in the rain.

She did the sum.

“Six thousand eight hundred,” said Elowen. “Prices went up.”

He counted out seven thousand. Then he picked up the bucket of red tulips, all twenty stems, dripping, and walked to the door, and opened it into the rain.

“Hey,” he called. Not loudly.

The girl stopped.

He held out the tulips.

The girl looked at the flowers, at his face, at the rain running down it. At the woman behind the counter, smiling. She took the tulips with both hands, and stared at him, and said, “I—I can’t pay for—it’s my mum’s birthday, I only wanted one, I can’t—”

“They’re paid for,” said Zhao.

The girl looked at the tulips in her arms. Then she looked back up at him, and her face did something complicated, and she said, “Thank you,” very quietly, and ran.

He came back in and shut the door and stood on the doormat. His sleeves were wet to the elbow.

“Those were my tulips,” said Elowen.

“They were my tulips,” said Zhao. “I paid.”

She opened her mouth to argue. Then she closed it, because he was right, and because she had just watched him do it again, after five years, without anyone asking, without anyone watching but her, and she knew exactly what to do with that now.

She came round the counter and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

They closed at eight.

He swept the floor. He did the corners with his fingers. She re-cut the roses that hadn’t sold, which was all of them, because he had bought them, and put them in the cooler for tomorrow, when she would sell them again and he would pretend not to notice that he had paid for them twice.

At the door, before she turned off the lights, she looked back at the shop.

The buckets. The cooler, humming. The second row of tulips, over a room under the floor with a light that stayed on. The counter, with a heavy old ring sitting beside the till, because she took it off to work and always put it in the same place. The drawer under the till with the sign in it. The orchid Evangeline had given her, on the windowsill. A narrow glass frame on the wall behind the counter with a pressed camellia floating in it, deep pink, every petal laid perfectly over the last.

And on the doormat by the door, a perfect wet outline of two shoes.

“Elowen,” he said behind her.

She turned.

He was holding out his wallet. Open. Behind his identity card, flat and faded almost to grey, she could see the ghost of a tiny blue flower, no bigger than a fingernail.

“Five years,” he said. “Today. Seven o’clock. The rain started at six.”

“You remember everything.”

“I’m very bad at forgetting things.” He closed the wallet and put it away, over his heart. “Do you know what I thought? That night. When you threw the towel at me.”

“What?”

He looked at her in the half-dark of her shop, with the rain on the window and the street lights coming through it, gold and soft.

“I thought,” said Zhao, “I would buy every flower in this shop every night for the rest of my life, if she would let me stand on the doormat.”

She looked at him.

“You can stand anywhere you like,” said Elowen. “Except behind the counter.”

“Except when you say so.”

“I always say so.”

He laughed, low and warm, and she turned off the lights, and they went out into the rain together. He held the coat over both their heads. She held his hand. Bao, under the noodle shop awning, finished his noodles and stood up and walked a little way behind them, the way he always did.

Behind them, the shop was dark and quiet, and full of flowers, every one of them paid for.

Twice.

chapters.title: Zhao Zhendong Tries to Arrange Flowers
chapters.desc: The florist has a fever. It’s Mother’s Day. The roses did not survive.
chapters.epigraph: “How hard can it be?” — Zhao Zhendong, 7:02 a.m.
chapters.content:
On the second Mother’s Day of their marriage, Elowen woke up with a fever of thirty-eight point nine and a throat like sandpaper, and found her husband standing at the end of the bed, fully dressed, holding the van keys.

“No,” she croaked.

“You can’t talk.”

“I have forty-three orders.”

“I know. I read the book.” He held up her order book. He had put sticky notes on it. “Xiao Pan is coming at seven. Bao is driving. Granny Su has the flowers ready. I called her at three.”

“You can’t arrange flowers.”

“I’ve watched you for a year.”

“You’ve watched me strip roses.”

He looked at her with an expression of calm, total confidence. It was the face he wore when he walked into rooms full of men with guns.

“How hard can it be?” said Zhao Zhendong.

She tried to get out of bed. He picked her up, put her back in it, pulled the duvet up to her chin, put a glass of water and two paracetamol on the bedside table, and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiao Pan told her about it afterwards. He told her in great detail, standing at the end of the bed that evening, still slightly pale, as if recounting a battle.

“The first hour was okay,” he said. “He did the wrapping ones. The simple ones. He just copied what you write in the book. ‘Twelve red roses, gypsophila, brown paper, red ribbon.’ He did exactly that. Exactly. He measured the ribbon with a ruler, Miss Lin.”

“A ruler.”

“To the centimetre. He said your bows are always eleven centimetres on each side.” Xiao Pan paused. “They are. I checked.”

Elowen closed her eyes.

“Then,” said Xiao Pan, “order nineteen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Order nineteen was an arrangement. A real one. A round, low, mixed bouquet in a ceramic bowl, for a customer who had written in the book, in Elowen’s handwriting: Something soft, for a mother who has everything. Use your judgment.

Zhao stood in front of the bowl for ten minutes.

Then he picked up a pink rose and put it in the foam.

He looked at it.

He took it out and put it in again, a centimetre to the left.

He looked at it.

“The thing is,” Xiao Pan told her, “he kept trying to make it symmetrical. Like a—like a gun on a cloth. Everything in a straight line. He put four roses at the top and four at the bottom and four on each side, exactly the same distance apart, and then he put the gypsophila in between them in perfect little rows, and then he stood back and looked at it, and it looked like—” Xiao Pan searched for the word. “Like a flower parade. Like soldiers. Like the roses were about to march.”

Elowen started laughing and had to stop because it hurt her throat.

“He knew it was wrong,” said Xiao Pan. “He didn’t say anything. He just stood there with his arms folded, looking at it, for a long time. And then he took everything out and started again.”

“How many times?”

Xiao Pan looked at the ceiling.

“Seven,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the seventh time, the roses were destroyed.

Not dead. Just—exhausted. Bruised from being pushed in and pulled out of the foam. Two of them had lost their heads entirely. The gypsophila had gone flat. There were petals all over the workbench, all over the floor, all over Zhao. He had a pink rose petal stuck in his hair and didn’t know it.

It was half past eleven. The customer was coming at twelve.

Xiao Pan, who had finished all the simple orders and was now standing at a safe distance by the cooler, watched his employer’s husband stare at the empty ceramic bowl.

“Mr. Zhao,” he said carefully. “Maybe I could call Miss Lin and ask—”

“No.”

“She wouldn’t mind—”

“She has a fever.” Zhao didn’t look away from the bowl. “She can’t talk. She went to the market every day for five years, sick, tired, on her wedding morning. I’m not calling her because I can’t put flowers in a bowl.”

He was quiet.

“What does she do?” he asked. “When she does this. I’ve watched her. She doesn’t measure. She doesn’t plan. She just—” He made a small, frustrated movement with his hand. “Picks things up. Puts them down. And it’s right. How does she know?”

Xiao Pan thought about it.

“She says,” he said slowly, “that you have to stop trying to make it look like flowers. You have to make it look like the person.”

Zhao turned his head and looked at him.

“‘A mother who has everything,’” said Xiao Pan. “Miss Lin would think about that. About what a mother like that would want. Not what looks nice. What she feels like.”

Zhao looked back at the bowl.

He stood there. Then he walked to the cooler, opened it, and stood inside, in the cold, looking at the buckets.

When he came out, he was holding things Xiao Pan didn’t expect. Not the pink roses. A handful of small white sweet peas. Three stems of pale blue scabious, slightly wild and messy. A sprig of rosemary from the herb pot on the windowsill. One single, slightly crooked peach rose that Elowen had put aside because its head was a little bent.

He put them in the bowl.

He didn’t measure. He didn’t line them up. He put them in quickly, without stopping to look, the way you’d put things into a bag in a hurry, and then he stopped.

It wasn’t symmetrical. It wasn’t neat. The scabious leaned to one side. The sweet peas were clumped together in one corner. The crooked peach rose sat a little off-centre, bowing its bent head.

It looked like someone’s garden in the morning. It looked like something picked by a child.

Zhao looked at it. Xiao Pan looked at it.

“That one,” said Xiao Pan, after a while, “is very good.”

“It’s a mess.”

“It looks like a mum,” said Xiao Pan. “Like a nice one. Like she’d keep the crooked rose because nobody else would.”

Zhao looked at the crooked rose for a long moment.

“Yes,” he said quietly. “That’s what I was thinking about.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The customer came at twelve. She was a middle-aged woman in an expensive coat, collecting the arrangement for her mother. She looked at the bowl on the counter for a long time.

Then she looked up at the large, silent, frightening man behind the counter, who had a pink rose petal in his hair.

“Did you make this?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“My mother had a garden,” said the woman. “When I was little. Before she was ill. Sweet peas. And rosemary by the door.” Her voice had gone strange. “How did you know?”

Zhao looked at her.

“I didn’t,” he said. “I thought about what she’d keep.”

The woman paid. She left a tip so large that Xiao Pan made a small sound. At the door, she turned back, and looked at the arrangement in her arms, and then at Zhao.

“Thank you,” she said, and went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Seven times,” said Elowen, from the bed, that evening.

“Seven times,” said Xiao Pan.

“And the roses?”

Xiao Pan looked at Zhao, who was standing in the doorway with a tray of congee and a very stiff face.

“The roses,” said Xiao Pan solemnly, “did not survive.”

He fled.

Zhao put the tray down on the bed. Elowen looked up at him. There was still a pink rose petal in his hair. She reached up and took it out and held it between two fingers.

“You made a mother cry,” she croaked.

“I made a bowl of flowers look like a garden,” he said. “By accident.”

“That’s not an accident. That’s the whole job.” She put the rose petal on the tray beside the congee. “I’m very proud of you.”

He looked at her.

“I’m never doing it again,” he said.

“Of course not.”

“I mean it.”

“I know you do.”

The next Mother’s Day, she had a fever again. Or said she did. He stood at the end of the bed with the van keys for a long time, looking at her suspiciously.

Then he went to the shop.

chapters.title: The Delivery Boy Who Saw Too Much
chapters.desc: Xiao Pan just wanted a tip. A complete list of things he has seen, and will never tell anyone, in order.
chapters.epigraph: “Please don’t make me say more, Miss Lin. I have to live.” — Xiao Pan
chapters.content:
My name is Pan Xiaodong. Everybody calls me Xiao Pan. I am twenty-two years old. I have worked at Elowen’s for five years. I deliver flowers. I am very good at it.

I would like to make it clear that I did not want to see any of this.

✦ ✦ ✦

1. The night of the rain.

I wasn’t there. I want that on the record. I had gone home early with a cold. But the next morning, there was five thousand in cash under the till that Miss Lin wouldn’t explain, and a wet shoe print on the doormat that she wouldn’t let me mop, and she kept looking at the delphiniums and smiling at nothing. I was seventeen. I thought she’d met a nice man.

I did not know, at the time, how wrong I was about the nice.

2. The first time I saw him.

He came in two weeks later. He didn’t buy anything. He stood in the doorway and looked at Miss Lin, and Miss Lin looked at him, and I was sweeping, and I stopped sweeping, because the whole shop had gone the way a field goes before thunder.

Then she said, “Xiao Pan, go and get lunch,” and I went, and I didn’t come back for two hours, because I am not stupid.

3. The van.

I don’t want to talk about the van.

My hands are fine now. I can hold a spoon. I can hold a cleaver; Old Ming’s nephew taught me, at the noodle shop. I can ride a motorbike. A small red one. A woman called Jinx built it. She has tattoos on both arms and she made me sit on it for an hour in her garage before she would let me start it, and she told me if I ever rode it without a helmet she would take the engine out with her bare hands.

I believe her. I wear the helmet.

He paid for everything. The hospital. The grafts I didn’t need. The exercises. The bike. He never said a word about it. When I tried to thank him, he hid behind a newspaper.

4. The house rules.

Miss Lin put a sign on the back wall. No frightening the customers. The husband is not allowed behind the counter.

He swept the floor instead. He did the corners with his fingers.

I have worked in this shop for five years. Nobody has ever done the corners. Not even Miss Lin.

5. The cooler.

I am not going to describe the cooler.

I will say that she went in to get lilies for a funeral order, and he followed her, and the door shut, and they were in there for nine minutes. It is one degree in the cooler. I timed it. When they came out, she had forgotten the lilies, and her face was pink, and he was carrying the bucket.

I wrapped the same bouquet four times while they were in there. I didn’t notice until the customer pointed out it had four ribbons.

6. The apron.

On the morning of the four hundred roses, she made him wear the green apron. It said ELOWEN’S on the front. It came to his ribs.

Then Mr. Chen came in, in a camel coat, and stopped dead in the doorway and said “Good morning” in the voice of a man who has just seen a dog walk on its hind legs.

Later, they stood on the pavement outside and Mr. Zhao laughed. Out loud. Two old ladies stopped to stare.

I have never told anyone about the apron. Nobody would believe me.

7. The hoodie.

He asked to borrow my hoodie. The grey one. I said yes, because you say yes. Then, as he was leaving, I said, “Mr. Zhao, it says FLOWER POWER on the back,” and he said, “I know,” and left anyway.

I found out later he wore it to a physics lecture. To spy on a man Miss Lin used to like at school.

When she asked me where my hoodie was, I tried to lie. I am very bad at lying. My ears go red. I said a man had borrowed it for an important mission, and she looked at me, and I said, “Please don’t make me say more, Miss Lin, I have to live.”

She laughed for ten minutes.

He gave it back washed and folded. With a note in the pocket. It said, Thank you. You were right about the back.

I still have the note.

8. The glass.

I don’t want to talk about the glass either.

I will say that there was a little girl called Mimi, buying sunflowers, and the window went white, and I didn’t think. I just went. I was lying on top of her and her mum with my hands over my head and glass falling on my back like hail, and it didn’t hurt, then. It hurt later. A nurse at the City Hospital took forty-one pieces out of me with tweezers.

When he came down the ladder into the room under the floor, he didn’t look at me. He looked at Miss Lin. Only at her. Like nothing else in the world existed.

Later, Miss Lin told me what he’d said on the phone, driving too fast to reach her: “Tell him his motorbike is going to be a very good one.”

It is. It is a very good one.

Mimi sends me a drawing every New Year. Last year it was me on the red motorbike, with a helmet, and a lot of sunflowers. I keep them all on my wall.

9. The night he came back.

I wasn’t there. I was at home, asleep. But I did the market every morning for those three days, with Granny Su, because somebody had to, and Miss Lin was in the basement and wouldn’t come out.

Granny Su made me count every bunch. Every single one. She said, “If you get it wrong, the girl’s husband will know when he comes back, and he’ll look at you.”

I said, “What if he doesn’t come back?”

Granny Su hit me on the back of the head with a bunch of eucalyptus.

“He comes back,” she said. “He carries too well not to.”

On the fourth morning, Miss Lin texted me one word. Home.

I cried on my motorbike at a red light and a taxi driver asked if I was all right.

10. The camellia.

On the sixteenth day after, she sent me home at five. There was a little white box on the workbench and she wouldn’t tell me what was in it, and her face was doing something I had never seen it do.

I don’t know what happened in the shop that night. I came in the next morning at six and the workbench had been cleared, and there were petals all over the floor, and stems, and a crushed pink flower I had never seen before sitting in a glass of water on the counter beside the till, like something important.

And the sign was still turned to CLOSED.

I turned it to OPEN. I swept the petals. I didn’t ask.

I am not stupid.

11. The tip.

Here is the thing nobody understands.

I have delivered flowers for five years. To weddings and funerals and hospitals and offices and once, terrifyingly, to a prison. I have been tipped well and badly and not at all.

The best tip I ever got was on the morning of their real wedding, in the shop, in September. I had put my helmet down by the door and was standing at the back with Mr. Yao the accountant, who was hiding.

At the end, when everyone was eating cake, Mr. Zhao came over to me. He didn’t say anything for a while. He just stood beside me, looking at Miss Lin across the room, laughing with her sisters, with the little gold lights on the ceiling.

Then he said, “The night of the van. When you tried to save the roses.”

“Yes, Mr. Zhao?”

“Why?”

I thought about it.

“Because they were for a wedding,” I said. “Two hundred people. Miss Lin worked until eleven on them. I didn’t want her to have to start again.”

He was quiet.

Then he put his hand on my shoulder. Just for a second. Heavy and warm.

“Thank you,” he said, “for looking after her before I knew how.”

That was the tip.

I know it doesn’t sound like much. But I have worked at Elowen’s for five years, and I have seen everything, and I can tell you: it was the best one I ever got.

I am still not telling anyone about the cooler.

chapters.title: Chen Si, Please Tell Your Wife to Stop
chapters.desc: A phone call between blood brothers, at two in the morning, about a building, a necklace, and a war neither of them can win.
chapters.content:
The phone on the bedside table buzzed at 2:04.

Zhao was awake. He was always awake at 2:04, or near it. He picked it up before it buzzed twice, and looked at the screen, and got out of bed very quietly so as not to wake his wife, and went out into the corridor in the dark.

“Si,” he said.

“Zhendong.” Chen Si’s voice. Calm. Very calm. Too calm. “Are you awake?”

“You know I’m awake.”

“I need you to do something for me.”

Zhao leaned against the wall beside the bedroom door. “What?”

“I need you,” said Chen Si, “to tell your wife to stop.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a pause.

“Stop what,” said Zhao.

“Don’t pretend. I know you know. Aurelia has been awake since midnight walking up and down the living room in a silk robe talking to herself in Italian.” Chen Si’s voice dropped. “She’s holding a printout. She’s been holding it for two hours. Every so often she stops and looks at it and says ‘Unbelievable’ and starts walking again.”

“What’s on the printout?”

“A property registration,” said Chen Si. “From this afternoon. The building next to your wife’s shop. The empty one, with the old tailor’s on the ground floor.” A pause. “Your wife bought it.”

Zhao didn’t say anything.

“Your wife,” said Chen Si, “bought the building next door to her own shop. With her own money. From the flower shop. And the tea estate. And apparently a very successful wedding season.” Another pause. “She’s going to knock through the wall and double the size of the shop. She told Aurelia at lunch. Casually. Over salad.”

“I know,” said Zhao.

“You know.”

“She told me last week. She showed me the drawings. Raiden did them.” He looked at the dark corridor. “It’s a good building. The roof is sound.”

“The roof is—Zhendong. Do you understand what this means?”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Explain,” said Zhao, who did, but liked hearing Chen Si explain things.

“Three weeks ago,” said Chen Si, “I gave Aurelia a necklace. For no reason at all. A very good one. Sapphires. From an estate sale in Geneva. It was in a magazine.” A pause. “On the same day, you took your wife to a mountain and stood in a walled garden with her in the rain looking at a flower.”

“It was the anniversary of the mountain,” said Zhao. “We go every year.”

“I know. Aurelia knows. Aurelia saw the photographs. Your wife posted one. One photograph. The two of you under an umbrella looking at a camellia.” Chen Si’s voice was very even. “It got more likes than the necklace.”

Zhao closed his eyes.

“Aurelia didn’t speak to me for a day,” said Chen Si. “Then she bought a jewellery workshop in Milan. As a treat. For herself. Because she deserves it. And she told your wife about it. At lunch. Over salad.” A pause. “And then your wife bought a building.”

“They’re competing,” said Zhao.

“They have been competing,” said Chen Si, “since they were fifteen years old and a list of exam results went up on a noticeboard. They are never going to stop competing. They will be competing in the nursing home. They will be competing about whose funeral has better flowers.” He breathed out. “And somehow, Zhendong, I am losing. I don’t understand how. I gave her sapphires.”

“You gave her something expensive,” said Zhao. “Elowen bought something for herself.”

Silence on the line.

“Explain that,” said Chen Si slowly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao looked at the bedroom door, open a hand’s width. Through the gap, he could see his wife asleep under the window over the sea, one arm flung out across his side of the bed where he had just been.

“The necklace is beautiful,” he said. “Aurelia will wear it and everyone will look at her and that’s what she likes. But you chose it. You bought it. It’s a gift.” He paused. “The building, Elowen chose. Elowen bought. With money she made. For a shop with her name on it. Nobody gave it to her.” He paused again. “Aurelia isn’t angry because the building is bigger than the necklace. She’s angry because she knows that if she’d bought the jewellery workshop first, she would have won.”

Chen Si was quiet.

“How do you know that?” he said finally.

“Because Elowen told me once,” said Zhao, “that in their final year, when she came first in the rankings, Aurelia didn’t mind losing. She minded that Elowen made it look like she didn’t try.” He shrugged in the dark. “Aurelia doesn’t want the best present. She wants to win something herself. Like Elowen did.”

The silence on the line went on for so long that Zhao thought it had cut out.

“Zhendong,” said Chen Si. “When did you start understanding women?”

“I don’t,” said Zhao. “I understand one. She talks in her sleep.”

Chen Si made a sound that might have been a laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

“So what do I do?” said Chen Si.

“Don’t buy her anything.”

“That seems like a terrible idea.”

“Don’t buy her anything,” said Zhao again. “Give her something to win. A problem. A real one. Something nobody else in the Syndicate can fix. Ask her to do it. Then stand back and let her.” He paused. “That’s what she married you for. You told me. At my wedding. A co-ruler.”

There was another long silence.

“The port authority,” said Chen Si slowly. “The new deputy director. He’s been blocking our permits for four months. I was going to deal with him myself next week.”

“Give it to Aurelia.”

“She’ll be terrifying.”

“She’ll be happy.”

“She’ll be terrifying and happy,” said Chen Si. “He won’t sleep for a month.” But his voice had changed. Zhao could hear it. Something lighter in it. Something almost fond. “Zhendong. Thank you.”

“You can thank me by telling her to stop calling my wife at midnight to argue about building permits.”

“I can’t promise that.”

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was about to hang up when Chen Si said, “Zhendong.”

“What.”

“Twelve years ago,” said Chen Si, “in Block C, you were fifteen and couldn’t read properly and had no front tooth and hit people when they looked at you. You didn’t understand anything. Not people. Not women. Not yourself.” A pause. “And now you’re standing in a corridor at two in the morning explaining my own wife to me.”

Zhao didn’t say anything.

“I’m very proud of you,” said Chen Si quietly. “I’ve never said that. I should have. I’m saying it now.”

Zhao stood in the dark corridor with the phone against his ear for a long moment.

“Go to bed, Si,” he said finally. His voice was rough.

“Yes.” Chen Si sounded like he was smiling. “Tell Elowen congratulations on the building. Tell her Aurelia is going to buy the one on the other side.”

“She already knows,” said Zhao. “She bought that one too. Last week. Under Raiden’s name. Aurelia won’t find out until the permits come through.”

There was a very long silence.

“God help us all,” said Chen Si, and hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao went back into the bedroom.

Elowen was awake. She was lying on her side with her eyes open, looking at him in the light from the Docks, and there was a small, satisfied smile on her face that he had seen on Granny Su once, when an apprentice cut a stem correctly the first time.

“Was that Chen Si?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“About the building?”

“Yes.”

“Did he ask you to tell me to stop?”

He got back into bed. She moved over and put her head on his chest, the way she always did.

“Yes,” he said.

“Are you going to?”

He thought about it. He put his hand on her hair.

“No,” said Zhao.

She laughed into his chest, and he held her, and somewhere across the city on the forty-fourth floor, Aurelia Chen was probably still walking up and down a marble living room in a silk robe, saying unbelievable in Italian, about to be handed the best present of her life: a port official who had no idea what was coming.

chapters.title: Anniversary Math
chapters.desc: Zhao has forgotten nothing. Not one date. Elowen finds the notebook.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m very bad at forgetting things.”
chapters.content:
She found the notebook by accident, looking for a pen.

It was in the drawer of his bedside table, the one where he kept the things she didn’t ask about. She had never opened that drawer. It was the last closed place in the house, the way the basement had been, once. But she needed a pen to write down an order Xiao Pan had texted her at eleven at night, and her own pens were downstairs, and he was in the shower, and she pulled the drawer open without thinking.

There was a pistol. She had expected that.

There was a box of the paracetamol she always forgot to buy. She hadn’t expected that.

And under the box, there was a small black notebook. The cheap kind, with an elastic band, that they sold at the stationery shop on the corner by the Docks.

She took it out. She meant only to see if there was a pen tucked into the band.

It fell open in her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first page said, in his square, blunt handwriting:

March 2. 7:00 p.m. Rain started at 6. Bought every flower in the shop. 4,200. She threw a towel.

She sat down on the edge of the bed.

The second line:

Delphiniums. Don’t put them near the door.

She turned the page.

March 9. 10:14 a.m. She came to the Docks. Found Kang. Read three dates and one initial. Did not look away. Coat buttoned wrong.

March 12. 11:40 p.m. She came back. Three pages. Terms. “You don’t touch me unless I ask.” Coat buttoned wrong again.

March 14. 9:41 a.m. Registry. Soil under her nails. Lily of the valley. Ring too big. She put her head on my shoulder in the photograph. She said yes. I looked at the clock.

Elowen put her hand over her mouth.

She turned the pages faster.

It went on. Year after year. Every date. Every time.

March 18. She named the dogs. Dumpling and Noodle.

March 20. Breakfast at the table. Fish belly. She gave it to me.

March 24. Market. 4 a.m. Granny Su. Soy milk man’s son is doing his exams.

April 2. She saw what I do. Maartens. Knife. She said “take it out.” Twenty per cent higher. For the tablecloth.

April 3. 2:00 a.m. She opened the door. I was sitting there. She left it open a hand’s width.

April 11. Van. Boy’s hands. Cold running water, twenty minutes. She held my arm under the tap.

April 19. Typhoon. Fever 39.4. She said “stay.” Held my hand all night. Asked about the scar.

April 20. 7:12 a.m. She kissed me. Page two, line six.

April 28. 12:20 a.m. Thermometer. 36.6. She asked again. She meant it.

April 29. She didn’t go to the market.

The handwriting on that line was different. Pressed harder into the paper. As if he had gone back over it more than once.

✦ ✦ ✦

She kept reading.

May 15. Taught me to hold the roses. Bled on 200. She took the thorns out with tweezers and kissed the plaster.

June 3. Lemon tree. Four lemons.

August 30. Magazine. Middlemist’s Red. Two in the world. Page forty.

September 19. The mountain. Rain. She cried in front of the flower. She said “I’m happy.” She did not say the other word.

She stopped.

She read that line again.

She did not say the other word.

He had written it down. On the night of the mountain, the night of the candles and the rain and the camphor quilt, after she fell asleep on his chest, he had got up, or lain there, and written down that she said happy and not the other one.

She turned the page.

October 4. Lin Jian. “She didn’t choose you. You were only the price.” I know.

October 21. Raiden asked. I said yes. To him. Not to her.

December 14. Reunion. Miles Wei said she doesn’t look like she wants to run.

March 14. One year. 9:41. Fourteenth key. She almost said something, after. She said happy anniversary instead.

She almost said it. I think. I don’t know. I don’t want to know in case I’m wrong.

Elowen was crying now. Silently. She turned the pages with shaking fingers.

The glass. 4:12. Six strips. I did them. My hands would not stop.

Forty-eight hours.

There was nothing else on that page. Just that. Forty-eight hours. And a long blank space underneath, as if he had started to write more, and stopped, and decided not to.

She came back through the front door. Tried to say it. I stopped her. “A boring day.”

Velde. Four pages. Samuel, 11. Into the bin.

And then, a page with only one line on it, in handwriting so shaky she almost couldn’t read it, as if written by a man with a fever, or with torn hands:

I came up the hill.

She held the notebook against her chest.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last entry was in steady handwriting again.

Day 15. Boring day. Fish. I asked. She said yes. She said “now ask me the other one.” I couldn’t.

And under that, the next day:

Day 16. 7:00 p.m. Rain started at 6.

Camellia. Lapel.

She said it.

She said it on a boring day, and nothing happened, and she meant it.

She said it nine times. I counted.

I don’t have to wonder anymore.

And then nothing. The rest of the notebook was blank.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bathroom door opened.

He came out with a towel round his waist and his hair wet, and stopped dead when he saw her sitting on the edge of the bed with the drawer open and the black notebook held against her chest and her face wet.

He didn’t say anything.

“You found it,” he said.

“I was looking for a pen.”

He came and sat down beside her on the bed. Slowly. Water dripping from his hair onto his shoulders. He looked at the notebook in her hands.

“I’m very bad at forgetting things,” he said quietly. “I told you.”

“You wrote down every date.”

“Yes.”

“Every single one. For three and a half years.” She looked at him. “Why?”

He was quiet.

“At the registry,” he said. “I looked at the clock. Nine forty-one. In case it was the only one. In case you changed your mind and I needed to know exactly when it started.” He looked at his hands. “And then you didn’t change your mind. And there was another one. And another. And I thought—if I write them down, then if it ever ends, I’ll have them. All of them. Every date. Nobody can take them.” He swallowed. “I didn’t think I’d be allowed to keep you. I thought I’d at least be allowed to keep the dates.”

She looked at him. At this big, scarred man sitting on the edge of their bed in a towel, who had written down she did not say the other word on the night of the mountain and carried it for two years.

She opened the notebook to the last page with writing on it.

She said it nine times. I counted.

She held out her hand.

“Pen,” she said.

He looked at her. Then he reached into the drawer, under the box of paracetamol, and found one, and gave it to her.

She wrote underneath his last line, in her small, neat, wedding-card handwriting:

Ten.

I love you.

Eleven. I love you.

Twelve.

She kept going. She wrote it down the page, and onto the next page, and the next, numbering each one, while he sat beside her in his towel and watched, and didn’t say anything, and didn’t move, until she had filled four pages, the same as the list of names in the grey folder, and the pen was running out of ink.

Two hundred and three. I love you.

She closed the notebook and gave it back to him.

“There,” she said. “Now you have more dates. And you don’t have to count any more. I’ll keep saying it. You can stop writing it down.”

He took the notebook. He held it in both hands. He didn’t open it.

“I’ll still write it down,” he said, after a long time. His voice had gone rough. “Not because I need to.”

“Then why?”

He looked at her.

“Because I like the dates,” said Zhao. “I like having all of them. Every one.” He put the notebook back in the drawer, on top of the paracetamol, very carefully, and closed it. “Today was a good one.”

She leaned against his wet shoulder.

“What will you write?” she asked.

He thought about it.

“She found the notebook,” he said. “She was looking for a pen.”

She laughed and cried at the same time and pulled him down onto the bed, wet hair and towel and all, and he went, laughing too, and the drawer stayed closed, and the notebook stayed inside it, full of every date, all of them, kept.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years Ago, Block C
chapters.desc: The riot in the detention centre, the blade he took for Chen Si, and the long crawl through the drains in the snow.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t leave them behind you, Zhendong. Not ever. Everything you leave behind you comes back.” — Chen Si, aged sixteen
chapters.content:
He was fifteen, and he had no front tooth, and he couldn’t read very well, and he hit people when they looked at him.

That was all anyone at the Northern Youth Correctional Facility knew about Zhao Zhendong, and it was all they needed to know. He had come in during the autumn, after stealing a truck full of copper wire and driving it into a wall. He didn’t talk. He didn’t cry at night, like some of the younger ones. He did his work in the laundry and ate his food very fast, bent over the tray with one arm around it, like a dog that has learned someone will take its bowl. And when one of the older boys tried to take his bread on the third day, he broke the boy’s nose against the edge of the table before anyone saw him move.

Nobody tried to take his bread again.

Block C was the worst block. It was where they put the boys nobody wanted: the violent ones, the ones whose families had stopped visiting, the ones the guards had given up on. It was cold. The heating broke every winter and nobody fixed it. There were sixty boys in a space built for thirty, in bunks three high, and the guards locked the doors at eight and didn’t come back until six.

Chen Si arrived in November.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao noticed him the way you notice a light in a window.

He was sixteen, and small for it, and thin, and he talked like someone from the television. He used words nobody else in Block C used. He held his chopsticks properly. On his first night, he sat on the edge of his bunk with his back very straight and a book in his lap, reading, as if he were in a library and not a concrete room that smelled of sweat and mould.

The other boys hated him immediately.

Zhao didn’t hate him. Zhao didn’t feel anything about him at all, at first. He watched him the way he watched everything, from his top bunk in the corner, with his back to the wall. He watched the older boys watch Chen Si. He watched them start to wait for him: in the showers, in the corridor to the laundry, in the dead corner of the yard where the cameras didn’t reach.

He watched Chen Si come back from the showers with a split lip, and sit on his bunk, and open his book, and keep reading.

That was the first thing Zhao ever felt about him: that he had never seen anyone do that.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a month before they spoke.

Zhao was in the laundry, alone, feeding sheets into the big press. Chen Si came in with a basket and put it down and stood there for a moment, watching him work.

“You hold the sheets very carefully,” said Chen Si.

Zhao didn’t look up.

“The others throw them,” Chen Si went on. “They get creased and the guards make them do it again. You fold them before you put them in. Every one.” He tilted his head. “Why?”

Zhao fed another sheet into the press.

“If you drop something,” he said, finally, “it costs.”

It was the most he had said to anyone since he arrived.

Chen Si looked at him. At his hands. At the burn scar low on his side, showing where his shirt had ridden up. At his face.

“Who told you that?” he asked.

Zhao didn’t answer. Chen Si didn’t ask again. But the next day, in the canteen, he sat down at the end of Zhao’s table, which nobody did, with his tray and his book. He didn’t say anything. He just sat there and read and ate, with his chopsticks held properly, and nobody came near him the whole meal, because nobody came near Zhao.

He did it the next day too. And the next.

After a week, Zhao said, without looking up from his tray: “What’s the book?”

Chen Si turned it so he could see. Zhao couldn’t read the title. He didn’t say so. Chen Si looked at his face and seemed to understand anyway.

“It’s about a war,” said Chen Si. “A long time ago. Two generals. One of them wins because he’s stronger. The other one wins because he knows where the river goes.” He closed the book. “I’ll read it to you, if you want.”

Zhao didn’t say yes. But he didn’t say no.

That night, Chen Si read to him. Quietly, in the dark, from the bunk below, so the others wouldn’t hear. Zhao lay on his back and looked at the ceiling and listened to a story about a general who knew where the river went.

Nobody had read him anything since he was very small, in the orphanage, before Old Zhao came.

✦ ✦ ✦

The riot was in January.

It started in Block A, over the heating, and spread. By nine at night, Block C could hear it through the walls: shouting, banging, something heavy being thrown. Then smoke. Somebody in Block B had set fire to the mattresses. The smoke came under the door in a thick grey line.

The guards didn’t come.

That was the thing Zhao would remember most, later. Not the fire. Not the blade. The guards. They locked the doors to the blocks and left. He found out afterwards that they had stood in the yard outside for two hours, in the snow, smoking, waiting for the boys inside to finish whatever they were going to do to each other, and for the fire brigade to come from the next town.

Inside Block C, sixty boys realised nobody was coming, and some of them decided it was a good time to settle things.

Three of them went for Chen Si.

Zhao saw them move. He was on his top bunk with his back to the wall, the way he always was. He saw them come down the aisle between the bunks through the smoke: three of the oldest boys, the ones who had been waiting in the showers. The biggest one, a boy called Gao who was seventeen and had killed a man in a fight before he was sent there, had something in his hand. A piece of metal, long and thin. A slat from a bed frame, sharpened against the concrete floor for weeks.

Chen Si was on his bunk with his book. He looked up. He saw them coming. And he didn’t run, and he didn’t shout. He closed the book and put it down very carefully on the blanket, the way you put down something you want to come back to.

Zhao came down off the top bunk.

He didn’t decide to. His body decided. One moment he was against the wall and the next he was on the floor in the aisle, between Chen Si’s bunk and Gao, in the smoke.

“Move,” said Gao.

Zhao didn’t move.

“This isn’t your business, dog.”

Zhao didn’t say anything. He had never been good at saying things. He stood there, fifteen and thin and gap-toothed, with his fists closed, between Gao and the only person who had ever read him a book.

Gao came at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t feel it at first.

He felt Gao’s weight hit him, and he felt himself hit back, once, hard, his fist going into something that cracked. He felt one of the other boys grab his arm. He felt the third go past him toward the bunk, toward Chen Si, and he twisted and got his hand into the boy’s collar and pulled him back and threw him into the bunks so hard the whole frame shook.

And then he felt something cold go into his side, under his left arm, and keep going. Down. A long, cold line, from his ribs almost to his hip.

He looked down.

Gao was holding the end of the bed slat. The rest of it was in him.

Zhao looked at it for a moment, in the smoke. Then he looked up at Gao. And Gao, who was seventeen and had killed a man, saw his face, and let go of the slat, and backed away.

Zhao pulled it out.

He didn’t remember much after that. He remembered the sound Gao made. He remembered the other two boys running. He remembered hitting Gao until somebody pulled him off, and it was Chen Si, small and thin, with both arms around him from behind, saying his name, over and over, Zhendong, Zhendong, stop, he’s down, stop, you’re bleeding, stop.

He stopped.

He sat down on the floor in the aisle between the bunks, in the smoke, and looked at his side, and it was all red, all of it, his shirt and his trousers and the floor. He felt very calm. Very tired.

“Si,” he said. It was the first time he had said Chen Si’s name. “You should go.”

“Go where?” Chen Si was kneeling in front of him, pressing his own shirt against the wound, both hands, as hard as he could. His face was white. His hands were red to the wrist. “The doors are locked.”

“Go anyway,” said Zhao. “Before they come back.”

Chen Si looked at him through the smoke.

Then he did something Zhao didn’t expect. He laughed. Short and shaky and fierce.

“Zhendong,” he said. “I know where the river goes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He had studied the plans of the building for two months.

He told Zhao afterward that it was the first thing he did when he arrived. He had bribed a guard with a watch his father had given him to let him look at the maintenance drawings in the office, and he had memorised them, every pipe and every drain and every vent, because he was sixteen and alone and his family had been erased, and he had decided on the first night in Block C that he would not die there.

There was a drain under the floor of the shower block. Old. Big. From when the building had been something else, a factory. It went under the yard, under the wall, and came out in a ditch by the road, half a kilometre away.

Chen Si got the grate up with a piece of the bed frame. He got Zhao into the drain.

Zhao didn’t remember most of it. He remembered darkness. Freezing water up to his chest. The smell. Chen Si’s voice in front of him, always in front of him, counting steps, forty, forty-one, forty-two, keep going, Zhendong, keep going. Chen Si’s shoulder under his arm, taking his weight, a thin sixteen-year-old boy carrying a bigger one through a pipe in the dark. Falling, and being pulled up. Falling again.

At one point, he stopped. He sat down in the freezing water and couldn’t get up.

“Leave me,” he said. “Go.”

“No.”

“Si. Go. You can make it on your own.”

Chen Si crouched down in front of him in the dark. Zhao couldn’t see him. He could only hear his voice, very close, very calm.

“You don’t leave them behind you,” said Chen Si. “Not ever. Do you understand? Everything you leave behind you comes back.” His hands found Zhao’s face in the dark and held it. “And you are not something I am leaving behind. Get up.”

Zhao got up.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they came out, it was snowing.

The ditch by the road was full of it. White, soft, falling straight down out of a black sky with no wind at all. Behind them, half a kilometre away, the detention centre was a dark shape with orange light in its windows and smoke going up into the snow.

Chen Si dragged him out of the drain and up the side of the ditch and laid him down in the snow by the road.

Zhao lay on his back and looked up at the snow falling.

It was very quiet. He couldn’t feel his legs. He couldn’t feel his side anymore. He could feel the snowflakes landing on his face, one at a time, cold and soft.

Chen Si was kneeling beside him, pressing both hands against his side again. He was covered in blood. All of it Zhao’s. His thin face was streaked with dirt and his hair was wet and he was shaking so hard his teeth chattered.

“Si,” said Zhao.

“Don’t talk.”

“If I’m dying,” said Zhao, “don’t take me to a hospital. Hospitals have records. They’ll send me back. Take me somewhere quiet. Let me go.”

Chen Si looked down at him.

“No,” he said.

Zhao closed his eyes.

He woke up three days later in a back room behind a clinic in the next town, with a drip in his arm and a long line of stitches down his side and a doctor who didn’t ask questions, because Chen Si had told him they were brothers and that their name was Wang, and paid him with the last thing he owned: the book. A first edition, worth more than the clinic, the only thing his father had left him.

Zhao looked at Chen Si, sitting in a chair beside the bed, asleep, his head tipped back against the wall, his hands still stained rust-brown at the knuckles.

He didn’t know what this was. He didn’t have a word for it. Nobody had ever carried him anywhere. Nobody had ever refused to leave him behind.

He would spend ten years not having a word for it.

Then a florist would throw a towel at him in the rain, and he would start to learn.

chapters.title: The Ring Was Too Heavy
chapters.desc: He has it resized without telling her. She notices in a minute. Then she reads the inside.
chapters.epigraph: “I told him I wanted something that wouldn’t break.”
chapters.content:
For three and a half years, she wore it on the wrong finger.

The heavy gold band with the square green stone. Two sizes too big for her ring finger, the morning he slid it on at the registry office, so that it went over her knuckle and kept going. She had moved it to her middle finger, where it fitted, just. She had told him to leave it.

So he had left it.

She took it off to work. Every morning, at the shop, she slipped it off and put it beside the till in the same place, a little dish Raiden had made her out of a piece of the old shipyard timber. Every evening, she put it back on. Her middle finger had a pale band around it now, a mark where the sun never reached.

It was ugly, honestly. Too heavy, too yellow, too old-fashioned. Granny Su said so every time she saw it. Aurelia said so at every gala, holding up her own hand with its perfect, delicate, diamond-crusted band that she had designed herself, and saying, “Darling, let me make you something. Please. It hurts me to look at it.”

Elowen always said no.

She couldn’t have explained why. Only that it was the ring of a man who had never been given anything that lasted, who had gone into a jeweller’s the day before his wedding and said, I want something that won’t break.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three weeks before the real wedding in the shop, she put it in the dish by the till on a Monday morning, the way she always did.

On Monday evening, it wasn’t there.

She looked in the dish. She looked under the till. She looked on the floor, behind the counter, in the cooler, in the bucket of offcuts, in every drawer. She made Xiao Pan look. She made Bao look. Bao looked for twenty minutes, very seriously, on his hands and knees, and then stood up and said, “Miss Lin, I don’t think it’s here,” in the careful voice of a man who knew something.

She looked at him.

“Bao,” she said.

“Miss Lin?”

“Where is my ring?”

Bao looked at the ceiling.

“I couldn’t say, Miss Lin,” he said.

She knew that voice. It was the voice he used when he had been told not to say something by the person who paid his wages, and was going to obey, and wanted her to know he was obeying.

She went home.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t say anything at dinner. Neither did he. He ate his fish, sitting down. He talked about the weather and a broker in the south and the lemon tree, which had nine lemons now. He didn’t mention the ring.

She noticed that he kept his left hand in his lap.

She didn’t say anything that night either. Or the next. Or the next. She went to the market at four and he carried the buckets and she worked all day with a bare middle finger and a pale stripe where the ring should be, and she felt its absence every time she picked up a stem, the way you feel a missing tooth with your tongue.

On Thursday night, at dinner, he put a small box on the table beside her bowl.

The same box. The same dark blue velvet, worn at the corners now, that he had opened on the steps of the registry office.

She looked at it.

“You took it,” she said.

“Yes.”

“From the dish. On Monday.”

“Bao took it. I asked him to.”

“You made Bao search the floor for twenty minutes, pretending.”

He looked faintly embarrassed. “He said it was the hardest thing I’ve ever asked him to do.”

She picked up the box. She opened it.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the same ring.

The same heavy band. The same deep yellow gold. The same square green stone, set deep, old-fashioned and solid and nothing like anything she would ever have chosen.

But smaller.

She took it out. She held it up in the light.

“You had it resized,” she said.

“For the wedding.” He wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at his fish. “You said leave it. Three and a half years ago. I left it. But we’re having a wedding now. A real one. Your father is walking you down an aisle. Everyone will look at your hand.” He paused. “I didn’t want them to see it on the wrong finger. I didn’t want them to think—” He stopped.

“Think what?”

“That I got it wrong.” He finally looked at her. “That I didn’t know your size. That I didn’t know you.”

She looked at him across the table for a long time.

Then she held out her left hand.

He looked at it. At the pale band on her middle finger. At her ring finger, bare.

He reached across the table and took the ring from her, and took her hand, and slid it on.

It went over her knuckle. And stopped. Exactly where it should. It fitted as if it had been made for her, as if it had always been made for her, as if it had only been waiting three and a half years for someone to measure.

“How did you know the size?” she asked. Her voice wasn’t steady.

“I measured,” said Zhao. “While you were asleep. With a piece of string.”

She laughed. It came out wet.

“You measured my finger with a string while I was asleep.”

“Four times,” he said. “To be sure.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took it off again, later, in bed. To look at it. She held it up in the light from the Docks, turning it, watching the green stone catch the light.

That was when she saw the inside.

There was writing. Engraved into the gold, on the inside of the band, where nobody would ever see it but her. Small, neat letters, cut very carefully by someone with very steady hands.

She tilted it to read.

9:41.

And then, beside it, smaller:

7:00 p.m. Rain.

She looked at it.

The time the clerk stamped the red book at the registry office. The time he walked into her shop, dripping on the floor, on the night it rained.

“Zhendong,” she said.

He was lying beside her on his back with his arm behind his head, watching her, the way he always watched her. He didn’t say anything.

“When did you have this done?”

“On Monday,” he said. “When I had it resized.”

“Not before?”

“No.” He looked at the ceiling. “Before, I didn’t think I was allowed. To put the times inside. In case—” He stopped.

“In case I changed my mind,” said Elowen. “And then it would just be a ring with two times in it that didn’t mean anything.”

He was quiet.

“I wasn’t sure,” he said finally, very low, “until the camellia. Until the shop. Until you said it on a boring day. I didn’t want to carve something into it that you might want to take off.” He turned his head on the pillow and looked at her. “Now I know you won’t.”

She looked down at the ring in her palm. At the two small times engraved inside it, where only she would ever see them.

Then she slid it back onto her ring finger, where it fitted, and turned onto her side, and put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart, with the heavy gold ring between them, warm from her skin.

“It’s still too heavy,” she said.

“I know.”

“Aurelia will hate it.”

“I know.”

“Granny Su will say it’s ugly.”

“She says that every week.”

She smiled in the dark.

“Good,” said Elowen. “I like that it’s heavy. I like that I can feel it.” She pressed her hand a little harder against his chest. “It’s the ring of a man who walked into a jeweller’s the day before his wedding and said he wanted something that wouldn’t break.”

He looked at her in the light from the Docks.

“It hasn’t,” he said.

“No,” said Elowen. “It hasn’t.”

She fell asleep like that, with her hand on his heart and the ring on the right finger, finally, after three and a half years. And he lay awake beside her, the way he always did for a while, and watched the light move on the ceiling, and did not have to wonder about anything at all.

chapters.title: Eliana Sleeps Over at the Big House
chapters.desc: The youngest Lin sister breaks the security system in forty minutes. For fun. Zhao is delighted.
chapters.epigraph: “Your cameras have a blind spot by the lemon tree. I’m telling you because I like you.” — Eliana Lin, 18
chapters.content:
Eliana came to stay at the house on the hill for a weekend in the second winter, because the heating at the house in the Walled City had broken and her father had asked Elowen, very stiffly, on the phone, whether her husband would mind.

“Mind what?” said Zhao, when Elowen asked him.

“My little sister. Sleeping here. Two nights.”

He thought about it.

“Does she eat fish?”

“She eats instant noodles and energy drinks and nothing else.”

“Then she can stay,” said Zhao, “and eat fish.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana arrived on Friday evening with one small bag of clothes and one enormous bag of equipment. She was eighteen. She wore the same hoodie she always wore, three sizes too big, the hood up even indoors. She stood in the hall by the lemon tree and looked at the house the way other people looked at a cake.

Then she looked up at the corner of the ceiling.

“That camera,” she said, “is pointing at the wrong place.”

Zhao, who had come out of the kitchen to say hello, stopped.

“It’s pointing at the door,” he said.

“It’s pointing at where the door was when someone installed it.” Eliana tilted her head. “You moved the door. About forty centimetres to the left. There’s a patch in the plaster. So the camera sees the door frame and about half of a person coming in. If they come in on the left side, it doesn’t see them at all.” She looked at him. “Also, there’s a blind spot by the lemon tree. I’m telling you because I like you. Don’t tell Baba I told you.”

Zhao looked up at the camera. Then at the patch in the plaster that he had walked past every day for four years without seeing.

Then he looked at his youngest sister-in-law with an expression Elowen had seen on him only once before: on the morning she found Kang in her father’s files.

“What else?” he said.

Eliana smiled. It was a small, slow, delighted smile. It was the first time Elowen had seen her sister smile in about a year.

“Can I have the Wi-Fi password?” said Eliana. “And about forty minutes?”

✦ ✦ ✦

It took her thirty-eight.

She sat cross-legged on the floor of the living room with three laptops open around her like a fortress and a can of energy drink at her knee, and typed, and muttered, and every so often said “oh, that’s bad” in a tone of deep personal joy.

Zhao sat on the black leather sofa behind her and watched.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t ask what she was doing. He just watched her hands, the way he had once watched Elowen’s hands cutting stems at closing time, and every so often, when she said “oh, that’s bad”, he leaned forward a little.

Elowen made dinner. Fish, ginger, rice. She carried the plates into the living room because she knew neither of them would come to the table, and found them both exactly where she had left them, except that Zhao had moved from the sofa to the floor beside Eliana and was looking at one of the laptop screens over her shoulder.

“That’s the guardhouse,” Eliana was saying, pointing. “That’s the gate. That’s the basement door—very good, by the way, I can’t get into that, it’s not on the network at all, who did it?”

“Raiden.”

“Of course.” She clicked. “But this. These cameras on the wall. They all run through one box in the guardhouse. If someone cuts the power to that box, you lose every camera on the east side. All at once. For about ninety seconds, until the backup kicks in.” She looked up at him. “Ninety seconds is a very long time.”

Zhao looked at the screen for a long moment.

“Show me,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven, Elowen went to bed.

At one, she woke up and the bed was empty.

She went downstairs. The living room light was on. Her husband and her little sister were sitting on the floor surrounded by laptops and empty energy drink cans and a printed diagram of the house’s security system covered in red ink, and Eliana was explaining something about network segments with her hands, very fast, and Zhao was nodding.

“Zhendong,” said Elowen from the doorway.

They both looked up. They both had exactly the same guilty expression.

“It’s one in the morning,” said Elowen.

“She found four more,” said Zhao.

“Five,” said Eliana. “The garage door opener uses a code from 2009. I could open it with my phone from the road.”

Zhao looked at Elowen with an expression of total, helpless delight. “From the road,” he said.

Elowen looked at them both. Then she went back upstairs and got her duvet and came down and lay on the sofa behind them, and fell asleep to the sound of her sister and her husband arguing quietly about firewalls.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday, when their father’s car came to collect Eliana, Zhao walked her to the door.

He carried her enormous bag of equipment. At the top of the steps, he stopped and put it down and looked at her.

“The guardhouse box,” he said. “I had it moved this morning. Split in two. One on each side of the house.”

Eliana nodded seriously. “Good.”

“And the garage.”

“I saw. New code. Sixteen digits.” She paused. “It’s my birthday backwards, isn’t it.”

He looked faintly embarrassed.

“I needed a number I’d remember,” he said.

Eliana looked at him for a long moment from under her hood. Then she did something nobody in her family had seen her do since she was small. She stepped forward and hugged him. Briefly, awkwardly, with her face against his chest and her arms barely reaching round, for exactly one second.

Then she let go, picked up her bag, and walked down the steps without looking back.

At the car, she stopped and turned round.

“Brother-in-law,” she called.

He waited.

“The lemon tree blind spot,” said Eliana. “Don’t fix that one.”

“Why not?”

She looked past him into the hall, where her sister was standing by the long window in the morning light, watering the lemon tree.

“Because that’s where you two always stand,” said Eliana, “when you think nobody’s looking.”

She got into the car. It drove away.

Zhao stood on the top step for a long time.

He never fixed the lemon tree blind spot.

chapters.title: Elowen Does the Armory’s Accounts
chapters.desc: From the private diary of Mr. Yao, accountant, who has worked for Zhao Zhendong for nine years and has never been this afraid.
chapters.epigraph: “She found an error from four years ago. With a pencil. In twenty minutes.” — Mr. Yao
chapters.content:
From the private diary of Yao Jianguo, accountant. Kept in a locked drawer. Never to be read by anyone.

Monday.

Mr. Zhao called me into the office today and said his wife would be reviewing the warehouse ledgers.

I said, “Of course, sir.”

I thought: a florist. How nice. She will look at the totals and say they are very impressive and go back to her roses.

I have been an accountant for twenty-six years. I have done the books for a man who sells rifles to generals. I have lied to tax inspectors in three provinces. I am not afraid of a florist.

Thursday.

I am afraid of the florist.

She came to the house on the hill at two in the afternoon. I brought eleven ledgers. She sat at the dining table with a pencil and a cup of jasmine tea and a calculator she did not use once.
