She asked for the third quarter of four years ago.

I gave it to her. She read it. She turned the pages slowly. She did not speak. Twenty minutes later, she put her pencil down on page forty-one and said, very politely:

“Mr. Yao. This figure should be one thousand two hundred and six. You’ve written one thousand two hundred and sixty. And then you carried it.”

I looked.

She was right.

I have been looking for that error for four years. It is the reason the north warehouse never balanced. I have lost sleep over it. I once dreamed about it. It was a six instead of a nothing.

She found it with a pencil, in twenty minutes, drinking tea.

Friday.

I told Mr. Zhao in the hall that I might be afraid of his wife.

He said, “Good.”

I don’t know what that means. I am choosing not to think about it.

The following Tuesday.

She has questions.

She writes them in the margins in very small, very neat handwriting. Like a wedding card. Every question is polite. Every question makes me feel like I am being slowly peeled.

Mr. Yao, why does warehouse seven always receive exactly eight hundred cases but ship six hundred and twelve?

Mr. Yao, who is Mr. Lam, and why does he receive a “consulting fee” every month but never appear in any meeting notes?

Mr. Yao, is this a five or an S?

It was an S. It stood for something I would rather not write here.

The following Thursday.

She found Mr. Lam.

Mr. Lam was a man in the south who had been receiving a consulting fee for three years for consulting on nothing. I had always assumed he was someone Mr. Zhao paid for reasons I didn’t want to know.

He wasn’t. He was someone Wu paid. With Mr. Zhao’s money. Wu, from warehouse seven.

Mrs. Zhao wrote this in the margin in pencil and then underlined it twice and then wrote underneath, very small: Don’t tell my husband yet, Mr. Yao. I’m saving it.

I asked her what she was saving it for.

She smiled at me. It was a very nice smile. It was the most frightening thing I have ever seen, and I once watched Mr. Zhao interview a customs officer.

“For when someone needs it,” she said.

I have not told Mr. Zhao. I am more afraid of her than of him. I did not think that was possible.

Three months later.

Wu called Mr. Zhao a dog in the office. In front of her.

She opened the ledger and read out every theft from warehouse seven, date by date, in her wedding-card voice, while Wu went grey.

I was not there. Bao told me. Bao does not usually tell me things. He came to my office specially. He stood in the doorway and said, “Mr. Yao. You should have seen it,” and then he laughed, which I have never heard Bao do, and went away.

I went home and told my wife I was going to buy her a necklace. She asked why. I said I had learned something important about marriage. She told me to sit down and explain.

I couldn’t. I bought her the necklace anyway.

One year later.

Mrs. Zhao reviews all the books on Thursdays now.

My error rate has fallen by ninety-one per cent. I calculated it. I do my sums twice. Sometimes three times. Before I send anything to the house on the hill, I read it aloud to myself in an empty room to see if it sounds like something she would put a pencil mark next to.

My wife says I have become a better man. My children say I have become very boring at dinner.

Last Thursday, when I brought the ledgers, Mrs. Zhao looked up from page twelve and said, “Mr. Yao, this is perfect.”

I had to go and stand in the garden for a while.

Mr. Zhao came out and stood next to me. He didn’t say anything for a long time. We looked at the lemon tree through the window.

Then he said, “She told me you were very good. Before she started. She said, ‘He’s careful. He just has no one to check him.’”

I said nothing. I could not.

“Nobody ever checked me either,” said Mr. Zhao. “For years. Then she did.” He looked at me. “It’s very frightening. And then it isn’t.”

He went back inside.

I have worked for Zhao Zhendong for ten years now. I have done the books for a man who sells rifles to generals. I have lied to tax inspectors in three provinces.

I have never once, until last Thursday, been told my work was perfect.

I am keeping this diary in a locked drawer. If anyone ever finds it, I would like it known that I was not afraid of the florist.

That is a lie. I am telling it to the diary.

It is the only one I have told all year.

chapters.title: The Language of Flowers, Studied in Secret
chapters.desc: He leaves her yellow roses. She explains what yellow means. He goes and buys a book.
chapters.epigraph: “Yellow roses mean jealousy, Zhendong. Or the end of a friendship.” “…Oh.”
chapters.content:
On the first morning of the second spring, Elowen came down to the kitchen at three-thirty and found a bunch of yellow roses on the counter, beside the two cups of coffee.

A dozen. Long-stemmed. Bright, clear, buttery yellow, the colour of the inside of a lemon. Wrapped in brown paper and tied with a piece of string, badly, the knot too tight.

Zhao was standing at the window with his coffee, very carefully not looking at them.

“You bought me roses,” said Elowen.

“I bought you roses.”

“From who?”

“A stall by the Docks. The man was opening at three.” He drank his coffee. “You buy everyone else roses. Nobody buys you any.”

She looked at the roses. They were good ones. Fresh, tight heads, straight stems. Someone had taken the thorns off, not very well; she could see the little torn places where a knife had gone in too deep. He had done it himself.

“They’re beautiful,” she said.

She meant it. She put them in water. She took them to the shop and put them on the counter by the till, where she would see them all day.

At eleven, an old woman came in to buy carnations, looked at the yellow roses on the counter, and said, “Oh dear. Who’s jealous?”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, at dinner, Elowen said, “The roses.”

He looked up from his fish.

“Do you know,” she said carefully, “what yellow roses mean?”

He looked blank. “Mean?”

“Flowers have meanings. It started in Europe, a long time ago. The Victorians were obsessed with it. They wrote whole dictionaries. Every flower meant something. Red roses for love. White for innocence. Forget-me-nots for—well, you can guess.” She turned her teacup. “Yellow roses meant jealousy. Or the end of a friendship. Or, sometimes, I am sorry I have done something I should not have done.”

He put down his chopsticks very slowly.

“Oh,” he said.

“It doesn’t matter. Nobody really uses it anymore. Most people think yellow just means happy.” She smiled. “Only old ladies and florists know. And the old lady at the shop today.”

He didn’t say anything else. He finished his fish. He washed his bowl.

She thought that was the end of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later, she found the book.

It was under the narrow bed in the small room at the top of the stairs, where he still went sometimes when he couldn’t sleep and didn’t want to wake her. She was changing the sheets. She lifted the mattress to tuck the corner and there it was, flat on the slats: a small, old, cloth-bound book with gold letters on the spine, faded almost to nothing.

The Language of Flowers. With Illustrations. 1884.

It was from an antique shop. She could tell from the smell. There was a pencilled price inside the cover that made her sit down on the bed.

She opened it.

Every page had a flower on it, a small painted illustration, and underneath, in old-fashioned type, the meaning. Acacia: concealed love. Aloe: grief. Amaryllis: pride. And on many of the pages, in the margins, in square blunt pencil, there were notes.

Next to Yellow Rose: Jealousy, decrease of love, he had written: NO.

Next to Red Rose: Love, he had written: Too obvious? She sells 400 a week.

Next to Lily of the Valley: Return of happiness, he had written: Granny Su. Every time. On the registry morning and the anniversary. Does Granny Su know this book?

Next to Delphinium: Ardent attachment, there was no note at all. Only a small, careful pencil line under the words, gone over and over, as if someone had traced it many times.

Elowen sat on the narrow bed and turned the pages, slowly, for a long time.

Next to Ranunculus: You are radiant with charms, he had written: She buys these every Tuesday. Does she know?

Next to Gardenia: Secret love, he had written: Too late.

Next to Camellia: My destiny is in your hands, he had written nothing. He had only drawn a small box around the words, very neatly, with a ruler.

She closed the book and held it in her lap.

Then she put it back under the mattress, exactly where it had been, and tucked the corner in, and went downstairs, and said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flowers started appearing a week after that.

One at a time. Never a bunch. One stem, on the kitchen counter beside her coffee, at three-thirty in the morning.

A sprig of rosemary. (Remembrance.)

One white tulip. (Forgiveness—the morning after they had argued about whether he should come to the market with a cold.)

A single stem of honeysuckle, which he must have cut from someone’s garden wall, because no florist in the city stocked it in March. (Bonds of love.)

A bunch of forget-me-nots so small and so badly tied that she knew he had picked them himself, by hand, somewhere on the hill. (She didn’t need the book for that one.)

She didn’t say anything. She put each one in a glass on the kitchen windowsill, a row of mismatched glasses that got longer every week. He didn’t say anything either. Every morning there was a new one. Every morning he stood at the window with his coffee, very carefully not looking at it.

It went on for two months.

Then one morning in May, there was a single stem of ranunculus beside her coffee. Pale apricot. Perfect.

You are radiant with charms.

She picked it up. She looked at him, standing at the window.

“I buy these every Tuesday,” she said.

He went very still.

“Did you know,” said Elowen, “that I buy them because of what they mean? My mother told me. When I was seven. She said, Buy yourself ranunculus once a week, so you remember somebody thinks you’re radiant, even if it’s only you.”

He turned round.

“I’ve bought them every Tuesday since she died,” said Elowen. “For eighteen years. So somebody would think it.” She held up the stem. “And now somebody does.”

He looked at her for a long time.

Then he crossed the kitchen and took the ranunculus out of her hand and tucked it behind her ear, the way he had once tucked a crushed camellia, on the floor of the shop, among the petals.

“You found the book,” he said.

“Under the mattress. In the small room.”

“I was going to stop after the camellia.” He touched the flower behind her ear. “I was saving that for last. For when I ran out of things to say.”

She reached up and put her hand over his.

“Then don’t run out,” she said.

He didn’t.

The row of glasses on the kitchen windowsill went all the way to the end, and round the corner onto the next one, and eventually Raiden had to come and build a shelf.

chapters.title: Valentine’s Day in a Flower Shop
chapters.desc: Fourteen hours, nine hundred roses, one till. The arms dealer works the counter. The customers are frightened and very polite.
chapters.epigraph: “Next.” — Zhao Zhendong, four hundred and twelve times
chapters.content:
Valentine’s Day was the worst day of the year.

Not emotionally. Physically. Elowen had done seven of them by the second February of her marriage, and every single one had nearly killed her. Nine hundred roses. Three hundred orders. A queue out of the door from seven in the morning until nine at night, every one of them a man who had forgotten until that morning and wanted twelve red roses right now, and every one of them sure he was the only one.

Xiao Pan did deliveries all day on the red motorbike. Xiao Pan’s cousin, the disastrous one from years ago, had been banned for life. There was nobody to work the till.

“I’ll work the till,” said Zhao.

She looked at him over the top of the order book.

“You can’t work the till.”

“Why not?”

“Because you’ll frighten everyone.”

He considered this. “They’ll be fast,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was behind the counter at six-fifty.

He wore the green apron. It still came to his ribs. He had found a pen and a notepad and a calculator he didn’t need, and he stood behind the till with his feet slightly apart and his hands flat on the counter, the way he had once stood at the whiteboard in the office at the Docks, looking at the door.

At seven, Elowen turned the sign to OPEN.

The first man in was about twenty-five, in a suit, holding his phone. He was already talking before he reached the counter. “Hi, yeah, I need a dozen red roses, the nice ones, and can you do it fast because I’m going to be late for—”

He looked up.

He stopped talking.

Zhao looked at him.

“Twelve red,” said Zhao. “Wrapped or in a box?”

The man stared at him. His mouth opened and closed.

“…Wrapped,” he said faintly. “Please.”

“Card?”

“…Yes. Please. Sir.”

Zhao slid a small card and a pen across the counter. The man wrote on it so fast his hand shook. Elowen, at the workbench behind, wrapped the roses in brown paper and red ribbon in forty seconds and passed them forward. Zhao took the money, gave the change, counted it twice, and said:

“Next.”

The man left. He didn’t run. But it was close.

✦ ✦ ✦

By nine, the queue was out of the door and down the street.

By ten, word had got round.

Elowen didn’t notice at first. She was wrapping roses at a speed that would have impressed a factory. But at some point she looked up and realised that the queue had gone very quiet. Usually on Valentine’s Day it was loud: men on phones, men arguing about colours, men asking if she could “do something special” for no extra charge. Today, forty men stood in a silent line, shuffling forward one step at a time, holding their wallets ready, looking straight ahead, like soldiers waiting to be inspected.

And every one of them, when he reached the counter, was very, very polite.

“Good morning, sir. Twelve red, please, if it’s not too much trouble.”

“Hello. I’d like the roses. Whichever ones you think are best. Thank you so much.”

“Sir. Sorry. I don’t mind what colour. Whatever’s easiest for you.”

Nobody asked for a discount. Nobody asked for anything special. Nobody complained about the price, which Elowen had raised by thirty per cent, as she did every year, and usually spent half the day defending.

One man, an older one in a good coat, reached the front, looked up at Zhao, went pale, and said, “I’ll take twenty-four. And the lilies. And—what are those? Those too.”

“Those are for a funeral,” said Zhao.

“…I’ll take them anyway,” said the man.

✦ ✦ ✦

At noon, she brought him a bowl of noodles from the shop across the street. He ate it standing behind the counter in four minutes without stopping serving. He said “Next” with his mouth full.

At two, a young woman came in. The only woman in the queue. She was about nineteen, in a school blazer, holding a handful of coins.

The line behind her shuffled.

She reached the counter and looked up at Zhao, and Elowen saw her flinch, and then saw her lift her chin.

“I want one rose,” the girl said. “One. Red. For a boy. In my class. I don’t know if he likes me. I just want to put it on his desk.” She put the coins on the counter. “That’s all I have.”

It was a third of the price of one rose on Valentine’s Day.

The whole queue had gone silent behind her.

Zhao looked at the coins. Then at the girl.

He reached into the bucket beside the till and took out one red rose. Then he looked at it, and put it back, and took out another one, and turned it in the light, and checked the head, and checked the stem, and ran his thumb down it for thorns the way Elowen had taught him on the first morning of the four hundred roses. He found one. He took it off with his thumbnail.

He held the rose out to the girl.

She took it. She looked at the coins on the counter.

“That’s not enough,” she whispered. “I know it’s not enough.”

Zhao looked at her for a moment.

“A boy,” he said. “In your class.”

“Yes.”

“You’re going to put it on his desk. Without telling him it’s from you.”

“Yes.”

“That’s very brave,” said Zhao. He picked up the coins and put them in the till and gave her no change. “Next.”

The girl stared at him. Then she clutched the rose to her chest and ran out of the shop, and the queue parted for her like water.

Behind the counter, Elowen was smiling so hard her face hurt.

✦ ✦ ✦

They closed at nine.

Nine hundred roses, gone. Three hundred and eleven orders. Four hundred and twelve customers, according to the till, every one of them served by a man in a green apron that came to his ribs. Not one complaint.

He sat on the stool behind the counter when the last man had gone, with his elbows on his knees and his head down, and didn’t move.

“Are you all right?” said Elowen.

“I said next four hundred and twelve times,” said Zhao, to the floor. “I’ve never said a word that many times in my life.”

She came round the counter. She stood between his knees and put her hands on his shoulders. He leaned his forehead against her stomach and closed his eyes.

“Every single one of them was polite,” she said into his hair. “Do you know how rare that is? On Valentine’s Day? I’ve been doing this for seven years. Nobody has ever been polite.”

“They were frightened.”

“They were polite because they were frightened.” She stroked his hair. “I’m hiring you every year. Forever. I don’t care. You’re the best till I’ve ever had.”

He laughed into her apron.

Then he reached behind him, under the counter, and brought out something he must have put there that morning, before the shop opened, while she was in the cooler.

One red rose.

Not the best one. Not the straightest. He had picked out, from nine hundred, one that was slightly crooked, with a bent head and a stem that curved to one side. The one nobody would have bought.

He held it up to her.

“I kept it back,” he said. “At seven. Before anyone came. It was the worst one in the bucket.” He turned it in his fingers. “I thought, everyone else gets the perfect ones. Nobody will want this one.” He looked up at her. “I wanted it.”

She took it.

She looked at the crooked rose in her hand. At the bent head and the curving stem. At her husband, sitting on her stool in a too-short green apron at nine o’clock at night, having said next four hundred and twelve times so that she wouldn’t have to.

“Happy Valentine’s Day,” said Zhao.

She put the crooked rose behind her ear. Then she bent down and kissed him, in the empty shop, among the bare buckets, with the sign turned to CLOSED.

Every year after that, on the fourteenth of February, he worked the till.

And every year, at seven in the morning, before anyone came, he went through all nine hundred roses and kept back the worst one.

For her.
